data.description: A 57-year-old female without any medical history was admitted for evaluation of a left ventricular tumor that was discovered incidentally. The patient was asymptomatic and had no relevant past medical history. Physical examination findings were not specifically described in the case report.

A benign primary cardiac tumor composed predominantly of fibroblasts and dense collagen. It usually arises within the ventricular myocardium or interventricular septum and can show prominent delayed enhancement on cardiac MRI because of its fibrous tissue content.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging appearance compatible with a fibrous lesion with delayed enhancement

data.description: A rare benign vascular tumor of the heart composed of capillary, cavernous, or mixed vascular channels. It may occur in the ventricular wall and can be asymptomatic when small.
symptoms_in_common: Histology showing vascular channels highlighted by endothelial immunostaining
Contrast enhancement of the mass on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly collagen-rich fibrous histology is less typical than for cardiac fibroma
No reported high-flow vascular features, bruit, or hemorrhagic symptoms

data.description: A benign mesenchymal tumor composed of spindle-shaped myofibroblasts, often with a biphasic pattern of fibrous tissue and branching vascular channels. Cardiac involvement is rare and is more often described in infants or children.
symptoms_in_common: Can present as an intramyocardial ventricular mass
Fibrous spindle-cell and vascular histologic components can overlap with the reported pathology
symptoms_not_in_common: Age of 57 years is atypical because myofibroma is much more common in pediatric patients
No symptoms of obstruction, arrhythmia, or heart failure

data.description: A rare benign fibrous tumor with a prominent vascular component, consisting of collagen-rich stroma containing small blood vessels. It can resemble a fibroma or hemangioma on imaging and pathology.
symptoms_in_common: Presence of small vascular channels within the tumor
symptoms_not_in_common: Cardiac angiofibroma is exceedingly rare and is not a common diagnosis for a left ventricular mass
No associated systemic manifestations

data.description: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with left upper quadrant abdominal pain that worsened with deep breathing or lying down, accompanied by fever. He also complained of mild cough and whitish sputum. On physical examination, the child was irritable but there were no other remarkable findings. Laboratory data showed elevated C-reactive protein (8.65 mg/dL) without leukocytosis and other findings were unremarkable.

Ischemic necrosis of splenic tissue caused by impaired splenic arterial or venous blood flow. Imaging commonly shows peripheral wedge-shaped hypoechoic or nonenhancing splenic lesions; the provided ultrasound and MRI appearances are most compatible with infarction.
symptoms_in_common: Acute left upper quadrant abdominal pain
Imaging appearance of peripheral wedge-like splenic lesions with reduced/absent perfusion
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild cough
Whitish sputum
Pain worsened by lying down

data.diagnosis: Splenic infarction associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
data.description: Mycoplasma pneumoniae respiratory infection can rarely cause extrapulmonary thrombosis or vasculitis, including splenic infarction. Respiratory symptoms accompanied by fever, inflammation, and imaging-confirmed splenic ischemic lesions support this possibility.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated C-reactive protein without marked leukocytosis
Left upper quadrant pain from splenic infarction
Pleuritic worsening of pain with deep breathing
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported sore throat
No reported diffuse malaise or generalized respiratory distress
No documented chest radiograph evidence of atypical pneumonia

data.description: A splenic abscess is a focal bacterial, fungal, or parasitic infection of the spleen that can cause fever and left upper quadrant pain. It may appear as a hypoechoic splenic lesion on ultrasound, although the wedge-shaped, perfusion-deficient MRI pattern more strongly favors infarction than abscess.
symptoms_not_in_common: No leukocytosis
No clear septic appearance or hemodynamic instability
No reported immunodeficiency, trauma, bacteremia, or predisposing infection
Mild cough and whitish sputum are not typical primary manifestations

data.description: A 38-year-old woman presented with a three-day history of fever, generalized myalgia and arthralgia, and the sensation of difficulty when breathing in. She had poorly localized discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration and loose stools over the preceding three days. Three days before presentation she had returned from a three-week trip to Western Australia, and 18 months earlier she had traveled to Vietnam. On examination she appeared well but was febrile at 38.0°C and tachypnoeic at 22 breaths/min, with all other observations normal. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable. Blood tests showed severe neutrophilia (18.9 × 10⁹/L; reference range 2.0-8.1), raised C reactive protein (354 mg/L; reference value <10), and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Chest radiography and urinalysis were normal. Blood cultures taken at presentation were negative.

data.diagnosis: Amoebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histolytica hepatic abscess)
data.description: An invasive intestinal amoebic infection that can spread through the portal circulation to cause a usually solitary liver abscess. It may occur months to years after travel to endemic regions and can cause diaphragmatic or pleuritic pain when the left hepatic lobe is involved.
symptoms_in_common: Marked inflammatory response with neutrophilia and elevated C-reactive protein
Poorly localized left diaphragmatic pain on deep inspiration
Travel history to Vietnam, an endemic region
Solitary hepatic lesion on CT consistent with a liver abscess
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized arthralgia
Prominent generalized myalgia

data.description: A bacterial infection producing a pus-filled collection in the liver, commonly caused by enteric organisms such as Klebsiella species, Escherichia coli, streptococci, or anaerobes. It often presents with fever and high inflammatory markers; left-lobe abscesses may cause upper abdominal or diaphragmatic discomfort.
symptoms_in_common: Pain/discomfort on deep inspiration near the diaphragm
Loose stools, which may suggest a gastrointestinal source
CT appearance of a focal hepatic lesion compatible with abscess
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized arthralgia
Generalized myalgia
Absence of focal right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain
Well appearance despite markedly raised inflammatory markers

data.diagnosis: Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkholderia pseudomallei infection)
data.description: Melioidosis is an infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, acquired from contaminated soil or water in endemic areas including parts of northern and western Australia and Southeast Asia. It can cause acute febrile illness, pneumonia, sepsis, and visceral abscesses involving the liver and spleen.
symptoms_in_common: Focal hepatic lesion that could represent an abscess
symptoms_not_in_common: Loose stools
Localized left diaphragmatic pain as the predominant focal symptom
No pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiography
No reported diabetes, chronic kidney disease, heavy alcohol use, or other typical melioidosis risk factor

data.diagnosis: Septic portal vein thrombophlebitis (pylephlebitis) associated with a hepatic abscess
data.description: Pylephlebitis is infected thrombosis of the portal venous system, usually arising from an intra-abdominal infection such as diverticulitis, appendicitis, or liver abscess. The CT image may suggest a focal hepatic abscess with adjacent portal venous involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Marked neutrophilia and elevated C-reactive protein
Loose stools suggesting possible gastrointestinal inflammation or infection
CT findings suspicious for hepatic abscess with possible portal venous abnormality
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized arthralgia
Generalized myalgia
No clear focal abdominal tenderness
No known preceding appendicitis, diverticulitis, pancreatitis, or other intra-abdominal source

data.description: A 60-year-old white Caucasian woman presented with a 4-year history of worsening gait and sensory disturbance accompanied by urinary urgency and nocturia. She reported slow deterioration in vision from age 50, though she could still drive. Her mother was registered blind and had Parkinson's disease with dementia. On examination, she had a spastic gait with normal power in lower limbs but increased tone and sustained ankle clonus. Reflexes were brisk with flexor plantar responses. She had mild reduction in visual acuity and dyschromatopsia, but no detectable visual field defect and preserved pupillary light reflexes. CSF analysis showed presence of oligoclonal bands. Routine hematological, biochemical and immunological blood tests were normal, including folate and vitamin B12. Anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies were negative in serum.

data.diagnosis: OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome (DOA+)
data.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by OPA1 variants, classically producing slowly progressive bilateral optic atrophy and sometimes additional neurologic features such as spastic paraplegia, ataxia, neuropathy, deafness, or parkinsonism.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly progressive visual decline beginning around age 50
Optic disc pallor and marked bilateral retinal nerve fiber layer thinning on OCT
Increased lower-limb tone, brisk reflexes, and sustained ankle clonus
Urinary urgency and nocturia consistent with upper motor neuron/spinal pathway involvement
Maternal history of blindness and parkinsonism/dementia, compatible with dominant familial mitochondrial optic neuropathy
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF oligoclonal bands are not a typical feature of OPA1-related disease
Preserved pupillary light reflexes despite optic atrophy are less characteristic but can occur with slowly progressive bilateral disease

data.diagnosis: SPG7-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic atrophy
data.description: A complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic SPG7 variants. It commonly causes adult-onset progressive lower-limb spasticity and may include optic neuropathy/optic atrophy, ataxia, neuropathy, and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Normal lower-limb power with increased tone and hyperreflexia
Bilateral optic atrophy and retinal nerve fiber layer loss on fundus examination and OCT
No clear brain or spinal cord demyelinating lesion on the provided MRI images
symptoms_not_in_common: A maternal pattern of blindness is less typical because SPG7 is usually autosomal recessive
CSF oligoclonal bands are not typical of SPG7-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia
Parkinsonism and dementia in the mother are not core SPG7 manifestations

data.description: An immune-mediated central nervous system demyelinating disease that can cause progressive spastic paraparesis, bladder dysfunction, sensory symptoms, and optic neuritis/optic atrophy. Oligoclonal bands in CSF support intrathecal immune activity.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive gait impairment with spasticity, hyperreflexia, and ankle clonus
Optic nerve damage/retinal nerve fiber layer thinning can occur after optic neuritis
symptoms_not_in_common: The long, gradual bilateral visual decline with optic atrophy and no reported episodes of painful optic neuritis is atypical
The provided brain and spinal MRI images do not show characteristic demyelinating lesions supporting multiple sclerosis
Strong family history of blindness suggests a hereditary optic neuropathy rather than typical multiple sclerosis
Normal pupillary light reflexes and absence of a visual field defect are less typical for clinically significant prior optic neuritis

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder affecting optic nerves and spinal cord, often associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies and causing severe optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis.
symptoms_in_common: Visual impairment with optic nerve atrophy
Spastic gait and upper motor neuron signs
symptoms_not_in_common: Serum anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies are negative
Visual deterioration was slow and chronic rather than a severe acute or subacute optic neuritis
No reported painful visual loss
The provided spinal MRI does not show a longitudinally extensive myelitis lesion
CSF oligoclonal bands are less typical for NMOSD than for multiple sclerosis
Familial blindness is not typical of NMOSD

data.description:
A 14-year-old female patient presented with generalized pruritus accompanied by scleral icterus and petechiae/ecchymoses on the extremities for over 2 months. She had no fever, abdominal pain, or distension. Past medical history included amenorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and acne. She had been taking Chinese herbal medicines (specific components unknown) for approximately 9 months. Physical examination revealed clear consciousness, facial acne and pigmentation, mild scleral and mucocutaneous jaundice, soft abdomen without tenderness or rebound tenderness, and no lower extremity edema. --- Imagen mixta 1: 03.jpg --- # 检测结果:

An autosomal-recessive disorder of impaired copper excretion caused by ATP7B mutations, resulting in copper accumulation in the liver, brain, cornea, and other tissues. The homozygous ATP7B c.2333G>T (p.Arg778Leu) pathogenic variant, Kayser-Fleischer corneal ring, and basal-ganglia MRI abnormalities strongly support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and ecchymoses, compatible with liver dysfunction/coagulopathy
Basal ganglia abnormalities on brain MRI consistent with copper deposition
Amenorrhea and menstrual irregularities, which may occur with chronic liver disease or Wilson disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported neurologic manifestations such as tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, gait disturbance, or psychiatric symptoms
No abdominal pain or abdominal distension

data.diagnosis: Herb-induced liver injury (drug-induced liver injury from Chinese herbal medicines)
data.description: Liver injury caused by hepatotoxic medications or herbal products, which can present with hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed hepatitis and may cause jaundice and pruritus.
symptoms_in_common: Nine-month history of Chinese herbal medicine use
Generalized pruritus, compatible with cholestatic liver injury
Petechiae and ecchymoses, potentially associated with severe hepatic synthetic dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Kayser-Fleischer corneal ring
Basal ganglia MRI findings suggesting metal deposition
Homozygous pathogenic ATP7B mutation
No fever, abdominal pain, or abdominal tenderness
Symptoms persisting for more than 2 months despite no stated acute medication-related onset

data.description: A chronic immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that often affects girls and young women and can cause jaundice, progressive liver dysfunction, and, in advanced disease, coagulopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and ecchymoses that may reflect impaired hepatic clotting-factor synthesis
Menstrual irregularities/amenorrhea that may accompany chronic systemic or liver disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized pruritus is less typical unless there is substantial cholestasis
Kayser-Fleischer corneal ring
Basal ganglia changes compatible with copper deposition
Homozygous pathogenic ATP7B mutation supporting Wilson disease
No reported fatigue, arthralgia, fever, hepatomegaly, or abdominal discomfort

data.description: Reduced bile formation or bile flow, from intrahepatic liver disease or obstruction, causing retention of bilirubin and bile acids that commonly produces jaundice and itching.
symptoms_in_common: Possible bleeding tendency manifested by petechiae and ecchymoses, potentially related to vitamin K deficiency or liver dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain, fever, abdominal tenderness, or abdominal distension suggestive of acute biliary obstruction or cholangitis
No reported pale stools, dark urine, hepatomegaly, or gallbladder-related symptoms
Kayser-Fleischer corneal ring
Basal ganglia MRI findings consistent with copper deposition
Homozygous pathogenic ATP7B mutation, which indicates Wilson disease as the underlying cause rather than isolated cholestasis

data.description: 66-year-old man with 2 days of fever, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash. History of hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis; started azathioprine 75 mg 10 days earlier. Exam showed ताप 38°C and bilateral tender knees with patellar tap. Labs: WBC 10,500/μL with neutrophilia, CRP 76 mg/L, ESR 69 mm/h, mildly elevated rheumatoid factor; anti-CCP, dsDNA, ENA, and anti-ASO negative. Renal function and urinalysis were normal, chest radiograph was normal, and synovial fluid was noninflammatory with no bacteria or crystals.

An idiosyncratic immune-mediated reaction to azathioprine, usually occurring within days to a few weeks of starting treatment, characterized by fever, malaise, rash, arthralgia, and elevated inflammatory markers.
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral knee effusions with patellar tap
Noninflammatory synovial fluid

data.diagnosis: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), potentially azathioprine-induced
data.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory dermatosis causing abrupt fever, neutrophilia, painful erythematous papules, nodules, or plaques, often accompanied by arthralgia. It can be drug-induced, including after azathioprine exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Painful erythematous plaques or nodular lesions on the legs/knees
Temporal relationship to recently initiated azathioprine
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral knee effusions
Noninflammatory synovial fluid
No reported biopsy showing dense neutrophilic dermal infiltrates

data.description: An inflammatory panniculitis presenting with painful erythematous subcutaneous nodules, classically on the anterior lower legs, often associated with fever, malaise, arthralgia, and elevated inflammatory markers.
symptoms_in_common: Tender painful red nodular or plaque-like lesions over the lower extremities
No bacterial growth or crystals in synovial fluid
symptoms_not_in_common: Very close onset after azathioprine initiation is more suggestive of a drug hypersensitivity reaction
Neutrophilia is not specific for erythema nodosum
Lesions appear to involve the knees rather than being confined to the classic anterior shins

data.description: A small-vessel immune-complex vasculitis that may be triggered by medications and commonly causes palpable purpura or painful erythematous lesions on dependent areas, sometimes with fever and arthralgia.
symptoms_in_common: Recent exposure to a new medication
Painful rash on the lower extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Rash does not clearly appear as palpable purpura
Normal urinalysis and renal function argue against systemic vasculitic involvement
No reported abdominal pain, neuropathy, or hematuria

data.description: An inflammatory arthritis occurring after an infection, typically involving asymmetric lower-extremity joints and sometimes associated with fever, skin lesions, conjunctivitis, urethritis, or gastrointestinal symptoms.
symptoms_not_in_common: Polyarticular rather than typical asymmetric oligoarticular arthritis
Synovial fluid is noninflammatory
No preceding gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection reported
No conjunctivitis, urethritis, or characteristic keratoderma reported
Painful erythematous rash and close azathioprine timing favor a drug reaction

data.description: A 60-year-old woman presented after sustaining direct trauma to the anterior neck from a fall. She developed progressively worsening hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, and pain with neck movement. Physical examination revealed visible neck swelling with bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall. There was no tenderness on palpation of the cervical spine. On flexible nasal endoscopy, swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall was observed, indicating potential airway compromise.

Hemorrhage into the retropharyngeal/prevertebral soft tissues after blunt neck trauma, which can expand and compress the pharynx and upper airway. The CT image shows marked prevertebral/retropharyngeal soft-tissue expansion consistent with hematoma.
symptoms_in_common: Bruising extending onto the anterior chest wall
Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling on flexible endoscopy
symptoms_not_in_common: No cervical spine tenderness

data.diagnosis: Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or hematoma
data.description: Injury to the larynx after anterior neck trauma may cause edema, mucosal bleeding, cartilage injury, and progressive airway narrowing.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent posterior pharyngeal wall swelling is more characteristic of a retropharyngeal process
No reported stridor
No reported subcutaneous emphysema
No reported hemoptysis

data.diagnosis: Prevertebral soft-tissue hematoma from occult cervical spine or ligamentous injury
data.description: Trauma to the cervical spine or its supporting ligaments can produce bleeding and prevertebral swelling, sometimes without obvious tenderness or fracture on initial examination.
symptoms_in_common: Marked prevertebral soft-tissue swelling on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No cervical spine tenderness
Hoarse voice is less typical unless the swelling affects the larynx or recurrent laryngeal nerve
Visible anterior neck bruising is more suggestive of direct soft-tissue neck injury

data.diagnosis: Traumatic pharyngeal injury with retropharyngeal edema
data.description: Blunt trauma can injure the pharyngeal wall and surrounding tissues, causing edema or hemorrhage in the retropharyngeal space and narrowing of the airway.
symptoms_not_in_common: Hoarseness is more suggestive of associated laryngeal involvement
No reported oral bleeding
No reported fever or infectious symptoms
No reported crepitus or subcutaneous emphysema

data.description: 37-year-old man with 3 months of recurrent episodes of weakness, irritability, poor concentration, craving for sweets, cold clammy fatigue, and occasional foggy sensorium/confusion, often occurring after several hours without food, especially at night or early morning. His wife noted strange behavior and memory loss; he gained 30 lb from drinking large amounts of cola for symptom relief. Past history was unremarkable aside from prior umbilical hernia repair and back surgery; no medication use. On examination he was confused, cold, and clammy, with otherwise unremarkable physical findings. Routine labs, HbA1c, adrenal testing, thyroid and gonadal hormones were normal; prolactin was mildly elevated. Glucose was 2.4 mmol/L with elevated insulin and C-peptide. Imaging showed a 1.8 × 1.3 cm hypervascular slightly exophytic lesion between the head and neck of the pancreas.
A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin autonomously, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia (endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia).
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent episodes after several hours without food, especially overnight or early morning
Craving sweets and relief with cola intake
Weight gain from frequent carbohydrate consumption
Documented hypoglycemia with glucose of 2.4 mmol/L
Elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Mildly elevated prolactin is not a typical direct manifestation of an isolated insulinoma

data.diagnosis: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) with insulinoma
data.description: An inherited endocrine tumor syndrome involving parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors; insulinoma may be the presenting pancreatic tumor.
symptoms_in_common: Weakness, confusion, behavioral changes, and memory impairment
Mild prolactin elevation, which can suggest pituitary involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No known family history of endocrine tumors
No reported hypercalcemia, kidney stones, bone disease, or other signs of hyperparathyroidism
No clear pituitary mass symptoms such as headaches, visual-field loss, or galactorrhea
A solitary small pancreatic lesion is more typical of sporadic insulinoma than MEN1-associated multifocal disease

data.description: Hypoglycemia caused by hidden ingestion of insulin secretagogue medications such as sulfonylureas, which stimulates endogenous insulin and C-peptide secretion.
symptoms_in_common: Weakness, confusion, irritability, and impaired concentration
Low glucose with elevated insulin and C-peptide
Symptom improvement after consuming sugary drinks
symptoms_not_in_common: He reports no medication use
A hypervascular pancreatic lesion strongly supports an insulin-secreting pancreatic tumor instead
The recurrent chronic pattern and pancreatic imaging finding make medication-induced hypoglycemia less likely

data.description: Hypoglycemia caused by administration of insulin from an external source, either accidental, intentional, or iatrogenic.
symptoms_in_common: Confusion, memory impairment, weakness, irritability, and sweating
symptoms_not_in_common: C-peptide is elevated; exogenous insulin typically suppresses C-peptide
No history of diabetes or insulin use
Pancreatic hypervascular lesion is not explained by exogenous insulin use
Weight gain from recurrent carbohydrate intake is possible but not specific

data.description: Hypoglycemia caused by tumors producing insulin-like growth factor 2 or consuming large amounts of glucose; it is usually associated with large mesenchymal, hepatic, or other non-pancreatic tumors.
symptoms_in_common: Weakness, confusion, cold clammy episodes, and behavioral changes
symptoms_not_in_common: Insulin and C-peptide are elevated, whereas they are usually suppressed in non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia
The lesion is a small pancreatic hypervascular mass rather than a large non-islet tumor
No evidence of a large systemic malignancy, liver mass, or weight loss

data.description: A 39-year-old male, with no prior relevant medical history, presents with atraumatic intermittent sharp pain in the lower segment of the right anterior thoracic wall. The symptoms began two months earlier when the patient started exercising (CrossFit), mostly triggered by training (especially abdominal crunches) whilst being asymptomatic in normal daily activities.

A mechanical pain syndrome caused by excessive mobility or subluxation of a false rib costal cartilage, usually involving ribs 8-10. Dynamic ultrasound may show abnormal movement/overlap of the involved rib cartilage relative to adjacent ribs.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent sharp pain in the lower anterior right thoracic wall
Pain provoked by abdominal crunches and exercise
Symptoms began after starting intense CrossFit training
Location involving the lower false ribs, particularly the 8th-9th rib region
Ultrasound appearance suggesting abnormal close relationship/mobility of the 8th rib relative to adjacent ribs
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported clicking, popping, or snapping sensation
No reported radiation of pain to the back or upper abdomen

data.description: Overstretching or microscopic tearing of the intercostal muscles, commonly caused by strenuous trunk movement, repetitive exercise, coughing, or twisting.
symptoms_in_common: Onset in association with new strenuous exercise
Pain provoked by abdominal exercises involving trunk flexion and chest-wall stabilization
No symptoms during normal low-demand daily activity
symptoms_not_in_common: Two-month intermittent course without a described acute muscle injury
Ultrasound emphasis on the relationship of the 7th, 8th, and 9th ribs rather than a clear muscle tear
Pain is specifically in the lower false-rib region, which favors slipping rib syndrome

data.description: Mechanical irritation or sprain at the junction between a rib and its cartilage, or between adjacent costal cartilages, often after repetitive loading of the chest wall.
symptoms_in_common: Provocation by forceful abdominal and trunk movements
Involvement of the lower anterior rib-cartilage region
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported focal swelling, bruising, or persistent tenderness
No known direct traumatic event
Apparent abnormal alignment/mobility of the 8th rib relative to neighboring ribs is more characteristic of slipping rib syndrome

data.diagnosis: Rib stress injury or occult stress fracture
data.description: A repetitive-load injury of a rib that can occur after abrupt increases in athletic activity; early stress injuries may be difficult to detect on plain radiographs.
symptoms_in_common: Pain developed after an increase in physical training intensity
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported persistent pain at rest
No reported pain with routine breathing, coughing, or normal daily activities
No described focal cortical disruption, periosteal reaction, or callus on the provided ultrasound images
No direct trauma

data.description: A 31-year-old woman underwent barium enema examination as part of a medical checkup. She had been healthy without specific complaints and had no significant past medical or family history. The patient was 161 cm in height and weighed 44 kg, appeared well, and the physical examination showed no abnormalities. Complete blood cell count and biochemical analysis of the blood for hepatic and renal function, urine analysis, and fecal occult blood test were all within normal limits. The tumor markers for CEA and CA 19-9 were also normal. No lesions were observed on the upper endoscopy and the abdominal ultrasound.

67-year-old previously healthy man with a 4-month history of dry cough, wheezing, and mild dyspnea, initially treated as eosinophilic asthma without improvement on inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids. No smoking or significant past medical history. On examination, he required 1 L/min nasal cannula oxygen (SaO2 96%), had decreased breath sounds and fine crackles in the right lower lung field, and no jugular venous distention, murmurs, gallop, or peripheral edema. Chest imaging showed right-sided ground-glass opacities on x-ray and ground-glass opacities with surrounding consolidation in the right lower lung on high-resolution CT.

data.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
data.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent eosinophilia, dysplastic/immature eosinophil precursors, blasts or other abnormal myeloid cells, and cytogenetic abnormalities. It can cause pulmonary eosinophilic infiltration and respiratory symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Fine crackles and decreased breath sounds over the right lower lung
Right lower-lung ground-glass opacities with surrounding consolidation
Blood-smear image showing abnormal eosinophilic maturation, including eosinophilic myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and bands
Image evidence of dysplastic hematologic findings, including irregular hypersegmented neutrophils and megaloblasts
Abnormal karyotype suggesting a clonal hematologic disorder
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly reported constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats
No reported splenomegaly or hepatomegaly

data.diagnosis: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine-kinase gene rearrangement
data.description: A group of clonal hematologic neoplasms, often involving PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, or PCM1-JAK2 rearrangements, that produce marked eosinophilia and may infiltrate the lungs, heart, skin, gastrointestinal tract, or nervous system.
symptoms_in_common: Respiratory symptoms caused by possible eosinophilic pulmonary infiltration
Ground-glass pulmonary opacities and focal consolidation
Peripheral-blood image showing increased eosinophilic cells at multiple stages of maturation
Cytogenetic abnormality on karyotype supporting a possible clonal myeloid process
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported splenomegaly
No reported cardiac manifestations such as heart failure, murmur, edema, or thromboembolism
No reported skin, gastrointestinal, or neurologic involvement

data.diagnosis: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with pulmonary involvement
data.description: A syndrome of persistent eosinophilia associated with organ damage after secondary causes and defined clonal eosinophilic neoplasms have been excluded. Lung involvement may mimic asthma or eosinophilic pneumonia.
symptoms_in_common: Cough, wheezing, and dyspnea initially resembling asthma
Failure to improve with inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids
Eosinophilic cells visible in the blood-smear image
symptoms_not_in_common: Abnormal eosinophil maturation and dysplastic blood-smear features are more suggestive of clonal eosinophilic leukemia than idiopathic HES
The karyotype abnormality is not typical of idiopathic HES
No reported involvement of other common target organs, such as heart, skin, gastrointestinal tract, or peripheral nerves

data.description: An eosinophilic lung disease characterized by subacute cough, dyspnea, wheezing, pulmonary infiltrates, and eosinophilic inflammation; it can be associated with adult-onset asthma but usually responds well to systemic corticosteroids.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute respiratory illness over several months
Ground-glass opacities and surrounding pulmonary consolidation
Initial clinical impression of eosinophilic asthma
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominantly unilateral right lower-lobe disease is less typical than the usual bilateral peripheral infiltrates
No improvement with inhaled corticosteroids
Blood-smear findings of immature/dysplastic eosinophilic precursors are not typical
Cytogenetic abnormality is not expected in reactive eosinophilic pneumonia

data.description: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of malaise, fevers, abdominal pain, and worsening pallor. His symptoms began with headache and abdominal pain, with an initial temperature of 38.6°C and pale skin. He experienced persistent upper abdominal pain and recurrent fevers. The patient reported nausea, occasional diarrhea, headache, myalgias, fatigue, and occasional dizziness. He described nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant, with occasional blood in stools. His height was 132 cm (1st percentile), weight 26.8 kg (1st percentile), with recent 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, distended abdomen with mild tenderness in right upper and left lower quadrants, and ecchymoses on the shins. He had visited the Dominican Republic 3 months prior. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP 143.2 mg/liter), and elevated ferritin (320 μg/L).

data.diagnosis: Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK-positive (ALCL)
data.description: An aggressive CD30-positive T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly affects children and adolescents. It often causes prolonged fever, systemic inflammation, anemia, lymphadenopathy, and extranodal disease. The imaging suggests extensive abdominal nodal disease, and the histology shows large atypical cells with strong CD30-type membranous/Golgi staining, supporting ALCL.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging evidence of extensive abdominal lymphadenopathy and possible extranodal involvement
Histology showing atypical large lymphoid cells with immunohistochemical findings consistent with a CD30-positive lymphoma
symptoms_not_in_common: Occasional diarrhea
Blood in stools
Recent travel to the Dominican Republic

data.description: A B-cell lymphoma characterized by malignant Reed-Sternberg cells, frequently associated with fever, weight loss, inflammatory-marker elevation, anemia, and lymph-node enlargement. CD30 expression can overlap with ALCL, although the histologic and immunophenotypic pattern shown is more suggestive of ALCL.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal discomfort from abdominal nodal disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent persistent periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant
Occasional diarrhea
Blood in stools
Ecchymoses
Marked microcytic anemia is less typical than anemia of chronic inflammation

data.diagnosis: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
data.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma that may present with rapidly enlarging abdominal masses or lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, bowel involvement, gastrointestinal bleeding, and anemia. However, the CD30-positive anaplastic histologic appearance favors ALCL rather than diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
symptoms_in_common: Possible bowel involvement with blood in stools
symptoms_not_in_common: One-month recurrent fever syndrome with very high inflammatory markers is more characteristic of systemic ALCL
Ecchymoses are not a usual presenting feature
Histologic CD30-dominant anaplastic-cell pattern is not typical for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving the peritoneum, bowel, or abdominal lymph nodes can cause prolonged fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and necrotic lymphadenopathy. Travel to an endemic region raises consideration, but the lymphoma-type histology and immunostaining argue against tuberculosis.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic abdominal pain and abdominal distension
symptoms_not_in_common: Ecchymoses
Histology showing atypical large malignant-appearing lymphoid cells rather than granulomas with caseous necrosis
CD30-positive lymphoma-type immunohistochemical staining pattern
No reported chronic cough, night sweats, or known tuberculosis exposure

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.title: Mixed cellularity classical Hodgkin lymphoma

data.description: 39-year-old man with 4 days of fever with shaking chills, diffuse headache, fatigue, lower back pain, weakness, anorexia, decreased urine output with dark urine, and blurry vision during febrile episodes, occurring after return from a 2-week trip to East Africa/Tanzania. During travel he had mosquito bites and ate cooked seafood and a small amount of raw tuna; he also developed nausea, vomiting, and nonbloody diarrhea near the end of the trip. Past history includes degenerative knee disease with prior glucocorticoid injections. On examination he was febrile (38.9°C), with facial flushing, mild scleral icterus, and dark brown urine.

Severe mosquito-borne malaria caused by P. falciparum, often acquired in sub-Saharan Africa and capable of causing hemolysis, jaundice, kidney injury, and cerebral or visual symptoms. The rapid malaria test and blood smear show findings consistent with P. falciparum, including multiple delicate ring forms within erythrocytes and an appliqué form.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to Tanzania, an area endemic for P. falciparum
Dark brown urine, compatible with hemoglobinuria from hemolysis
Decreased urine output, concerning for malaria-associated acute kidney injury
Mild scleral icterus, compatible with hemolysis and hyperbilirubinemia
Peripheral smear showing intraerythrocytic ring-stage parasites, including multiple rings and an appliqué form
Positive malaria rapid diagnostic test pattern consistent with P. falciparum
symptoms_not_in_common: Nonbloody diarrhea is possible but is less characteristic than fever and hemolytic manifestations
Lower back pain is nonspecific and not a classic defining feature

data.diagnosis: Severe falciparum malaria with blackwater fever
data.description: A severe hemolytic manifestation of P. falciparum malaria characterized by massive intravascular red-cell destruction, dark hemoglobin-containing urine, jaundice, and possible acute kidney injury.
symptoms_in_common: Fever with rigors after travel to a malaria-endemic region
Lower back pain, which may occur with hemolysis or renal involvement
Blood smear and rapid test evidence of P. falciparum infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Diarrhea is not a typical core feature of blackwater fever
Raw tuna and cooked seafood exposure do not explain this syndrome
Blurry vision is not a defining feature, although it may occur in severe malaria

data.description: A zoonotic spirochetal infection acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with animal urine. Severe disease can cause fever, headache, jaundice, dark urine, and acute kidney injury.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported freshwater, floodwater, rodent, or animal-urine exposure
Mosquito exposure and Tanzania travel more strongly support malaria
Blood smear showing intraerythrocytic malaria parasites is not compatible with leptospirosis
Positive malaria rapid diagnostic testing is not expected in leptospirosis

data.description: A mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause abrupt fever, severe headache, fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms, and occasionally hepatitis or kidney injury. It is an important alternative diagnosis in febrile returning travelers.
symptoms_in_common: Possible dark urine and mild jaundice if hepatic involvement occurs
symptoms_not_in_common: Dark brown urine with oliguria from marked hemolysis is less typical of dengue
No rash, myalgias, retro-orbital pain, mucosal bleeding, or reported thrombocytopenic bleeding
Blood smear with ring-form intraerythrocytic parasites is not a feature of dengue
Positive malaria rapid diagnostic testing supports malaria rather than dengue

data.description: 24-year-old male with quadriplegia from a car accident 5 years prior that required cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. Presented with dysphagia, odynophagia, neck pain, fever, and chills. Medical history significant for quadriplegia requiring cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. CT and MRI showed large paraspinal abscess extending from cervical spine 4 to thoracic spine 11.

data.diagnosis: Esophageal perforation caused by erosion of cervical spine hardware
data.description: A delayed complication of anterior cervical spine fixation in which a plate or screw erodes into the pharynx or esophagus, producing a perforation and allowing contamination of deep neck and mediastinal spaces.
symptoms_in_common: History of cervical spine stabilization with metal plates
Endoscopic appearance of exposed/eroding hardware and a communicating defect
Paraspinal abscess extending from the cervical spine to T11
symptoms_not_in_common: Quadriplegia from prior trauma

data.description: A severe infection of the mediastinum caused by spread of infection from the neck, pharynx, or esophagus; it may produce purulent mediastinal collections and systemic illness.
symptoms_in_common: Endoscopic images showing pus draining into the mediastinum
Large infection extending from the cervical region into the thoracic spine/mediastinal region
symptoms_not_in_common: Quadriplegia
Cervical metal plates are not a typical primary feature, although they may be the underlying cause

data.diagnosis: Cervical spinal instrumentation infection with extensive paraspinal abscess
data.description: Infection involving prior cervical fixation hardware and adjacent soft tissues, causing a deep paraspinal abscess that can spread longitudinally through fascial planes into the thorax.
symptoms_in_common: Prior cervical spine stabilization with metal plates
Large paraspinal abscess from the cervical spine to T11
Possible exposure of hardware on endoscopic imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Dysphagia and odynophagia are less typical unless the infection erodes into or compresses the esophagus
Quadriplegia is due to the prior injury rather than the acute infection

data.diagnosis: Retropharyngeal/deep neck space abscess with extension to the mediastinum
data.description: A purulent infection in the retropharyngeal or prevertebral deep neck spaces that may descend into the mediastinum and cause life-threatening mediastinal sepsis.
symptoms_in_common: Extension of infection from the neck into the thoracic region
symptoms_not_in_common: Remote cervical fixation hardware is not typical for a primary retropharyngeal abscess, but may be the source in this case
Quadriplegia is not a typical manifestation

data.description: A 58-year-old male with worsening nausea for the past 72 hours presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back in the context of 4 recent episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis. He was afebrile, diaphoretic, and mildly tachycardic. Cardiac workup, complete blood count, and electrolytes were normal.

A full-thickness rupture of the esophagus, usually in the distal thoracic esophagus, caused by a sudden rise in intrathoracic pressure during forceful vomiting. It can cause mediastinal air, pleural contamination, pleural effusions, and rapidly progressive mediastinitis.
symptoms_in_common: Severe chest pain radiating to the back after repeated vomiting
Acute worsening nausea with multiple episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis
Subcutaneous emphysema in the lower neck/supraclavicular regions on imaging
Left-sided pleural fluid and pleural air-fluid abnormality consistent with hydropneumothorax or contaminated pleural effusion
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile presentation
Normal complete blood count
Normal electrolytes

data.diagnosis: Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophageal perforation
data.description: Inflammation and infection of the mediastinum caused by leakage of esophageal contents after perforation. Early cases may initially have normal laboratory values before fever and leukocytosis develop.
symptoms_in_common: Pleural effusions, particularly on the left
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
Normal complete blood count without leukocytosis
Only 72 hours of symptoms without described systemic toxicity or sepsis

data.description: Air in the mediastinum caused by alveolar rupture or, less commonly, esophageal injury after increased intrathoracic pressure from vomiting or Valsalva. It may produce chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema.
symptoms_not_in_common: Large left pleural fluid collection/hydropneumothorax
Bilateral pleural effusions
Severe persistent chest pain after repeated emesis is more concerning for esophageal rupture than uncomplicated pneumomediastinum
Diaphoresis

data.diagnosis: Aspiration pneumonitis or aspiration pneumonia following emesis
data.description: Chemical lung injury or infection caused by inhalation of gastric contents during vomiting. It commonly affects dependent lower-lobe lung regions and may cause hypoxemia, cough, fever, and infiltrates.
symptoms_in_common: Left lower-lung opacity/atelectatic or infiltrative change on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe chest pain radiating to the back
Pneumomediastinum
Cervical subcutaneous emphysema
Pleural air-fluid abnormality suggesting hydropneumothorax
No fever
Normal complete blood count
No cough, dyspnea, or hypoxemia reported

data.description: 27-year-old man with 2-year history of recurrent convulsive episodes. Events began with shaking of the trunk, arms, and legs lasting 4–5 minutes, preceded by occipital pain radiating to the neck, blurred vision, palpitations, nausea, and difficulty concentrating. Four months before admission, he had a generalized stiffening episode with fall and 5–8 minutes of shaking with urinary incontinence while drinking alcohol. Despite levetiracetam, he continued to have episodes about weekly; one month before admission he was found on the floor with shaking and clenching movements lasting about 2 minutes. On examination, he was awake and alert but nonverbal, with a stiff posture and intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements of the trunk and limbs. He had extensive burn scars on the face, trunk, back, arms, and legs. Past history included febrile seizure in childhood, multiple concussions, asthma, major depressive disorder, chronic PTSD, and panic disorder with agoraphobia. Laboratory studies were normal except for mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase.

Functional seizures are paroxysmal episodes that resemble epileptic seizures but are not caused by abnormal epileptic cortical discharges. They are commonly associated with trauma-related, mood, anxiety, and dissociative disorders. The EEG image is most consistent with prominent movement/electrode artifact during an event without a convincing evolving ictal epileptiform pattern.
symptoms_in_common: Stiff posture with nonverbal behavior during examination
History of significant trauma suggested by extensive burn scars
EEG appearance dominated by movement artifact rather than a clear ictal electrographic seizure pattern
symptoms_not_in_common: Urinary incontinence during one episode
Mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase after convulsive activity
Childhood febrile seizure history
Multiple prior concussions

data.description: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures involve sudden loss of consciousness, tonic stiffening followed by bilateral rhythmic clonic jerking, and often a postictal period. They may cause falls, injuries, urinary incontinence, lactate elevation, and creatine kinase elevation.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral shaking of the trunk, arms, and legs
Mild elevation of lactate and creatine kinase
History of febrile seizure in childhood
symptoms_not_in_common: Episodes frequently last 4-8 minutes, which is longer than many typical generalized tonic-clonic seizures
Intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements rather than consistently rhythmic clonic jerking
Continued frequent events despite antiseizure medication
Prominent psychiatric trauma-related comorbidity
EEG image does not show a clear generalized evolving ictal discharge and is dominated by artifact

data.diagnosis: Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, possibly occipital onset
data.description: Focal seizures arise from one cerebral region and may spread to produce bilateral tonic-clonic convulsions. Occipital seizures can include visual symptoms, and focal autonomic symptoms can include nausea and palpitations before convulsive activity.
symptoms_in_common: Occipital pain radiating to the neck before events
Fall and urinary incontinence during a convulsive episode
History of multiple concussions, which can increase seizure risk
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly described stereotyped focal neurologic onset such as visual hallucinations, forced head/eye deviation, unilateral jerking, or focal impaired awareness
Nonrhythmic tremulous movements during examination
Prominent PTSD, depression, panic disorder, and agoraphobia favoring a functional contribution
EEG image lacks a definite focal evolving ictal rhythm
Event duration of several minutes with variable motor activity is less typical of a single focal epileptic seizure

data.description: Convulsive syncope is transient loss of consciousness from reduced cerebral perfusion, often due to vasovagal or cardiac causes, with brief stiffening or myoclonic jerks that can mimic a seizure. Palpitations may suggest a cardiac trigger.
symptoms_in_common: Brief shaking or clenching movements can occur with syncope
symptoms_not_in_common: Repeated prolonged convulsive episodes lasting 4-8 minutes
Sustained generalized shaking
Urinary incontinence is less typical
Persistent nonverbal stiff posture and intermittent tremulous movements
Mild creatine kinase elevation after events
No described brief loss of consciousness with rapid recovery, orthostatic trigger, or documented arrhythmia

data.description: 92-year-old woman with BMI 14.2 kg/m². Past history: no abdominal surgery, five children by normal vaginal delivery. Presenting with: 2-day history of sudden onset right knee pain, 1-day history of nausea and vomiting. Physical exam: no knee swelling/tenderness, patient frequently flexed right knee for pain relief, abdominal distension present, tenderness to deep palpation but no peritoneal irritation signs, no abdominal mass. Rectal exam revealed small extraluminal mass on right side. Initial abdominal radiograph showed small-bowel obstruction.

data.diagnosis: Right obturator hernia with incarcerated small bowel causing small-bowel obstruction
data.description: A pelvic hernia in which small bowel protrudes through the obturator canal. It classically occurs in thin, elderly multiparous women and may compress the obturator nerve, producing medial thigh or knee pain (Howship-Romberg sign). The CT images show a bowel-containing hernia in the right obturator region.
symptoms_in_common: Elderly thin woman with very low BMI
Right knee pain without local knee swelling or tenderness
Flexion of the right knee for pain relief
Right-sided extraluminal mass on rectal examination
Deep abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs
symptoms_not_in_common: No palpable abdominal mass
No peritoneal irritation signs

data.diagnosis: Strangulated or incarcerated right obturator hernia
data.description: An obturator hernia may trap bowel tightly within the obturator canal, causing incarceration and potentially bowel ischemia or strangulation. It commonly presents as an acute mechanical small-bowel obstruction in frail elderly women.
symptoms_in_common: Right pelvic extraluminal mass on rectal examination
Right knee pain suggestive of obturator nerve compression
CT evidence of right obturator-region bowel herniation
symptoms_not_in_common: No peritoneal irritation signs
No reported fever
No reported hemodynamic instability
No reported severe continuous abdominal pain

data.description: A femoral hernia is protrusion of abdominal contents through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. It is more common in older women and can incarcerate bowel, although the imaging location and knee pain more strongly favor an obturator hernia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Right knee pain relieved by knee flexion is not typical
No described groin bulge or tender femoral mass
Very low BMI and multiparity more strongly support obturator hernia
CT appearance is more consistent with an obturator-canal hernia

data.description: 23-year-old Korean female with 6 months of recurrent bilateral visual field defects and headache, worsened 1 month before presentation. She presented with 1 day of left eye visual disturbance and left visual field defect, followed 2 days later by sudden left-sided hearing loss. Three weeks later, she developed right eye visual field defect, then tinnitus, severe headache, and arm numbness. No history of diabetes, hypertension, connective tissue disease, tuberculosis, hematologic or cardiovascular disease, oral contraceptive use, or pregnancy. Initial exam showed reactive pupils without RAPD, visual acuity 20/20 right and 20/25 left, normal intraocular pressure, and normal anterior segment exam. Labs including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, ESR, and CRP were normal; CSF showed mildly elevated protein (74.4 mg/dL) without oligoclonal bands.

A rare autoimmune endotheliopathy causing microvascular occlusion in the brain, retina, and cochlea; classically presents with encephalopathy/headache, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss. MRI commonly shows characteristic corpus callosum lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Young woman with recurrent visual field defects
Retinal arterial branch occlusion/retinal ischemic lesion on fundus photography and fluorescein angiography
Sudden unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus
MRI lesions involving the corpus callosum and periventricular region
Mildly elevated CSF protein without oligoclonal bands
Normal inflammatory markers and negative antiphospholipid antibody testing
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear encephalopathy, confusion, or cognitive decline described
No retinal vasculitis or uveitis described

data.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that commonly affects young women and can cause episodic visual, sensory, and other neurologic deficits with white-matter lesions on MRI.
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is uncommon
Retinal branch arterial occlusion is not typical of multiple sclerosis
Fluorescein angiographic retinal arterial ischemia is atypical
CSF lacks oligoclonal bands
The combination of retinal ischemia and cochlear hearing loss is more characteristic of Susac syndrome

data.description: An autoimmune hypercoagulable disorder that can produce arterial or venous thrombosis, including retinal vascular occlusion and cerebral ischemic lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Retinal arterial occlusion with visual field loss
Focal neurologic symptom of arm numbness
Brain ischemic-appearing lesions on diffusion-weighted MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies were normal
No pregnancy morbidity or prior thrombotic history
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is less typical
Recurrent bilateral retinal and cochlear microvascular involvement with corpus callosum lesions is more suggestive of Susac syndrome

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with retinal vasculopathy
data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that may cause retinal vascular occlusion, central nervous system involvement, headache, and neurologic deficits, often with systemic inflammatory or connective-tissue manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Retinal vascular ischemia causing visual field defects
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of connective-tissue disease or systemic lupus manifestations
Normal ESR and CRP
Negative lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibody testing
No rash, arthritis, renal disease, oral ulcers, or serositis described
Sensorineural hearing loss is not a typical dominant feature

data.description: A rare inflammatory disorder characterized mainly by interstitial keratitis and audiovestibular dysfunction, including sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo; systemic vasculitis can occur.
symptoms_in_common: Headache and possible systemic vascular inflammatory manifestations
symptoms_not_in_common: No interstitial keratitis, ocular pain, photophobia, or anterior-segment inflammation
Retinal branch arterial occlusions are not the classic ocular manifestation
Corpus callosum lesions and recurrent retinal ischemia are more characteristic of Susac syndrome
No vertigo or vestibular symptoms described

data.description: A 73-year-old woman with a 10-year history of severe paraspinal muscle atrophy and cerebellar ataxia. Symptoms began at age 63 with slight stooping posture, then progressed to gait instability requiring a walking stick by age 68 and difficulty climbing stairs by age 70. Exam showed moderate neck flexion weakness, mild proximal limb weakness, poor tandem gait balance without limb ataxia, and MMSE 25/30. Labs revealed elevated creatine kinase, normal blood and CSF lactate, low-normal TSH, elevated antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, elevated rheumatoid factor, and mildly positive antinuclear antibody. EMG showed mild myopathic changes. Audiometry showed sensorineural high-frequency hearing loss, and Holter monitoring showed frequent premature contractions.

data.diagnosis: Mitochondrial myopathy due to an mtDNA mutation (likely MELAS-spectrum or m.3243A>G-related disease)
data.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder causing impaired oxidative phosphorylation. It can produce proximal and axial myopathy, ragged-red/oxidative-enzyme-abnormal muscle fibers, hearing loss, cardiac conduction abnormalities, cognitive changes, and variable cerebellar involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly progressive axial and proximal muscle weakness
Severe paraspinal muscle atrophy with stooped/bent-spine posture
Cerebellar ataxia and poor tandem gait
Maternal-pattern family history with affected female relatives and elevated CK in descendants
Muscle biopsy appearance consistent with mitochondrial abnormalities, including ragged-red/oxidative-enzyme-abnormal fibers
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal blood and cerebrospinal-fluid lactate
No reported diabetes mellitus
No reported stroke-like episodes
No reported recurrent migraine, vomiting, or encephalopathy

data.diagnosis: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF syndrome)
data.description: A mitochondrial disease, most often associated with an MT-TK mutation, characterized by myoclonus, generalized epilepsy, ataxia, myopathy, hearing impairment, and ragged-red fibers on muscle biopsy. Clinical severity can vary considerably within maternal families.
symptoms_in_common: Mitochondrial-type muscle biopsy abnormalities including ragged-red fibers
Progressive myopathy with axial and proximal weakness
Possible maternal inheritance pattern in the pedigree
symptoms_not_in_common: No seizures or myoclonus reported in the patient
Very late onset at age 63 is less typical
Bent-spine syndrome with marked paraspinal atrophy is not a classic dominant feature
Frequent premature cardiac contractions are less characteristic than neurologic manifestations

data.diagnosis: Mitochondrial spinocerebellar ataxia with myopathy (POLG-related or other nuclear mitochondrial disease)
data.description: Nuclear-gene mitochondrial disorders can cause cerebellar ataxia, external ophthalmoplegia, neuropathy, seizures, myopathy, and mitochondrial abnormalities on muscle biopsy. POLG-related disease may present in adulthood but is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive or dominant nuclear pattern rather than a maternal mtDNA pattern.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive myopathy with elevated creatine kinase
Family history including a relative with seizures
symptoms_not_in_common: Pedigree suggests maternal transmission rather than typical nuclear-gene inheritance
No reported epilepsy in the patient
No ophthalmoplegia or ptosis reported
No peripheral neuropathy reported
No liver dysfunction or valproate sensitivity reported

data.diagnosis: Myofibrillar myopathy presenting as bent-spine syndrome
data.description: Myofibrillar myopathies are inherited muscle diseases that can preferentially affect paraspinal, neck-flexor, and proximal muscles, causing camptocormia or bent-spine syndrome. Some forms are associated with cardiomyopathy or arrhythmias and modest CK elevation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Cerebellar ataxia is not typical
Sensorineural hearing loss is not typical
Mitochondrial ragged-red or oxidative-enzyme-abnormal fibers are not typical primary findings
Maternal inheritance pattern is less typical for most myofibrillar myopathies
Mild cognitive impairment is not a usual feature

data.description: A lysosomal glycogen-storage myopathy caused by acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. Adult-onset disease produces slowly progressive limb-girdle and axial weakness, including paraspinal involvement, often with respiratory muscle weakness and sometimes elevated CK.
symptoms_in_common: Paraspinal weakness and severe axial muscle atrophy
symptoms_not_in_common: Cerebellar ataxia is not typical
Sensorineural hearing loss is not typical in adult-onset disease
Cardiac premature contractions are not a usual adult-onset feature
Mitochondrial ragged-red/oxidative-enzyme-abnormal muscle fibers would not be expected
Maternal-pattern pedigree is not compatible with autosomal recessive inheritance
No respiratory insufficiency or diaphragmatic weakness is reported

data.description: A 2-year-old Korean male was admitted for evaluation and management of left hip pain. Physical examination revealed several palpable lymph nodes in the left inguinal area and an ill-defined heterogeneous mass-like lesion in the left anteromedial muscle. Peripheral blood examination showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.83 × 10^9/L, platelet count 182 × 10^9/L, and 5 atypical lymphocytes per 100 white blood cells. Immunophenotyping of neoplastic cells showed positivity for CD45 (99.0%), CD19 (94.84%), CD10 (27.64%), CD20 (94.24%), HLA-DR (95.70%), surface IgG lambda (96.45%), CD13 (22.46%), and CD117 (22.22%), and negativity for CD34 (0.01%), Tdt (0.64%), myeloperoxidase (0.01%), and various T-cell and myeloid markers.

data.diagnosis: Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia (mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with MYC rearrangement)
data.description: An aggressive mature germinal-center B-cell lymphoma of childhood, commonly associated with MYC rearrangement, often involving lymph nodes, extranodal soft tissue, bone marrow, and peripheral blood. The images show highly proliferative atypical lymphoid cells with basophilic/vacuolated cytoplasm and cytogenetic/FISH findings compatible with a MYC-associated rearrangement.
symptoms_in_common: Age of 2 years, consistent with pediatric Burkitt lymphoma
Atypical circulating lymphoid cells in peripheral blood
Mature monoclonal B-cell phenotype: CD45+, CD19+, CD20+, HLA-DR+, surface IgG lambda+
Partial CD10 expression, compatible with germinal-center B-cell differentiation
Negative TdT and CD34, supporting mature rather than precursor B cells
Cytoplasmic vacuolation in atypical lymphoid cells on the image, characteristic of Burkitt-type cells
Cytogenetic/FISH findings suggestive of a MYC-associated chromosomal rearrangement
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal mass or ileocecal involvement was reported
No jaw or facial mass was reported
No tumor lysis syndrome, markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase, or renal dysfunction was reported
White blood cell count is not markedly elevated despite circulating atypical cells

data.diagnosis: High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rearrangement
data.description: A category of aggressive mature B-cell lymphomas with MYC rearrangement that can resemble Burkitt lymphoma morphologically and immunophenotypically but may have more complex cytogenetic abnormalities or atypical clinical/pathologic features.
symptoms_in_common: Aggressive soft-tissue mass involving the left anteromedial muscle
Strong mature B-cell marker expression including CD19, CD20, CD45, HLA-DR, and surface lambda light-chain restriction
Chromosomal/FISH abnormalities compatible with MYC rearrangement
symptoms_not_in_common: This category is less common than Burkitt lymphoma in a 2-year-old child
No explicit evidence of concurrent BCL2 or BCL6 rearrangement was provided
The vacuolated Burkitt-like morphology and pediatric presentation favor classic Burkitt lymphoma over this broader category

data.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-center B-cell type
data.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma composed of large transformed B cells. It can present as nodal or extranodal soft-tissue disease and may express CD20 and CD10, although classic pediatric Burkitt lymphoma is more strongly favored here.
symptoms_in_common: Hip pain related to local soft-tissue involvement
Mature B-cell immunophenotype with CD19+, CD20+, CD45+, HLA-DR+, and surface immunoglobulin light-chain restriction
Possible germinal-center marker expression with CD10 positivity
symptoms_not_in_common: Very young age is less typical for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Marked cytoplasmic vacuolation of tumor cells is more typical of Burkitt lymphoma
A MYC-associated rearrangement with Burkitt-like morphology more strongly supports Burkitt lymphoma
Peripheral blood atypical lymphoid cells/leukemic involvement is less typical at presentation

data.description: A malignancy of immature B-cell precursors that commonly affects children and may involve bone marrow, blood, lymph nodes, and bone. It is an important differential diagnosis for pediatric lymphoid malignancy but is poorly supported by the mature B-cell phenotype in this case.
symptoms_in_common: Atypical lymphoid cells in peripheral blood
Musculoskeletal pain or soft-tissue involvement can occur in lymphoblastic neoplasms
Expression of B-cell markers CD19 and CD45
symptoms_not_in_common: TdT is negative, whereas B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma is usually TdT positive
CD34 is negative, whereas precursor B-cell neoplasms often express CD34
Strong CD20 expression is more characteristic of mature B cells
Surface IgG lambda restriction indicates mature clonal B cells rather than precursor lymphoblasts
Cytoplasmic vacuolation and MYC-type cytogenetic findings favor Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

data.description: A 12-year-old Malagasy boy consulted for a fever that had been evolving for two months, with a notion of trauma and pain in the right upper quadrant as well as chronic diarrhoea. A parasitological examination of the stool found eggs of Schistosoma mansoni. An ultrasound and a CT scan were then ordered.

data.diagnosis: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni with periportal fibrosis (Symmers fibrosis)
data.description: Chronic intestinal schistosomiasis can cause egg deposition in portal tracts, producing characteristic periportal fibrosis, hepatosplenomegaly, and portal hypertension. Ultrasound and CT commonly show echogenic/thickened periportal tracts and a heterogeneous liver with periportal bands.
symptoms_in_common: Stool examination positive for Schistosoma mansoni eggs
Imaging appearance consistent with periportal fibrosis
Enlarged liver and spleen on CT appearance
symptoms_not_in_common: Two months of persistent fever
History of trauma

data.diagnosis: Portal hypertension secondary to schistosomal periportal fibrosis
data.description: Periportal fibrosis from chronic S. mansoni infection may obstruct portal venous flow while preserving hepatocellular function, causing portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and potentially varices or ascites.
symptoms_in_common: Evidence of chronic Schistosoma mansoni infection
Periportal hepatic changes on ultrasound and CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic diarrhoea is not a direct manifestation of portal hypertension
Persistent fever is not typical unless another infection is present
Recent trauma is not a typical cause

data.diagnosis: Intestinal schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni
data.description: S. mansoni infection involves the mesenteric venous circulation; eggs lodged in the intestinal wall cause chronic inflammatory colitis, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and may progress to hepatosplenic disease.
symptoms_in_common: Schistosoma mansoni eggs identified in stool
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked periportal fibrosis and hepatosplenic imaging abnormalities indicate advanced hepatosplenic involvement rather than isolated intestinal disease
Persistent fever is not a usual feature of chronic intestinal schistosomiasis
History of trauma

data.description: A 44-year-old man presented with 1 hour of severe substernal burning chest pain radiating to the left arm, awakening him from sleep, with nausea and nonbilious, nonbloody vomiting. He reported a 1-month history of intermittent, less intense similar chest pain lasting hours to days, not exertional, with temporary relief from antacids and omeprazole. He denied dyspnea, fever, cough, trauma, leg swelling, immobility, tobacco/alcohol/drug use, and family history of premature coronary disease. Past history was unremarkable, though he recalled being told 12 years earlier that his platelet count was about 600,000/mm³; he also noted intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers and denied bleeding, thrombosis, or neurologic symptoms. On exam, he was afebrile, in distress clutching his chest, with normal vital signs otherwise, regular cardiac rhythm, no JVD or edema, normal lung exam, and a nontender chest and abdomen. Labs showed leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, elevated hemoglobin, and mild hyperglycemia, with troponin 0.08 ng/mL.

data.diagnosis: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (anterior STEMI)
data.description: Acute myocardial infarction due to coronary arterial occlusion, with ECG evidence of marked ST-segment elevation in the anterior precordial leads (especially V3-V5/V6).
symptoms_in_common: Radiation of pain to the left arm
Anterior precordial ST-segment elevation on ECG
symptoms_not_in_common: One-month history of intermittent pain lasting hours to days
Temporary relief of prior episodes with antacids and omeprazole
No traditional coronary risk factors reported
Marked thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, and elevated hemoglobin
Pruritus after hot showers

data.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by increased red blood cell mass and often associated leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, commonly causing aquagenic pruritus and arterial or venous thrombosis.
symptoms_in_common: Acute arterial thrombotic event causing myocardial infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe acute substernal burning chest pain is not a primary presenting symptom unless caused by thrombosis
Radiation of chest pain to the left arm
Nausea and vomiting
No reported headache, dizziness, visual symptoms, erythromelalgia, splenomegaly, or prior thrombosis

data.description: A myeloproliferative neoplasm with persistent excessive platelet production that can cause microvascular symptoms and major arterial thrombosis, including coronary thrombosis and myocardial infarction.
symptoms_in_common: Acute myocardial infarction potentially caused by arterial thrombosis
Leukocytosis can occur in this disorder
Absence of conventional cardiovascular risk factors
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated hemoglobin favors polycythemia vera rather than isolated essential thrombocythemia
Aquagenic pruritus is more characteristic of polycythemia vera
Severe chest pain, left-arm radiation, nausea, and vomiting reflect the infarction rather than essential thrombocythemia itself
No reported erythromelalgia, headache, visual disturbance, or bleeding symptoms

data.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary thrombosis associated with a myeloproliferative neoplasm
data.description: Acute coronary ischemia caused by thrombotic coronary occlusion in the setting of a hypercoagulable myeloproliferative disorder, most likely polycythemia vera in this case.
symptoms_in_common: Aquagenic pruritus suggesting an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm
Lack of typical atherosclerotic risk factors
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior intermittent nonexertional chest pain lasting hours to days
Partial relief of previous pain with antacids and omeprazole
No previous thrombotic history

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

data.description: Newborn girl admitted to the NICU after cardiorespiratory arrest at delivery. Pregnancy was complicated by maternal hepatitis C infection, treated Chlamydia trachomatis infection, gestational hypertension, and prenatal right urinary tract dilatation on serial ultrasounds. Delivery occurred at 40 weeks after prolonged labor for nonreassuring fetal status; amniotic fluid was meconium-stained and the infant was delivered breech. At birth she was limp, apneic, and required 16 minutes of resuscitation with intubation, CPR, epinephrine, and saline boluses before spontaneous circulation returned. Apgar scores were 1, 0, 0, 1, and 3 at 1, 5, 10, 15, and 20 minutes. On NICU arrival she was hypothermic (34.9°C) and mechanically ventilated; therapeutic hypothermia was started.

data.diagnosis: Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with intrathoracic liver herniation
data.description: A congenital defect in the diaphragm allowing abdominal organs, particularly the liver, to enter the thorax, causing lung compression, pulmonary hypoplasia, and severe respiratory failure at birth.
symptoms_in_common: Severe respiratory failure and apnea immediately after birth
Prenatal abnormality detected on serial ultrasound
Chest radiographs showing abnormal thoracic lucency and asymmetric lung appearance
Cross-sectional imaging suggesting diaphragmatic abnormality with abdominal tissue extending into the thorax
Potential pulmonary hypoplasia/compression on the affected side
symptoms_not_in_common: Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Breech delivery
Maternal hepatitis C infection
Previously treated maternal Chlamydia trachomatis infection
Prenatal right urinary tract dilatation

data.description: Abnormal elevation and thinning or paralysis of the diaphragm that permits cephalad displacement of abdominal contents without a true diaphragmatic defect, potentially causing neonatal respiratory distress.
symptoms_in_common: Asymmetric diaphragmatic contour and abnormal lower thoracic appearance on chest radiographs
Possible upward displacement of abdominal contents into the lower chest
Possible compression of adjacent lung tissue
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound cardiorespiratory arrest is less typical than with a large congenital diaphragmatic hernia
Marked intrathoracic herniation of abdominal organs would favor a true hernia rather than eventration
Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Breech delivery
Maternal hepatitis C infection
Prenatal urinary tract dilatation

data.diagnosis: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM), possibly with air trapping
data.description: A developmental cystic malformation of the lung that may appear as a hyperlucent, cystic, or mass-like lesion and can cause respiratory distress through compression of normal lung tissue.
symptoms_in_common: Asymmetric lung lucency on serial chest radiographs
Possible focal hyperinflation or cystic-appearing region in the lower thorax
symptoms_not_in_common: Imaging evidence of diaphragmatic/abdominal content displacement is not typical for isolated CPAM
Profound arrest at delivery is possible but not the usual presentation
Prenatal urinary tract dilatation
Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Maternal hepatitis C infection

data.description: Nonfunctioning congenital lung tissue, usually in a lower lobe, that receives anomalous systemic arterial blood supply from the aorta and may be associated with other thoracoabdominal malformations.
symptoms_in_common: Possible abnormal systemic arterial vessel demonstrated on Doppler ultrasound or contrast imaging
Respiratory distress in the neonatal period
Potential association with congenital diaphragmatic abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: Massive cardiorespiratory arrest at birth is uncommon for isolated sequestration
Diffuse/asymmetric hyperlucent thoracic appearance is less typical than a focal lower-lobe mass
Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Breech delivery
Maternal hepatitis C infection
Prenatal urinary tract dilatation

data.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse; in a ventilated or resuscitated neonate it can rapidly worsen respiratory and cardiovascular status.
symptoms_in_common: Mechanical ventilation and extensive resuscitation, which increase pneumothorax risk
Hyperlucent hemithorax appearance on chest radiographs
Possible compressed lung at the thoracic periphery or base
symptoms_not_in_common: Prenatal thoracoabdominal abnormality would not be explained by pneumothorax
Persistent abnormal diaphragmatic/abdominal anatomy on CT or ultrasound is not typical
Pneumothorax would not explain congenital anomalous vascular findings
Prenatal right urinary tract dilatation
Maternal hepatitis C infection

data.description: 54-year-old man with a history of polysubstance abuse and treatment-naïve hepatitis C presented with altered mental status. Family history included a sister with renal failure of unknown cause requiring dialysis at age 45. On examination he was afebrile, drowsy, and hypertensive (172/110 mmHg), with jugular venous distension and basal crackles.
