Laboratory studies showed severe renal dysfunction (creatinine 16.0 mg/dL, BUN 99 mg/dL), mild anemia, elevated LDH, proteinuria, and rare schistocytes on blood film; urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 1.9. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine and metabolites. Complement C3 was low with normal C4, and low C3 persisted during hospitalization. Renal ultrasound showed echogenic kidneys measuring 9.8 cm and 10.3 cm.

data.diagnosis: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, aHUS)
data.description: A complement-dysregulation disorder causing endothelial injury, arteriolar and glomerular thrombosis, hemolysis, severe hypertension, and acute kidney injury. The biopsy images show thrombotic microangiopathy with concentric intimal thickening ('onion-skin' arteriolopathy).
symptoms_in_common: Severe acute kidney dysfunction with creatinine 16.0 mg/dL and BUN 99 mg/dL
Rare schistocytes on peripheral blood film
Persistently low C3 with normal C4, suggesting alternative-complement-pathway activation
Family history of unexplained renal failure requiring dialysis
Renal biopsy appearance consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive cocaine toxicology, which may instead represent a trigger or an alternative cause of thrombotic microangiopathy
Chronic hepatitis C infection
Small echogenic kidneys, which suggest substantial chronic kidney disease in addition to the acute presentation

data.description: Severe hypertension can cause endothelial damage, fibrinoid vascular injury, microangiopathic hemolysis, and rapidly progressive kidney failure. Renal pathology commonly shows marked arteriolar intimal thickening with onion-skin lesions, as seen in the images.
symptoms_in_common: Altered mental status, compatible with hypertensive encephalopathy or uremia
Jugular venous distension and basal crackles consistent with volume overload from renal failure
Mild anemia, elevated LDH, and schistocytes compatible with microangiopathic hemolysis
Biopsy findings consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent isolated low C3 is not typical of hypertension alone and raises concern for underlying complement-mediated disease
Family history of renal failure at a relatively young age is not typical of isolated essential hypertension
Cocaine exposure may be a precipitating contributor rather than malignant hypertension alone

data.diagnosis: Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangiopathy and malignant hypertension
data.description: Cocaine can cause intense vasoconstriction, severe hypertension, endothelial injury, platelet activation, and thrombotic microangiopathy, resulting in acute kidney injury and hemolysis.
symptoms_in_common: Urine toxicology positive for cocaine and metabolites
Renal biopsy findings of thrombotic microangiopathy
Pulmonary congestion and volume overload findings
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistently low C3 with normal C4 is not a usual isolated feature of cocaine toxicity
Family history of unexplained dialysis-dependent renal failure suggests a possible inherited complement abnormality
Small echogenic kidneys suggest pre-existing chronic kidney disease rather than a purely acute cocaine-induced process

data.diagnosis: Hepatitis C-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (often cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis)
data.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, often with low complement levels, proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension, and progressive renal impairment.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal C4 is less typical because hepatitis C cryoglobulinemic disease often causes marked C4 reduction
Severe microangiopathic features including elevated LDH and schistocytes are not typical
The renal biopsy images show thrombotic microangiopathy with onion-skin arteriolar lesions rather than a classic immune-complex membranoproliferative pattern
Abrupt extreme renal failure and malignant hypertension are less characteristic as the primary presentation

data.description: 44-year-old Chinese woman with 7 weeks of progressively worsening nausea and vomiting with 13 kg weight loss. She denied abdominal pain, distension, and diarrhea. Symptoms did not improve after 3 weeks of treatment with antidepressants, prokinetics, and anti-emetics. Eight days after admission, she developed metabolic alkalosis, acute respiratory failure, and neurological deficits. Examination showed right-sided limb paralysis, horizontal nystagmus, absent pharyngeal reflex, decreased tendon reflexes on the right, and bilateral Babinski signs. Past workup including gastroscopy and abdominal CT was normal. Laboratory tests showed normal liver, kidney, thyroid, autoimmune, and glucose studies; serum AQP4-IgG was negative, but cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG was positive.

data.diagnosis: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system, usually associated with aquaporin-4 (AQP4) antibodies. Involvement of the dorsal medulla/area postrema can cause otherwise unexplained persistent nausea, vomiting, and hiccups. The sagittal MRI images are consistent with a lesion in the dorsal medulla near the area postrema.
symptoms_in_common: Intractable progressive nausea and vomiting for 7 weeks
Marked weight loss due to persistent vomiting
Normal gastrointestinal investigations despite severe vomiting
Failure to respond to prokinetics and anti-emetics
Brainstem neurological signs including horizontal nystagmus and absent pharyngeal reflex
Right-sided limb paralysis and decreased right-sided tendon reflexes
Bilateral Babinski signs indicating central nervous system involvement
Acute respiratory failure, compatible with severe medullary/brainstem involvement
MRI evidence of a dorsal medullary/area postrema-region lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: Serum AQP4-IgG negativity, although CSF positivity can still support the diagnosis
Metabolic alkalosis is a secondary consequence of prolonged vomiting rather than a primary NMOSD manifestation

data.diagnosis: Area postrema syndrome due to NMOSD
data.description: Area postrema syndrome is a core clinical manifestation of NMOSD caused by inflammatory lesions in the area postrema of the dorsal medulla. It presents with otherwise unexplained persistent nausea, vomiting, and/or hiccups and may precede other neurological deficits.
symptoms_in_common: No abdominal pain, distension, or diarrhea suggesting a non-gastrointestinal cause
Poor response to conventional gastrointestinal and anti-emetic treatment
Dorsal medullary lesion on MRI in the expected area postrema location
symptoms_not_in_common: Right-sided paralysis and bilateral Babinski signs are not required for isolated area postrema syndrome, but may occur when adjacent brainstem or corticospinal tracts are involved
Acute respiratory failure is uncommon in isolated area postrema syndrome and suggests more extensive medullary involvement
Metabolic alkalosis is secondary to recurrent vomiting rather than a defining neurological feature

data.diagnosis: Brainstem encephalitis/demyelinating lesion involving the medulla
data.description: Inflammation or demyelination of the brainstem can produce vomiting, nystagmus, bulbar dysfunction, long-tract signs, weakness, and respiratory compromise. In this case, the AQP4-IgG-positive status and area postrema lesion make NMOSD the most likely specific cause.
symptoms_in_common: Nausea and vomiting from medullary involvement
Absent pharyngeal reflex indicating bulbar dysfunction
Decreased tendon reflexes on the right
Acute respiratory failure due to brainstem involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe prolonged vomiting as the initial dominant symptom is more characteristic of area postrema involvement than many other forms of brainstem encephalitis
CSF AQP4-IgG positivity specifically favors NMOSD over nonspecific infectious or autoimmune brainstem encephalitis
Normal autoimmune testing outside of AQP4 testing is less supportive of some alternative autoimmune encephalitides

data.description:
47-year-old male with 2-month history of fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and malaise. History of inguinal hernia repair surgery 10 years ago and cardiac disease. On admission, body temperature was 37.3°C. Physical examination revealed aortic valve diastolic murmurs at the precordium. --- Imagen documental 1: 01.jpg --- # Antibiotics # Minimal inhibitory concentrations (ug/ml)
Ampicillin 1.5
Penicillin 0.5
Cefazolin > 256
Cefuroxime > 256
Ceftriaxone > 256
Meropenem 16
Imipenem 1
Vancomycin > 256
Levofloxacin 1

data.diagnosis: Lactobacillus infective endocarditis of the aortic valve
data.description: Subacute bacterial endocarditis caused by Lactobacillus species, an uncommon opportunistic Gram-positive bacillus. Lactobacilli may show intrinsic high-level vancomycin resistance and poor susceptibility to cephalosporins; infection can cause destructive native-valve disease and severe aortic regurgitation.
symptoms_in_common: Aortic diastolic murmur, consistent with aortic regurgitation
Echocardiographic evidence of major aortic-valve/aortic-root structural abnormality and regurgitant flow
Antibiotic profile with susceptibility to penicillin/ampicillin and imipenem but marked resistance to vancomycin and cephalosporins
symptoms_not_in_common: Only low-grade temperature at admission (37.3 degrees C), although indolent endocarditis can have intermittent or low-grade fever

data.description: A rare Gram-positive bacillary infection that can cause severe, often subacute native-valve endocarditis, frequently involving the aortic valve. The organism is characteristically resistant to vancomycin and generally susceptible to penicillin-class agents.
symptoms_in_common: Echocardiographic findings compatible with destructive valvular infection and aortic regurgitation
Vancomycin resistance with penicillin and ampicillin susceptibility
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported occupational or animal exposure, such as contact with fish, swine, poultry, or meat
No reported localized erysipeloid skin lesion at the presumed inoculation site

data.diagnosis: Enterococcus faecalis native aortic-valve infective endocarditis
data.description: A common cause of subacute infective endocarditis, particularly in patients with underlying cardiac disease. It can involve the aortic valve and produce progressive valvular destruction and aortic regurgitation.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute fever over weeks to months
Constitutional symptoms including malaise, headache, myalgia, and arthralgia
New or worsening aortic diastolic murmur
Echocardiographic abnormalities suggestive of infective endocarditis with aortic regurgitation
Potential susceptibility to ampicillin and penicillin
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked high-level vancomycin resistance is less typical for many Enterococcus faecalis isolates
Extreme resistance to multiple cephalosporins is expected intrinsically in enterococci but does not specifically identify Enterococcus
No reported genitourinary, gastrointestinal, biliary, or recent healthcare-associated source

data.description: 51-year-old man undergoing venesection for haemochromatosis. During procedure, experienced sudden gurgling sensation up his arm, followed by severe central crushing chest pain with radiation to jaw and left arm, severe dyspnoea, and left sided hemiparesis and dysphasia. On arrival to hospital: hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), left hemiplegia (resolved within 15 minutes). Initial ECG showed T-wave inversion inferiorly. Troponin I was raised at 0.14 μg/L (ref 0-0.08 μg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study showed right-to-left shunting during normal respiration and Valsalva. Baseline right heart pressures were normal. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed patent foramen ovale with passage of bubbles.

data.diagnosis: Venous air embolism with paradoxical systemic embolization through a patent foramen ovale
data.description: Entry of air into the venous circulation during venesection, with passage from the right to left atrium through a patent foramen ovale, allowing air emboli to reach the coronary and cerebral arterial circulations.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden gurgling sensation in the arm during venesection
Abrupt severe central crushing chest pain
Pain radiating to the jaw and left arm
Hypoxia with oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
Documented right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale
symptoms_not_in_common: None of the major presenting features are inconsistent; the transient neurologic deficit and myocardial injury are explained by paradoxical embolization

data.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow by embolic material. The CT pulmonary angiographic image shows an intraluminal filling defect in a left pulmonary arterial branch, compatible with pulmonary embolism; in this clinical context, embolic air may have contributed.
symptoms_in_common: CT pulmonary angiographic filling defect in a left pulmonary arterial branch
Troponin elevation, which can occur with acute right-heart strain
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient left hemiplegia and dysphasia are not typical of an isolated pulmonary embolism
Chest pain radiating to the jaw and left arm is more suggestive of myocardial ischemia than pulmonary embolism
Normal baseline right-heart pressures do not suggest chronic pulmonary hypertension
The immediate onset during venesection and arm gurgling sensation are more suggestive of iatrogenic air entry than conventional thromboembolism

data.diagnosis: Paradoxical embolic transient ischemic attack or acute ischemic stroke
data.description: A transient cerebral arterial occlusion caused by embolic material crossing a right-to-left intracardiac shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale. Air emboli or thromboemboli can produce this mechanism.
symptoms_in_common: Abrupt onset during a procedure with potential venous air entry
Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunting
Resolution of neurologic deficits within 15 minutes, consistent with a transient ischemic attack
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe dyspnoea and hypoxia are not typical primary manifestations of an isolated cerebral transient ischemic attack
Crushing chest pain with jaw and left-arm radiation is not typical of isolated stroke or transient ischemic attack
Raised troponin and inferior ECG T-wave inversion suggest concurrent cardiac involvement

data.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome due to paradoxical coronary air embolism
data.description: Acute myocardial ischemia caused by embolic obstruction of a coronary artery, potentially from air entering the venous system and crossing a patent foramen ovale into the systemic arterial circulation.
symptoms_in_common: Radiation of pain to the jaw and left arm
Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunting, providing a route for paradoxical coronary embolization
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient left hemiplegia and dysphasia are not typical of isolated acute coronary syndrome
Marked hypoxia and severe dyspnoea suggest simultaneous pulmonary vascular involvement
The arm gurgling sensation is not typical of spontaneous atherosclerotic acute coronary syndrome

data.description: 41-year-old right-handed man with neurologic history dating to his early twenties when he presented with seizures. In 2009, he developed headaches. Initial biopsy/resection pathology showed PXA (WHO grade 2) with BRAF V600E mutation confirmed by PCR testing.

data.diagnosis: Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), WHO grade 2, BRAF V600E-mutant
data.description: A rare, usually superficial cerebral astrocytic tumor that often arises in the temporal lobe of younger patients and commonly presents with longstanding seizures. BRAF V600E mutation is frequent. The MRI appearance may include a cortical or superficial temporal lesion with T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and variable enhancement.

data.diagnosis: Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (anaplastic PXA, WHO grade 3)
data.description: A higher-grade or transformed form of PXA characterized by increased mitotic activity and more aggressive behavior. It may develop after an initially grade 2 PXA and can show enlarging or newly enhancing tumor on follow-up MRI. BRAF V600E mutations are also common.
symptoms_in_common: Enhancing temporal brain lesion on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented rapid neurologic decline, focal neurologic deficit, or pathology demonstrating anaplastic features

data.description: A typically low-grade mixed neuronal-glial tumor that often occurs in the temporal lobe and causes chronic focal seizures. Some gangliogliomas harbor BRAF V600E mutations and may have cystic, solid, or variably enhancing MRI appearances.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior tissue diagnosis favored pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma rather than a mixed neuronal-glial tumor

data.description: A rare aggressive glioblastoma subtype that can occur in younger patients, often involves the temporal lobe, and may carry a BRAF V600E mutation. Imaging commonly shows an enhancing lesion with surrounding FLAIR abnormality and mass effect.
symptoms_in_common: BRAF V600E mutation can occur in this tumor type
symptoms_not_in_common: Very long clinical course dating to the early twenties is less typical of glioblastoma
Prior pathology showed WHO grade 2 PXA rather than glioblastoma
No reported rapid progression, marked neurologic deficits, or extensive mass effect

data.description: 32-year-old man with a 10-week history of violaceous rash and progressive muscle weakness. The rash began on the eyelids, elbows, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and knees, followed one week later by intense generalized myalgias and worsening weakness with difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs. Exam showed heliotrope rash, periungual edema/erythema, erythematous papules on the fingertips and extensor surfaces of the fingers, elbows, and knees, pitting edema of the arms and legs, diminished breath sounds at both lung bases, and severe proximal weakness with inability to lift arms, legs, or head against gravity; grip and ankle strength were mildly reduced. Sensation, reflexes, muscle tone, and bulk were normal. Past history included meniscal repair 10 years earlier; he did not smoke or use illicit drugs.
An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by distinctive cutaneous findings and symmetric proximal muscle weakness due to muscle inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Violaceous heliotrope rash on the eyelids
Papules over the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints consistent with Gottron papules
Erythematous lesions on extensor surfaces of the fingers, elbows, and knees
Progressive severe symmetric proximal muscle weakness
Difficulty rising from a squat, climbing stairs, and walking
Inability to lift the arms, legs, or head against gravity
Preserved sensation, reflexes, muscle tone, and muscle bulk
Pitting edema, which can occur in severe edematous dermatomyositis
Diminished breath sounds at both lung bases, potentially reflecting associated interstitial lung disease or pleural fluid
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild reduction in grip and ankle strength is less prominent than the typical proximal-predominant pattern

data.description: A dermatomyositis subtype often associated with painful ulcerative or violaceous skin lesions, periungual changes, arthritis, and a high risk of rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease; muscle disease can range from absent to severe.
symptoms_in_common: Gottron-like papules over finger joints and extensor surfaces
Possible pulmonary involvement suggested by diminished breath sounds at the lung bases
Myalgias and muscle weakness can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe classic proximal muscle weakness is less typical because anti-MDA5 disease is often clinically amyopathic or has relatively mild muscle involvement
No reported skin ulceration, palmar papules, arthritis, fever, or respiratory symptoms

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy syndrome associated with myositis, interstitial lung disease, inflammatory arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and mechanic's hands; it may overlap with dermatomyositis.
symptoms_in_common: Possible interstitial lung involvement suggested by diminished breath sounds at both lung bases
Periungual and hand skin abnormalities can occur in overlap disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash and classic Gottron papules are more characteristic of dermatomyositis than antisynthetase syndrome
No reported mechanic's hands
No reported inflammatory arthritis
No reported Raynaud phenomenon
No reported fever or dyspnea

data.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy, sometimes associated with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies, that causes rapidly progressive symmetric proximal weakness and markedly elevated muscle enzymes but usually has little or no rash.
symptoms_in_common: Rapidly progressive severe proximal muscle weakness
Difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a squat, and lifting the limbs
Normal sensation and reflexes despite profound weakness
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash is not typical
Gottron papules over the finger joints, elbows, and knees are not typical
Periungual edema and erythema are not typical
Fingertip papules are not typical
Pitting peripheral edema is not a usual feature

data.description: An inflammatory myopathy causing subacute symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes, without the characteristic skin manifestations of dermatomyositis.
symptoms_in_common: Difficulty walking, climbing stairs, and rising from a squat
Difficulty lifting the head and extremities against gravity
Normal sensation and generally preserved reflexes
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash is not typical
Gottron papules and extensor-surface papules are not typical
Periungual edema and erythema are not typical
Fingertip lesions are not typical
Pitting edema is uncommon

data.description: 59-year-old woman with a longstanding history of epilepsy with complex partial seizures, treated with phenytoin for more than 20 years, presented with a 3-year history of progressive muscle weakness and generalized bone and muscle pain, worsening proximal muscle pain and weakness, and increasing bone pain with significant limitation in daily activities. Physical examination showed normal renal and liver function, and radiographs revealed bilateral Looser’s zones in the femoral neck.

Metabolic bone disease caused by long-term phenytoin use, often through accelerated vitamin D metabolism leading to vitamin D deficiency, impaired mineralization of osteoid, bone pain, muscle weakness, and insufficiency fractures.
symptoms_in_common: More than 20 years of phenytoin treatment
Multifocal increased skeletal uptake on bone scintigraphy consistent with insufficiency fractures/pseudofractures
symptoms_not_in_common: Longstanding complex partial epilepsy itself is not a manifestation of osteomalacia

data.description: A disorder of defective bone mineralization caused by inadequate vitamin D availability, resulting in hypocalcemia or hypophosphatemia, diffuse bone pain, proximal myopathy, and Looser's zones.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral Looser's zones in the femoral neck
Imaging pattern compatible with multiple insufficiency fractures or pseudofractures
Normal renal and liver function does not exclude nutritional or medication-related vitamin D deficiency
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented dietary deficiency, malabsorption, low sunlight exposure, or measured low vitamin D level
Epilepsy is not typically caused by vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia

data.description: Bone loss and impaired mineralization associated with enzyme-inducing antiseizure medications such as phenytoin; the spectrum includes vitamin D deficiency, osteomalacia, osteoporosis, and fragility fractures.
symptoms_in_common: Long-term exposure to phenytoin, an enzyme-inducing antiseizure medication
Multifocal skeletal tracer uptake suggesting stress or insufficiency injuries
Functional decline due to pain and weakness
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented low bone mineral density measurement
No documented biochemical calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone, or vitamin D abnormalities

data.description: Reduced bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration causing fragility or insufficiency fractures, which can produce focal or multifocal pain and increased uptake on bone scans.
symptoms_in_common: Bone scan findings that may reflect multifocal insufficiency fractures
Reduced ability to perform daily activities
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent generalized muscle pain and proximal muscle weakness are more characteristic of osteomalacia than uncomplicated osteoporosis
Looser's zones are classically associated with osteomalacia rather than primary osteoporosis
Long-term phenytoin exposure strongly favors medication-related osteomalacia/metabolic bone disease

data.description: A previously healthy 50-year-old man presented with acute-onset dysarthria and was found to be febrile with respiratory distress and lethargy. He performed poorly in the right hand alternating movement test. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg and heart rate of 116 beats per minute. The apex beat was located in the sixth intercostal space, 1.5 cm outside the midclavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur that was most prominent at the apex. Laboratory findings showed normal troponin T, creatine kinase (CK), and CK-myoglobin (CK-MB) levels, but elevated N-terminal-pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) levels at 3277 pg/ml. The leukocyte count was 10,620/mm³ with neutrophils at 10,350/mm³, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Blood culture was positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischemia.

data.diagnosis: Group A streptococcal native mitral-valve infective endocarditis
data.description: Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, here most consistent with a large vegetation on the mitral valve caused by group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus. The echocardiographic image shows a valvular mass compatible with vegetation.
symptoms_in_common: Positive blood culture for group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus
New grade 4/6 systolic murmur maximal at the apex
Evidence of mitral-valve vegetation on echocardiography
Systemic embolic complication causing cerebral infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute respiratory distress is not a universal presenting feature, although it may occur with severe mitral regurgitation or heart failure
Normal leukocyte count is not present; the patient instead has mild leukocytosis with marked neutrophilia

data.diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke due to septic embolism
data.description: An acute cerebral infarction caused by embolization of infected material from a left-sided cardiac valve vegetation. The brain MRI image shows an acute infarct in the left cerebral hemisphere, consistent with the patient's focal neurologic deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Poor right-hand alternating movements, consistent with contralateral hemispheric dysfunction
Brain MRI evidence of an acute left cerebral infarction
Documented mitral-valve infective endocarditis, a source of septic emboli
symptoms_not_in_common: Fever and positive streptococcal blood cultures are not typical of a noninfectious thromboembolic stroke but support septic embolic stroke
Apical systolic murmur is not caused by the cerebral infarct itself
Respiratory distress is not a typical direct manifestation of ischemic stroke

data.diagnosis: Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to infective endocarditis
data.description: Mitral-valve infection can damage leaflets or chordae and produce severe mitral regurgitation. The apical pansystolic murmur, displaced apex beat, elevated NT-pro-BNP, respiratory distress, and color Doppler regurgitant jet support significant mitral regurgitation.
symptoms_in_common: Grade 4/6 systolic murmur loudest at the apex
Displaced apex beat in the sixth intercostal space lateral to the midclavicular line
Color Doppler echocardiographic evidence of a substantial mitral regurgitation jet
Mitral-valve vegetation capable of causing valvular destruction
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute dysarthria and impaired right-hand coordination are not typical consequences of mitral regurgitation alone
Fever, neutrophilia, and positive blood cultures indicate the underlying infective endocarditis rather than isolated mitral regurgitation
Normal troponin T and CK-MB do not specifically support or exclude mitral regurgitation

data.diagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure due to infective mitral-valve disease
data.description: Acute severe mitral regurgitation from endocarditis can elevate cardiac filling pressures and cause congestive heart failure. The elevated NT-pro-BNP, dyspnea/respiratory distress, tachycardia, and displaced apex beat are compatible with this complication.
symptoms_in_common: Displaced apex beat suggesting cardiac enlargement or volume overload
Severe apical systolic murmur due to mitral regurgitation
Normal cardiac injury markers, making acute myocardial infarction less likely as the cause of cardiac decompensation
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute dysarthria and right-hand incoordination are not typical manifestations of heart failure
Positive group A streptococcal blood cultures and elevated inflammatory markers point to infective endocarditis as the precipitating condition rather than primary heart failure
Focal brain infarction is not caused by heart failure alone, although it may occur from embolism related to the underlying endocarditis

data.description: 3.5-year-old male with proteinuria, hematuria, and glycosuria noted in the early neonatal period; UTI at 12 months; at 3 years developed bronchopneumonia with elevated creatinine. Persistent proteinuria, glycosuria, and hematuria with reduced eGFR, elevated serum creatinine, uric acid, urea, total cholesterol, and triglycerides; normal CBC, blood glucose, albumin, thyroid and liver tests. Renal ultrasound showed increased cortical echogenicity and decreased corticomedullary differentiation. Physical findings included dolichocephaly, frontal bossing, broad nasal bridge, long/flat philtrum, narrow upper lip, low-set/protruding ears, narrow chest, pectus excavatum, rhizomelic limb shortening, short humeri/fibulae, brachydactyly, overlapping toes, joint laxity, sparse hair, small teeth, thin/short nails, and protuberant abdomen. Ophthalmologic findings: hyperopia, strabismus, and nystagmus. Development and intelligence were reported as normal.

A rare autosomal-recessive ciliopathy characterized by cranial shape abnormalities, distinctive facial appearance, ectodermal abnormalities of hair, teeth and nails, skeletal dysplasia with a narrow thorax and short limbs, and progressive renal disease, often resembling nephronophthisis or tubulointerstitial nephropathy.
symptoms_in_common: Early-onset chronic kidney disease with reduced eGFR and elevated creatinine, urea and uric acid
Increased renal cortical echogenicity and poor corticomedullary differentiation
Broad nasal bridge, long flat philtrum and narrow upper lip
Small teeth and thin short nails
Rhizomelic limb shortening and short humeri/fibulae
symptoms_not_in_common: Hematuria is less characteristic than the usual tubulointerstitial/nephronophthisis-like urinary findings
Renal abnormalities beginning in the early neonatal period are earlier than in many reported cases
Normal development and intelligence, although possible, are not universal

data.description: A rare autosomal-recessive disorder caused by SMARCAL1 variants, characterized by steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome or progressive renal failure, disproportionate short stature from skeletal dysplasia, facial differences and variable immune deficiency with recurrent infections.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated serum creatinine, urea and reduced eGFR
Short limbs and disproportionate skeletal appearance
Facial dysmorphism including frontal prominence and low-set ears
symptoms_not_in_common: Glycosuria is not a typical hallmark
Hematuria is not a dominant feature
Sparse hair, abnormal teeth and thin short nails are not typical
Brachydactyly, overlapping toes and marked joint laxity are not classic findings
Normal CBC and no documented immune deficiency
No reported spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia or severe growth failure

data.description: An X-linked disorder caused by OCRL variants that produces proximal renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome), ocular abnormalities and neurodevelopmental impairment; affected boys may develop chronic kidney disease.
symptoms_in_common: Early-onset glycosuria suggesting proximal tubular dysfunction
Hypothetically compatible with rickets-like skeletal changes or short stature from renal tubular disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Congenital cataracts, a major feature of Lowe syndrome, were not reported
Normal development and intelligence are atypical because developmental delay is common
Hematuria is not typical
Dolichocephaly, narrow thorax, ectodermal abnormalities of hair/teeth/nails and brachydactyly are not characteristic
Nystagmus without reported cataracts is less typical
No reported hypotonia, metabolic acidosis, phosphaturia or aminoaciduria

data.description: A ciliopathy characterized by nephronophthisis-related kidney disease, skeletal dysplasia with cone-shaped epiphyses and shortened phalanges, and retinal dystrophy; some individuals have cerebellar or hepatic involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive chronic kidney disease with abnormal renal ultrasound
Facial dysmorphism can occur in ciliopathy-associated skeletal dysplasias
symptoms_not_in_common: Retinal dystrophy, night blindness or visual loss was not reported
Glycosuria and neonatal onset of renal findings are not typical defining features
Hematuria is not a usual major manifestation
Sparse hair, small teeth and thin short nails are not typical
No documented cone-shaped epiphyses or phalangeal radiographic abnormalities

data.description: A severe congenital nephrotic syndrome due to LAMB2 variants, classically associated with diffuse mesangial sclerosis, early renal failure and characteristic ocular abnormalities such as microcoria; neurologic involvement may occur.
symptoms_in_common: Proteinuria recognized in the neonatal period
Progressive renal impairment with elevated creatinine and reduced eGFR
Hyperlipidemia, which can accompany heavy urinary protein loss
Ocular abnormalities including strabismus and nystagmus
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal serum albumin is atypical for classic congenital nephrotic syndrome
Glycosuria is not typical
Hematuria is not a central feature
Microcoria was not reported
Skeletal dysplasia, narrow chest, brachydactyly and overlapping toes are not typical
Sparse hair, abnormal teeth and nail abnormalities are not typical
Normal development is more compatible with milder forms but not classic severe Pierson syndrome

data.description: A 58-year-old man presented with a six-week history of muscle weakness, dysphagia, and a symmetrical widespread rash on the face, torso, and limbs. Laboratory testing revealed elevated creatine kinase of 7070 u/L (reference range 30-175). An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed and showed abnormal findings, and a PET CT scan was arranged.

An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle inflammation and distinctive cutaneous lesions, including Gottron papules over the finger joints. It can cause severe creatine kinase elevation and dysphagia.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia due to pharyngeal and esophageal muscle involvement
Violaceous/scaly papules over the knuckles consistent with Gottron papules in the hand image
Rash involving the face, torso, and limbs
symptoms_not_in_common: Abnormal oesophagogastroduodenoscopy findings suggesting a possible structural gastrointestinal lesion
Focal fluorodeoxyglucose-avid lesion on PET-CT in the thoracic esophageal/mediastinal region, which raises concern for an associated malignancy rather than uncomplicated dermatomyositis

data.description: Dermatomyositis may occur as a paraneoplastic autoimmune syndrome, particularly in older adults. The classic skin findings and inflammatory myopathy can precede or accompany detection of an internal malignancy.
symptoms_in_common: Gottron papules over the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints
Symmetrical erythematous rash on the face, trunk, and limbs
PET-CT focal avid abnormality suspicious for an underlying malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported weight loss
No reported anorexia
No reported gastrointestinal bleeding
No reported lymphadenopathy

data.diagnosis: Esophageal carcinoma, potentially associated with paraneoplastic dermatomyositis
data.description: Esophageal cancer is a malignant tumor of the esophagus that commonly presents with progressive dysphagia. In this context, an abnormal endoscopy and focal PET uptake raise suspicion for an esophageal malignancy, which could be associated with paraneoplastic dermatomyositis.
symptoms_in_common: Focal increased tracer uptake in the thoracic esophageal/mediastinal region on PET-CT
Age and sex consistent with a higher-risk demographic for esophageal malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Symmetrical scaly rash and Gottron papules are not typical direct manifestations of esophageal carcinoma
Severe muscle weakness is not typical of localized esophageal carcinoma
Marked creatine kinase elevation is not typical of esophageal carcinoma except through associated inflammatory myopathy/paraneoplastic dermatomyositis
No reported weight loss, odynophagia, anemia, or gastrointestinal bleeding

data.description: An 8-year-old boy presented to his general practitioner with limping and complaints of occasional leg pain. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On physical examination, he walked with a limp and demonstrated painful, reduced internal rotation and abduction of his right hip. Plain radiographs were obtained to evaluate his symptoms.

Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, causing sclerosis, fragmentation, flattening, and possible deformity of the femoral head. The radiographs show changes consistent with femoral-head collapse/fragmentation on the symptomatic side.
symptoms_in_common: Radiographic femoral-head irregularity, sclerosis, flattening, and fragmentation
symptoms_not_in_common: No major symptoms are atypical; occasional mild pain can occur in Perthes disease

data.description: Displacement of the femoral-head epiphysis relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, usually occurring in older children or adolescents and often associated with obesity.
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 8 years, which is younger than the usual age group
Otherwise healthy presentation without typical adolescent growth-related risk factors
Radiographs show femoral-head fragmentation/flattening rather than the typical epiphyseal slip

data.description: A self-limited inflammatory hip effusion, commonly following a viral illness, that causes acute hip pain and a limp in children.
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms appear persistent enough to prompt radiography rather than abruptly transient
Marked loss of internal rotation and abduction
Radiographic femoral-head sclerosis, fragmentation, and flattening are not typical of transient synovitis
No preceding viral illness is described

data.description: A bacterial infection within the hip joint that usually causes acute severe pain, inability to bear weight, fever, systemic illness, and rapidly progressive joint damage if untreated.
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile
Otherwise healthy and not systemically unwell
Occasional rather than severe acute pain
No reported inability to bear weight
Radiographic femoral-head fragmentation and remodeling favor chronic avascular necrosis rather than acute septic arthritis

data.description: A 62-year-old fit and well Romanian man presented with a two-week history of worsening acute localized pain in the upper abdomen and vomiting. His surgical history included an open appendectomy as a child and laparoscopic cholecystectomy 20 years ago. On presentation, he had fever (39°C) and tachycardia (104 beats/min), with blood pressure of 125/73 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness, worse in the right upper quadrant, with localized guarding in the right upper quadrant. Blood tests showed a raised white cell count of 16 × 10⁹/L (reference range 4-10 × 10⁹/L) and a C reactive protein concentration of 277 mg/L (reference value <9 mg/L). A frontal projection erect chest radiograph was initially reported as showing pneumoperitoneum, but showed a normal bowel gas pattern under the left hemidiaphragm.

A bacterial collection of pus within the liver, sometimes containing gas-producing organisms. The imaging shows a large gas-containing fluid collection in the right hepatic lobe, explaining the apparent subdiaphragmatic free air on chest radiography.
symptoms_in_common: Right upper quadrant and upper abdominal pain
Right upper quadrant guarding and tenderness
symptoms_not_in_common: None prominent; generalized abdominal tenderness may suggest severe inflammation or extension beyond the liver

data.description: A liver abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica, typically producing fever and right upper quadrant pain and most often involving the right lobe of the liver.
symptoms_in_common: Large right-lobe liver collection on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Gas within the liver collection is unusual unless there is secondary bacterial infection
Marked tachycardia and severe systemic inflammatory response are more suggestive of pyogenic infection
No reported diarrhoea or dysentery
No reported travel or exposure history suggestive of amoebiasis

data.description: Perforation of a gastric or duodenal ulcer releases air and gastrointestinal contents into the peritoneal cavity, causing acute peritonitis and free subdiaphragmatic air.
symptoms_in_common: Initial chest radiograph concern for air beneath the right hemidiaphragm
symptoms_not_in_common: The CT images show gas within a large hepatic collection rather than free intraperitoneal air
Two weeks of gradually worsening symptoms is less typical of an untreated perforated ulcer
No reported history of peptic ulcer disease, dyspepsia, melena, or hematemesis

data.description: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree, usually due to biliary obstruction, causing fever, abdominal pain, and systemic inflammation; it can occasionally lead to hepatic abscess formation.
symptoms_in_common: Right upper quadrant pain and tenderness
Possible hepatic abscess as a complication
symptoms_not_in_common: No jaundice is reported
No abnormal liver function tests or biliary dilatation are reported
Prior cholecystectomy reduces, but does not eliminate, gallstone-related biliary obstruction
A large gas-containing liver abscess is more directly explanatory than uncomplicated cholangitis

data.description: A 1-year and 4-month-old girl was admitted for evaluation of psychomotor retardation and an operation for exotropia. She was born at term (gestational age: 40 weeks) by cesarean delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, and was the first child of healthy, unrelated parents. The family history was unremarkable. On admission, she presented with a characteristic high-pitched cry and microcephaly. She showed delayed motor functions and crawling, was able to sit unassisted but unable to stand, with developmental characteristics lagging behind for normal chronologic age. On neurologic examination, she had left leg hypotonia, with normal tendon reflexes and normal cranial nerve signs. When she was 6 months old, ventricular septal defect was detected by echocardiography. Chromosome analysis revealed 46,XX,del (5) (p15.2) one month after delivery.

A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically associated with a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, characteristic facial features, and variable congenital heart and brain abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Marked psychomotor and motor developmental delay
Unable to stand independently at 16 months
MRI findings compatible with neurodevelopmental brain abnormalities, including apparent brainstem/pons hypoplasia and delayed white-matter maturation
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal tendon reflexes are not a defining feature, although they can be normal
Unilateral left-leg hypotonia is less typical than generalized hypotonia

data.description: A chromosomal deletion syndrome caused by loss of material from chromosome 4p. It causes growth and developmental delay, microcephaly, hypotonia, congenital heart defects, seizures, and characteristic craniofacial features.
symptoms_in_common: Congenital heart defect including ventricular septal defect
Possible structural brain-development abnormalities on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Chromosome testing demonstrates a 5p deletion rather than a 4p deletion
High-pitched cat-like cry is much more characteristic of cri-du-chat syndrome
No seizures reported
No typical 'Greek warrior helmet' facial appearance described
No prenatal or postnatal growth restriction described

data.description: A genetic microdeletion disorder with variable developmental delay, hypotonia, congenital heart defects, palatal abnormalities, immune dysfunction, and characteristic facial features.
symptoms_in_common: Congenital heart disease with ventricular septal defect
symptoms_not_in_common: The demonstrated chromosomal abnormality is del(5p15.2), not a 22q11.2 deletion
High-pitched cat-like cry is not typical
Microcephaly is less characteristic
No palatal anomaly, feeding difficulty, recurrent infections, hypocalcemia, or immune deficiency reported

data.description: An X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder, usually caused by pathogenic MECP2 variants, characterized by apparently normal early development followed by developmental regression, loss of purposeful hand use, stereotypic hand movements, impaired gait, and acquired microcephaly.
symptoms_in_common: Hypotonia and delayed ability to stand or walk
symptoms_not_in_common: A confirmed 5p chromosomal deletion provides a more direct alternative diagnosis
High-pitched cat-like cry is not typical
Congenital ventricular septal defect is not a usual Rett syndrome feature
No developmental regression described
No loss of purposeful hand skills or stereotyped hand movements reported

data.description: 7-year-old girl with no past medical history presented with intermittent abdominal pain لمدة approximately 1 month, unrelieved by anti-inflammatory treatment. Abdominal CT showed peritoneal effusion and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Serum AFP was elevated to 1,210 ng/mL. Ultrasound revealed multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal hypoechoic lymph nodes; the uterus and adnexa were unremarkable. Surgical resection found a 4 cm jejunal mass involving the full thickness of the jejunum.

data.diagnosis: Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragonadal yolk sac tumor)
data.description: A rare malignant germ-cell tumor arising outside the gonads, capable of producing very high alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). In this case, the jejunal full-thickness mass, markedly elevated AFP, metastatic abdominal lymphadenopathy, peritoneal fluid, PET-avid lesion, and histology with glandular/reticular tumor architecture support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Jejunal mass involving the full thickness of the bowel wall
Normal uterus and adnexa, supporting an extragonadal rather than ovarian primary

data.description: A rare AFP-producing adenocarcinoma with morphologic and immunohistochemical features resembling hepatocellular differentiation. It can arise in the gastrointestinal tract and metastasize to lymph nodes, but it is exceptionally uncommon in children and in the jejunum.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very young age (7 years), whereas hepatoid adenocarcinoma usually occurs in adults
No described liver mass or underlying hepatic disease
Jejunal location is less typical than gastric location

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine that can produce a circumferential or full-thickness bowel mass and spread to regional or retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Conventional small-bowel adenocarcinoma generally does not cause substantial AFP elevation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 7 years, as small-bowel adenocarcinoma is predominantly an adult disease
Marked AFP elevation is not typical
No reported bowel obstruction, gastrointestinal bleeding, weight loss, or anemia

data.diagnosis: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the small bowel
data.description: Pediatric non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve the bowel wall and produce abdominal pain, bowel masses, ascites, and extensive abdominal lymphadenopathy. However, lymphoma would not usually produce markedly elevated AFP or a glandular epithelial histology.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal lymph nodes
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked AFP elevation is not typical of lymphoma
Reported glandular/epithelial tumor histology is not typical of lymphoma
No reported fever, night sweats, weight loss, or other systemic B symptoms

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

data.description: 6-month-old boy with 2 days of intermittent abdominal pain awakening him from sleep, crying and drawing his legs to his chest, with a rigid abdomen during episodes. He had three bloody stools progressing to nearly all blood with a large clot. On presentation he was tachycardic with diffuse abdominal tenderness, worse on the right, and later appeared pale with worsening hypotension. History of infantile colic and gastroesophageal reflux treated with ranitidine; recently started pureed foods and was on low-lactose cow milk-based formula. Laboratory tests showed severe anemia and leukocytosis.

data.diagnosis: Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
data.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain acid-secreting ectopic gastric mucosa, causing adjacent ulceration and significant lower gastrointestinal bleeding. The radionuclide images show a right-sided abdominal focus with uptake timing similar to the stomach, supporting ectopic gastric mucosa in a Meckel diverticulum.
symptoms_in_common: Tachycardia and hypotension consistent with hemorrhagic shock
Radionuclide uptake in the right abdomen synchronous with gastric uptake
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent colicky episodes with drawing the legs to the chest are more characteristic of intussusception
Rigid abdomen during pain episodes may suggest obstruction, ischemia, or peritonitis rather than uncomplicated bleeding

data.description: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, most often ileocolic in infants. It causes episodic severe colicky abdominal pain, vomiting or lethargy, and may produce bloody mucus stools due to bowel ischemia.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent severe abdominal pain awakening the infant
Crying and drawing legs to the chest during episodes
Rigid or tense abdomen during painful episodes
Tachycardia, pallor, and hypotension can occur with advanced bowel ischemia or shock
symptoms_not_in_common: Nearly all-blood stool with a large clot and severe anemia is more suggestive of brisk Meckel diverticulum bleeding than typical currant-jelly stool
The nuclear medicine scan demonstrates focal uptake compatible with ectopic gastric mucosa, which is not a typical finding in isolated intussusception
No vomiting, palpable abdominal mass, or described lethargy between episodes

data.diagnosis: Meckel diverticulum acting as a lead point for intussusception
data.description: A Meckel diverticulum can serve as a pathologic lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception. This can combine features of Meckel-related bleeding with episodic obstructive abdominal pain.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent colicky abdominal pain with legs drawn to the chest
Severe anemia, pallor, tachycardia, and hypotension from gastrointestinal hemorrhage
Abdominal tenderness, worse on the right
Right abdominal focus on technetium-pertechnetate imaging consistent with ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel diverticulum
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented vomiting or abdominal distension
No reported palpable sausage-shaped mass
The imaging provided is a Meckel scan rather than an ultrasound or contrast enema demonstrating bowel telescoping

data.diagnosis: Acute lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage from an intestinal duplication containing ectopic gastric mucosa
data.description: An enteric duplication cyst or tubular duplication can contain ectopic gastric mucosa, producing ulceration, abdominal pain, and gastrointestinal bleeding; it can occasionally be positive on technetium-pertechnetate scintigraphy.
symptoms_in_common: Severe anemia, pallor, tachycardia, and hypotension
Possible focal technetium-pertechnetate uptake from ectopic gastric mucosa
symptoms_not_in_common: The classic right lower abdominal scintigraphic appearance is more typical of a Meckel diverticulum
No known abdominal mass, chronic obstructive symptoms, or recurrent infection
The episodic legs-to-chest pain pattern is more typical of intussusception

data.description: A 69-year-old female non-smoker presented with a 6-month history of progressive breathlessness. She had no relevant past medical history or drug history. Spirometry showed FEV1 32% predicted and a flow-volume loop suggesting severe small airway disease. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.

data.diagnosis: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)
data.description: A rare proliferative disorder of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells that occurs predominantly in older nonsmoking women and commonly causes constrictive bronchiolitis. CT typically shows multiple small pulmonary nodules with mosaic attenuation and air trapping.
symptoms_in_common: Severe obstructive/small-airway pattern on spirometry with FEV1 32% predicted
CT appearance of multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules
CT mosaic attenuation/patchy low-attenuation regions consistent with air trapping
Normal echocardiogram, supporting a noncardiac cause of dyspnea

data.description: Fibrotic narrowing and obliteration of small bronchioles, often caused by DIPNECH in older nonsmoking women. It produces fixed airflow obstruction and mosaic attenuation from regional air trapping.
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple discrete pulmonary nodules are not typical of isolated constrictive bronchiolitis and suggest an associated process such as DIPNECH

data.diagnosis: Pulmonary carcinoid tumor(s) arising in the setting of DIPNECH
data.description: Pulmonary carcinoid tumors are well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors. DIPNECH can progress from neuroendocrine-cell hyperplasia and tumorlets to one or more carcinoid tumors, which may appear as larger rounded pulmonary nodules.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple pulmonary nodules, including relatively larger rounded nodules on CT
Breathlessness may occur when associated DIPNECH causes small-airway obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe diffuse small-airway obstruction is not usually caused by an isolated carcinoid tumor
Mosaic attenuation/air trapping is more characteristic of associated DIPNECH-related bronchiolitis than of a solitary carcinoid

data.diagnosis: Asthma or non-smoking-related chronic obstructive airway disease
data.description: Chronic inflammatory airway disease can cause airflow limitation, wheeze, dyspnea, and air trapping. In this case, the imaging pattern and patient demographic make this less likely as the primary diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Obstructive spirometry with markedly reduced FEV1
symptoms_not_in_common: No smoking history, making conventional COPD less likely
Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules are not a typical feature of asthma or uncomplicated COPD
Older nonsmoking female demographic with nodules plus mosaic attenuation is more suggestive of DIPNECH

data.description: Hematogenous spread of malignancy to the lungs may produce multiple rounded pulmonary nodules. However, metastatic disease alone would not usually explain marked obstructive small-airway physiology and mosaic air trapping.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple rounded pulmonary nodules on CT
Progressive breathlessness can occur with extensive pulmonary metastatic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No known prior malignancy or relevant medical history
Severe small-airway obstruction is not typical of uncomplicated pulmonary metastases
Mosaic attenuation/air trapping is more consistent with bronchiolitis associated with DIPNECH

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

data.description: 27-year-old man, previously healthy, presented with a few days of cough, hemoptysis, and low-grade fever. He denied night sweats and weight loss. He had a history of left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement that had intermittently enlarged and regressed since age 15. On examination, he was thin, with low-grade fever, mild hypoxemia, left upper lung crackles, and a 2 cm left supraclavicular lymph node that was nontender, firm, nonfixed, circumscribed, and rubbery. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated ESR and CRP, and elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor. Blood and sputum cultures were negative, and autoimmune, HIV, and tumor marker tests were negative. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation without identifiable pathogens.

data.diagnosis: Pulmonary tuberculosis with possible coexisting unicentric hyaline-vascular Castleman disease
data.description: Pulmonary tuberculosis commonly causes upper-lobe cavitary infiltrates, hemoptysis, fever, and granulomatous inflammation. The longstanding supraclavicular node and its image appearance with regressed follicles and concentric mantle zones are compatible with a separate unicentric hyaline-vascular Castleman disease.
symptoms_in_common: Upper-lobe infiltrative and cavitary lung abnormalities on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Repeatedly enlarging and regressing left supraclavicular lymph node since age 15
Negative sputum cultures and no pathogen identified on biopsy
Absence of night sweats and weight loss

data.description: Nontuberculous mycobacteria can produce chronic upper-lobe cavitary disease, bronchiectatic change, cough, hemoptysis, fever, and granulomatous lung inflammation; repeated mycobacterial cultures are usually needed for confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Upper-lobe cavitary and bronchiectatic-appearing lung abnormalities
Granulomatous inflammation without organisms initially identified
symptoms_not_in_common: Previously healthy young man without known structural lung disease or immune deficiency
Intermittent supraclavicular lymph node enlargement since adolescence
Negative sputum cultures
Acute presentation over only a few days

data.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most often involving the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes. Cavitary lung disease and substantial hemoptysis are uncommon but can occur in advanced or atypical pulmonary disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: Hemoptysis
Prominent unilateral upper-lobe cavitary destruction
Neutrophilic leukocytosis
A single supraclavicular node that has waxed and waned since adolescence
No reported bilateral hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy

data.description: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that can cause pulmonary nodules or cavities, cough, hemoptysis, systemic inflammation, and granulomatous inflammation on tissue biopsy.
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative autoimmune testing
No reported chronic sinus, nasal, ear, eye, renal, skin, or neurologic manifestations
Longstanding intermittently enlarged supraclavicular lymph node
Bronchiectatic/cystic rather than nodular cavitary imaging pattern

data.description: Unicentric Castleman disease is a localized benign lymphoproliferative disorder, usually presenting as a single enlarged lymph node. Hyaline-vascular histology typically shows small regressed germinal centers with concentric mantle-zone lymphocytes and prominent vascular proliferation.
symptoms_in_common: Solitary left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement
Node is firm, rubbery, circumscribed, mobile, and nontender
Long history of intermittent node enlargement and regression
Lymph-node histology image compatible with hyaline-vascular Castleman-type architecture
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute cough
Hemoptysis
Upper-lobe cavitary pulmonary infiltrates
Granulomatous inflammation in lung tissue
Mild hypoxemia
Neutrophilic leukocytosis and acute inflammatory syndrome

data.description: A 31-year-old Caucasian man with multiple sclerosis who had received 24 natalizumab infusions and was switched to fingolimod due to persistent high anti-JCPyV antibody index (3.61). After 40 days of fingolimod treatment, he developed seizures and visual field defects. Neurological examination revealed lateral nystagmus to the left, homonymous hemianopia, distal tremor and spasm of the upper limbs. data.diagnosis: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC polyomavirus
data.description: A severe opportunistic demyelinating brain infection caused by reactivation of JC polyomavirus, typically occurring in immunosuppressed individuals. Natalizumab exposure, high anti-JCPyV antibody index, subsequent fingolimod treatment, and profound leukopenia substantially increase risk.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute onset of visual field defects
Recent natalizumab exposure with high anti-JCPyV antibody index
CSF findings with low cell count, which can occur in PML
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly reported cognitive decline, aphasia, personality change, or progressive paresis
Upper-limb spasms are less characteristic than focal weakness or cognitive deficits

data.description: An acute or subacute episode of new inflammatory demyelination in a person with multiple sclerosis, causing new focal neurological deficits lasting more than 24 hours in the absence of infection or another explanation.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute development of focal neurological deficits
symptoms_not_in_common: Seizures are relatively uncommon in a typical MS relapse
Homonymous hemianopia is less common than optic neuritis, diplopia, sensory symptoms, or limb weakness in MS relapse
Very high anti-JCPyV antibody index and prior natalizumab exposure strongly raise concern for PML rather than routine MS activity
Marked leukopenia is not a typical feature of an MS relapse

data.description: An inflammatory worsening of pre-existing or recently developing JC-virus PML that can occur after withdrawal of natalizumab or changes in immunomodulatory therapy, as immune surveillance returns and produces inflammation around infected brain tissue.
symptoms_in_common: Recent discontinuation of natalizumab and switch to fingolimod
High risk for underlying JC-virus reactivation/PML
Visual field loss and focal neurological deficits
symptoms_not_in_common: The presentation occurred while receiving fingolimod, which may continue to suppress lymphocyte trafficking rather than produce robust immune reconstitution
No reported MRI contrast enhancement, edema, mass effect, fever, or CSF pleocytosis to specifically support inflammatory IRIS
Profound leukopenia is less compatible with a strong immune-reconstitution response

data.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, usually affecting posterior cerebral regions, that commonly presents with seizures, visual disturbances, headache, and altered mental status. It is often associated with severe hypertension, renal disease, cytotoxic drugs, or immune-modulating treatments.
symptoms_in_common: Possible posterior cerebral involvement suggested by visual symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported hypertension
No reported headache, encephalopathy, nausea, vomiting, or altered consciousness
Nystagmus, distal tremor, and upper-limb spasms are not typical dominant manifestations
Natalizumab exposure with high anti-JCPyV antibody index and leukopenia favor PML over PRES

data.description: A 39-year-old Korean male presented with intermittent and atypical chest discomfort symptoms. His medical history included burning pain originating in the extremities and radiating inwards to the limbs since childhood, which was previously dismissed as 'growing pains'. He also experienced ringing in the ears, had angiokeratomas on his trunk, and cornea verticillata. Physical examination revealed proteinuria (P/C ratio 0.501) without hematuria and normal renal function. His plasma αGal-A activity was markedly lower than controls at 4.1 nmoL/hr/mg protein (normal cutoff >35 nmoL/hr/mg protein). Genetic testing identified a hemizygous mutation in exon 4 of GLA, c.617T>C (p.Leu206 Pro).

data.diagnosis: Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency)
data.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic GLA variants resulting in deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity and accumulation of globotriaosylceramide. It causes neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, corneal verticillata, kidney disease, and cardiomyopathy. The ECG/echocardiographic findings are compatible with Fabry cardiac involvement, and the electron microscopy appearance is consistent with lamellar lysosomal inclusions (zebra bodies).
symptoms_in_common: Burning extremity pain since childhood consistent with acroparesthesias
Markedly reduced plasma alpha-galactosidase A activity
ECG and echocardiographic evidence suggestive of left ventricular hypertrophy/cardiac involvement
Electron microscopy findings compatible with glycolipid storage inclusions

data.description: Cardiac involvement from Fabry disease, characterized by glycosphingolipid accumulation in cardiomyocytes that commonly produces concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, repolarization abnormalities, chest pain, arrhythmias, and later myocardial fibrosis or heart failure.
symptoms_in_common: ECG abnormalities compatible with ventricular hypertrophy and repolarization changes
Echocardiographic appearance suggestive of left ventricular hypertrophy
symptoms_not_in_common: Childhood burning extremity pain
Angiokeratomas
Cornea verticillata
Tinnitus
Proteinuria

data.description: A myocardial disease characterized by unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, often due to sarcomeric gene variants, which can cause chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, and ECG evidence of hypertrophy. Fabry disease is an important metabolic mimic of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
symptoms_in_common: ECG findings suggestive of left ventricular hypertrophy with repolarization abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: Burning neuropathic extremity pain since childhood
Angiokeratomas
Cornea verticillata
Tinnitus
Proteinuria
Markedly low alpha-galactosidase A activity
Hemizygous GLA mutation
Renal electron microscopy findings compatible with lysosomal glycolipid accumulation

data.description: Renal involvement of Fabry disease caused by glycolipid accumulation in podocytes, tubular epithelial cells, endothelial cells, and vascular cells. It commonly presents initially with proteinuria and may progress to chronic kidney disease.
symptoms_in_common: Proteinuria with a protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.501
No hematuria, which is compatible with Fabry-related proteinuria
Normal renal function, compatible with early-stage Fabry nephropathy
Electron microscopy findings compatible with lysosomal storage material
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent atypical chest discomfort
ECG/echocardiographic cardiac hypertrophy findings
Tinnitus
Cornea verticillata
Angiokeratomas
Burning extremity pain

data.description: A multitrauma patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to an intrahepatic hematoma. On the 7th day of ICU hospitalization, he presented fever. Laboratory blood tests showed leucocytosis and elevated liver function values.

A traumatic liver hematoma can become secondarily infected during ICU admission, forming an abscess-like collection. Ultrasound may show a complex hypoechoic intrahepatic collection with internal debris.
symptoms_in_common: Recent liver trauma with intrahepatic hematoma
Fever on the seventh ICU day
Intrahepatic complex fluid collection on ultrasound
symptoms_not_in_common: No focal right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain was reported
No jaundice was reported
No positive blood or collection culture was provided

data.description: A biloma is an encapsulated collection of bile caused by disruption of intrahepatic bile ducts, often after liver trauma. It may become infected and cause fever and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Blunt liver injury with intrahepatic hematoma
Delayed presentation several days after trauma
symptoms_not_in_common: No jaundice or bilirubin elevation was specifically reported
No abdominal pain or abdominal distension was reported
The ultrasound appearance is complex and could also represent hematoma or abscess rather than simple bile

data.description: A pyogenic liver abscess is a localized bacterial infection within the liver, producing a fluid-containing lesion and systemic inflammatory signs. In this setting, it may arise from infection of a traumatic hepatic collection.
symptoms_in_common: Complex intrahepatic hypoechoic collection on ultrasound
Critical-care hospitalization, which increases risk of nosocomial infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No right-upper-quadrant pain was reported
No chills, septic shock, or bacteremia were reported
The lesion is associated with a known traumatic hematoma, favoring secondary infection of hematoma over a primary spontaneous abscess

data.description: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. Several hours after intravenous urography was performed with iodinated contrast material, generalized pustular eruptions developed, with multiple coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae observed on the trunk, arms, and legs. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and mild eosinophilia with 55% neutrophils and 8% eosinophils, and a white-cell count of 6500 per cubic millimeter. Histopathological examination of the lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Microbiologic studies were negative.

A rare severe cutaneous hypersensitivity/toxic reaction to iodinated compounds, including radiographic contrast, characterized by pustules, vesicles, bullae, and sometimes vegetating plaques with neutrophilic inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Abrupt eruption several hours after iodinated contrast exposure
Generalized pustules, coalescing vesicles, and pus-filled bullae
Marked involvement of the face, ears, trunk, arms, and legs
symptoms_not_in_common: Hematuria is not a typical manifestation of iododerma

data.diagnosis: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) induced by iodinated contrast
data.description: An acute drug-induced pustular eruption, commonly caused by medications and occasionally iodinated contrast media, with numerous sterile nonfollicular pustules and neutrophilia.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid onset after exposure to iodinated contrast material
Pustules on the trunk and extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Large coalescing vesicles and extensive pus-filled bullae are less typical than small pinpoint pustules
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis is not typical of classic AGEP
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is not a usual AGEP finding
Hematuria is not a typical feature

data.diagnosis: Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption caused by iodinated contrast
data.description: A severe drug eruption in which well-demarcated erythematous or dusky plaques blister after medication exposure; generalized bullous forms can mimic epidermal necrolysis and may occur after contrast agents.
symptoms_in_common: Temporal relationship to iodinated contrast administration
symptoms_not_in_common: Numerous pustules and purulent bullae are less typical
Diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate is less characteristic than an interface/lymphocytic pattern
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is unusual
No recurrent fixed-site lesions or residual hyperpigmentation are described
Hematuria is not typical

data.diagnosis: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-like drug reaction
data.description: A life-threatening severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction marked by widespread keratinocyte death, epidermal detachment, bullae, and frequent mucosal involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: Sterile pustules are not a dominant feature of TEN
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is not typical
A diffuse neutrophilic infiltrate is less typical than sparse inflammatory infiltrates
No mucosal erosions, skin detachment, or systemic toxicity are reported
Very rapid onset within hours is less typical for first-exposure TEN
Hematuria is not a typical feature

data.description: 54-year-old female with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented to cardiology clinic for follow-up 20 months since her most recent office visit. She was being evaluated for follow-up of cardiac risk factors and medication management. The patient was in her usual state of health and asymptomatic without changes in her exercise tolerance, weight, or energy levels. She did not have any gross hematuria or flank pain.

45-year-old man with acute nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting დაწყ after being well until the day before admission. Three days earlier, he had dog bites to the hands and forearms while bathing his dog; he also had head trauma from a rusty nail a few days earlier and dental extractions 1–2 weeks earlier. Past history: asthma, mild COPD, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and alcohol abuse (up to 18 beers daily, stopped 3 days before admission). On exam, he was ill-appearing, anxious, and diaphoretic, with hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and delayed capillary refill. He had multiple lacerations with necrotic edges and scratch marks on the hands and forearms, including a 3–4 cm right forearm wound with a 5–7 cm purplish surrounding area.

data.diagnosis: Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant sepsis with purpura fulminans
data.description: A rapidly progressive bloodstream infection caused by a dog-associated, fastidious gram-negative fusiform bacillus. It is particularly severe in people with heavy alcohol use, impaired splenic function, or other immune compromise and can cause septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, purpuric skin necrosis, and multiorgan failure.
symptoms_in_common: Dog bites to the hands and forearms 3 days before illness
Heavy alcohol use, a major risk factor for severe Capnocytophaga infection
Abrupt severe systemic illness with nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain
Hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, delayed capillary refill, diaphoresis, and ill appearance consistent with septic shock
Purplish ecchymotic and necrotic skin lesions on the extremities, compatible with purpura fulminans/DIC
Skin lesions extending beyond the bite wounds, including discoloration of thighs and lower legs in the images
Gram-stain image showing slender fusiform gram-negative rods, consistent with Capnocytophaga species
symptoms_not_in_common: Recent rusty-nail head trauma
Recent dental extractions
Alcohol cessation 3 days before admission, which could also raise concern for withdrawal

data.diagnosis: Purpura fulminans due to sepsis-associated disseminated intravascular coagulation
data.description: A life-threatening thrombotic and bleeding disorder, usually triggered by severe sepsis, in which widespread microvascular clotting causes rapidly progressive purpura, ecchymoses, skin necrosis, shock, and possible limb ischemia.
symptoms_in_common: Rapidly progressive purplish discoloration and ecchymotic lesions of the hands, forearm, thigh, and lower legs
Necrotic edges of traumatic skin wounds
Cold-appearing distal extremities and delayed capillary refill suggesting impaired peripheral perfusion
Severe systemic toxicity with hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and shock physiology
Multifocal rather than purely localized skin involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Dog bites are a trigger for the underlying infection rather than a defining feature of purpura fulminans
Nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain are nonspecific and not characteristic skin findings
Fusiform gram-negative rods identify an infectious cause rather than purpura fulminans itself

data.diagnosis: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection of the forearm from dog-bite wound
data.description: A rapidly progressive bacterial infection involving deep skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, or muscle. It can follow animal bites and may produce severe pain, necrosis, violaceous discoloration, systemic toxicity, and septic shock.
symptoms_in_common: Recent dog bites with multiple lacerations and scratches on hands and forearms
A 3–4 cm forearm wound with a 5–7 cm surrounding purplish area
Ill appearance and shock-like vital signs
Rapid progression over a few days
symptoms_not_in_common: Diffuse purpura/ecchymoses of thighs and both lower legs suggest systemic coagulopathy rather than a solely localized soft-tissue infection
No reported crepitus or soft-tissue gas on the provided extremity radiograph
No described severe focal pain out of proportion to examination
Fusiform gram-negative rods and alcohol-associated dog-bite sepsis more strongly support Capnocytophaga bloodstream infection

data.diagnosis: Pasteurella multocida infection after dog bite
data.description: A gram-negative coccobacillary infection commonly transmitted through dog or cat bites. It typically causes rapidly developing cellulitis at the bite site and can occasionally cause bacteremia or severe sepsis in medically vulnerable patients.
symptoms_in_common: Forearm and hand wounds with surrounding discoloration and tissue injury
Acute systemic illness with tachycardia and tachypnea
Potential for invasive infection in a patient with chronic alcohol abuse and chronic lung disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Extensive purpura fulminans-like lesions on distant extremities are uncommon
Hypothermic septic shock is much less typical than localized cellulitis
The Gram-stain morphology shown is fusiform rod-like rather than the usual small coccobacillary appearance of Pasteurella
Heavy alcohol use and dog exposure are especially characteristic risk factors for severe Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection

data.description: 27-year-old female, 162cm tall, 30kg weight. Born after normal pregnancy/delivery. No family history of neurological diseases. Normal early development. At age 6, developed general muscle weakness and gait disturbance with decreased muscle tone/strength and atrophic muscle mass. At age 8, muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type. At age 24, had sudden syncope. At age 26, had stroke with general weakness, aphagia, and dysarthria. Current presentation at age 27 with left hemiplegia and aphasia. Lab findings: plasma lactate 21.8 mg/dL (elevated), normal CBC/electrolytes/BUN/creatinine, free T4 1.76 ng/dL, TSH 0.04 μIU/mL, C3 13 mg/dL (low), C4 18 mg/dL (normal).
