Negative for ASO antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulants, and anti-cytoplasmic antibody. DNA sequencing showed m.3303C>T mutation in mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene.

data.diagnosis: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS syndrome) due to MT-TL1 m.3303C>T mutation
data.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by impaired oxidative phosphorylation, characterized by myopathy, lactic acidosis, neurologic deficits, and recurrent stroke-like episodes at a young age. MT-TL1 mutations affecting mitochondrial tRNA leucine are a well-established cause.
symptoms_in_common: Gait disturbance with reduced muscle tone and muscle atrophy
Muscle biopsy showing mitochondrial myopathy with pleoconial changes
Young-onset neurologic event with aphasia, dysarthria, and hemiplegia
Recurrent episodes of syncope and stroke-like neurologic deficits
Diffusion-weighted brain MRI lesion consistent with an acute stroke-like cerebral injury
Pathogenic mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene mutation (m.3303C>T)
symptoms_not_in_common: Low complement C3
Suppressed TSH with relatively high free T4
Possible large-vessel arterial occlusion on MR angiography
Intracardiac thrombus suggested by echocardiography

data.diagnosis: Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke due to left ventricular thrombus
data.description: An ischemic stroke caused by embolization of a thrombus from the heart into a cerebral artery. The brain diffusion MRI demonstrates an acute right hemispheric infarct, while MR angiography suggests major intracranial arterial obstruction and echocardiographic images appear to show a left ventricular intracavitary thrombus.
symptoms_in_common: Brain MRI with acute diffusion-restricted right cerebral infarction
MR angiographic evidence of intracranial arterial flow interruption or occlusion
Echocardiographic appearance concerning for a left ventricular thrombus
symptoms_not_in_common: Childhood-onset progressive generalized muscle weakness
Muscle atrophy and gait disturbance beginning at age 6
Mitochondrial myopathy on muscle biopsy
Elevated lactate
Mitochondrial MT-TL1 m.3303C>T mutation
Very low body weight

data.diagnosis: Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy with left ventricular thrombus formation
data.description: Cardiac involvement in mitochondrial disease can include cardiomyopathy, impaired ventricular contractility, arrhythmia, and intracardiac thrombus formation. A ventricular thrombus can lead to systemic embolism and ischemic stroke.
symptoms_in_common: Known mitochondrial disease with MT-TL1 mutation
Syncope, which may reflect arrhythmia or cardiac dysfunction
Echocardiographic intracavitary left ventricular mass compatible with thrombus
Neurologic deficits following stroke, including aphasia and left hemiplegia
symptoms_not_in_common: Low complement C3
Suppressed TSH and elevated free T4
Childhood muscle biopsy findings are not specific for cardiac involvement
No reported palpitations, chest pain, edema, or overt heart-failure symptoms

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

data.description: 29-year-old woman with 7 weeks of progressive generalized pruritus, nausea, bloating, and watery mustard-colored diarrhea սկս after eating sushi. Three weeks later she developed jaundice, right upper quadrant discomfort, decreased appetite, and amber urine. Initial urgent care treatment with methylprednisolone, hydroxyzine, and diphenoxylate-atropine did not help. Four weeks before presentation, labs showed elevated ALT 327 U/L, AST 104 U/L, total bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, and CA 19-9 73 U/mL. Past history: anxiety and depression; no medications or drug allergies. On exam, she was thin, jaundiced with scleral icterus and diffuse excoriations from scratching.

data.diagnosis: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head
data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the pancreas. A tumor in the pancreatic head can obstruct the distal common bile duct, causing painless or minimally painful obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, gallbladder distention, and elevated CA 19-9. The imaging and pathology are consistent with an infiltrative pancreatic-region adenocarcinoma with biliary obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging evidence of biliary obstruction with gallbladder distention and a pancreatic-region obstructing lesion
Adenocarcinoma-like cytology/histology with desmoplastic stromal reaction
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age of 29 years
Watery mustard-colored diarrhea beginning abruptly after sushi consumption
Seven-week subacute course following a suspected foodborne exposure

data.description: Cholangiocarcinoma is an adenocarcinoma arising from biliary duct epithelium. Distal common-bile-duct tumors produce obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, anorexia, and biliary dilatation; CA 19-9 may be elevated.
symptoms_in_common: Biliary ductal obstruction and gallbladder distention on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Watery diarrhea as the initial dominant symptom
Abrupt onset after eating sushi
Very young age for cholangiocarcinoma
Bloating is nonspecific rather than a characteristic presentation

data.description: Ampullary carcinoma arises at the ampulla of Vater, where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct drain into the duodenum. It can cause early biliary obstruction, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and elevated CA 19-9, often with less extensive symptoms than pancreatic cancer.
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive watery diarrhea after sushi exposure
Diffuse generalized itching preceding obvious jaundice by several weeks
Age 29 years is unusual
Marked bloating is not a classic defining feature

data.diagnosis: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor causing biliary obstruction
data.description: A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor is a neoplasm arising from endocrine cells of the pancreas. A nonfunctioning tumor in the pancreatic head may compress the bile duct and cause jaundice, although its pathology is usually neuroendocrine rather than conventional ductal adenocarcinoma.
symptoms_not_in_common: Adenocarcinoma-like gland-forming/desmoplastic histology would be atypical
CA 19-9 elevation is less characteristic
Watery diarrhea is not typical unless the tumor is a functional hormone-secreting subtype
Abrupt onset after sushi consumption is not typical

data.description: A patient with known Crohn's disease presented with difficulties to pass stool, a sensation of a foreign body in the rectum and limited rectal bleeding. An endoscopy was performed as the first examination. A gallstone was found in the rectum and it was removed without complications.

data.diagnosis: Gallstone ileus with rectal gallstone impaction
data.description: Mechanical intestinal obstruction caused by a gallstone that has entered the bowel, usually through a biliary-enteric fistula, and has become impacted distally in the rectum.
symptoms_in_common: Sensation of a foreign body in the rectum
Endoscopically confirmed gallstone in the rectum
Limited rectal bleeding, likely from local mucosal irritation by the impacted stone
symptoms_not_in_common: Known Crohn's disease is not required for gallstone ileus
No typical proximal small-bowel obstruction symptoms were reported, such as vomiting, abdominal distension, or colicky abdominal pain

data.diagnosis: Cholecystoenteric fistula, most likely cholecystoduodenal fistula
data.description: An abnormal communication between the gallbladder and bowel that permits a gallstone to migrate directly into the gastrointestinal tract. The abdominal images are consistent with a biliary-enteric fistulous route near the gallbladder and adjacent duodenum.
symptoms_in_common: A gallstone was found within the rectum, supporting prior passage through the bowel
Imaging suggests an abnormal communication in the gallbladder/duodenal region
The stone could produce downstream obstructive rectal symptoms after passage through the fistula
symptoms_not_in_common: Difficulty passing stool is a consequence of distal stone impaction rather than a typical direct symptom of the fistula
Foreign-body sensation in the rectum is not typical until the stone reaches the rectum
Rectal bleeding is not a usual primary manifestation of a cholecystoenteric fistula

data.diagnosis: Crohn's disease with possible intestinal stricture or anorectal involvement
data.description: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can cause bowel-wall inflammation, strictures, fissures, and anorectal symptoms. It may contribute to impaired intestinal passage and increase the likelihood of a migrating stone becoming impacted.
symptoms_in_common: Difficulty passing stool can occur with Crohn-related colonic, rectal, or anal stricture
Limited rectal bleeding can occur with active anorectal inflammation, ulceration, or fissuring
symptoms_not_in_common: A sensation of a discrete foreign body in the rectum is not typical of Crohn's disease alone
The endoscopically identified rectal gallstone is not explained by Crohn's disease alone
No reported abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, weight loss, or other clear features of an active Crohn's flare

data.description: 15-year-old boy presented after injuring his left knee while carrying a tray of food at a fast food restaurant. He felt his knee 'wobble' and fell to the floor, unable to bear weight due to pain. Medical history included chronic fatigue syndrome. Had a Beighton score of 6 (indicating joint laxity) but no history of joint dislocations. On examination: laterally dislocated patella, moderate effusion, pain on palpation around medial patellofemoral ligament, range of movement reduced to extension-flexion of 0/10/60 degrees, ligamentous tests unremarkable. Two weeks later: complained of intermittent locking in left knee, had joint effusion and palpable loose body under patella.
Displacement of the patella to the lateral side of the knee, commonly occurring in adolescents with ligamentous laxity and often associated with injury to the medial patellofemoral ligament.
symptoms_in_common: Knee felt unstable or 'wobbled' before the fall
Pain around the medial patellofemoral ligament
Generalized joint laxity with Beighton score of 6
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent mechanical locking two weeks later
Palpable loose body beneath the patella

data.description: A fracture involving articular cartilage and underlying bone, typically from the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle after a lateral patellar dislocation. A fragment may detach and become an intra-articular loose body.
symptoms_in_common: Acute traumatic knee injury associated with lateral patellar dislocation
Palpable loose body under the patella
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic fatigue syndrome
Generalized joint hypermobility is not itself a typical manifestation of an osteochondral fracture

data.diagnosis: Intra-articular osteochondral loose body of the knee
data.description: A free fragment of cartilage and bone within the knee joint, often produced by an osteochondral injury after patellar dislocation. It can cause episodic locking, swelling, and pain.
symptoms_in_common: Palpable mobile loose body beneath the patella
Recent patellar dislocation, a common cause of osteochondral loose bodies
symptoms_not_in_common: Initial visible lateral patellar dislocation
Medial patellofemoral ligament tenderness
Generalized joint laxity

data.description: 45-year-old female with 13-year history of papular spiny eruptions on trunk and limbs with severe pruritus. Patient was otherwise in good health. Family history positive for psoriasis in sister. Treatment history included topical steroids and oral antihistamines without relief. Papular lesions on body presented before the alopecia of scalp and pubis, while axillae had been involved for 6 years.

A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by the triad of cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring alopecia of axillary/pubic hair, and widespread follicular keratotic or spiny papules (lichen spinulosus-like eruption).
symptoms_in_common: Long-standing intensely pruritic follicular papular/spiny eruption on trunk and limbs
Papular eruption preceding scalp and pubic alopecia
Scalp alopecia with clinical appearance consistent with scarring hair loss
Dermoscopic follicular keratotic plugs/spines and perifollicular changes
Histology compatible with lichenoid perifollicular inflammation and follicular fibrosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Family history of psoriasis
Otherwise good general health is not specifically diagnostic

data.description: A primary lymphocytic cicatricial alopecia in which inflammation targets the upper hair follicle, causing permanent hair loss; it can be associated with perifollicular scale, itching, and follicular keratotic papules.
symptoms_in_common: Scalp alopecia developing after the cutaneous eruption
Follicular fibrosis/scarring compatible with cicatricial alopecia
symptoms_not_in_common: Widespread spiny papules on trunk and limbs are not typical of classic isolated lichen planopilaris
Axillary and pubic alopecia is more characteristic of the Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur variant
Family history of psoriasis

data.description: A follicular keratotic disorder producing groups of tiny rough, spine-tipped papules, often on the trunk and extremities; it may resemble keratosis pilaris but has more prominent follicular spines.
symptoms_in_common: Papular spiny/keratotic eruption on the trunk and limbs
Follicular keratotic plugs visible clinically and dermoscopically
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe persistent pruritus is less typical
Scarring scalp alopecia is not a feature of isolated lichen spinulosus
Pubic and axillary alopecia are not typical
Histologic lichenoid perifollicular inflammation and fibrosis suggest lichen planopilaris-spectrum disease rather than isolated lichen spinulosus

data.description: A lichen planus variant with follicular hyperkeratotic papules and perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation; when the scalp is involved, it may overlap clinically and histologically with lichen planopilaris.
symptoms_not_in_common: No classic violaceous polygonal lichen planus papules or mucosal lesions were described
Axillary and pubic alopecia are more specifically suggestive of Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome
Family history of psoriasis

data.description: 35-year-old woman with severe hypertension, edema, and renal failure. She had preeclampsia during pregnancy 12 months earlier, requiring Caesarean delivery at 29 weeks, followed by poorly controlled hypertension and proteinuria (>1 g/day). Six months before admission, she developed fatigue, headaches, severe hypertension, and facial and pedal edema. She denied fever, neurologic symptoms, or diarrheal prodrome. On examination, she was pale and hydrated with blood pressure 151/103 mmHg. Labs showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, marked renal dysfunction, reticulocytosis, schistocytes, heavy proteinuria (4.9 g/24 h), microscopic hematuria, elevated LDH and bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and negative Coombs test; liver enzymes, immunologic tests, viral screening, and antiphospholipid antibodies were normal.

data.diagnosis: Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), pregnancy-associated
data.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulated complement activation, often triggered by pregnancy or the postpartum period. It produces microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, severe kidney injury, hypertension, and may cause thrombotic skin lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Reticulocytosis, elevated LDH and bilirubin, and low haptoglobin
Necrotic ulcerative ankle skin lesions compatible with cutaneous thrombotic microangiopathy
Skin histology consistent with thrombotic small-vessel injury
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly documented complement levels, anti-factor H antibodies, or pathogenic complement-gene variant
The prolonged course beginning many months after delivery is less typical than abrupt early postpartum presentation

data.description: Severe uncontrolled hypertension can damage small arteries and arterioles, causing endothelial injury, platelet consumption, mechanical hemolysis, renal failure, and ischemic skin injury.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated LDH, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and low haptoglobin
Skin ulcers/necrosis that may reflect ischemic thrombotic vasculopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: The degree of thrombocytopenia and hemolysis may be more prominent than in many cases of hypertension-associated thrombotic microangiopathy
Pregnancy-associated onset raises concern for an underlying complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy rather than hypertension alone
Heavy nephrotic-range proteinuria is not a defining feature

data.description: A life-threatening thrombotic microangiopathy usually caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, with variable neurologic, renal, fever, and skin manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Possible ischemic cutaneous lesions due to microvascular thrombosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe renal failure is more characteristic of HUS/aHUS than classic TTP
No neurologic deficits, confusion, seizures, or focal symptoms
No fever
Marked hypertension, heavy proteinuria, and hematuria suggest a primary renal thrombotic microangiopathy
No reported severe ADAMTS13 deficiency

data.diagnosis: Pregnancy-related HELLP syndrome or persistent preeclampsia-associated thrombotic microangiopathy
data.description: Preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome are pregnancy-related endothelial disorders causing hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, and sometimes kidney injury. They usually improve after delivery.
symptoms_in_common: History of severe preeclampsia requiring premature Caesarean delivery
Hemolytic anemia with elevated LDH, bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and schistocytes
symptoms_not_in_common: Disease persisted and progressed for approximately 12 months after delivery
Liver enzymes were normal
There is no reported right upper quadrant pain, nausea, or hepatic involvement
Severe ongoing renal failure and necrotic skin lesions are atypical after resolved preeclampsia/HELLP
The postpartum persistence favors complement-mediated aHUS

data.diagnosis: Antiphospholipid syndrome with thrombotic vasculopathy (including catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome)
data.description: An autoimmune hypercoagulable condition that can cause pregnancy morbidity, hypertension-related placental disease, renal thrombotic microangiopathy, thrombocytopenia, and ischemic skin ulcers.
symptoms_in_common: Renal dysfunction with proteinuria and hematuria
Necrotic ulcerative skin lesions suggestive of vascular occlusion
Histologic appearance of small-vessel thrombotic injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Antiphospholipid antibody testing was negative
No documented arterial, venous, or placental thrombosis
Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with prominent schistocytes is more suggestive of a thrombotic microangiopathy
No multiorgan acute thrombotic syndrome characteristic of catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome

data.description: 45-year-old woman presented with syncope and severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL) with lower GI bleeding. A diagnostic colonoscopy was negative. CT scan of abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.2 x 3 x 2.9 cm contrast-enhancing right lower-quadrant mass arising from the wall of the ileum. No evidence of metastatic disease. Subsequent laparotomy found a 3.5 cm mass that was resected with negative margins. Molecular studies showed a 42-base pair deletion in exon 11 of the KIT gene (V559_D572del) that would delete all or part of codons 558 to 572 and would change the 558-encoding amino acid from Lys to Asn (K558N).
A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract derived from interstitial cells of Cajal. Ileal GISTs commonly express KIT (CD117) and may harbor activating KIT exon 11 mutations, as in this case.
symptoms_in_common: Syncope likely secondary to acute or chronic blood-loss anemia
Contrast-enhancing mass arising from the ileal wall
Submucosal small-bowel lesion not detected on colonoscopy
Strong immunohistochemical staining consistent with KIT expression

data.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise from the intestinal wall and present as a bleeding small-bowel mass. It is generally positive for smooth-muscle markers such as desmin and SMA rather than KIT-driven.
symptoms_not_in_common: KIT exon 11 activating deletion mutation
Strong KIT/CD117-type immunohistochemical staining
Features favoring a GIST rather than a smooth-muscle neoplasm

data.description: A neuroendocrine neoplasm frequently arising in the distal ileum. These tumors may cause obstruction, mesenteric fibrosis, or metastatic disease and can occasionally bleed.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe bleeding causing hemoglobin of 6 g/dL is less typical
No reported carcinoid syndrome symptoms such as flushing, diarrhea, or wheezing
No mesenteric desmoplastic reaction or metastatic disease
KIT exon 11 activating deletion mutation
Histology and KIT-positive immunostaining favoring GIST

data.description: An epithelial malignancy of the small intestine that can produce anemia, bleeding, abdominal pain, obstruction, or weight loss. It usually has gland-forming histology rather than a KIT-mutant mesenchymal phenotype.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported obstructive symptoms, abdominal pain, or weight loss
Well-circumscribed wall-based mass with mesenchymal-appearing histology
Strong KIT/CD117-type immunostaining
KIT exon 11 deletion mutation, which strongly supports GIST

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

data.description: A 73-year-old man presented with abdominal distention and maldigestion for 1 month. The patient had a medical history of diabetes and hypertension. On physical examination, an intraabdominal mass was palpated in the epigastric area, and the patient did not complain of pain and tenderness. Laboratory findings showed no abnormalities except an elevated fasting glucose level.

A rare malignant exocrine pancreatic tumor, usually occurring in older adults, often presenting as a large, well-circumscribed pancreatic mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. Histology typically shows acinar or solid growth of relatively uniform cells with granular cytoplasm.
symptoms_in_common: Maldigestion consistent with pancreatic exocrine dysfunction
Large heterogeneous pancreatic mass with necrotic or hemorrhagic areas on CT
Gross yellow-tan, hemorrhagic and necrotic tumor appearance
Histology showing solid/acinar-appearing sheets of relatively uniform tumor cells
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of abdominal pain
Normal laboratory findings apart from elevated fasting glucose
No reported lipase-hypersecretion manifestations such as panniculitis, polyarthritis, or eosinophilia

data.description: A pancreatic neoplasm arising from neuroendocrine cells. Nonfunctioning tumors can become large before causing symptoms and may produce abdominal fullness, digestive symptoms, or a palpable mass.
symptoms_in_common: Relatively well-demarcated mass with areas of degeneration or hemorrhage possible
symptoms_not_in_common: Histologic appearance favors acinar differentiation rather than classic nested or trabecular neuroendocrine architecture
No hormone-related syndrome such as hypoglycemia, gastrinoma-related ulcer disease, diarrhea, flushing, or glucagonoma rash
Normal laboratory findings except hyperglycemia
Very large infiltrative-appearing tumor is less typical than for acinar cell carcinoma

data.diagnosis: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
data.description: A low-grade malignant pancreatic tumor that is typically large, encapsulated, and contains mixed solid, hemorrhagic, and cystic areas. It most often occurs in young women but can rarely occur in older men.
symptoms_in_common: Gross hemorrhagic and necrotic areas within the tumor
Relatively indolent presentation without marked laboratory abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: Age of 73 years is highly atypical
Male sex is atypical
Maldigestion is less characteristic
Histology does not clearly show the typical pseudopapillary architecture with delicate fibrovascular cores

data.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy, arising from pancreatic ductal epithelium. It commonly causes obstructive, digestive, and constitutional symptoms and is often associated with diabetes in older patients.
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain or back pain
No jaundice or reported biliary obstruction
No weight loss or anorexia reported
Normal laboratory findings aside from glucose elevation
Large well-circumscribed hemorrhagic tumor and acinar-pattern histology are not typical of conventional ductal adenocarcinoma

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

data.description: A 58-year-old overweight African American male presented with a 5-year history of a slightly pruritic and painful rash that worsened during summers, and blisters sometimes developed. Emollients were unhelpful. The patient was otherwise healthy, performed indoor manual labor as a maintenance engineer, and had no significant sun exposure. His sister had diabetes mellitus and a similar rash in her axillae. Physical examination revealed irregularly thickened skin containing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, multiple acrochordons (skin tags), malodorous crust, and areas of maceration and erosion. Further examination showed pseudofolliculitis barbae in the submental and mandibular regions bilaterally. The nails, oral cavity, and mucosal membranes appeared normal.

An autosomal-dominant acantholytic blistering disorder caused by ATP2C1 mutations, producing recurrent painful erosions, fissures, crusting, and maceration in flexural areas. It commonly worsens with heat, sweating, and friction. Histology typically shows widespread suprabasal acantholysis with a "dilapidated brick wall" appearance.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic recurrent rash in an intertriginous/axillary location
Family history of a similar axillary rash in a first-degree relative
Clinical image showing thickened eroded flexural plaques
Histology showing marked acantholysis consistent with Hailey-Hailey disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Pseudofolliculitis barbae
Multiple acrochordons/skin tags
Prominent hypopigmentation and hyperpigmentation

data.description: An inherited acantholytic keratinization disorder caused by ATP2A2 mutations. It causes persistent greasy, crusted keratotic papules in seborrheic and flexural areas and may worsen with heat and sweating. Histology shows acantholysis with dyskeratosis, including corps ronds and grains.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic inherited-appearing rash with an affected sibling
Possible erosions and secondary malodor in flexural areas
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominantly localized axillary/intertriginous disease rather than widespread seborrheic papules
Painful macerated erosions and blisters are more characteristic of Hailey-Hailey disease
No characteristic nail abnormalities such as red-and-white longitudinal streaks or V-shaped nicking
No mucosal papules
Histology does not describe prominent dyskeratosis, corps ronds, or grains
Pseudofolliculitis barbae
Multiple skin tags

data.description: A rare vegetating form of pemphigus vulgaris in which flaccid bullae evolve into painful, malodorous, vegetating erosions and plaques, often in intertriginous regions. It is autoimmune and usually has mucosal involvement; histology may show acantholysis with eosinophilic inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Painful and mildly pruritic flexural eruption
Blistering followed by erosions and crusting
Macerated, malodorous, thickened or vegetating plaques in the axilla
symptoms_not_in_common: Five-year familial history with a sister affected, favoring an inherited disorder
Summer/friction-related exacerbations are more typical of Hailey-Hailey disease
Normal oral cavity and mucous membranes
No reported widespread flaccid bullae
No reported eosinophilic pustules or vegetating plaques with characteristic autoimmune features
Pseudofolliculitis barbae
Multiple acrochordons

data.diagnosis: Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or candidal infection
data.description: Inflammation of opposing skin surfaces caused by moisture, heat, friction, and sweating, often complicated by Candida or bacterial overgrowth. It produces erythema, maceration, fissuring, erosions, odor, and discomfort in axillae, groin, or inframammary folds.
symptoms_in_common: Overweight status with a skin-fold eruption
Worsening during hot weather and sweating
Maceration, erosions, crusting, malodor, itching, and pain
Possible secondary infection contributing to odor and crust
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent blistering over five years
Affected sibling with a similar chronic rash
Histologic acantholysis
Irregular thickened plaques with a pattern suggestive of a primary acantholytic disorder
No mention of satellite pustules typical of candidal intertrigo
Pseudofolliculitis barbae

data.description: A velvety hyperpigmented thickening of flexural skin, commonly associated with obesity, insulin resistance, or diabetes mellitus. Skin tags may coexist, particularly in the axillae and neck.
symptoms_not_in_common: Painful and pruritic rash
Summer exacerbations with blister formation
Maceration, erosions, crusting, and malodor
Family history of a similar inflammatory axillary rash
Histologic acantholysis
Pseudofolliculitis barbae

data.description: A 22-year-old female presented with a gradually increasing pelvic mass with tenderness for 1 month. There was no evidence of previous trauma or fever, and no history of other medical or surgical disease and no evidence of pregnancy. On physical examination, there was a palpable mass with tenderness in her left pelvic area.

A rare malignant cartilage-forming soft-tissue tumor that often occurs in young adults and may arise in the pelvis. Imaging commonly shows a lobulated soft-tissue mass with prominent calcified chondroid matrix, adjacent bone erosion or invasion, and increased FDG uptake.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging evidence of a calcified lobulated pelvic soft-tissue mass
High uptake on FDG PET imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No systemic symptoms are reported

data.description: A malignant soft-tissue sarcoma that produces osteoid or bone outside the skeleton. It can present as a calcified pelvic mass with local invasion and marked metabolic activity, although it is more common in older adults.
symptoms_in_common: Dense mineralization/calcification within the mass on radiographs and CT
Possible erosion of adjacent iliac bone
Increased uptake on bone scintigraphy and FDG PET
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 22 years is much younger than the typical patient
Only a 1-month symptom duration is relatively short for many cases

data.description: A malignant mesenchymal soft-tissue tumor affecting adolescents and young adults. It may occur near the hip or pelvic joints, can contain calcifications, and may cause pressure erosion of adjacent bone.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly enlarging tender pelvic soft-tissue mass
symptoms_not_in_common: The degree of extensive chondroid-appearing calcification is less typical than for chondrosarcoma
No specific joint-related limitation or periarticular origin is reported

data.diagnosis: Conventional chondrosarcoma of the ilium with extraosseous soft-tissue extension
data.description: A malignant cartilaginous tumor arising from bone, often in the pelvis, with lobulated architecture and characteristic rings-and-arcs or stippled calcification. Larger lesions can extend into surrounding soft tissues.
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 22 years is younger than the usual age for conventional chondrosarcoma
Very rapid clinical recognition over 1 month is less typical for a conventional low-grade tumor

data.diagnosis: Chondroblastoma of the pelvic bone with soft-tissue extension
data.description: A benign but locally aggressive cartilage tumor that usually affects adolescents and young adults. It can show matrix calcification and bone-scan uptake, although pelvic location and a large soft-tissue mass are uncommon.
symptoms_not_in_common: Large palpable extraosseous pelvic mass is uncommon
Marked FDG avidity and extensive soft-tissue invasion would be concerning for malignancy rather than typical chondroblastoma
Iliac location is less typical than epiphyseal lesions of long bones

data.description: 36-year-old female with no past medical history who developed lower-limb and paraspinal muscle spasms over 3 months, progressively worsening over 6 months to wheelchair dependence. She later required regular IVIG every 12 days, diazepam 30 mg/day, and morphine up to 60 mg/day for pain. Examination showed brisk reflexes and severe clonus, and the spasms were severe enough to impair breathing, requiring intermittent oxygen.

A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and limb muscle rigidity, painful stimulus-sensitive spasms, hyperreflexia, and exaggerated startle responses; it is often associated with antibodies to GAD65 or related inhibitory-synapse proteins. The electrophysiology shown is compatible with excessive stimulus-triggered muscle activation and an enhanced late blink-reflex response.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive paraspinal and lower-limb muscle spasms
Severe painful muscle contractions requiring diazepam and morphine
Progression to severe gait impairment and wheelchair dependence
Spasms involving axial musculature and impairing breathing
Need for maintenance IVIG, consistent with immune-mediated SPS treatment
Image evidence of widespread stimulus-triggered muscle activity and exaggerated blink-reflex R2 responses
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear report of persistent fixed axial rigidity or hyperlordosis between spasms
No stated anxiety, phobic avoidance, or stimulus-triggered falls
No reported anti-GAD65, anti-amphiphysin, or anti-glycine-receptor antibody result

data.diagnosis: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
data.description: A severe autoimmune stiff-person-spectrum disorder, frequently associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, causing rigidity, painful spasms, myoclonus or exaggerated startle, hyperreflexia, brainstem involvement, and sometimes autonomic or respiratory dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive rigidity/spasm syndrome involving the trunk and legs
Severe stimulus-related muscle overactivity on electrophysiologic recordings
Clinical need for immunotherapy with IVIG
Enhanced brainstem reflex physiology suggested by large/repetitive blink-reflex R2 activity
symptoms_not_in_common: No encephalopathy, confusion, or altered consciousness reported
No clear myoclonus reported
No documented autonomic instability, such as severe sweating, tachycardia, or blood-pressure fluctuations
No cranial-nerve, eye-movement, or bulbar symptoms described

data.diagnosis: Glycine receptor antibody-associated stiff-person spectrum disorder
data.description: An autoimmune disorder of inhibitory glycinergic neurotransmission that may present as stiff-person syndrome or PERM, with exaggerated startle, axial and limb spasms, hyperexcitability of brainstem/spinal reflex circuits, and potential respiratory involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Brisk reflexes and clonus indicating motor-system hyperexcitability
Exaggerated reflex-related electrophysiologic activity in the images
Improvement-oriented treatment pattern with IVIG and diazepam
symptoms_not_in_common: No glycine-receptor antibody testing result is provided
No prominent startle-triggered falls explicitly described
No reported brainstem, autonomic, or cognitive features

data.description: A disorder of impaired glycinergic inhibition, usually genetic but occasionally acquired/autoimmune, causing an excessive startle reflex with generalized stiffening after unexpected stimuli. Electrophysiology may show abnormal startle-related recruitment across multiple muscles.
symptoms_in_common: Electrophysiologic evidence of widespread muscle activation following stimulation
Potential breathing difficulty during severe generalized stiffening
symptoms_not_in_common: Typical hereditary hyperekplexia usually begins in infancy or childhood, whereas this began at age 36
The prolonged progressive course with severe painful axial spasms is more typical of stiff-person-spectrum disease
No explicit history of exaggerated startle to sound, touch, or surprise is provided
Need for regular IVIG suggests an autoimmune disorder rather than classic genetic hyperekplexia

data.diagnosis: Hereditary spastic paraplegia or other upper-motor-neuron spastic paraparesis
data.description: A group of disorders causing progressive bilateral lower-limb spasticity, weakness, hyperreflexia, and clonus due to corticospinal-tract dysfunction. Some forms can produce substantial gait disability.
symptoms_in_common: Paraspinal muscle overactivity can occur with marked spasticity
symptoms_not_in_common: Painful episodic spasms involving axial and respiratory muscles are less typical
The apparent exaggerated startle/blink-reflex physiology is not characteristic
Regular IVIG responsiveness or dependence is not typical
No family history, urinary symptoms, sensory findings, or progressive weakness pattern is reported

data.description: 46-year-old woman presented with frequent collapse. Medical history included carotid endarterectomy in 2005 following a small right hemispheric stroke, and hypercholesterolaemia. No previous dermatological or scalp problems. Current medications: clopidogrel 75mg, aspirin 80mg, and simvastatin 40mg daily.

data.diagnosis: Takayasu arteritis (aortic arch syndrome) with carotid/subclavian arterial stenosis
data.description: A large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, often causing stenosis or occlusion of carotid and subclavian arteries. Reduced scalp and cerebral perfusion can cause scalp ischemia, ulceration, syncope, and stroke.
symptoms_in_common: Frequent collapse, consistent with cerebral hypoperfusion
Previous hemispheric ischemic stroke at a relatively young age
Scalp ischemia with ulceration/necrosis visible in the image
Angiographic appearance of major arch-vessel/carotid disease with collateral circulation
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypercholesterolaemia is not a typical primary feature
No reported constitutional or inflammatory symptoms

data.diagnosis: Severe carotid artery occlusive disease causing scalp ischemic necrosis
data.description: Critical stenosis or occlusion of the common or internal carotid circulation can impair flow through the external carotid branches supplying the scalp, producing ischemic scalp ulceration and cerebral hypoperfusion symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Scalp ulcer with a necrotic appearance
Vascular imaging showing severe disease affecting major neck vessels
symptoms_not_in_common: No prior scalp symptoms despite development of a marked scalp lesion

data.diagnosis: Atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease with recurrent carotid stenosis or occlusion
data.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the carotid and great vessels can recur after carotid endarterectomy and may cause transient cerebral hypoperfusion, ischemic stroke, and rarely external-carotid territory ischemia such as scalp necrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Frequent collapse compatible with cerebral hypoperfusion
Angiographic evidence of significant arterial narrowing/occlusive disease
Scalp ulceration potentially caused by poor external carotid perfusion
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe scalp necrosis is an uncommon manifestation of routine atherosclerotic carotid disease
Age 46 is relatively young for advanced diffuse atherosclerotic disease

data.diagnosis: Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia/necrosis
data.description: Giant cell arteritis is an inflammatory vasculitis of medium and large arteries that can cause scalp tenderness, ischemic scalp ulceration or necrosis, and ischemic neurologic complications. It usually occurs in adults older than 50 years.
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 46 years is younger than typical for giant cell arteritis
Frequent collapse is not a typical presenting feature
No reported headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual symptoms, or systemic inflammatory symptoms

data.description: 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and adalimumab. Four months before admission, she developed pain and stiffness in the MCP and IP joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission, she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the malleoli. Labs then showed anemia, leukopenia, neutropenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, high rheumatoid factor, ANA 1:640, low C4, mildly elevated anti-dsDNA, and positive cryoglobulins; HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests were negative. On admission after a burn from an electric heater, she had fever and pancytopenia without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Blood film, cultures, chest/abdomen/pelvis CT, CMV PCR, and tuberculin skin test were negative. She had traveled to Athens seven months earlier and stayed with relatives who kept several dogs.

A systemic protozoal infection transmitted by sandflies, often acquired in Mediterranean regions. In immunosuppressed patients, it can cause fever, pancytopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, autoimmune-like serology, and may occur without splenomegaly. The image is consistent with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes within macrophages, and the serum appearance is compatible with hypergammaglobulinemia.
symptoms_in_common: Pancytopenia including anemia, leukopenia, and neutropenia
Positive ANA and mildly elevated anti-dsDNA that can occur as infection-related autoantibodies
Travel to Athens, a Mediterranean endemic area
Exposure to dogs, an important reservoir for Leishmania infantum
Microscopic image showing macrophages containing numerous small intracellular amastigote-like organisms
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of hepatosplenomegaly
Absence of lymphadenopathy
Livedo reticularis
Purpuric lesions around the malleoli

data.description: A complication of longstanding seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia, usually splenomegaly, and increased susceptibility to infection. It may be associated with anemia, thrombocytopenia, high rheumatoid factor, and hypergammaglobulinemia.
symptoms_in_common: Fever in the setting of neutropenia
symptoms_not_in_common: No splenomegaly
Pancytopenia rather than predominantly neutropenia
Travel to a Mediterranean leishmaniasis-endemic area
Dog exposure
Positive cryoglobulins
Low C4 and mildly elevated anti-dsDNA
Intracellular amastigote-like organisms in the image

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis-systemic lupus overlap syndrome (rhupus)
data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause inflammatory polyarthritis, fever, cytopenias, hypocomplementemia, positive ANA, anti-dsDNA antibodies, cryoglobulins, and cutaneous vasculitic lesions. In this case, some lupus-like laboratory findings may instead be induced by visceral leishmaniasis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Travel to an endemic Mediterranean area with dog exposure
Marked hypergammaglobulinemia with fever and pancytopenia suggestive of infection
Image showing macrophages filled with amastigote-like organisms
Lack of typical lupus manifestations such as nephritis, photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, or serositis

data.diagnosis: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), potentially secondary to visceral leishmaniasis
data.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome characterized by persistent fever, cytopenias, immune activation, and macrophage activation. Infections, including visceral leishmaniasis, can trigger secondary HLH in immunosuppressed adults.
symptoms_in_common: Immunosuppression due to methotrexate and adalimumab
Potential infectious trigger from visceral leishmaniasis
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported hepatosplenomegaly
No reported markedly elevated ferritin
No reported hypertriglyceridemia or hypofibrinogenemia
No reported hemophagocytosis
Cryoglobulinemic vasculitic lesions are not typical primary features
Image more directly supports Leishmania infection than HLH alone

data.description: A 25-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department for evaluation of a hyperpigmented lesion on the shin. The lesion appeared as a small reddish-brown macule 3 years ago and has gradually increased in size. During the past several months, the lesion has become indented and increasingly tender. The patient denies systemic symptoms, including fevers and chills, and is primarily concerned about the changing appearance of the lesion and the new-onset tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a random blood glucose level of 217 mg/dL (12 mmol/L).

A chronic granulomatous dermatosis strongly associated with diabetes mellitus. It typically presents on the shins as slowly enlarging red-brown plaques that develop a yellow-brown, atrophic, indented center with a raised erythematous border. Histology shows dermal collagen degeneration (necrobiotic collagen) with granulomatous inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Initially reddish-brown macule that gradually enlarged over years
Hyperpigmented/yellow-brown lesion with an erythematous rim
New tenderness, which can occur with inflammation or impending ulceration

data.description: A benign granulomatous inflammatory skin disorder that may produce slowly enlarging papules or plaques, often on the extremities. Histology can show palisading granulomas around degenerated collagen, but lesions are usually annular and lack the prominent yellow atrophic center typical of necrobiosis lipoidica.
symptoms_not_in_common: Location specifically on the shin with a centrally indented atrophic plaque
Yellow-brown atrophic center with a red inflammatory border
Association with diabetes mellitus
Increasing tenderness

data.description: A common diabetes-associated skin finding consisting of small, round or oval, brown, slightly depressed macules on the shins, often called shin spots. It is related to diabetic microangiopathy and usually causes no symptoms.
symptoms_not_in_common: Single lesion progressively enlarging over 3 years
Prominent erythematous border
Yellow-brown plaque-like center
Scaling
New tenderness
Histologic granulomatous inflammation and necrobiosis rather than nonspecific microangiopathic changes

data.description: A chronic inflammatory and fibrosing disorder of the lower legs caused by chronic venous insufficiency. It can produce tender, hyperpigmented, indurated plaques and eventually atrophic or scarred skin, most often around the lower calves and ankles.
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age
Solitary localized shin plaque rather than diffuse lower-leg involvement
No reported edema, varicosities, venous stasis changes, or ankle involvement
Reddish-yellow plaque with a raised inflammatory border
Diabetes-associated necrobiotic granulomatous histology

data.description: 14-year-old boy with 2 days of acute fear of choking when swallowing after choking on chicken at dinner, followed by vomiting with attempted eating, marked reduction in oral intake and fluids, and sleepiness. Mother also reported inspiratory stridor during sleep for several weeks. Past history included infantile gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, sensory-integration training in childhood, incomplete immunizations after age 2.5 years, keratosis pilaris, and eczema. On examination he was alert but anxious, with persistent involuntary burping, drooling, and dry oral mucosa; neurologic exam was otherwise normal. Later exam showed hypertonic leg muscles and a mildly positive left Chvostek sign. Labs showed severe hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia, elevated parathyroid hormone, and low urine calcium.

data.diagnosis: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP1B), likely due to a GNAS methylation defect
data.description: An inherited or sporadic disorder of parathyroid-hormone resistance, primarily in the renal proximal tubules. It causes hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated PTH despite adequate parathyroid hormone production. The image shows abnormal GNAS methylation in the patient, supporting PHP1B.
symptoms_in_common: Hypertonic leg muscles consistent with neuromuscular irritability
Inspiratory stridor, potentially from hypocalcemia-related laryngospasm
Difficulty swallowing and fear of choking, potentially worsened by pharyngeal or laryngeal muscle irritability
Anxiety and sleepiness during severe electrolyte disturbance
Abnormal GNAS methylation pattern on the provided image
symptoms_not_in_common: Long-standing eczema
Keratosis pilaris
History of milk-protein allergy
History of sensory-integration training

data.description: Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability and can cause muscle stiffness, tetany, dysphagia, laryngospasm or stridor, anxiety, vomiting, and reduced oral intake. In this case, the hypocalcemia is most likely secondary to pseudohypoparathyroidism.
symptoms_in_common: Inspiratory stridor during sleep, compatible with intermittent laryngospasm
symptoms_not_in_common: Hyperphosphatemia and elevated PTH are not explained by hypocalcemia alone and suggest an underlying PTH-resistance disorder
Abnormal GNAS methylation is not a feature of nonspecific hypocalcemic tetany
Keratosis pilaris
Eczema
Milk-protein allergy history

data.diagnosis: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A) / Albright hereditary osteodystrophy spectrum
data.description: A GNAS-related disorder causing resistance to PTH and sometimes other hormones, usually associated with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features such as short stature, obesity, brachydactyly, and subcutaneous ossifications. It is a differential diagnosis for hypocalcemia with elevated PTH, but the methylation findings favor PHP1B rather than PHP1A.
symptoms_in_common: Neuromuscular irritability with hypertonia and positive Chvostek sign
Possible stridor or swallowing difficulty related to hypocalcemia
symptoms_not_in_common: The provided image demonstrates abnormal GNAS methylation, which is more characteristic of PHP1B than PHP1A
No reported short stature
No reported obesity
No reported brachydactyly
No reported round face or subcutaneous ossifications
Drooling and acute choking fear are not classic primary manifestations of PHP1A

data.description: 57-year-old woman with resected stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma presented with recurrent fever. Four months before admission, she developed bleeding from a right scalp lesion; evaluation showed ulcerated melanoma with positive margins. Three months before admission, she underwent wide local excision and neck lymph-node dissection, with metastatic melanoma in 2 of 26 lymph nodes and a BRAF V600E mutation. One month before admission, she started adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib; fever and nausea began the day after treatment initiation, improved after stopping the drugs and taking antipyretics, then recurred two weeks before admission. On presentation, temperature was 40.2°C with tachycardia, diaphoresis, ill appearance, mild right upper quadrant tenderness, and no rash.

Systemic infection with Histoplasma capsulatum, often involving the lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, and reticuloendothelial system. Tissue typically shows granulomatous inflammation with small intracellular yeasts highlighted by fungal stains.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple liver and splenic lesions on CT
Fungal organisms demonstrated on special staining in tissue
symptoms_not_in_common: Very close onset of fever the day after dabrafenib and trametinib initiation
No reported respiratory symptoms such as cough or dyspnea
No reported hepatosplenomegaly

data.description: A common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibition, characterized by recurrent fever, chills, diaphoresis, malaise, nausea, and occasionally hypotension or laboratory inflammatory abnormalities. Symptoms often improve with treatment interruption and antipyretics.
symptoms_in_common: Fever beginning the day after starting dabrafenib and trametinib
symptoms_not_in_common: Granulomatous inflammation in liver tissue
Fungal organisms identified by special stains
Multiple hepatic and splenic lesions
Pulmonary nodular or inflammatory CT abnormalities
Right upper quadrant tenderness is not a defining feature

data.description: An invasive Candida infection that can produce persistent fever and multiple small liver and splenic lesions, particularly in patients with malignancy or immunosuppression. Histology may show granulomas and fungal elements.
symptoms_in_common: Liver and splenic lesions on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported neutropenia or recent prolonged neutrophil recovery
No reported mucositis, candidemia, or central-line infection
Pulmonary findings are less characteristic
The small intracellular yeast-like tissue morphology is more suggestive of Histoplasma than Candida

data.diagnosis: Sarcoid-like granulomatous reaction induced by BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy
data.description: BRAF and MEK inhibitors can rarely trigger sarcoid-like inflammatory reactions, with noncaseating granulomas involving the skin, lungs, lymph nodes, liver, or other organs.
symptoms_in_common: Recent initiation of dabrafenib and trametinib
Possible hepatic involvement causing right upper quadrant tenderness
symptoms_not_in_common: Fungal organisms seen on special stains argue against a sterile sarcoid-like reaction
Very high fever of 40.2°C is less typical
Multiple liver and splenic lesions are more concerning for disseminated infection
Nausea and severe systemic toxicity are not typical primary features

data.description: 59-year-old man with history of prostate cancer metastatic to lumbar spine and periaortic lymph nodes diagnosed in 2001, with initial PSA of 11.3 ng/mL. In August 2011, presented to emergency room with abdominal pain. Lab tests showed elevated lipase (874 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (289 IU/L), and ALT (222 IU/L), with normal bilirubin. Later returned with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tachycardia but afebrile. Physical exam showed positive Murphy's sign and palpable gallbladder. Labs showed elevated alkaline phosphatase of 357 IU/L and normal serum lipase.

Metastatic spread of prostate cancer to the gallbladder, an extremely uncommon site of involvement. The imaging demonstrates a gallbladder mass, and the cytology/histology with prostate-lineage immunostaining is consistent with metastatic prostatic adenocarcinoma rather than a primary gallbladder tumor.
symptoms_not_in_common: Initial markedly elevated lipase
Normal bilirubin despite biliary-region symptoms
Afebrile presentation

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from the gallbladder mucosa, often presenting late with right upper quadrant pain, biliary obstruction, cholecystitis-like symptoms, or a gallbladder mass. In this case it is less favored because pathology supports prostatic origin.
symptoms_not_in_common: Known metastatic prostate cancer with pathology favoring prostate origin
Positive Murphy's sign suggesting acute gallbladder inflammation
Initial elevated lipase
Normal bilirubin

data.diagnosis: Acute cholecystitis due to malignant cystic-duct obstruction
data.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder caused by obstruction of cystic-duct outflow, in this case potentially from a gallbladder metastatic deposit or tumor rather than gallstones. It can mimic typical calculous cholecystitis clinically.
symptoms_in_common: Gallbladder lesion capable of causing obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever reported
No reported leukocytosis
No gallstones described on imaging
Initial marked lipase elevation is not typical of isolated cholecystitis

data.description: 13-year-old boy with a history of congenital bilateral cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, hypospadias, early tear deficiency, global developmental delay with mild intellectual disability, and Addison’s disease diagnosed at age 4 after recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive, hyperpigmentation, hypotonia, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia. He later developed muscle weakness and excessive fatigue, gait ataxia, and severe progressive dysphagia beginning at age 11, requiring liquids to swallow. On examination he had severe hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis of the elbows and knuckles, facial dysmorphism, dysarthria, nasal speech, saccadic eye movements with horizontal gaze nystagmus, dilated pupils with poor light response, mild bilateral optic atrophy, distal muscle wasting and weakness in the arms, milder pyramidal weakness in the legs, unsteady gait, hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated ACTH with normal electrolytes, aldosterone, and renin.

A rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by alacrima, achalasia, ACTH-resistant primary adrenal insufficiency, and progressive neurologic/autonomic dysfunction. A '4A' phenotype may include amyotrophy and other neurologic manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Primary adrenal insufficiency with markedly elevated ACTH
Hypoglycemia, vomiting, hypotonia, hypothermia, and failure to thrive at adrenal presentation
Preserved aldosterone, renin, and electrolytes, consistent with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency
Progressive severe dysphagia requiring liquids, compatible with achalasia or esophageal dysmotility
Muscle weakness, distal muscle wasting, excessive fatigue, and amyotrophy
Hyperreflexia and bilateral extensor plantar responses
Saccadic eye movements, nystagmus, poorly reactive dilated pupils, and optic atrophy
Cervical spinal-cord atrophy/signal abnormality on MRI, compatible with progressive neurologic involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Congenital bilateral cryptorchidism
Hypospadias
Inguinal hernia
Facial dysmorphism
Global developmental delay and mild intellectual disability

data.diagnosis: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, including adolescent cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy or early adrenomyeloneuropathy
data.description: An X-linked peroxisomal disorder caused by ABCD1 variants that produces adrenal insufficiency and progressive central nervous system white-matter or spinal-cord disease. It can cause spasticity, weakness, gait impairment, and visual or cognitive decline.
symptoms_in_common: Childhood-onset primary adrenal insufficiency with hyperpigmentation and elevated ACTH
Hypoglycemia and vomiting during adrenal crises
Pyramidal signs including hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses
Optic atrophy and visual pathway involvement
Possible spinal-cord involvement on cervical MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Congenital tear deficiency/alacrima
Severe progressive dysphagia suggestive of achalasia
Normal mineralocorticoid studies are less characteristic than in Allgrove syndrome
Dilated pupils with poor light response and prominent autonomic ocular findings
Congenital bilateral cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and inguinal hernia
Marked elbow/knuckle hyperkeratosis

data.diagnosis: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency with neurologic involvement
data.description: A group of inherited causes of ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency, usually presenting in childhood with severe cortisol deficiency, hyperpigmentation, hypoglycemia, and typically preserved mineralocorticoid function. Certain genetic forms can include developmental or neurologic abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent vomiting and failure to thrive
Normal electrolytes, aldosterone, and renin, supporting selective glucocorticoid deficiency
Possible developmental delay and neurologic impairment in selected genetic subtypes
symptoms_not_in_common: Early tear deficiency/alacrima
Severe dysphagia likely due to achalasia
Progressive combined peripheral and pyramidal neurologic syndrome with distal amyotrophy
Saccadic eye movements, gaze-evoked nystagmus, poorly reactive dilated pupils, and optic atrophy
Cervical spinal-cord atrophy/signal abnormality
Congenital cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and inguinal hernia
Hyperkeratosis of elbows and knuckles

data.description: 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, stage IV with metastases to bone, lungs, and liver, status post mastectomy and multiple systemic therapies including stem-cell transplantation 8 years earlier. She had been taking anastrozole for 3 months and paracetamol for pain. She developed progressive generalized weakness and episodic confusion over several days, rapidly worsening to unresponsiveness. On admission, she was found on the floor, disoriented, with lower leg weakness and inability to understand basic instructions. Examination showed her awake but unresponsive and uncooperative, without focal neurologic deficits initially; vital signs were notable for mild tachycardia, with normal blood pressure and no fever. A brain MRI 2 weeks earlier was normal.

data.diagnosis: Cerebral fat embolism syndrome secondary to metastatic bone disease/bone marrow necrosis
data.description: A neurologic manifestation of fat embolism in which marrow fat enters the circulation and causes diffuse cerebral microvascular occlusion, edema, and petechial hemorrhage. MRI commonly shows numerous bilateral diffusion-restricting lesions (the "starfield" pattern) and microhemorrhages on susceptibility imaging.
symptoms_in_common: Rapidly progressive encephalopathy with confusion progressing to unresponsiveness
Acute neurologic deterioration without an initial focal neurologic deficit
History of extensive bone metastases, which can predispose to marrow necrosis and fat embolization
MRI appearance of multifocal bilateral diffusion-restricting lesions with petechial/microhemorrhagic abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported recent long-bone fracture, orthopedic surgery, or major trauma
No documented respiratory distress, hypoxemia, or petechial skin rash
No fever

data.diagnosis: Multifocal embolic ischemic stroke due to cancer-associated hypercoagulability
data.description: Advanced malignancy can produce a hypercoagulable state, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, or tumor-associated thrombosis, leading to multiple acute embolic cerebral infarcts in different vascular territories.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced metastatic adenocarcinoma, a strong risk factor for cancer-associated thrombosis
Multifocal diffusion restriction on MRI compatible with acute ischemic injury
Lesions involving both cerebral hemispheres and multiple vascular distributions
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear focal neurologic syndrome such as unilateral hemiparesis, aphasia, or visual-field loss at presentation
Petechial microhemorrhages and diffuse starfield-like lesion distribution are more suggestive of fat embolism than typical thromboembolic infarction
No known atrial fibrillation, valvular disease, or documented arterial embolic source

data.diagnosis: Cerebral tumor embolism from metastatic breast carcinoma
data.description: Tumor cells can embolize to cerebral arteries in patients with disseminated cancer, causing multifocal ischemic lesions and occasionally hemorrhagic infarction. It is rare but can occur in advanced metastatic breast cancer.
symptoms_in_common: Long-standing stage IV invasive ductal breast carcinoma with lung, liver, and bone metastases
Hemorrhagic components can occur in tumor-related embolic infarcts
symptoms_not_in_common: No identified intracardiac tumor, pulmonary venous invasion, or other demonstrated source of tumor emboli
The diffuse punctate diffusion-restriction and microbleed pattern is more characteristic of cerebral fat embolism
No persistent focal deficit typical of a dominant large-vessel tumor embolus

data.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, usually involving posterior cerebral regions, associated with hypertension, renal dysfunction, cytotoxic therapies, eclampsia, or severe systemic illness. It can cause seizures and altered mental status.
symptoms_in_common: Acute confusion and decreased level of consciousness
Posterior cerebral white-matter/cortical MRI signal abnormalities
History of malignancy and prior systemic cancer therapies
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood pressure was reported as normal rather than severely elevated
No reported seizures, headache, or visual disturbance
Prominent diffusion restriction and susceptibility microhemorrhages are less typical than vasogenic edema in classic PRES
The rapidly progressive coma-like presentation with widespread punctate lesions favors embolic microvascular injury

data.description: Breast cancer may spread to the brain, producing focal or multifocal enhancing masses with vasogenic edema, seizures, headache, and focal neurologic deficits. Some metastases can bleed.
symptoms_not_in_common: Brain MRI performed 2 weeks earlier was normal
The current lesions appear as acute multifocal diffusion-restricting abnormalities rather than discrete mass lesions with surrounding vasogenic edema
No initial focal neurologic deficit, headache, vomiting, or signs of increased intracranial pressure
The abrupt progression over days is less typical of newly developed diffuse parenchymal metastases

data.description: 54-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 1 month of progressive weakness and sensory changes in all four extremities, followed by urinary difficulty. Exam showed hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffmann and Tromner signs, positive Babinski sign, and asymmetric weakness (MRC 2/5 on the right, 4/5 on the left). Sensory loss involved pinprick and temperature below C4, predominantly on the left, and decreased vibration and proprioception, predominantly on the right. Serologic autoimmune studies and CSF analysis were normal; ACE was mildly elevated. Brain MRI, chest/abdominal CT, and nerve conduction study showed no other organ involvement.

Neurosarcoidosis is granulomatous inflammation caused by sarcoidosis involving the nervous system. In this case, imaging shows an enhancing cervical intramedullary lesion and pathology shows noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells; absence of systemic organ involvement supports isolated spinal neurosarcoidosis.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute progressive weakness in all four extremities
Upper motor neuron signs including hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffmann/Tromner signs, and Babinski sign
Dissociated sensory abnormalities involving pain/temperature and proprioception/vibration
Urinary difficulty from spinal cord involvement
Cervical intramedullary MRI lesion with enhancement
Noncaseating granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells on pathology
No evidence of systemic sarcoidosis on chest-abdominal imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No pulmonary, skin, ocular, or lymph-node manifestations of systemic sarcoidosis
Normal CSF analysis

data.description: Idiopathic transverse myelitis is an inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord causing acute or subacute motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction, usually with a sensory level and MRI evidence of myelitis.
symptoms_in_common: Hyperreflexia and Babinski signs indicating myelopathy
Intramedullary cervical spinal cord lesion on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked asymmetry of weakness and sensory abnormalities
Mass-like focal enhancing lesion rather than typical longitudinal inflammatory cord signal change
Noncaseating granulomas with giant cells on biopsy
Mildly elevated ACE suggesting granulomatous disease

data.diagnosis: Cervical intramedullary spinal cord tumor (especially ependymoma or astrocytoma)
data.description: Intramedullary tumors such as ependymoma or astrocytoma can produce a slowly progressive cervical myelopathy through expansion and compression of spinal cord tracts and may enhance on MRI.
symptoms_in_common: Hyperreflexia, Hoffmann/Tromner signs, and Babinski sign
Sensory loss below a cervical level
Focal cervical intramedullary lesion with contrast enhancement
symptoms_not_in_common: Subacute onset over only 1 month is less typical for many intramedullary tumors
Noncaseating granulomas and multinucleated giant cells on pathology rather than neoplastic cells
Mild ACE elevation
No reported tumor-associated cyst, syrinx, or hemorrhagic cap sign

data.diagnosis: Infectious granulomatous myelitis (tuberculous or fungal myelitis)
data.description: Tuberculosis and certain fungal infections can cause granulomatous inflammation of the spinal cord, sometimes forming an intramedullary tuberculoma or inflammatory mass with enhancing MRI abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells on pathology
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported fever, night sweats, weight loss, pulmonary symptoms, or infectious exposure
Normal CSF analysis
No other lesions or systemic infection on chest-abdominal imaging
Pathology appears noncaseating rather than necrotizing/caseating granulomatous inflammation
No reported organisms on special stains or microbiologic testing

data.description: 33-year-old male with 20 days of cough and sputum production after a cold, with small amounts of yellow-white sticky sputum. No hemoptysis, fever, chills, chest pain, or dyspnea initially. Treated at a local clinic with intravenous therapy without improvement. Cough worsened 7 days before admission, especially at night causing sleep disturbance, sometimes with right-sided chest pain. Past history unremarkable; smoker for over 10 years, about 10 cigarettes/day, no alcohol use. Physical exam: T 36.2℃, P 112/min, R 19/min, BP 126/85 mmHg. Chest exam showed symmetric thorax and respiratory movements, normal vocal fremitus and percussion, coarse breath sounds in both lungs, and a small amount of wet rales in the right lung.

data.diagnosis: Right lower lobe lung abscess / necrotizing bacterial pneumonia
data.description: A destructive bacterial lung infection causing consolidation with areas of tissue necrosis and cavitation; imaging commonly shows a thick-walled cavity or multiple small cavities within an area of pneumonia.
symptoms_in_common: Worsening cough despite prior intravenous treatment
Wet rales in the right lung
CT appearance of right lower lobe consolidation with multiple cavitary or necrotic areas
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No chills
No marked dyspnea
No hemoptysis

data.description: A chronic suppurative lung infection caused by Actinomyces species, often producing mass-like consolidation, abscesses, cavitation, and extension across tissue planes. Histology may show suppurative inflammation and sulfur-granule-like bacterial colonies.
symptoms_in_common: Failure to improve with nonspecific initial treatment
Right lower lobe mass-like consolidation with cavitary/abscess-like changes on CT
Smoking history, which may increase risk through poor airway clearance
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or systemic constitutional symptoms
No hemoptysis
No reported poor dentition, aspiration event, or alcohol use

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause persistent cough, sputum production, focal consolidation, cavitation, and granulomatous inflammation. Although classically upper-lobe predominant, lower-lobe disease can occur.
symptoms_in_common: Lack of improvement after initial empiric treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No night sweats
No weight loss reported
No hemoptysis
Imaging is predominantly in the right lower lobe rather than the typical upper lobes

data.description: Bacterial pneumonia produces cough, purulent sputum, focal crackles, and lobar consolidation. More severe infections, including those caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or anaerobic organisms, may cavitate.
symptoms_in_common: Cough after an apparent upper respiratory infection
Right lower lobe consolidation on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or chills
No leukocyte count or inflammatory-marker elevation provided
Prolonged course and cavitary changes are less typical of uncomplicated pneumonia
No dyspnea

data.diagnosis: Pulmonary fungal infection, including pulmonary cryptococcosis
data.description: Pulmonary fungal infections can present with subacute cough and focal nodules, consolidation, or cavitary lesions. Histologic evaluation may demonstrate granulomatous inflammation with yeast-containing macrophages, depending on the organism.
symptoms_in_common: Minimal systemic symptoms despite radiologically significant lung disease
Failure to improve with routine antibacterial treatment
Focal right lower lobe consolidation and cavitary lesions on CT
Inflammatory/granulomatous-appearing changes in the provided pathology image
symptoms_not_in_common: No known immunosuppression
No fever
No reported exposure to birds, soil, mold, or endemic fungi
No neurologic symptoms suggestive of disseminated cryptococcosis

data.description: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. He had no travel outside Croatia but spent recreational time in forests and islands near his residence and owned a pet dog. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed total blood counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein within normal values. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

data.diagnosis: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
data.description: A zoonotic filarial nematode infection transmitted by mosquitoes, usually involving dogs as reservoir hosts. In humans, Dirofilaria repens commonly causes a solitary or migrating painless subcutaneous nodule. Histology typically shows a nematode with a thick multilayered cuticle and characteristic external longitudinal ridges.
symptoms_in_common: Painless well-demarcated nodule in the upper arm
Exposure to a pet dog, an important reservoir host
Recreational exposure to forested and island environments where mosquito exposure may occur
Normal blood counts and inflammatory markers
Negative serology for other helminth infections
Histologic image appearance of a filarial nematode with thick cuticle and external ridging

data.diagnosis: Human subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria immitis
data.description: An uncommon human infection with the dog heartworm, transmitted by mosquitoes. Human infection more often causes pulmonary nodules, but rare subcutaneous lesions can occur. Histology may show a Dirofilaria species, although D. immitis is less consistent with the cuticular morphology and clinical presentation than D. repens.
symptoms_in_common: Potential mosquito exposure during outdoor recreation
Normal routine laboratory tests can occur in human dirofilariasis
symptoms_not_in_common: Migrating brachial subcutaneous nodules are more typical of Dirofilaria repens
No pulmonary symptoms or pulmonary nodule reported
Histologic external longitudinal cuticular ridges favor Dirofilaria repens rather than Dirofilaria immitis

data.description: A tissue infection caused by larval Spirometra tapeworms, acquired through ingestion of contaminated water or undercooked intermediate hosts. It may present as slowly migrating subcutaneous nodules, but the parasite morphology differs substantially from the filarial nematode shown.
symptoms_in_common: Routine blood tests may be normal
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported ingestion of untreated water, frogs, snakes, or other typical exposure sources
Dog ownership is not a characteristic exposure for human sparganosis
The histologic image is more consistent with a round nematode than a cestode larva
External cuticular ridges support Dirofilaria rather than Sparganum

data.description:
66-year-old man admitted in March 2007 for dysphagia with repeated aspiration. Symptoms began around 2000 with unexplained falls while riding a motorcycle, later followed by blurred vision, photophobia, and worsening imbalance and unsteadiness. He had bilateral cataract surgery with lens implantation in 2000 without benefit. Over time he developed frequent falls requiring a cane, retracted head, slurred speech, inability to look down, and swallowing difficulty.

On examination in 2003, pupils were irregular with sluggish direct light reflexes. Vertical voluntary gaze and pursuit were slow and limited, while passive head movement preserved full eye movements; horizontal gaze was slow with bilateral adduction paresis, but convergence was normal. He was slow with distal rapid alternating movements and tended to fall backward. By March 2007, he had severe limitation of vertical and medial eye movements, absent convergence, no Bell’s phenomenon or optokinetic nystagmus, absent caloric and doll’s eye responses, severe nuchal rigidity and retrocollis, inability to sit independently, marked backward falls, axial rigidity, minimally brisk symmetric reflexes, and bilateral flexor plantar responses.

A rapidly progressive atypical parkinsonian tauopathy characterized by early unexplained backward falls, axial rigidity, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dysarthria, dysphagia, and frontal-subcortical dysfunction. The MRI appearance is compatible with midbrain atrophy, often termed the 'hummingbird' or 'penguin' sign.
symptoms_in_common: Early unexplained falls with marked backward instability
Progressive gait imbalance requiring a cane and later inability to sit independently
Vertical gaze slowing followed by severe vertical gaze limitation, especially impaired downgaze
Initially preserved passive eye movements despite impaired voluntary gaze, consistent with supranuclear gaze palsy
Later loss of vestibulo-ocular and doll's-eye responses
Slow horizontal eye movements and bilateral adduction impairment
Minimal limb-predominant parkinsonism relative to severe axial/postural impairment
MRI features suggestive of midbrain-predominant atrophy
symptoms_not_in_common: Irregular pupils with sluggish direct light reflexes
Blurred vision and photophobia as early presenting complaints
History of cataract surgery without visual benefit

data.description: An alpha-synuclein neurodegenerative disorder causing parkinsonism, autonomic failure, gait impairment, dysarthria, dysphagia, and sometimes eye-movement abnormalities. However, severe early vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and early backward falls favor PSP over MSA.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal eye movements can occur in advanced disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention/incontinence, erectile dysfunction, or other prominent autonomic failure
Early and profound backward falls
Prominent vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with impaired downgaze
Severe retrocollis and axial rigidity predominating over limb signs
MRI appearance more suggestive of midbrain atrophy than pontocerebellar or putaminal MSA changes
No documented cerebellar ataxia, stridor, or characteristic MSA respiratory symptoms

data.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy that usually causes asymmetric parkinsonism, limb dystonia, apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien-limb phenomena, and cognitive impairment; eye-movement abnormalities and dysphagia may occur later.
