symptoms_not_in_common: No marked asymmetric limb rigidity or bradykinesia described
No limb apraxia
No alien-limb behavior
No cortical sensory loss
No myoclonus
Early severe vertical gaze palsy and backward falls are more characteristic of PSP
Prominent axial rigidity and retrocollis are more typical of PSP-Richardson syndrome

data.description: A common alpha-synuclein disorder causing bradykinesia with rigidity, resting tremor, and later postural instability. Advanced disease can produce dysarthria and dysphagia, but early falls and vertical gaze palsy are not typical.
symptoms_in_common: Slow rapid alternating movements consistent with bradykinesia
Dysphagia and aspiration in advanced parkinsonism
symptoms_not_in_common: Falls began early in the disease course
Marked backward falls and severe early postural instability
Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, particularly inability to look down
Absent convergence and severe ophthalmoplegia
Retrocollis and severe axial rigidity
No resting tremor described
Rapid progression to profound disability
MRI midbrain atrophy pattern favors PSP rather than idiopathic Parkinson disease

data.description: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3°C and neck stiffness. CT of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 29 cm of water (ref: <20 cm). CSF analysis revealed: cell count 340 cells/µL (90% mononuclear cells, predominantly lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, and protein 0.80 g/L. HIV antibody test was positive with viral load 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL.

data.diagnosis: Cryptococcal meningitis due to Cryptococcus neoformans
data.description: Opportunistic fungal meningitis caused by encapsulated Cryptococcus yeast, especially in advanced HIV/AIDS. The images show round budding yeasts with prominent clear capsules/halos, characteristic of Cryptococcus on India ink or capsule-staining microscopy.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute 2-week course of fever and headache
Photophobia and neck stiffness consistent with meningitis
Markedly elevated CSF opening pressure (29 cm water)
Advanced untreated HIV infection with CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL
Microscopy showing encapsulated yeast forms with clear halos

data.description: A subacute meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, typically producing lymphocytic CSF inflammation, elevated protein, reduced glucose, and elevated intracranial pressure. It is more common in people with advanced HIV.
symptoms_not_in_common: Microscopy demonstrates encapsulated budding yeasts with clear halos rather than acid-fast bacilli
CSF glucose of 46 mg/dL is not markedly low for typical tuberculous meningitis
No reported pulmonary tuberculosis symptoms, cranial nerve palsies, or focal neurologic deficits

data.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes with brain involvement, caused by viruses such as herpesviruses, enteroviruses, or HIV-associated infections. CSF usually has lymphocytic pleocytosis with relatively preserved glucose.
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated opening pressure is more characteristic of cryptococcal meningitis
Advanced CD4 depletion strongly predisposes to opportunistic fungal meningitis
Microscopy shows encapsulated yeast organisms, which is not a feature of viral infection
CSF protein elevation is more prominent than in many uncomplicated viral meningitis cases

data.description: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Acute left pontine ischemic infarction causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia
data.description: A small acute ischemic stroke in the left medial pons involving the medial longitudinal fasciculus, producing impaired left eye adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus. The diffusion-weighted MRI appearance is consistent with an acute pontine infarct.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to adduct the left eye
Nystagmus of the right eye during attempted leftward gaze
Clinical pattern consistent with left internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Acute focal lesion in the pons on diffusion-weighted MRI
Atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation, increasing embolic stroke risk
symptoms_not_in_common: No limb weakness or sensory deficit
No dysarthria, dysphagia, or facial weakness
No altered consciousness

data.description: A disorder of horizontal eye movement caused by interruption of the medial longitudinal fasciculus. It produces ipsilateral impaired adduction and nystagmus of the opposite abducting eye; in this case it is most likely due to a small pontine infarct.
symptoms_in_common: Right eye abducting nystagmus when attempting horizontal gaze
symptoms_not_in_common: Diplopia described as occurring only when looking through the right eye
No mention of impaired convergence testing
No chronic or fluctuating eye movement symptoms

data.diagnosis: Posterior-circulation transient ischemic attack or ischemic stroke due to atrial fibrillation
data.description: Atrial fibrillation can cause cardioembolic ischemia in the posterior circulation, including small brainstem infarcts. Persistent focal eye movement findings and diffusion restriction favor completed ischemic stroke rather than transient ischemia.
symptoms_in_common: MRI evidence of an acute pontine ischemic lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: No other posterior-circulation symptoms such as vertigo, ataxia, dysarthria, or dysphagia
No motor or sensory deficits
Symptoms persisted for several hours rather than resolving rapidly, making transient ischemic attack less likely

data.description: Multiple sclerosis can produce internuclear ophthalmoplegia through demyelination of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, but it is substantially less likely in an elderly patient with abrupt symptoms and an acute diffusion-restricting pontine lesion.
symptoms_in_common: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia pattern with impaired left adduction
symptoms_not_in_common: Age of 83 years
Sudden onset over hours
No prior relapsing neurological episodes
No other demyelinating symptoms
Atrial fibrillation provides a stronger vascular explanation
MRI appearance favors acute infarction rather than typical multifocal demyelinating plaques

data.description: 35-day-old male infant, born at 37.5 weeks as a fraternal twin by cesarean section for breech presentation, previously healthy and fed breast milk plus formula, presented after 1 day of fussiness, pallor, warmth, and vomiting, followed by fever, tachycardia, mottled skin, and respiratory distress on admission. Exam showed temperature 39.1°C, pulse 176/min, respiratory rate 68/min with retractions, pallor, listlessness, a grade 2/6 holosystolic-flow murmur, splenomegaly 2–3 cm below the costal margin, and cool mottled extremities. Urinalysis showed dark red cloudy urine with large blood, protein, and granular casts. Labs revealed severe anemia (hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, hematocrit 20.9%), thrombocytopenia (36,000/mm³), elevated LDH, AST, and D-dimer, and peripheral smear with polychromasia, anisocytosis, and intracellular parasites with multiple ring forms. CSF was clear with 11 WBC/mm³, normal protein and glucose, and no organisms on Gram stain; Wright stain showed intraerythrocytic ring forms.

Malaria acquired transplacentally or during delivery, most often presenting in early infancy with fever, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and parasitemia. The smear appearance of multiple delicate ring forms within individual erythrocytes strongly supports P. falciparum.
symptoms_in_common: Dark red urine consistent with hemoglobinuria
Respiratory distress during severe systemic illness
Shock-like features including tachycardia, cool mottled extremities, and poor perfusion
Peripheral blood smear showing intraerythrocytic parasites with multiple ring forms
Multiple ring forms in individual red blood cells on the image
symptoms_not_in_common: Very early age at presentation is less common for malaria overall but is compatible with congenital malaria
A holosystolic-flow murmur is not a primary malaria feature and may reflect severe anemia or an incidental cardiac finding

data.diagnosis: Congenital malaria due to Plasmodium vivax
data.description: A transplacentally acquired malaria infection that can cause fever, anemia, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, and parasitemia in neonates. P. vivax typically infects enlarged young red cells and usually has only one parasite per erythrocyte, unlike the multiple-ring-form pattern seen here.
symptoms_in_common: Intraerythrocytic ring forms on blood and CSF Wright stains
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple ring forms within individual erythrocytes favor Plasmodium falciparum rather than P. vivax
Severe hemoglobinuria with dark red urine is less typical of P. vivax
Profound thrombocytopenia and severe shock-like illness are more characteristic of severe falciparum malaria
No described enlarged erythrocytes, Schuffner dots, or amoeboid trophozoites

data.description: Babesia is an intraerythrocytic protozoal infection that causes hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, and splenomegaly. It may resemble malaria on smear; however, Babesia classically shows tetrads forming a Maltese-cross pattern and is generally acquired by tick exposure, transfusion, or rarely vertically.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated LDH and evidence of hemolysis
Tachycardia and respiratory distress in severe illness
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple delicate ring forms within the same erythrocyte are more suggestive of Plasmodium falciparum
No Maltese-cross tetrads are described or visible in the provided smear images
Congenital babesiosis is rare
The clinical context and smear interpretation specifically favor malaria

data.diagnosis: Late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
data.description: Systemic bacterial infection in an infant can cause fever, tachycardia, respiratory distress, poor perfusion, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, anemia, and multiorgan dysfunction. It is an important initial consideration in a toxic-appearing febrile infant but does not explain malarial parasites on smear.
symptoms_in_common: Tachypnea with retractions and respiratory distress
Cool mottled extremities and shock-like appearance
symptoms_not_in_common: Intraerythrocytic multiple ring-form parasites are not a feature of bacterial sepsis
Marked hemolytic anemia with polychromasia and parasite-containing erythrocytes is not typical
Splenomegaly is less characteristic of acute bacterial sepsis
CSF Gram stain showed no organisms and CSF chemistry was not strongly suggestive of bacterial meningitis

data.description: 70-year-old man with history of Gleason 9 (4+5) adenocarcinoma treated with radical prostatectomy 10 years ago. Presented to primary care with rectal pain persisting for several weeks. Patient had lost 20 lbs over 3-4 weeks and complained of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, severe tenesmus, and rectal pain. Patient had been living independently on West Coast but relocated to East Coast to be closer to adult children.

data.diagnosis: Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with rectal involvement
data.description: Late recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after prostatectomy, with locally invasive pelvic/rectal disease and distant metastases. The CT images appear to show a pelvic rectal-region mass, hepatic lesion, and multiple pulmonary nodules, compatible with disseminated malignancy.
symptoms_in_common: History of Gleason 9 high-grade prostate adenocarcinoma
Imaging appearance of pelvic disease with liver and lung lesions suggestive of metastases
symptoms_not_in_common: Rectal pain and tenesmus are less common than urinary obstruction, hematuria, or bone pain in typical recurrent prostate cancer
No urinary symptoms are reported
No bone pain is reported despite bone being a common metastatic site

data.diagnosis: Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with hepatic and pulmonary metastases
data.description: A colorectal malignancy arising in the rectum can cause tenesmus and rectal pain and commonly metastasizes to the liver and lungs. The pelvic abnormality and distant lesions on CT are compatible with advanced metastatic rectal cancer.
symptoms_in_common: Liver lesion and multiple lung nodules compatible with metastatic spread
symptoms_not_in_common: No rectal bleeding is reported
No change in bowel caliber, constipation, diarrhea, or overt bowel obstruction is reported
Prior high-grade prostate cancer makes recurrent prostate malignancy an important competing explanation

data.diagnosis: Metastatic malignancy of uncertain primary origin involving rectum, liver, and lungs
data.description: Widespread cancer can present with constitutional decline and focal symptoms from pelvic or rectal involvement. The combination of a pelvic lesion, liver mass, and pulmonary nodules suggests disseminated malignant disease, although tissue diagnosis is needed to establish the primary site.
symptoms_in_common: CT findings concerning for lesions in the pelvis, liver, and lungs
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever, night sweats, or infectious symptoms are reported
No specific symptoms identifying another primary tumor site are reported
The prior history of aggressive prostate cancer provides a more specific likely source

data.description: 27-year-old man with 3 days of progressive myalgias in the upper legs followed by acute weakness in the legs and arms on the day of presentation, unable to lift his legs or stand. For several months he had difficulty sleeping, loose stools, ~5 kg weight loss, and hand tremors. He started an herbal stress-reducing supplement 4 days before presentation. Examination showed bilateral conjunctival injection, proximal muscle weakness (upper extremities 4/5, lower extremities 3/5), brisk patellar reflexes, and fine hand tremor. Labs showed severe hypokalemia (K 1.8 mmol/L), mild transaminitis and elevated alkaline phosphatase, mildly elevated bilirubin, mild CK and aldolase elevation, and venous pH 7.29.

data.diagnosis: Graves disease causing thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis
data.description: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins. The ultrasound appearance of diffuse thyroid enlargement with marked hypervascularity ('thyroid inferno') and histology showing diffuse hyperplastic follicles with scalloped colloid are consistent with Graves disease. Severe thyrotoxicosis can cause intracellular potassium shifting and acute flaccid weakness.
symptoms_in_common: Acute proximal muscle weakness involving the legs and arms
Mild transaminitis and elevated alkaline phosphatase
Diffuse hypervascular thyroid appearance on Doppler ultrasound
Thyroid histology compatible with diffuse hyperplasia
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral conjunctival injection is nonspecific and is not the classic Graves orbitopathy finding
Myalgias are less prominent than weakness in typical thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
Venous acidemia is not a defining feature of Graves disease

data.description: An episodic, potentially life-threatening neuromuscular complication of thyrotoxicosis in which thyroid hormone excess increases cellular potassium uptake, producing profound hypokalemia and sudden weakness. It commonly affects young men and may be precipitated by medications, supplements, carbohydrate intake, exertion, or stress.
symptoms_in_common: Abrupt progression to severe limb weakness
Predominantly proximal leg weakness with inability to stand or lift the legs
Extension of weakness to the arms
Hyperthyroid symptoms preceding the attack: tremor, weight loss, diarrhea, and insomnia
Brisk reflexes can occur early in thyrotoxic states
Recent herbal supplement as a possible precipitating exposure
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive upper-leg myalgias for 3 days are not always present
Conjunctival injection is not typical
Thyroid enlargement/hypervascularity indicates the underlying cause rather than periodic paralysis itself
Mild liver enzyme elevation is not a core manifestation

data.diagnosis: Herbal supplement-associated thyrotoxicosis or thyroid hormone exposure
data.description: Some herbal or 'stress-reducing' supplements may contain undisclosed thyroid hormone, iodine, stimulants, or other compounds that precipitate or worsen hyperthyroidism. In a person with underlying Graves disease, such exposure can trigger a thyrotoxic periodic paralysis episode.
symptoms_in_common: Symptoms worsened shortly after starting an herbal supplement
Acute hypokalemic weakness compatible with thyrotoxicosis-related potassium shifting
symptoms_not_in_common: Hyperthyroid symptoms were present for several months before the supplement was started
Diffuse thyroid hypervascularity and hyperplastic histology favor endogenous Graves disease rather than isolated exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion
No specific ingredient or confirmed thyroid hormone contamination is provided

data.description: An inherited skeletal-muscle ion-channel disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of weakness with low serum potassium, often triggered by carbohydrate intake, rest after exertion, stress, or certain medications. Thyroid disease can mimic or exacerbate this syndrome.
symptoms_in_common: Acute severe weakness affecting proximal limbs
Potential trigger from a recent supplement or physiologic stress
symptoms_not_in_common: Several months of hyperthyroid symptoms including tremor, weight loss, diarrhea, and insomnia
Diffuse hypervascular thyroid and thyroid histology consistent with Graves disease
No family history or prior recurrent attacks is described
Mild liver enzyme abnormalities are not typical

data.description: An acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy that causes progressive, usually symmetric weakness and classically reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes. It is an important alternative diagnosis for acute limb weakness but does not explain the severe hypokalemia or thyroid findings well.
symptoms_in_common: Leg weakness that became severe enough to prevent standing
Myalgias can occur in some patients
symptoms_not_in_common: Brisk patellar reflexes rather than reduced or absent reflexes
Severe hypokalemia provides a more direct explanation for weakness
Prominent tremor, diarrhea, insomnia, and weight loss suggest thyrotoxicosis instead
Diffuse hypervascular thyroid and Graves-compatible histology are not features of Guillain-Barre syndrome
No sensory symptoms, cranial neuropathies, respiratory symptoms, or preceding infection are described

data.description: A 70-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a routine examination. The patient reported that this mass had been present since birth. Her symptoms were minimal, with occasional difficulty cleaning the area and halitosis from entrapped food, but she was otherwise asymptomatic regarding the lesion.
A benign, non-neoplastic bony exostosis arising from the midline hard palate. It is often nodular or lobulated, covered by normal mucosa, slowly enlarges over time, and is usually asymptomatic.
symptoms_in_common: Large midline palatal mass with a multilobulated appearance
Long-standing lesion reportedly present since birth
symptoms_not_in_common: Halitosis is not a primary feature of torus palatinus, although it can occur secondarily from retained food

data.description: A benign localized overgrowth of mature bone on the palate. Palatal exostoses can resemble torus palatinus but may be less strictly midline or have an irregular nodular contour.
symptoms_in_common: Food retention and cleaning difficulty caused by the contour of the mass
symptoms_not_in_common: A lesion reportedly present since birth is less typical, since many exostoses become more evident later in life
Halitosis is not a usual direct manifestation

data.description: A benign, slow-growing tumor composed of mature bone. In the oral cavity it typically presents as a firm, painless, well-circumscribed bony mass.
symptoms_in_common: Possible functional inconvenience from a large mass, including food trapping
symptoms_not_in_common: Reported presence since birth is atypical because osteomas generally arise later
The broad, symmetric multilobulated midline appearance is more characteristic of torus palatinus than an osteoma
Halitosis is not typical of osteoma

data.diagnosis: Fibrous hamartoma or congenital oral hamartoma
data.description: A benign developmental overgrowth of normal tissue components that can be present from birth and may form a painless, soft-tissue mass in the oral cavity.
symptoms_in_common: Difficulty maintaining hygiene around a bulky lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: The image suggests a firm, broad-based, symmetric palatal prominence rather than a typical soft-tissue hamartoma
Most oral hamartomas are not specifically centered on the midline hard palate

data.diagnosis: Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary gland
data.description: A benign salivary-gland tumor that commonly occurs on the palate and usually presents as a painless, slowly enlarging, firm submucosal mass.
symptoms_in_common: Potential interference with oral hygiene if large
symptoms_not_in_common: Presence since birth is very atypical
The symmetric, multilobulated midline configuration is not typical of pleomorphic adenoma
Food entrapment and halitosis are not usual presenting features
Pleomorphic adenoma more often presents as a unilateral posterior palatal mass

data.description: A 52-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of lower back pain radiating into her left leg with associated leg weakness. She had a history of chronic back pain. Neurological examination revealed reduced power in her left leg (3/5), but was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Large L4-L5 lumbar disc herniation with nerve-root compression
data.description: A protruded or extruded degenerative disc at L4-L5 compressing the thecal sac and adjacent lumbar nerve roots. The sagittal MRI shows a prominent posterior L4-L5 disc herniation with marked central canal narrowing.
symptoms_in_common: Pain radiating into the left leg (sciatica/radiculopathy)
MRI evidence of a large lower-lumbar posterior disc abnormality causing canal/nerve-root compression
symptoms_not_in_common: No sensory loss was reported
No reduced reflexes were reported
No bowel or bladder dysfunction was reported

data.diagnosis: Lumbar radiculopathy, likely involving the L5 nerve root
data.description: Radiculopathy is pain, weakness, or sensory disturbance caused by compression or irritation of a spinal nerve root. In this case it is most likely due to the large L4-L5 disc herniation seen on MRI, which commonly affects the traversing L5 root.
symptoms_in_common: Lower back pain radiating down one leg
MRI evidence of lower-lumbar disc disease with nerve-root/canal compression
symptoms_not_in_common: No dermatomal sensory symptoms such as numbness or tingling were described
No reflex abnormality was reported
The exact distribution of leg pain and specific weak muscle groups were not provided

data.diagnosis: Degenerative lumbar spinal canal stenosis, exacerbated by L4-L5 disc protrusion
data.description: Lumbar spinal stenosis is narrowing of the spinal canal from degenerative disc disease, disc bulging/herniation, and facet or ligamentous degeneration. The MRI demonstrates substantial lower-lumbar central canal narrowing, most pronounced at L4-L5.
symptoms_in_common: Leg pain associated with lumbar pathology
MRI evidence of degenerative lower-lumbar disc changes and central canal narrowing
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms developed abruptly over two days, whereas stenosis often causes more gradually progressive symptoms
No neurogenic claudication, such as pain provoked by walking or standing and relieved by flexion, was reported
No bilateral leg symptoms were reported

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

data.description: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

data.diagnosis: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with multiorgan involvement
data.description: A disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia causing eosinophil-mediated injury to organs, commonly the heart, nervous system, lungs, skin, and gastrointestinal tract. In this case, cerebral ischemic lesions and cardiac injury are compatible with eosinophilic vascular and cardiac involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Marked hypereosinophilia of 5,500/μL (41% of white blood cells)
No identifiable secondary cause of eosinophilia such as parasitic infection, malignancy, allergy, or vasculitis
Disorientation, attention deficit, and immediate memory disturbance
Multifocal acute cerebral infarct-like lesions on diffusion-weighted MRI
Small hemorrhagic cerebral lesion on susceptibility-sensitive MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No typical chronic constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats were reported
No skin rash, urticaria, angioedema, or gastrointestinal symptoms were reported

data.diagnosis: Eosinophilic myocarditis/endomyocardial disease secondary to hypereosinophilic syndrome
data.description: Eosinophil infiltration of the myocardium and endocardium can produce myocardial injury, ventricular dysfunction, mural thrombus formation, and systemic embolic stroke. It is a major cardiac complication of hypereosinophilic syndrome.
symptoms_in_common: Multifocal cerebral ischemic lesions that may reflect cardioembolism
Neurologic deficits including dysarthria, weakness, and hemiparetic gait
symptoms_not_in_common: No chest pain was reported
No palpitations, dyspnea, edema, or overt heart failure symptoms were reported
No definite intracardiac thrombus was described on echocardiography

data.diagnosis: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA; Churg-Strauss syndrome)
data.description: A necrotizing eosinophilic small- and medium-vessel vasculitis that commonly causes asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, peripheral eosinophilia, lung infiltrates or nodules, neuropathy, cardiac disease, and occasionally cerebral infarction or hemorrhage.
symptoms_in_common: Cardiac injury with elevated cardiac enzymes and wall-motion abnormality
Neurologic involvement with multifocal cerebral ischemic lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of asthma
No sinusitis or chronic rhinosinusitis
No reported allergic rhinitis
No peripheral neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex, skin purpura, renal disease, or gastrointestinal vasculitic symptoms
No established systemic vasculitis was identified

data.diagnosis: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS)
data.description: An inflammatory vasculitis limited to cerebral and spinal cord vessels that can cause multifocal ischemic strokes, intracranial hemorrhage, encephalopathy, and segmental arterial narrowing or irregularity on angiography.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute cognitive dysfunction with disorientation and attention deficit
Upper-extremity weakness, hyperreflexia, and right hemiparetic gait
Multifocal cerebral diffusion-restricted lesions consistent with acute ischemia
Intracranial arterial irregularity/stenosis suggested by vascular imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked peripheral eosinophilia is not typical of isolated PACNS
Cardiac enzyme elevation and left ventricular hypokinesia are not typical of disease confined to the CNS
Pulmonary nodules are not typical of PACNS

data.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia or other clonal myeloid hypereosinophilic neoplasm
data.description: A clonal hematologic disorder in which excessive eosinophil production can lead to tissue infiltration, thrombosis, cardiac damage, pulmonary abnormalities, and central nervous system ischemic events. It must be excluded in otherwise unexplained hypereosinophilia.
symptoms_in_common: Possible thromboembolic or vascular cerebral infarcts
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis beyond eosinophilia, or abnormal blood-cell morphology
No reported splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, fever, weight loss, or night sweats
No bone marrow or molecular evidence of a clonal myeloid disorder was provided

data.description: A 44-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with abnormal findings on 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging. She had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer (T1N2M0, Stage IIIa, intraductal carcinoma, triple negative cancer) and had undergone adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy after a right breast conserving surgery 2 years prior. She was a non-smoker with no specific occupational or environmental exposure to known carcinogens and had been taking tamoxifen after chemotherapy. Laboratory results revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 mg/dL) and leucopenia (3,300/μL), with all other results within normal limits. Additional laboratory findings included an elevated angiotensin I-converting enzyme level of 101 U/L, and her purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. The biopsy sample was also negative for tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon gamma.

A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving intrathoracic lymph nodes and lungs. Stage II disease includes bilateral hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy with pulmonary parenchymal involvement.
symptoms_in_common: FDG-avid bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy on PET
No major systemic infectious symptoms reported
symptoms_not_in_common: History of triple-negative breast cancer, which initially raises concern for metastatic disease
Prior chemotherapy and radiation therapy, which may also contribute to alternative inflammatory or treatment-related processes

data.diagnosis: Sarcoid-like reaction associated with prior breast cancer or cancer therapy
data.description: A noninfectious granulomatous reaction resembling sarcoidosis that can occur in regional or distant lymph nodes after malignancy, chemotherapy, radiation, or other immune-modulating treatments, without representing tumor recurrence.
symptoms_in_common: FDG-avid mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes that can mimic cancer recurrence
Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level can occur in granulomatous inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Pulmonary parenchymal nodules and diffuse thoracic lymph-node involvement are more characteristic of systemic sarcoidosis than a purely localized sarcoid-like reaction
Mild leukopenia may be more suggestive of systemic sarcoidosis or prior treatment effect

data.diagnosis: Metastatic breast cancer to mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes and lungs
data.description: Recurrent breast carcinoma can metastasize to thoracic lymph nodes and lungs and may show intense FDG uptake on PET imaging.
symptoms_in_common: History of stage IIIA triple-negative breast cancer
FDG-avid thoracic lymphadenopathy on PET imaging
Mild anemia and leukopenia can occur in patients with prior cancer treatment or advanced malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Biopsy demonstrates noncaseating granulomas rather than malignant epithelial breast-cancer cells
Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level is not typical of metastatic breast cancer
Symmetric bilateral hilar and mediastinal nodal involvement is more typical of sarcoidosis
Negative infectious studies and granulomatous histology favor sarcoidosis rather than metastasis

data.description: Tuberculosis is a mycobacterial infection that can cause pulmonary infiltrates and granulomatous lymphadenitis; granulomas are classically caseating but may occasionally be noncaseating.
symptoms_in_common: Mild anemia and leukopenia can occur with chronic infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Purified protein derivative skin test is negative
Tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon-gamma testing of the biopsy is negative
Histology shows noncaseating rather than caseating granulomas
No fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough, or other constitutional tuberculosis symptoms are reported
Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level favors sarcoidosis over tuberculosis

data.description: 78-year-old woman with 2 months of lethargy and easy fatigue, referred for anemia and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Past history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, treated with perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination showed normal cardiac, respiratory, and neurologic findings, with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy; ECOG performance status 1. Blood tests revealed hemoglobin 99 g/L, normal white cell and platelet counts, ESR 120 mm/h, creatinine 110 mmol/L, calcium 2.81 mmol/L, and mildly elevated LDH 333 U/L. Further studies showed IgG kappa paraprotein 32 g/L, β₂-microglobulin 6.3 mg/L, free kappa light chains 1,400 mg/L, kappa/lambda ratio 280, and urine Bence-Jones protein (kappa); 24-hour urine protein was normal. Vitamin D, parathyroid hormone, and alkaline phosphatase were normal.

A malignant plasma-cell disorder characterized by clonal bone-marrow plasma-cell infiltration, monoclonal immunoglobulin production, osteolytic bone disease, anemia, hypercalcemia, and possible renal impairment. The marrow images show extensive plasma-cell infiltration, and the pelvic radiograph shows lytic bone lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly elevated serum free kappa light chains of 1,400 mg/L
Pelvic radiograph showing lytic bone abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported bone pain
No recurrent infections reported
No organomegaly or lymphadenopathy

data.description: An asymptomatic plasma-cell neoplasm with a substantial monoclonal protein and/or increased marrow plasma cells but without myeloma-defining end-organ damage. It may progress to symptomatic multiple myeloma.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly abnormal serum free kappa light chains and kappa/lambda ratio
symptoms_not_in_common: Anemia attributable to plasma-cell disease
Hypercalcemia
Radiographic lytic bone lesions
Lethargy and fatigue associated with anemia
Possible renal impairment
These myeloma-defining features favor active multiple myeloma rather than smoldering disease

data.diagnosis: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), IgG kappa type
data.description: A premalignant clonal plasma-cell condition with a low-level monoclonal protein and no attributable anemia, hypercalcemia, renal injury, bone lesions, or significant marrow plasma-cell burden.
symptoms_not_in_common: Paraprotein concentration of 32 g/L, which is high for MGUS
Marked free kappa light-chain elevation and kappa/lambda ratio of 280
Bence-Jones proteinuria
Anemia
Hypercalcemia
Possible renal impairment
Bone-marrow plasma-cell infiltration
Lytic pelvic bone lesions
Lethargy and fatigue
Overall findings strongly argue against MGUS and support active multiple myeloma

data.description: 20-year-old male with 3 years of bilateral breast enlargement without nipple discharge. Over the prior 4 years he had polydipsia, increased fluid intake, and polyuria that had recently improved. He also reported blurred vision corrected with glasses, occasional post-exertion headaches, and decreased facial hair growth. Past history included generalized nocturnal tonic-clonic seizures and focal right leg seizures from ages 6–13, treated with carbamazepine until age 14. Recent constipation and a chronic pilonidal cyst were noted. Examination showed minimal facial hair, small testes, bilateral breast enlargement without nipple retraction or masses, a small posterior anal fissure, and a small coccygeal lump with a central punctum.

data.diagnosis: Bifocal intracranial germinoma (suprasellar and pineal germinoma)
data.description: A primary central nervous system germ-cell tumor that commonly affects adolescent and young adult males. It often involves the pineal region and/or suprasellar-hypothalamic-pituitary region, producing diabetes insipidus, hypopituitarism, visual-field defects, and sometimes multifocal enhancing brain lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Several years of polydipsia, increased fluid intake, and polyuria consistent with central diabetes insipidus
Bilateral gynecomastia due to pituitary-hypothalamic endocrine dysfunction
MRI showing enhancing lesions in the suprasellar/hypothalamic-pituitary region and pineal region, a characteristic bifocal distribution for germinoma
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic pilonidal cyst
Posterior anal fissure
Constipation

data.diagnosis: Suprasellar germinoma with multifocal intracranial dissemination
data.description: A suprasellar germinoma is a germ-cell tumor involving the pituitary stalk, hypothalamus, or posterior pituitary. It frequently presents with central diabetes insipidus and anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies; additional pineal or ventricular lesions may represent synchronous or disseminated disease.
symptoms_in_common: Polydipsia and polyuria compatible with posterior pituitary dysfunction
Possible spontaneous improvement in diabetes insipidus symptoms can occur with changing hypothalamic-pituitary involvement
Reduced facial hair and small testes compatible with gonadotropin deficiency
MRI evidence of an enhancing suprasellar lesion with other intracranial enhancing lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Long remote history of childhood focal and generalized seizures is not a typical initial presentation of an isolated suprasellar lesion
Pilonidal cyst
Anal fissure
Constipation

data.diagnosis: Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
data.description: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is an infiltrative inflammatory-neoplastic disorder that can involve the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus, most often causing central diabetes insipidus and pituitary hormone deficiencies. It is a differential diagnosis for pituitary-stalk thickening, although the pineal and multifocal intracranial imaging pattern is more suggestive of germinoma.
symptoms_in_common: Polydipsia and polyuria consistent with central diabetes insipidus
Hypogonadal features including sparse facial hair and small testes
symptoms_not_in_common: Bifocal pineal and suprasellar enhancing lesions are more characteristic of intracranial germinoma
No reported bone lesions, skin rash, pulmonary disease, or ear involvement
Blurred vision is less characteristic unless there is substantial suprasellar mass effect
Pilonidal cyst
Anal fissure

data.description: A 50-year-old man with a history of injecting drug use presented to the emergency department with reduced level of consciousness and left arm weakness following five days of swinging fever, rigors, and headache. His past medical history included hepatitis C infection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and a recent hospital admission for discitis and psoas abscess. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C but he was hemodynamically stable and alert. Physical findings included a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border, splinter hemorrhages, a small digital infarct of the left third toe, and mild upper motor neuron pattern weakness in the left arm. Laboratory investigations revealed normocytic anemia and leukocytosis, with blood cultures growing methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

data.diagnosis: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus native aortic-valve infective endocarditis
data.description: Infection of the native aortic valve by MRSA, producing valvular vegetations and systemic embolic phenomena. The echocardiographic images are consistent with aortic-valve vegetation, and the clinical findings fulfill major features of infective endocarditis.
symptoms_in_common: Five days of swinging fever and rigors
Headache and reduced level of consciousness
New early diastolic decrescendo murmur consistent with aortic regurgitation
Digital infarct of the left third toe
Recent discitis and psoas abscess, which may represent metastatic staphylococcal infection
symptoms_not_in_common: None; the presentation is highly typical of complicated infective endocarditis

data.diagnosis: Aortic root abscess complicating aortic-valve infective endocarditis
data.description: A periannular infection extending from aortic-valve endocarditis into the aortic root, potentially causing abscess formation, aortic regurgitation, and conduction-system disturbance. The ECG images suggest PR-interval prolongation/conduction delay, while echocardiography suggests periannular involvement adjacent to the aortic valve.
symptoms_in_common: Early diastolic murmur suggesting aortic regurgitation
Evidence of aortic-valve infective endocarditis on echocardiography
ECG conduction abnormality consistent with PR prolongation/first-degree atrioventricular block
Systemic embolic signs including splinter hemorrhages and digital infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: Left arm upper motor neuron weakness is more directly explained by cerebral embolism than by the abscess itself
Reduced consciousness and headache are not specific manifestations of an aortic root abscess

data.diagnosis: Septic cerebral embolic stroke secondary to infective endocarditis
data.description: Embolization of infected valvular material from endocarditis to cerebral arteries, causing acute ischemic stroke and potentially cerebral infection. This is a common neurological complication of left-sided infective endocarditis.
symptoms_in_common: Left arm weakness with an upper motor neuron pattern
Aortic-valve infective endocarditis with likely vegetation
Peripheral embolic evidence, including a digital toe infarct
symptoms_not_in_common: Early diastolic decrescendo murmur is due to aortic-valve disease rather than stroke
Splinter hemorrhages are manifestations of endocarditis rather than cerebral stroke
PR-interval/conduction abnormality is more suggestive of periannular aortic-root involvement

data.description: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

data.diagnosis: Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency; glycogen storage disease type II)
data.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal glycogen-storage disorder caused by severe deficiency of acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA), resulting in glycogen accumulation in cardiac, skeletal, and respiratory muscle. The classic infantile form commonly causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, muscle weakness, and markedly reduced GAA activity.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly deficient confirmatory lymphocyte GAA activity
Compound-heterozygous pathogenic GAA variants in trans: c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T
Elevated CK, consistent with skeletal-muscle injury
Elevated ALT, which can occur with muscle and/or cardiac involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No poor feeding
No poor activity
No weak cry
Normal muscle power
Normal reflexes
No macroglossia
Only mildly decreased facial folds rather than obvious hypotonic facies

data.diagnosis: CRIM-negative or functionally CRIM-deficient infantile-onset Pompe disease
data.description: A severe subtype of infantile-onset Pompe disease in which little or no endogenous immunologically detectable GAA protein is produced, often due to null or severe splice variants. It carries a high risk of anti-drug antibody formation during enzyme-replacement therapy and requires early immune-tolerance consideration.
symptoms_in_common: Severely reduced GAA enzyme activity on newborn screening and lymphocyte confirmation
Two severe GAA variants, including a canonical splice-site variant c.2040+1G>T
Western blot image shows absent or markedly reduced mature GAA protein band, supporting severely impaired GAA processing/expression
Cardiac biomarker elevation with high pro-BNP
symptoms_not_in_common: No overt hypotonia at day 7
Normal muscle strength
Normal reflexes
No feeding difficulty
No respiratory symptoms described
No macroglossia

data.description: Cardiac involvement from glycogen accumulation in Pompe disease, typically producing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and an enlarged cardiac silhouette in infants. Cardiac disease may be detectable before substantial skeletal-muscle symptoms appear.
symptoms_in_common: Chest radiograph with enlarged cardiac silhouette/cardiomegaly
Elevated CK and ALT, which may accompany systemic muscle involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported heart-failure symptoms
No poor feeding
No poor activity
No respiratory distress reported
No hepatomegaly reported
No weak cry

data.description: A milder GAA-deficiency phenotype that usually presents later in childhood or adulthood with progressive proximal muscle weakness and respiratory muscle weakness, typically without severe infantile cardiomyopathy.
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation in the neonatal period
Very severe residual GAA deficiency
Elevated pro-BNP
Cardiomegaly on chest radiograph
Elevated ALT
Large birth weight
Absence of the typical later-onset pattern of progressive proximal weakness and respiratory insufficiency

data.description: 6-year-old girl with a 1-year history of intermittent migratory bone and joint pain after a fall on her left hand, including rib pain, right knee pain with limping, and left flank pain radiating to the left leg. Six days before admission, she developed back pain, worsening limp, and intermittent fever up to 39.8°C. The day before admission, she developed periorbital swelling, abdominal distention, and periumbilical discoloration. On examination, she was febrile (38.7°C) with bilateral periorbital discoloration, slight limping, and pain on external rotation of the right hip; abdomen was soft and nontender. Past history included infant gastroesophageal reflux and pollen allergy with allergic rhinitis. Labs showed anemia and elevated inflammatory markers.

A malignant proliferation of immature B-lymphoblasts involving bone marrow and potentially extramedullary sites. The marrow morphology and flow-cytometry images showing a blast population with B-cell markers including CD19 and CD10 strongly support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent migratory bone and joint pain
Possible bone marrow involvement causing skeletal pain
Periorbital swelling and discoloration from extramedullary leukemic infiltration or bleeding
Imaging findings consistent with multifocal soft-tissue/extramedullary lesions
Bone marrow images showing numerous blasts
Flow cytometry showing CD19-positive and CD10-positive blast population
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain beginning after a minor fall, which may be coincidental rather than caused by leukemia
Long 1-year intermittent course before acute presentation is less typical of overt acute leukemia

data.description: An embryonal tumor of sympathetic nervous system origin, usually arising from the adrenal gland or paraspinal sympathetic chain. It can metastasize to bone marrow, bone, orbit, liver, and lymph nodes, causing bone pain and periorbital ecchymoses.
symptoms_in_common: Age of 6 years, within the pediatric age range for neuroblastoma
Flank pain radiating to the leg
Possible multifocal lesions on CT/PET imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Bone marrow flow cytometry showing CD19-positive and CD10-positive blasts is not typical of neuroblastoma
Marrow morphology dominated by lymphoblast-like cells is not typical of neuroblastoma
No clearly described adrenal or primary paraspinal mass
Migratory joint pain over a year is less characteristic than persistent pain from osseous metastases

data.diagnosis: Burkitt lymphoma with bone marrow involvement
data.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can involve the abdomen, bone marrow, central nervous system, and extranodal soft tissues. It may produce abdominal enlargement, constitutional symptoms, anemia, and bone pain when marrow is involved.
symptoms_in_common: Bone marrow involvement by malignant B-lineage cells could produce skeletal symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: Periorbital ecchymosis is less typical than in metastatic neuroblastoma
The immunophenotypic pattern with CD10 and CD19 alone is insufficient for Burkitt lymphoma and may instead indicate precursor B-lymphoblasts
No reported rapidly enlarging abdominal mass, jaw mass, or markedly elevated tumor-lysis markers
One-year intermittent migratory pain is atypical for the usually rapidly progressive course of Burkitt lymphoma

data.diagnosis: Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarcoma
data.description: Acute myeloid leukemia is a clonal myeloid blast malignancy that can infiltrate marrow and form extramedullary tumor masses called myeloid sarcomas. Such lesions can involve bone, orbit, soft tissue, and lymph nodes.
symptoms_in_common: Periorbital swelling or discoloration can occur with orbital myeloid sarcoma
symptoms_not_in_common: Flow cytometry with strong CD19 and CD10 expression favors B-lymphoblastic leukemia rather than AML
No reported myeloid-marker pattern sufficient to support AML
Migratory pain over one year is less typical of AML
Periumbilical discoloration is not a characteristic AML finding

data.description: 54-year-old woman without comorbidities presented to emergency department with 12-hour history of redness and painful swelling in left gluteal region. Denied trauma. At admission: afebrile (36.2°C), normal blood pressure (109/65 mmHg), heart rate 89 bpm, mild peripheral oxygen desaturation (92% on room air) without respiratory distress. Rest of physical exam normal.

data.diagnosis: Acute bacterial cellulitis of the gluteal region
data.description: A bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, most often caused by streptococci or staphylococci. The photographs show diffuse erythema and swelling, while ultrasound appears consistent with subcutaneous edema/cobblestoning without a well-defined drainable collection.
symptoms_in_common: Acute painful swelling of the left gluteal region
No reported trauma or alternative local trigger
Ultrasound appearance compatible with subcutaneous inflammatory edema
Absence of a clear focal abscess on ultrasound
Afebrile presentation can occur, especially early in localized cellulitis
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild oxygen desaturation is not typical of uncomplicated localized cellulitis
No fever or systemic inflammatory symptoms were reported

data.description: A superficial acute bacterial skin infection, usually due to beta-hemolytic streptococci, characterized by painful erythema and edema. It is closely related to cellulitis but more often involves the upper dermis and lymphatics.
symptoms_not_in_common: The erythema appears relatively diffuse rather than sharply demarcated and raised
No fever, chills, or systemic illness were reported
Mild oxygen desaturation is not typical of erysipelas

data.description: A rapidly progressive, potentially life-threatening infection involving deep fascia and soft tissue. Early disease may initially resemble cellulitis, but worsening pain, systemic toxicity, skin necrosis, bullae, crepitus, or fascial fluid/gas would raise concern.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid onset of painful swelling and redness
Progressive-appearing erythematous and violaceous skin discoloration
Gluteal location can be involved in necrotizing soft-tissue infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever, hypotension, tachycardia, or toxic appearance
No pain out of proportion to examination was reported
No bullae, skin necrosis, crepitus, or anesthesia described
Ultrasound does not show obvious soft-tissue gas or a deep fascial fluid collection
Mild isolated oxygen desaturation is nonspecific

data.description: A localized collection of pus within soft tissue, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, which can produce painful erythema and swelling and may coexist with surrounding cellulitis.
symptoms_not_in_common: No fluctuance, drainage, or focal pustule was described
Ultrasound does not demonstrate a well-circumscribed fluid collection typical of an abscess
No fever or systemic symptoms were reported
Mild oxygen desaturation is not typical of a localized abscess

data.description: 41-year-old white male with history of myelofibrosis. Past medical history includes splenectomy and allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from single-antigen mismatched unrelated donor 2 years prior. After sun exposure during sailing trip, developed nonpruritic rash on face, trunk and extremities, associated with intermittent fever, muscle pain and weakness. Only current medication is daily oral acyclovir. Vital signs normal. Physical exam showed impaired ability to dorsiflex wrists while bringing palms together ('prayer sign'). Lab results showed: AST 41 U/L, ALT 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 147 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Antinuclear antibody test positive (1:320) with speckled pattern.

data.diagnosis: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD), sclerodermatous/dermatomyositis-like cutaneous phenotype
data.description: A late immune-mediated complication of allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. Cutaneous cGVHD can cause lichenoid or sclerodermoid skin changes, pigmentary changes, restricted joint mobility, and occasionally dermatomyositis-like eruptions.
symptoms_in_common: Allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation 2 years earlier
Diffuse nonpruritic rash involving face, trunk, and extremities
Facial erythema and widespread papular/poikilodermatous-appearing eruption in the images
Skin tightening with impaired wrist dorsiflexion and positive prayer sign
Mild elevation of AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase, compatible with possible hepatic involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent fever is less specific and may suggest an inflammatory, infectious, or autoimmune overlap process

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and characteristic photosensitive skin findings, including facial erythema, shawl-distribution rash, Gottron papules/sign, and periungual changes. It may occur after transplantation or in association with chronic GVHD.
symptoms_in_common: Photosensitive rash after sailing-related sun exposure
Facial erythema resembling a malar or heliotrope-like eruption
Erythematous eruption over the upper chest and trunk, compatible with a shawl-sign distribution
Papular erythematous lesions over the dorsal hands, compatible with Gottron-like papules
Mild AST and ALT elevation, which can occur with muscle inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Prayer sign and restricted wrist dorsiflexion due to skin tightening are more characteristic of sclerodermatous chronic GVHD than classic dermatomyositis
No creatine kinase elevation, aldolase elevation, electromyography findings, or muscle-biopsy findings are provided
Intermittent fever is not a defining manifestation

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lupus-like autoimmune syndrome
data.description: A systemic autoimmune connective-tissue disease that can cause photosensitive facial and generalized rashes, constitutional symptoms, musculoskeletal complaints, and positive antinuclear antibodies. A lupus-like syndrome may rarely occur in the post-transplant setting.
symptoms_in_common: Facial erythema with a malar distribution
Positive antinuclear antibody with speckled pattern
Mild liver-enzyme abnormalities can occur in systemic autoimmune disease or overlap syndromes
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive prayer sign with restricted wrist motion suggests skin sclerosis/fascial involvement rather than typical lupus
No arthritis, oral ulcers, alopecia, nephritis, cytopenias, serositis, or neurologic manifestations are reported
The timing after allogeneic transplantation strongly favors chronic GVHD as an alternative explanation

data.diagnosis: Systemic sclerosis-like chronic GVHD / eosinophilic fasciitis-like syndrome
data.description: A fibrosing disorder of skin and fascia that can occur as a manifestation of chronic GVHD after stem-cell transplantation. It causes skin induration, reduced joint range of motion, contractures, and a positive prayer sign; inflammatory rash may coexist.
symptoms_in_common: Impaired wrist dorsiflexion while pressing palms together, producing a positive prayer sign
Skin changes over the hands and extremities that may reflect fibrosis or sclerosis
Muscle pain and perceived weakness, which may occur with fascial inflammation and restricted movement
Positive antinuclear antibody can be present in connective-tissue-disease-like cGVHD
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute photosensitive facial and truncal eruption is less typical of isolated systemic sclerosis-like disease
Intermittent fever is not a classic feature
Gottron-like dorsal hand papules and a shawl-like chest eruption would favor dermatomyositis or dermatomyositis-like cGVHD
No Raynaud phenomenon, digital ulcers, dysphagia, or pulmonary fibrosis is reported

data.description: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.

Keratoacanthomas are rapidly growing crateriform keratinizing epidermal tumors that can occur as multiple lesions in eruptive forms. They may be associated with immunologic dysfunction, chronic renal failure, medications, ultraviolet exposure, or trauma.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple pruritic papules and nodules on the sun-exposed extensor surfaces of the arms and hands
Centrally crusted and keratin-filled crateriform lesions visible in the images
Progressive eruption of numerous lesions over months
Terminal kidney disease and long-term dialysis, which may contribute to immune dysregulation
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported history of habitual ultraviolet-light exposure
Marked sleep impairment from pruritus is not a defining feature of keratoacanthoma
Some lesions were histologically verrucae rather than keratoacanthomas

data.description: A rare eruptive keratoacanthoma syndrome characterized by the development of many small keratinizing papules, often with severe itch and prominent involvement of sun-exposed skin. Lesions may be persistent and difficult to manage.
symptoms_in_common: Numerous keratotic papules and crateriform nodules
Progressive appearance of lesions over approximately 10 months
Clinical improvement or disease control with topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions appear concentrated mainly on the upper extremities rather than being clearly generalized over the entire body
No reported facial predominance or ectropion
Age 51 years is younger than the typical later-adult presentation
No known familial or syndromic history is reported

data.diagnosis: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma type
data.description: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a keratinocyte malignancy that may present as a hyperkeratotic papule, nodule, ulcer, or crateriform keratoacanthoma-like lesion. Multiple tumors can occur in patients with immune dysfunction or prior immunosuppression.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple persistent hyperkeratotic, crusted, ulcerated papules and nodules
Sun-exposed distribution on the dorsal hands and forearms
Crateriform architecture with keratin plugs on clinical and histologic images
History of kidney transplantation and prior immunosuppressive exposure
Chronic renal failure and dialysis-associated immune dysregulation
symptoms_not_in_common: Reported histology favored keratoacanthoma and verruca rather than invasive conventional squamous cell carcinoma
No metastases or lymphadenopathy were identified on computed tomography
Severe generalized itch is less typical as the principal symptom of squamous cell carcinoma
No reported habitual ultraviolet exposure or known carcinogen exposure

data.diagnosis: Acquired perforating dermatosis associated with chronic renal failure (Kyrle disease spectrum)
data.description: Acquired perforating dermatosis is an intensely pruritic disorder seen particularly in patients with diabetes or end-stage renal disease on dialysis. It causes excoriated hyperkeratotic papules, often on the extremities, due to transepidermal elimination of dermal material.
symptoms_in_common: End-stage kidney disease with long-term hemodialysis
Multiple excoriated and crusted papules on the extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: The lesions are prominently crateriform and keratin-filled rather than typical umbilicated perforating papules
Histology demonstrated keratoacanthomas and verrucae rather than transepidermal elimination
Sun-exposed localization is more characteristic of keratoacanthoma-related disease than acquired perforating dermatosis
Large tumor-like nodules and repeated excisions are less typical

data.description: 15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst. Initially presented with left arm pain, frontal headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia without fever or neurological deficits. Seven days later developed acute lower back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission: mild left-sided weakness, proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, afebrile, no meningism, GCS 15. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia. By day 2, developed dysuria, urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, loss of temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffman signs. CSF and electromyography were normal.

data.diagnosis: Anterior spinal artery syndrome due to spinal cord infarction
data.description: Acute ischemic injury of the spinal cord, usually involving the anterior two-thirds of the cord and producing motor weakness, loss of pain/temperature sensation, and autonomic dysfunction. The MRI appearances are compatible with intramedullary T2 hyperintensity in an ischemic distribution.
symptoms_in_common: Acute severe lower back and limb pain
Loss of temperature sensation below thoracic sensory levels
Bilateral Hoffman signs suggesting corticospinal tract involvement
Normal electromyography early in the course
symptoms_not_in_common: Frontal headaches
Conjunctival hyperaemia
Leukocytosis with neutrophilia

data.diagnosis: Fibrocartilaginous embolism causing spinal cord infarction
data.description: A rare cause of spinal cord infarction in children and young adults, caused by embolization of intervertebral-disc fibrocartilage into spinal cord vessels. It typically presents with abrupt spinal or limb pain followed by rapidly progressive motor, sensory, and bladder dysfunction, often with normal CSF.
symptoms_in_common: Paraesthesia and dissociated loss of temperature sensation
Upper motor neuron signs including bilateral Hoffman signs
MRI spinal cord signal abnormality compatible with infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: Frontal headaches before the spinal symptoms
Conjunctival hyperaemia
No clearly reported preceding trauma, heavy exertion, or Valsalva-type event
Leukocytosis with neutrophilia

data.description: An inflammatory spinal cord disorder causing acute or subacute motor weakness, sensory impairment with a spinal sensory level, and autonomic dysfunction. MRI usually shows intramedullary T2-hyperintense lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute progression of neurological deficits over days
Thoracic sensory levels with impaired temperature sensation
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent acute severe pain at onset is more suggestive of spinal cord ischemia
Normal CSF without inflammatory abnormalities
Markedly asymmetric left-sided presentation
Frontal headaches
Conjunctival hyperaemia

data.description: An autoimmune demyelinating disorder that can cause severe myelitis with weakness, sensory loss, pain, and bladder dysfunction. It often produces longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesions, although confirmatory antibody testing and clinical correlation are required.
symptoms_in_common: Sensory disturbance with a defined thoracic level
Intramedullary spinal cord T2 signal abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: No optic neuritis or visual loss reported
No vomiting, hiccups, or area-postrema symptoms reported
Normal CSF is possible but does not specifically support NMOSD
Abrupt painful onset and ischemic-appearing clinical pattern favor spinal cord infarction
Conjunctival hyperaemia is not typical

data.description: 27-year-old male presented with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days before admission. Physical examination showed no palpable lymph-node enlargement or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed: WBC count 49.5×109/L, hemoglobin 161 g/L, platelet count 36×109/L, with 95% blasts in peripheral blood smear. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was markedly elevated to 13,022 IU/L. Flow cytometry showed leukemic blasts were positive for CD2, CD7, CD5, and CD3, and negative for TdT, CD34, CD13, CD33, CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22.

data.diagnosis: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL), with TCRAD-associated chromosomal rearrangement
data.description: An aggressive precursor T-lymphoid neoplasm characterized by marrow and blood replacement by lymphoblasts. The images show blast-rich peripheral blood and marrow, while the immunophenotype demonstrates T-lineage markers (cytoplasmic/surface CD3, CD2, CD5, and CD7). The karyotype/FISH findings support rearrangement involving the T-cell receptor alpha/delta locus at 14q11, with additional involvement of Xq22.3/IRS4.
symptoms_in_common: Acute presentation with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting
Very high proportion of circulating blasts (95%)
Blast-rich bone marrow and peripheral blood morphology
T-cell immunophenotype: CD2+, CD3+, CD5+, and CD7+
Negative B-cell markers (CD10, CD19, CD20, CD22)
symptoms_not_in_common: TdT negativity is less typical for precursor T-ALL, although it can occur
CD34 negativity is less typical for very immature T-lymphoblastic leukemia
No palpable lymph-node enlargement
No hepatosplenomegaly

data.description: A mature, aggressive T-cell leukemia that commonly presents with marked lymphocytosis and a mature post-thymic T-cell phenotype, often expressing CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7. It is usually a disease of older adults and frequently has splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and skin involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 27 years, whereas T-PLL usually occurs in older adults
Predominance of blast-like cells rather than typical prolymphocytes
Severe thrombocytopenia at presentation
No hepatosplenomegaly
No lymph-node enlargement
Chromosomal findings involving TCRAD/IRS4 rather than the more typical T-PLL-associated TCL1 rearrangements

data.description: A mature peripheral T-cell malignancy caused by human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). Leukemic ATLL generally expresses mature T-cell markers, often CD2, CD3, CD4, and CD25, and may present with high LDH, blood involvement, lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, hypercalcemia, and organ enlargement.
symptoms_in_common: Peripheral blood involvement by malignant T cells
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age is atypical for ATLL
Blast morphology is not typical; ATLL more often shows pleomorphic 'flower' cells
CD7 expression is often absent in ATLL
No reported CD4 or CD25 expression
No hypercalcemia reported
No lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly
No reported HTLV-1 infection
TCRAD-associated chromosomal rearrangement is more supportive of T-lymphoblastic leukemia than ATLL

data.description: 36-year-old Chinese man with a 1-month history of persistent fever. Previously healthy, with no significant past medical history, no prior TB, chronic illness, liver or kidney disease, transfusions, malignancy, or immune disease; no regular medications and no recent travel abroad. On admission, he was acutely ill with tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, and hypoxemia; physical examination showed bilateral pulmonary rales. He had persistent fever with pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, and clinical deterioration to acute respiratory failure. Initial labs showed leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, and markedly elevated ferritin.

A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells, leading to cytokine storm, hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, coagulopathy, multiorgan failure, and very high ferritin. The marrow images show hemophagocytosis.
symptoms_in_common: Pancytopenia including leukopenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia
symptoms_not_in_common: None; bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and severe hypoxemia are not required diagnostic features but can occur with severe HLH

data.description: Widespread infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis can trigger secondary HLH, especially when there is bone-marrow, hepatic, splenic, and pulmonary involvement. It may present with prolonged fever, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, diffuse lung infiltrates, and hemophagocytosis.
symptoms_in_common: Hyperferritinemia and hypofibrinogenemia consistent with secondary HLH
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported prior tuberculosis history
No reported chronic cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, or known tuberculosis exposure
No clearly described cavitary pulmonary lesions or classic miliary nodules

data.description: Disseminated Histoplasma capsulatum infection can involve the reticuloendothelial system, including bone marrow, liver, and spleen, and may trigger HLH. It commonly causes fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, markedly elevated ferritin, and diffuse pulmonary disease.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and respiratory failure
Bone-marrow hemophagocytosis compatible with infection-triggered HLH
symptoms_not_in_common: No stated exposure to bat or bird droppings, caves, or an endemic exposure setting
No reported immunosuppression
No described mucocutaneous lesions, lymphadenopathy, or gastrointestinal symptoms

data.description: Visceral leishmaniasis is a systemic protozoal infection involving macrophages in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow. It can produce prolonged fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, and secondary HLH.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported travel to or exposure in a leishmaniasis-endemic region
Severe diffuse pulmonary infiltrates and acute respiratory failure are less typical
No reported marked weight loss, darkening of the skin, or chronic constitutional symptoms

data.diagnosis: Severe viral infection causing infection-associated HLH, especially Epstein-Barr virus-associated HLH
data.description: Acute Epstein-Barr virus infection and other systemic viral infections can trigger HLH in previously healthy adults. EBV-associated HLH commonly causes persistent fever, cytopenias, liver/spleen enlargement, coagulopathy, hyperferritinemia, and rapid multiorgan deterioration.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid deterioration with shock and respiratory failure
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, rash, or infectious-mononucleosis-like illness
No viral serology or viral-load result is provided
Extensive bilateral lung consolidation is less characteristic of uncomplicated EBV infection

data.description: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand. He was reported to have been in perfect health during the cruise. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C) and comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. He exhibited hemiplegia of the left side, paresis of the right upper limb, normal tendon reflexes, and a Babinski sign on the left side. A transient rash was observed within 48 hours of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed leukocyte count of 41/mm³ (98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein level of 76 mg/dL, and CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.75.

data.diagnosis: Dengue virus encephalitis with cerebral vasculitis/ischemic strokes
data.description: A severe neurologic complication of dengue infection in which encephalitis and inflammatory vascular injury can cause multifocal cerebral ischemia. Dengue is endemic in several Pacific islands, including Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to dengue-endemic Pacific islands
Focal neurologic deficits including hemiplegia and right arm paresis
CSF pleocytosis with elevated protein and relatively preserved glucose
Brain imaging compatible with multifocal ischemic/inflammatory lesions and possible cerebral vasculopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported thrombocytopenia, bleeding, shock, severe myalgia, or arthralgia
Predominantly polymorphonuclear CSF cells are less typical than lymphocytic pleocytosis in viral encephalitis

data.diagnosis: Chikungunya virus encephalitis with cerebral vasculitis
data.description: Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne alphavirus infection that can cause fever and rash; severe encephalitis, encephalopathy, and vascular complications occur particularly in older adults.
symptoms_in_common: Travel to Pacific regions where chikungunya transmission can occur
Focal weakness and upper motor neuron signs
CSF inflammation with elevated protein and normal glucose ratio
Imaging findings suggestive of inflammatory vascular involvement and ischemic brain injury
symptoms_not_in_common: No prominent severe polyarthralgia or arthritis was reported
No reported myalgia or joint swelling
Neutrophil-predominant CSF is less typical than lymphocytic CSF inflammation

data.diagnosis: Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with VZV cerebral vasculopathy
data.description: Varicella-zoster virus can infect cerebral arteries, producing vasculopathy with multifocal infarctions, encephalitis, altered consciousness, and focal deficits; rash may be absent, remote, or transient.
symptoms_in_common: Fever and severe altered mental status/coma
Focal neurologic deficits including hemiplegia and Babinski sign
Vascular imaging findings compatible with cerebral arterial inflammation or narrowing
CSF pleocytosis and elevated protein with preserved glucose
Transient rash could represent a subtle or atypical zoster eruption
symptoms_not_in_common: No typical painful dermatomal vesicular rash was described
No history of recent shingles or chickenpox was provided
Travel exposure is not specifically required for VZV reactivation

data.description: West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne flavivirus that can cause severe meningoencephalitis in older adults, with fever, coma, focal neurologic deficits, and occasionally rash.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced age, which markedly increases risk of severe neuroinvasive disease
CSF pleocytosis with elevated protein and relatively normal glucose
symptoms_not_in_common: The imaging pattern of multifocal ischemic lesions and suspected arterial vasculopathy is not the classic West Nile pattern
No tremor, parkinsonism, or acute flaccid paralysis was reported
Neutrophil predominance can occur early but is less typical later in West Nile neuroinvasive disease

data.diagnosis: Bacterial meningitis with infectious cerebral vasculitis or septic embolic infarction
data.description: Acute bacterial meningitis can cause coma and focal deficits through meningeal inflammation, vasculitis, arterial thrombosis, or septic emboli, producing ischemic lesions on brain imaging.
symptoms_in_common: Coma with low Glasgow Coma Scale score
Focal neurologic deficits and Babinski sign
Imaging findings that may reflect inflammatory vasculopathy and cerebral infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF leukocyte count is relatively low for typical pyogenic bacterial meningitis
CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.75 is not typical of untreated bacterial meningitis, which usually lowers CSF glucose
Transient rash and recent tropical travel more strongly suggest an arboviral illness
No meningismus, purpura, hypotension, or documented bacteremia was reported

data.description: 20-year-old man with Crohn’s disease diagnosed at age 10, previously treated with prolonged glucocorticoids and improved over the past 3 years on weekly adalimumab. He presented with 2 weeks of progressive left calf pain and swelling that extended to the foot, along with a purpuric/erythematous rash on the dorsum of both feet. Three weeks before presentation, he had sore throat, nonproductive cough, rhinorrhea, and chills. He also reported multiple prior self-limited episodes of similar upper respiratory symptoms. On examination, he was uncomfortable from left leg pain and had left ankle synovitis with normal peripheral pulses.

An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis characterized by IgA deposition in vessel walls. It commonly follows an upper respiratory infection and causes palpable purpura of the lower extremities, arthralgia or arthritis, gastrointestinal involvement, and sometimes kidney disease. The biopsy images show leukocytoclastic vasculitis with vascular IgA, C3, and fibrin deposition, strongly supporting this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Purpuric erythematous rash on both feet and lower legs
Painful swelling of the left calf extending to the foot
Recent sore throat, cough, rhinorrhea, and chills preceding the rash
