New rapidly recognized maxillary soft-tissue swelling
symptoms_not_in_common: Pathology images show atypical lymphoid rather than gland-forming epithelial tumor cells
BCL6 and MUM1 immunoreactivity favors lymphoid differentiation rather than colorectal adenocarcinoma
No reported gastrointestinal symptoms or evidence of recurrent systemic colorectal cancer
Slight CRP elevation is nonspecific

data.description: An aggressive lymphoma with plasmablastic morphology that commonly involves the oral cavity, particularly in immunocompromised patients. It usually shows plasma-cell-associated markers and often lacks conventional B-cell marker expression.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid swelling with nonhealing extraction sites
Aggressive-appearing atypical large-cell neoplasm on cytology/histology
symptoms_not_in_common: The reported BCL6 and MUM1 staining pattern is more supportive of DLBCL than classic plasmablastic lymphoma
No reported immunodeficiency, HIV infection, or transplant-related immunosuppression
No reported plasma-cell marker findings such as CD138 or CD38 positivity
No reported EBV association

diagnoses.name: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.title: Diffuse large B-cell lymphomas

data.description: 24-year-old man presents with severely itchy rash that spread over two months. Had previously used an over-the-counter cream containing clobetasol, ofloxacin, terbinafine, and ornidazole which helped initially.

data.diagnosis: Tinea incognito (steroid-modified tinea corporis and tinea cruris)
data.description: A dermatophyte fungal infection whose usual ring-shaped, scaly border has been altered and allowed to spread by potent topical corticosteroid use. It commonly affects the groin, thighs, and trunk.
symptoms_in_common: Large annular and polycyclic erythematous plaques with peripheral scale and partial central clearing in the images
Involvement of the groin and inner thighs
Initial improvement after a cream containing terbinafine and clobetasol, followed by persistence/spread consistent with steroid masking

data.diagnosis: Extensive tinea corporis with tinea cruris
data.description: A superficial dermatophyte infection of glabrous skin and the groin, typically producing pruritic expanding annular plaques with an active scaly edge and relative central clearing.
symptoms_in_common: Expanding rash over weeks to months
Annular plaques with raised erythematous scaly margins
Distribution on proximal thighs and groin
Partial response to topical terbinafine-containing treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: The plaques appear unusually extensive and less sharply scaly than classic untreated tinea, likely because of prior clobetasol use

data.description: A reactive inflammatory eruption characterized by slowly enlarging ring-shaped erythematous lesions, sometimes with trailing scale inside the advancing border.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute spread over approximately two months
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent groin/inner-thigh involvement is more suggestive of dermatophyte infection
Peripheral active scaling and the very large polycyclic plaques favor tinea
Initial improvement with a terbinafine-containing cream supports fungal infection
Severe itch is less typical than in tinea

data.description: A pruritic eczematous disorder causing coin-shaped erythematous, scaly plaques, often on the limbs; lesions may become widespread but usually lack a true advancing ring border.
symptoms_in_common: Possible temporary improvement with potent topical clobetasol
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple lesions have annular/polycyclic shapes with central clearing
The lesions appear to have an advancing scaly edge rather than uniformly eczematous scaling
Groin-centered distribution is less typical
Progression despite steroid-containing treatment and response to antifungal treatment favor tinea

data.description: 72-year-old man with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease controlled on daily omeprazole until 11 months before admission, when heartburn recurred despite treatment. He then developed postprandial nausea and early satiety with gradual worsening over 9 months, progressing from solid foods to soft solids, then blended foods, then liquids over the following months. Two months before admission, EGD was limited by large residual gastric food despite 24-hour fasting, with no intraluminal mass seen. When he became unable to tolerate liquids, he presented to the emergency department. On examination, he was thin, mildly febrile, tachycardic, with mild epigastric tenderness and a nasogastric tube in place.

An infiltrative gastric cancer, often composed of poorly cohesive/signet-ring cells, that diffusely thickens and stiffens the stomach wall and may cause gastric outlet obstruction without a discrete intraluminal mass.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive inability to tolerate solids and then liquids
Large retained gastric food contents despite prolonged fasting
Marked gastric distension consistent with gastric outlet obstruction
CT and endoscopic appearance of diffuse gastric-wall thickening with enlarged folds and no discrete intraluminal mass
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild fever
Tachycardia
Recurrent heartburn despite omeprazole

data.description: A subtype of diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma characterized histologically by mucin-containing signet-ring cells. It commonly infiltrates the gastric wall diffusely, producing linitis plastica and obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Progression from solid-food intolerance to liquid intolerance
Persistent retained food in the stomach after fasting
Diffuse thickened, rigid-appearing gastric wall without an obvious luminal tumor
Histologic appearance compatible with poorly cohesive mucin-producing malignant cells
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild fever
Tachycardia
Longstanding GERD symptoms

data.diagnosis: Gastric outlet obstruction due to infiltrative gastric malignancy
data.description: Mechanical obstruction at the distal stomach or pylorus caused by an infiltrating gastric tumor. This produces delayed gastric emptying, severe gastric retention, vomiting or nausea, and inability to tolerate oral intake.
symptoms_in_common: Large residual food burden on endoscopy despite 24-hour fasting
Thin appearance consistent with poor nutritional intake
symptoms_not_in_common: No prominent vomiting is described
No overt gastrointestinal bleeding is described
No discrete obstructing intraluminal mass was seen

data.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the stomach that can cause wall thickening, enlarged folds, early satiety, and occasionally gastric outlet obstruction. It is a differential diagnosis for diffuse gastric infiltration but is less supported when pathology shows carcinoma-type cells.
symptoms_not_in_common: Progression to severe complete obstruction is less typical
Histology appears more consistent with infiltrative adenocarcinoma/signet-ring carcinoma than lymphoid cells
No lymphadenopathy, night sweats, or other lymphoma-associated systemic symptoms are described
No discrete ulcerated gastric mass is described

data.description: A male full-term neonate was admitted to the hospital 4 hours after birth for ecchymosis and petechiae. The infant was delivered by cesarean section at 40+5 weeks gestation due to failed induction, with birth weight 4000g and Apgar scores of 10. Physical examination revealed stable vital signs, weight 3850g, length 52cm, head circumference 35cm. The infant was alert and responsive with no special facial features. Skin examination showed large areas of ecchymosis on the chest, back, and upper limbs, with ecchymosis at the hepatitis B vaccine and vitamin K1 injection sites, and scattered pinpoint hemorrhages on the buttocks and lower limbs. The umbilical cord ligation site showed no bleeding, and cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal, and neurological examinations were normal.

A rare inherited bone-marrow failure disorder caused most often by biallelic MPL variants, resulting in markedly reduced megakaryocytes and severe thrombocytopenia beginning at birth. The parent-child sequencing image supports consideration of an inherited genetic disorder.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae beginning within hours of birth
Large ecchymoses on the chest, back, and upper limbs
Bleeding/bruising at vitamin K1 and hepatitis B injection sites
Otherwise well-appearing full-term infant with normal vital signs and normal general examination
No obvious traumatic explanation for the extensive bruising
symptoms_not_in_common: No umbilical-cord bleeding was observed, although this can occur in severe thrombocytopenia

data.description: An immune disorder in which maternal antibodies against paternally inherited fetal platelet antigens cross the placenta and destroy fetal/neonatal platelets. It commonly presents in an otherwise healthy newborn with severe petechiae, purpura, and bruising.
symptoms_in_common: Bruising or bleeding at injection sites
Normal vital signs and normal neurological examination
Healthy-appearing term neonate despite prominent skin bleeding
symptoms_not_in_common: The provided sequence image suggesting a familial genetic variant would be less characteristic than an immune platelet-antigen incompatibility
No intracranial hemorrhage or mucosal bleeding is described, although these are not required for FNAIT

data.description: An X-linked inherited platelet disorder affecting males, caused by WAS gene variants. It can produce congenital thrombocytopenia with petechiae and bruising; eczema and immune dysfunction may develop later.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and ecchymoses in the neonatal period
Potentially supportive family-based genetic sequencing findings
symptoms_not_in_common: No eczema is described
No recurrent infections or immunodeficiency features are described
No small-platelet finding is provided
Extensive bruising immediately after birth is possible but less specifically suggestive than for severe neonatal immune thrombocytopenia or CAMT

data.description: A rare inherited platelet adhesion disorder involving the GPIb-IX-V complex. It causes thrombocytopenia with giant platelets and mucocutaneous bleeding, including petechiae, bruising, and bleeding after procedures.
symptoms_in_common: Possible inherited genetic basis suggested by parent-child sequencing
symptoms_not_in_common: No mucosal bleeding is described
No prolonged umbilical-stump bleeding is described
No laboratory evidence of giant platelets or platelet-function abnormality is provided

data.diagnosis: Neonatal thrombocytopenia due to maternal immune thrombocytopenia (maternal ITP-associated neonatal thrombocytopenia)
data.description: Maternal antiplatelet autoantibodies can cross the placenta and cause neonatal platelet destruction. Affected newborns may develop petechiae, purpura, and bruising soon after delivery.
symptoms_in_common: Otherwise stable and clinically well newborn
symptoms_not_in_common: No maternal history of immune thrombocytopenia, autoimmune disease, or maternal thrombocytopenia is provided
The family genetic sequencing image favors consideration of an inherited thrombocytopenia rather than isolated passive maternal autoantibody transfer

data.description: 50-year-old man presented with 2-week history of constant worsening headache affecting the whole head. No history of head trauma, but reported headbanging at a Motörhead concert 4 weeks prior to presentation. Medical history was unremarkable and patient denied substance misuse. Neurological examination and laboratory studies, including coagulation screening, were normal.

data.diagnosis: Subacute/chronic subdural hematoma related to repetitive headbanging
data.description: A subdural hematoma is blood collected between the dura and brain surface, often from tearing of bridging veins after acceleration-deceleration forces. The CT appearance of a crescentic extra-axial collection and the delayed progressive headache after vigorous headbanging strongly support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Symptoms beginning days to weeks after repetitive acceleration-deceleration head movement
Normal neurological examination can occur in a relatively small or slowly developing subdural hematoma
CT evidence of a crescent-shaped extra-axial subdural collection with mass effect
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported direct head impact or conventional head trauma
No focal neurological deficits
Normal coagulation studies

data.diagnosis: Traumatic cerebral contusion with associated intracranial hemorrhage
data.description: A cerebral contusion is bruising and bleeding within brain tissue caused by rapid head acceleration or deceleration. Temporal and frontal regions are common sites, and contusions may coexist with subdural bleeding after repetitive head movement.
symptoms_in_common: CT suggestion of focal hemorrhagic brain injury in the temporal region
Potential association with an adjacent subdural hematoma
symptoms_not_in_common: No loss of consciousness reported
No focal neurological deficits
No documented direct head strike
Delayed presentation several weeks after the event is less typical for an isolated acute contusion

data.description: An acute-on-chronic subdural hematoma occurs when recent bleeding develops into a pre-existing or evolving chronic subdural collection. It can cause progressively worsening headache and may follow seemingly minor or repetitive mechanical head trauma.
symptoms_in_common: Repetitive head movement capable of causing bridging-vein injury
CT appearance compatible with subdural blood products of differing density or age
Neurological examination may remain normal early in the course
symptoms_not_in_common: No known prior head injury or prior subdural hematoma
No anticoagulant use, substance misuse, or coagulation abnormality reported
No confusion, weakness, gait disturbance, or reduced consciousness

data.description: A 35-year-old woman presented to the emergency room with a clinically incarcerated umbilical hernia. Fourteen days after the initial hernia repair surgery, she developed strong pain in the right lower abdomen and complained of umbilical secretion. Physical examination revealed the patient was afebrile. Blood analysis showed a slight elevation in leukocyte count at 11.05 × 10^9/L, while other parameters were unexceptional. Ultrasound of the abdominal wall detected a semisolid infraumbilical mass with a diameter of 5.5 cm. Initial histologic examination of the resected omental fat from the hernia repair revealed malignant cells with neuroendocrine differentiation. Immunohistochemical analysis was positive for synaptophysin and protein gene product 9.5. Fluorescent in situ hybridization revealed a rearrangement of the EWSR1 gene.

data.diagnosis: Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor (pPNET) of the omentum or abdominal wall
data.description: A malignant small round cell sarcoma occurring in soft tissue rather than bone. It commonly harbors an EWSR1 gene rearrangement and may show neural/neuroendocrine marker expression, including synaptophysin and PGP9.5. The imaging shows a sizable anterior intra-abdominal/abdominal-wall soft-tissue mass.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal wall or right lower abdominal pain
Mass involving omental fat/abdominal soft tissue
symptoms_not_in_common: Umbilical secretion shortly after hernia repair
Clinically incarcerated umbilical hernia at presentation
Only slight leukocytosis

data.description: A rare aggressive small round cell sarcoma that usually arises in the peritoneum or omentum of young people and can present as an abdominal mass. It is genetically characterized by an EWSR1-WT1 fusion rather than the classic Ewing-family fusion.
symptoms_in_common: Malignant small round cell-type neoplasm may be considered on initial histology
EWSR1 rearrangement can be present in this tumor
symptoms_not_in_common: Female sex is less typical because DSRCT predominantly affects males
Neuroendocrine differentiation with synaptophysin and PGP9.5 positivity is not the typical defining immunophenotype
Solitary small abdominal-wall/infraumbilical mass is less typical than multifocal peritoneal disease
Umbilical secretion after surgery
Incarcerated umbilical hernia presentation

data.description: An aggressive epithelial malignancy composed of poorly differentiated neuroendocrine cells, often arising in the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, or other organs. These tumors typically express neuroendocrine markers such as synaptophysin.
symptoms_in_common: PGP9.5 positivity can occur in tumors with neural/neuroendocrine differentiation
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 35 is younger than typical for poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma
EWSR1 gene rearrangement is not typical for neuroendocrine carcinoma
Presentation as a lesion in resected omental fat during umbilical hernia repair is unusual
No identified primary epithelial gastrointestinal or pancreatic lesion
Umbilical secretion and postoperative timing are not characteristic

data.description: 60-year-old Japanese woman presented with a black nodule on the right postauricular area. Initial staging after radical resection and sentinel node biopsy was pT3aN0M0 stage IIA. At 19 months post-surgery, imaging detected right jugular lymph node and lung metastases. Seven courses of pembrolizumab treatment later, evaluation showed further lung metastasis and new liver metastasis. Tumor harbored BRAF V600E mutation. Thirteen days after starting dabrafenib/trametinib, patient developed fever and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, increased liver enzyme levels, and coagulation abnormalities.

data.diagnosis: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) secondary to dabrafenib plus trametinib
data.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by excessive activation of macrophages and T cells, resulting in cytokine release, hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, and hyperferritinemia. In this case, the rapid onset after dabrafenib-trametinib strongly supports drug-associated HLH.
symptoms_in_common: Fever beginning 13 days after initiation of dabrafenib-trametinib
Bone marrow image showing macrophages with hemophagocytosis
Diffuse erythematous skin eruption with inflammatory infiltrates on skin histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive lung and liver metastases from melanoma
BRAF V600E mutation

data.diagnosis: Dabrafenib-trametinib-associated drug hypersensitivity reaction with rash
data.description: A medication-related immune reaction to BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy that can produce fever, diffuse morbilliform erythema, liver injury, and systemic inflammation. Severe reactions may overlap with or trigger HLH.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse faint erythematous rash on the arm
Skin biopsy showing superficial inflammatory cell infiltration
symptoms_not_in_common: Hepatosplenomegaly
Pancytopenia
Marked hyperferritinemia
Coagulation abnormalities
Bone marrow hemophagocytosis

data.diagnosis: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome
data.description: A severe delayed drug hypersensitivity syndrome characterized by fever, widespread rash, hematologic abnormalities, and internal-organ involvement, especially hepatitis. It can occasionally be associated with hemophagocytic syndromes.
symptoms_in_common: Fever after a new systemic medication
symptoms_not_in_common: Very rapid onset at 13 days is less typical than the usual 2-8 week latency
No eosinophilia reported
No facial edema reported
No lymphadenopathy reported at the time of reaction
Hepatosplenomegaly and hemophagocytosis are more characteristic of HLH
Pancytopenia rather than eosinophilia

data.description: HLH can be triggered by advanced malignancy, including metastatic melanoma, through tumor-driven immune dysregulation. It produces the same inflammatory and hematologic pattern as drug-induced HLH.
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt onset 13 days after dabrafenib-trametinib strongly favors treatment-associated HLH
Concurrent diffuse drug-type skin eruption is more suggestive of a medication reaction
No evidence provided that melanoma directly infiltrated the bone marrow

data.description: 14-year-old boy presented to trauma unit with gunshot wound to left eye. Alert and hemodynamically stable, blind in left eye, no CSF rhinorrhea. Pubertal status: Tanner stage S3, height: 1.7m (75th percentile). Laboratory findings: 8am serum cortisol 28 nmol/L (normal 171-536), thyroid-stimulating hormone 0.63 mIU/L (normal 0.27-4.20), free thyroxine 13.5 pmol/L (normal 13.6-23.2), luteinising hormone 0.7 IU/L (normal 1.3-9.8), insulin-like growth factor 1 19.4 nmol/L (normal 28.8-127.3), prolactin 13.04 pmol/L (normal 174-660.9), testosterone undetectable <0.1 nmol/L (normal 1-38.5).

data.diagnosis: Traumatic panhypopituitarism due to transorbital gunshot injury involving the sellar/pituitary region
data.description: Loss of multiple anterior pituitary hormone functions caused by direct traumatic injury to the pituitary gland or pituitary stalk. Imaging shows a retained metallic projectile in the central skull base/sellar region, supporting pituitary-region trauma.
symptoms_in_common: Very low 8 am cortisol, consistent with ACTH deficiency
Low-normal TSH with low free thyroxine, consistent with central hypothyroidism
Low luteinising hormone with undetectable testosterone, consistent with central hypogonadism
Low insulin-like growth factor 1, suggesting growth hormone deficiency
Markedly low prolactin, supporting pituitary/stalk injury
Pubertal delay or incomplete puberty relative to age (Tanner stage S3 at age 14)
Imaging evidence of a retained projectile near the sellar/central skull-base region
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute unilateral blindness of the left eye is more directly attributable to the ocular gunshot injury than to panhypopituitarism
No reported polyuria or polydipsia to indicate associated diabetes insipidus
Normal height percentile does not suggest longstanding severe childhood growth hormone deficiency
No reported hypotension, hypoglycaemia, vomiting, or altered consciousness despite severe cortisol deficiency

data.description: Adrenal cortisol deficiency resulting from inadequate pituitary ACTH secretion, most likely from traumatic pituitary damage. It can be life-threatening during acute illness or trauma.
symptoms_in_common: Severely low 8 am serum cortisol of 28 nmol/L
Central nervous system trauma involving the sellar/pituitary region
Possible pituitary hormone deficiencies in other hormonal axes
symptoms_not_in_common: He is alert and haemodynamically stable rather than hypotensive or in adrenal crisis
No reported nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, hypoglycaemia, or hyponatraemia
Low free thyroxine, low gonadotropins, low IGF-1, and low prolactin indicate broader pituitary dysfunction beyond isolated central adrenal insufficiency
Left-eye blindness is not a typical manifestation of central adrenal insufficiency

data.description: Deficient gonadotropin secretion from pituitary or hypothalamic injury causes inadequate testosterone production and delayed or arrested pubertal development.
symptoms_in_common: Incomplete pubertal maturation for age (Tanner stage S3 at 14 years)
Trauma affecting the pituitary-region structures on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe low cortisol is not explained by isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
Low free thyroxine is not explained by isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
Low IGF-1 and very low prolactin suggest multiple pituitary-axis involvement
Acute blindness in the left eye is not typical of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
Height at the 75th percentile is not typical of longstanding severe gonadotropin deficiency alone

data.diagnosis: Central hypothyroidism due to traumatic pituitary dysfunction
data.description: Insufficient pituitary TSH stimulation of the thyroid gland, producing low free thyroxine with a TSH level that is inappropriately normal or low rather than elevated.
symptoms_in_common: TSH of 0.63 mIU/L, which is inappropriately low-normal in the setting of low free thyroxine
Evidence of pituitary-region trauma on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, or weight gain
Profound cortisol deficiency and hypogonadism suggest panhypopituitarism rather than isolated central hypothyroidism
Acute left-eye blindness is not typical of central hypothyroidism
Normal-to-tall height percentile does not suggest longstanding severe untreated hypothyroidism

data.description: 14-month-old girl with a 3-month history of recurrent episodic vomiting starting at 11 months old, with four episodes lasting 3–5 days and associated lethargy, decreased oral intake, and intermittent diarrhea. Over the same period, she had developmental regression, stopping attempts to walk and crawling unsteadily with occasional falls. Parents also reported brief morning symmetric “shakes” lasting seconds over about 10 minutes without loss of consciousness. Born full-term without complications. On exam, she was alert and interactive but had frontal bossing, a full fontanelle with visible pulsations when supine, head circumference 51.5 cm, decreased tone in the legs, brisk 3+ patellar reflexes, and flexor plantar responses; eye movements and pupils were normal.

data.diagnosis: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to congenital aqueductal stenosis
data.description: Cerebrospinal-fluid flow is blocked at the cerebral aqueduct, producing enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles with relative sparing of the fourth ventricle. The MRI appearance is consistent with severe triventricular hydrocephalus and aqueductal obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Progressively enlarged head circumference crossing percentiles, reaching 51.5 cm at 14.6 months
Lethargy and decreased oral intake during episodes
Developmental regression with loss of walking attempts
Brief shaking episodes that could represent seizures related to raised intracranial pressure
MRI showing marked enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles with relative fourth-ventricle sparing
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent diarrhea
No persistent altered consciousness between episodes
Normal eye movements and pupils despite severe hydrocephalus

data.diagnosis: Raised intracranial pressure secondary to severe hydrocephalus
data.description: Increased intracranial pressure occurs when excessive cerebrospinal fluid enlarges the ventricles and stretches the skull in infants with open sutures and fontanelles. It can cause episodic vomiting, somnolence, developmental decline, and motor abnormalities.
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent diarrhea
Brief symmetric morning shakes without loss of consciousness are not a classic direct manifestation of raised intracranial pressure
Alert and interactive examination between episodes

data.description: Severe hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure can lower the seizure threshold. The reported brief symmetric shaking events may represent epileptic myoclonus, tremulousness, or another seizure-like phenomenon, although EEG would be needed for confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Severe structural brain abnormality with marked hydrocephalus on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No loss of consciousness
Shaking lasting only seconds over approximately 10 minutes is not specific for epileptic seizures
Vomiting, macrocephaly, frontal bossing, and full fontanelle are better explained by hydrocephalus than by seizures alone
Intermittent diarrhea

diagnoses.name: Aqueductal stenosis
diagnoses.title: Stenosis of the aqueduct of Sylvius

data.description: 31-year-old man with sleep apnea and a 20 pack-year smoking history, referred for newly diagnosed hypertension with repeated elevated readings up to 173/110 mm Hg. He reported 6 months of lethargy and intermittent headaches. On examination, pulse was 106 bpm and BMI 34; otherwise exam was unremarkable, with no cushingoid features, hyperpigmentation, bruits, or tremor. Full blood count, urea, electrolytes, and renal artery Doppler were normal. Endocrine testing showed elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio, with normal urinary metanephrines and mildly elevated 24-hour urinary cortisol; dexamethasone suppression was normal.

A form of secondary hypertension caused by autonomous excess aldosterone production, usually from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. It commonly produces hypertension with suppressed renin and an elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio.
symptoms_in_common: New-onset severe hypertension with readings up to 173/110 mm Hg
Normal renal artery Doppler, making renovascular hypertension less likely
Normal electrolytes do not exclude primary aldosteronism
symptoms_not_in_common: Sleep apnea
Obesity with BMI of 34
Tachycardia with pulse 106 bpm
Mildly elevated 24-hour urinary cortisol

data.description: Obstructive sleep apnea can cause persistent and resistant hypertension through recurrent nocturnal hypoxia, sympathetic nervous system activation, and sleep fragmentation.
symptoms_in_common: Lethargy, which may reflect poor sleep quality and daytime sleepiness
Headaches, which can occur with sleep apnea
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Mildly elevated urinary cortisol
Normal renal artery Doppler is not specifically supportive or exclusionary
Tachycardia is not a typical defining feature

data.description: Essential hypertension is the most common form of hypertension and is multifactorial, influenced by obesity, smoking, sleep apnea, genetic susceptibility, diet, and lifestyle factors.
symptoms_in_common: Sleep apnea, a strong contributing risk factor
Normal renal function tests and renal artery Doppler
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio, which raises concern for a secondary endocrine cause
Mildly elevated 24-hour urinary cortisol
Young age with relatively marked hypertension may be less typical

data.description: Cushing syndrome results from chronic glucocorticoid excess and may cause hypertension, weight gain, fatigue, glucose intolerance, proximal muscle weakness, and characteristic physical features.
symptoms_in_common: Headaches can occur in some causes of Cushing syndrome, particularly pituitary lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal dexamethasone suppression test
No cushingoid physical features
No proximal muscle weakness reported
No skin thinning, easy bruising, purple striae, or diabetes reported
Elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio is not typical of Cushing syndrome

data.description: These catecholamine-secreting tumors can cause episodic or sustained hypertension, headaches, palpitations, sweating, anxiety, and tachycardia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal urinary metanephrines
No reported episodic palpitations, sweating, tremor, panic-like episodes, or pallor
Elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio is not typical
Lethargy is less characteristic than episodic adrenergic symptoms

data.description: 46-year-old woman who experienced chest pain before having an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Pre-arrest rhythm strip showed sinus tachycardia. Initial troponin I was 5.9 μg/L (normal: 0-0.04 μg/L). Medical history included similar chest pain episode one year prior after taking sumatriptan for migraine, with transient inferior and lateral ST elevation on ECG but negative troponin at that time. Previous coronary angiography showed normal left coronary system and dominant right coronary artery with minor ostial spasm and slow flow. Negative bubble study for right to left shunting. Current medications: oral diltiazem, nicorandil, lansoprazole, and beclometasone inhaler. Patient was a former smoker.

data.diagnosis: Coronary vasospasm (vasospastic/Prinzmetal angina) causing acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction
data.description: Transient intense constriction of an epicardial coronary artery, likely involving the left anterior descending artery, causing severe ischemia, ST elevation, myocardial injury, and potentially malignant ventricular arrhythmia/cardiac arrest.
symptoms_in_common: Acute chest pain preceding cardiac arrest
Marked troponin I elevation consistent with myocardial injury
Transient ST-segment elevation during the prior chest-pain episode
Current ECG with prominent anterior ST-segment elevation/hyperacute ischemic changes in V1-V4
Prior angiography with no significant fixed coronary obstruction
Previously observed coronary ostial spasm and slow coronary flow
Prior episode temporally associated with sumatriptan, a medication capable of provoking coronary vasoconstriction
Use of diltiazem and nicorandil, medications commonly used for vasospastic angina
Former smoking history, a risk factor for coronary vasospasm
symptoms_not_in_common: None strongly atypical; cardiac arrest is an uncommon but recognized severe complication of coronary vasospasm

data.diagnosis: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction due to acute left anterior descending coronary artery occlusion
data.description: Acute interruption of blood flow in the left anterior descending coronary artery, most often from plaque rupture and thrombosis, producing anterior myocardial infarction and risk of ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest.
symptoms_in_common: Anterior precordial ischemic/ST-elevation changes, most prominent in V1-V4
symptoms_not_in_common: Previous coronary angiography showed no significant obstructive coronary artery disease
Previous chest-pain episode had transient ST elevation with negative troponin
Previous angiography documented ostial spasm and slow flow, favoring vasospasm rather than fixed atherosclerotic obstruction
Relatively limited documented atherosclerotic risk profile apart from former smoking

data.diagnosis: Sumatriptan-associated coronary vasospasm with myocardial infarction
data.description: A medication-triggered coronary vasospastic reaction caused by a triptan, which can constrict coronary arteries and produce transient ST elevation, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, or cardiac arrest even in patients without obstructive coronary disease.
symptoms_in_common: Prior chest-pain event occurred after taking sumatriptan
Prior transient inferior and lateral ST-segment elevation after sumatriptan exposure
Previously normal major coronary arteries on angiography
Current presentation is compatible with recurrent severe vasospasm causing ischemia and cardiac arrest
symptoms_not_in_common: No sumatriptan use is specifically reported immediately before the current cardiac-arrest event
Current ECG changes are predominantly anterior, whereas the prior episode involved inferior and lateral ST elevation

data.description: A nonatherosclerotic tear or intramural hematoma within a coronary artery that can abruptly obstruct coronary blood flow, causing acute myocardial infarction, ST elevation, and ventricular arrhythmias; it occurs disproportionately in women.
symptoms_in_common: Cardiac arrest can occur in severe presentations
Absence of known obstructive coronary disease on previous angiography
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior documented coronary spasm and sumatriptan-associated transient ST elevation more strongly support vasospasm
No angiographic evidence of dissection is provided
Prior symptoms were transient with negative troponin, which is more typical of reversible vasospasm than SCAD

data.description: A 44-year-old woman with cerebral palsy and multiple sclerosis (diagnosed at age 16) presented to the emergency department with four days of acute constipation and vomiting. She had a history of chronic constipation due to neurogenic bowel dysfunction secondary to her underlying conditions, initially managed with laxatives. Her constipation had become severe enough to warrant insertion of a sacral anterior root stimulator in the last year. On examination, her abdomen was markedly distended, diffusely tender, with absent bowel sounds. There was no guarding, rigidity, or previous incisions, and all hernia orifices were intact. Vital signs showed tachycardia (140 beats/min), tachypnea, normal blood pressure (130/60 mmHg), and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Laboratory findings revealed normal pH of 7.36, hypocapnea (PCO2 29mmHg), hyperlactataemia (20 mg/dL), normal PO2 (), white blood cell count of 10,500 cells/mm3 (73% neutrophils), and elevated C-reactive protein of 3.25 mg/dL.

data.diagnosis: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) with megacolon
data.description: Functional obstruction of the colon caused by severe autonomic and neuromuscular dysmotility without a mechanical obstructing lesion. It can cause massive colonic dilatation, ischemia, and perforation.
symptoms_in_common: Underlying neurologic disease causing neurogenic bowel dysfunction
Imaging showing massive gaseous colonic dilatation with air-fluid levels
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic constipation severe enough to require a sacral anterior root stimulator
Fecal loading/impaction in the distal colon on CT may suggest an additional mechanical fecal obstruction
Hyperlactataemia raises concern for ischemia or perforation rather than uncomplicated pseudo-obstruction

data.diagnosis: Fecal impaction causing acute large-bowel obstruction (fecaloma-associated megacolon)
data.description: A large, hardened accumulation of stool obstructs the distal colon or rectum, producing proximal colonic dilatation, vomiting, abdominal pain, and potentially ischemia or perforation.
symptoms_in_common: Neurogenic bowel dysfunction from cerebral palsy and multiple sclerosis
CT appearance of substantial stool burden in the distal colon/rectum with marked proximal gaseous colonic dilatation
symptoms_not_in_common: Tachypnea with hypocapnea is not a primary feature of uncomplicated fecal impaction
Hyperlactataemia suggests possible bowel ischemia or perforation, a complication rather than a typical early finding
Only mild leukocytosis despite severe obstructive findings

data.diagnosis: Stercoral colitis with impending or contained colonic perforation
data.description: Inflammation, pressure necrosis, ulceration, and possible perforation of the colon caused by prolonged fecal impaction. It occurs particularly in patients with chronic constipation and neurologic impairment.
symptoms_in_common: Hyperlactataemia suggesting bowel hypoperfusion or ischemia
Fecal impaction with marked colonic dilatation on CT
Possible small extraluminal gas focus on CT, concerning for perforation
symptoms_not_in_common: No guarding or rigidity despite concern for perforation
Normal blood pressure
Only mildly elevated white blood cell count
No reported fever

data.description: 64-year-old man with 5 months of cough with thin yellow sputum, exertional dyspnea, chest tightness, and wheezing, followed 10 days before presentation by lethargy, myalgias, chills, headaches, anorexia, and night sweats. He presented with dyspnea, wheezing, cough, headaches, neck stiffness, and photophobia. On examination he was febrile and tachycardic, mildly ill-appearing, with neck stiffness, bilateral inspiratory crackles, and mild chronic synovial thickening in the hands. History included fibromyalgia, L5 radiculopathy with foot drop, carpal tunnel syndrome, knee and neck osteoarthritis, cervical spondylosis, sleep apnea, and peptic ulcer disease. He worked in a healthcare facility, had recent travel to Florida and Europe/Caribbean, and had a sister with systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma, and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated ESR, mild hyponatremia, and microscopic hematuria.

A necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis, usually associated with cytoplasmic ANCA/PR3-ANCA, that can involve the lungs, kidneys, upper airways, joints, eyes, and nervous system. The CT abnormalities may represent pulmonary capillaritis/alveolar hemorrhage or inflammatory pulmonary nodules, and the immunofluorescence image is compatible with ANCA staining.
symptoms_in_common: Fever, chills, lethargy, anorexia, myalgias, and night sweats
Headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia, which can occur with neurologic or meningeal vasculitic involvement
Pulmonary CT abnormalities with multifocal ground-glass/nodular inflammatory changes
symptoms_not_in_common: Thin yellow sputum suggestive of a concurrent infectious bronchitis or pneumonia
Mild hyponatremia

data.description: A pauci-immune ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis, commonly associated with MPO-ANCA, that frequently causes pulmonary capillaritis with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
symptoms_in_common: Dyspnea, cough, chest symptoms, and crackles compatible with pulmonary capillaritis or alveolar hemorrhage
Fever, malaise, myalgias, anorexia, and night sweats
Ground-glass pulmonary CT changes that can occur with alveolar hemorrhage
symptoms_not_in_common: Prolonged wheezing with thin yellow sputum
Neck stiffness and photophobia are less typical manifestations
Chronic hand synovial thickening is less characteristic than in some connective-tissue diseases

data.diagnosis: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (anti-GBM disease/Goodpasture syndrome)
data.description: An autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome caused by antibodies directed against the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. It produces rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage, often with diffuse ground-glass lung opacities.
symptoms_in_common: Dyspnea and cough with bilateral crackles
Pulmonary ground-glass abnormalities that could reflect diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
Constitutional symptoms including fatigue and fever can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Wheezing and chronic thin yellow sputum are not classic
Headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia are not typical
Chronic synovial thickening is not typical
Night sweats and travel-associated infectious symptoms are less characteristic

data.description: Legionella is an atypical bacterial pneumonia acquired from contaminated water aerosols or healthcare-associated water systems. It can cause fever, cough, dyspnea, headache, myalgias, hyponatremia, and occasionally encephalopathy or aseptic-meningitis-like symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Fever, chills, lethargy, myalgias, anorexia, and night sweats
Cough with sputum, dyspnea, chest tightness, crackles, and wheezing
Healthcare-facility employment and recent travel, which may increase exposure risk
symptoms_not_in_common: Five months of preceding cough is longer than typical acute Legionella pneumonia
Microscopic hematuria is not a typical primary feature
Chronic hand synovial thickening is not typical

data.description: 47-year-old woman admitted for left lumbar pain and macroscopic hematuria. Past medical history was unremarkable. Physical examination showed pallor without peripheral edema, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, and diuresis of 1000 mL/day. Laboratory studies showed moderate normocytic anemia, marked proteinuria and hematuria, and impaired renal function. Autoimmune, antiphospholipid, vasculitis, anti-GBM, cryoglobulin, hepatitis B/C, HIV, and monoclonal protein studies were negative.

A renal vascular injury pattern caused by endothelial damage, platelet-rich microthrombi, arteriolar intimal swelling or concentric 'onion-skin' thickening, and glomerular ischemia. The biopsy images are most consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy, including vascular thrombotic/occlusive lesions and endothelial injury on electron microscopy.
symptoms_in_common: Histologic vascular thrombotic lesions and arteriolar concentric intimal thickening
Electron-microscopy evidence of endothelial injury and subendothelial widening
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal blood pressure
Absence of reported thrombocytopenia
No peripheral edema

data.description: A complement-mediated form of thrombotic microangiopathy that predominantly affects the kidneys and may occur without diarrheal illness. It causes microvascular thrombosis, hemolytic anemia, acute kidney injury, hematuria, and proteinuria; some cases are renal-limited.
symptoms_in_common: Renal thrombotic microangiopathy pattern on biopsy
Negative autoimmune, vasculitis, anti-GBM, viral, cryoglobulin, and monoclonal-protein studies
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported thrombocytopenia
No documented biochemical evidence of hemolysis such as elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, or schistocytes
No hypertension reported
Left lumbar pain is not a classic presenting feature

data.description: A systemic thrombotic microangiopathy usually caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, leading to platelet-rich microthrombi, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and variable renal, neurologic, and febrile manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Hematuria and proteinuria can occur with renal involvement
Thrombotic microangiopathy-type vascular lesions on renal biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported thrombocytopenia
No neurologic manifestations
No fever
Marked renal-predominant disease is more characteristic of HUS/aHUS than classic TTP
No documented evidence of hemolysis or ADAMTS13 deficiency

data.description: Severe hypertension can injure renal arterioles and glomeruli, producing fibrinoid vascular injury, thrombotic microangiopathy, ischemic glomerular collapse, renal dysfunction, hematuria, and proteinuria.
symptoms_in_common: Anemia may accompany severe thrombotic microangiopathy
Concentric arteriolar intimal thickening and thrombotic vascular lesions on biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg rather than severely elevated
No history of hypertension
No peripheral edema
No hypertensive retinal, cardiac, or neurologic manifestations reported

data.description: A 31-year-old female, G3P2, came in with 5-day history of severe menorrhagia. She was treated medically and discharged. She was readmitted 2 days later with menorrhagia and anaemia (haemoglobin of 77). The patient had suffered a spontaneous miscarriage a few months earlier.

An abnormal high-flow connection between uterine arteries and veins, often acquired after pregnancy-related uterine trauma such as miscarriage, curettage, or delivery. It can cause recurrent, severe, sometimes life-threatening uterine bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Bleeding that recurred shortly after medical treatment

data.description: Persistent placental or fetal tissue within the uterus after miscarriage, which may remain vascular and cause prolonged or heavy vaginal bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: History of spontaneous miscarriage a few months earlier
Recurrent bleeding after initial medical management
symptoms_not_in_common: Bleeding occurring several months after the miscarriage is less typical than bleeding in the immediate post-miscarriage period

data.description: A contained injury to a uterine arterial wall that forms a vascular sac and can rupture intermittently, causing sudden severe vaginal bleeding. It may occur after miscarriage, uterine instrumentation, or pregnancy.
symptoms_in_common: Failure of routine medical treatment to control bleeding
symptoms_not_in_common: No preceding uterine procedure, delivery, or pelvic trauma is reported

data.description: Abnormal persistence or proliferation of pregnancy-related trophoblastic tissue after a pregnancy event, which can present with irregular or heavy bleeding and a highly vascular uterine lesion.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent or recurrent heavy vaginal bleeding
symptoms_not_in_common: No elevated beta-hCG level is provided
No symptoms of hyperemesis, uterine enlargement, or metastatic disease are reported

data.description: 28-year-old man with abdominal pain and diarrhea after completing azithromycin for pneumonia, initially with 10–12 watery stools per day. Six weeks later, after bowel habits returned to baseline, he developed 3 weeks of recurrent abdominal discomfort relieved by bowel movements with increased stool frequency to 4–5 stools per day. At the second presentation, vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable; C. difficile PCR was positive, with otherwise normal blood counts and albumin.
A recurrence of antibiotic-associated C. difficile infection causing toxin-mediated colitis, often occurring within weeks after an initial episode.
symptoms_in_common: Initial episode of frequent watery diarrhea
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms are relatively mild at the second presentation
Abdominal discomfort is relieved by bowel movements
Normal vital signs
Normal blood counts
Normal albumin
No reported fever or systemic illness

data.description: A functional bowel disorder that can develop after infectious gastroenteritis or colitis, characterized by recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent abdominal discomfort relieved by bowel movements
Symptoms developing after a prior diarrheal illness
No reported fever, weight loss, or systemic toxicity
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive C. difficile PCR
Initial severe watery diarrhea of 10–12 stools per day after antibiotic use
Recent antibiotic exposure can suggest active C. difficile infection rather than functional bowel disease

data.diagnosis: Asymptomatic Clostridioides difficile colonization with post-infectious bowel symptoms
data.description: Presence of C. difficile detected by PCR without active toxin-mediated infection; bowel symptoms may instead be due to post-infectious dysmotility or irritable bowel syndrome.
symptoms_in_common: Mild recurrent increase in stool frequency
Abdominal discomfort relieved by bowel movements
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms are not expected in truly asymptomatic colonization
Initial episode of severe watery diarrhea may have represented active C. difficile infection rather than colonization

data.diagnosis: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea not caused by Clostridioides difficile
data.description: Diarrhea related to disruption of normal intestinal microbiota by antibiotic treatment, usually mild and self-limited, without toxin-mediated colitis.
symptoms_in_common: Normal vital signs and laboratory results at the later presentation
symptoms_not_in_common: Initial stool frequency of 10–12 watery stools per day is more severe than typical uncomplicated antibiotic-associated diarrhea
Symptoms recurred six weeks after bowel habits returned to baseline
Positive C. difficile PCR suggests possible C. difficile involvement
Abdominal discomfort relieved by bowel movements is more suggestive of irritable bowel syndrome

diagnoses.name: Clostridioides difficile colonization
diagnoses.title: Intestinal infections due to Clostridioides difficile

data.description: 29-year-old man with 6 weeks of unintentional 10 kg weight loss, severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the throat and worsened by eating, followed by 3 weeks of nausea, occasional vomiting, decreased oral intake, one episode of hematemesis, sore throat, and fever. Past history included a respiratory illness 2 years earlier; long-standing macular hyperpigmentation on the feet and legs for 10 years. On examination he was cachectic, febrile to 38.3°C, tachycardic (114–119 bpm), with low blood pressure (101/68 mm Hg), weight 47.6 kg, BMI 18.6, coarse breath sounds with fine rales at both lung bases, white exudate on the underside of the tongue, and multiple 1–2 cm nontender mobile submandibular, submental, and cervical lymph nodes. Laboratory findings showed anemia, lymphopenia, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, low albumin, elevated globulins, positive HIV-1 serology with HIV-1 RNA 172,000 copies/mL, and CD4 count of 10/mm3.

Systemic infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, especially severe in advanced HIV/AIDS. It can involve the lungs, gastrointestinal tract, lymph nodes, bone marrow, skin, liver, and spleen, and may produce diffuse pulmonary micronodules.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced HIV infection with CD4 count of 10/mm3
Marked unintentional weight loss and cachexia
Diffuse fine pulmonary nodular or miliary-pattern opacities on chest radiograph and CT
Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and poor oral intake due to possible gastrointestinal involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Long-standing macular hyperpigmentation of the feet and legs for 10 years
Single episode of hematemesis is less characteristic, although gastrointestinal ulceration can cause bleeding
White tongue exudate is more suggestive of concomitant oral candidiasis

data.diagnosis: Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary pulmonary tuberculosis
data.description: Hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis causing innumerable tiny lung nodules and possible involvement of lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, abdomen, and other organs. It is common in profoundly immunocompromised patients.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse bilateral micronodular or miliary pulmonary pattern on imaging
Abdominal pain and possible abdominal lymph node involvement
Advanced HIV/AIDS with profound CD4 lymphopenia
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the throat and worsened by eating is not a classic pulmonary tuberculosis symptom
Hematemesis is uncommon unless there is specific gastrointestinal tuberculosis
White tongue exudate is not typical of tuberculosis
Long-standing hyperpigmented macules on the legs are not typical of tuberculosis

data.description: Disseminated infection with nontuberculous mycobacteria, usually occurring in patients with AIDS and CD4 counts below 50/mm3. It commonly causes fever, weight loss, anemia, hepatosplenic disease, lymphadenopathy, and gastrointestinal symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and reduced food intake
symptoms_not_in_common: Diffuse miliary pulmonary micronodules are less typical for disseminated MAC than for miliary tuberculosis or histoplasmosis
Acute severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the throat is not a typical presentation
Hematemesis is uncommon
Long-standing hyperpigmented skin lesions are not typical

data.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia in advanced HIV/AIDS, usually producing progressive dyspnea, nonproductive cough, fever, hypoxemia, and bilateral diffuse ground-glass pulmonary infiltrates.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced HIV/AIDS with CD4 count of 10/mm3
Diffuse bilateral pulmonary interstitial or hazy abnormalities on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No prominent dyspnea is reported
No cough is reported
Miliary discrete micronodules are less typical than diffuse ground-glass opacity
Cervical lymphadenopathy is not typical
Severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and hematemesis are not typical
Long-standing hyperpigmented macules are not typical

data.diagnosis: AIDS-related lymphoma, such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma
data.description: Aggressive B-cell lymphomas can occur in advanced HIV and may involve lymph nodes, gastrointestinal organs, bone marrow, lungs, and abdominal lymph nodes. They often cause constitutional symptoms and abdominal pain.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple nontender cervical, submandibular, and submental lymph nodes
Abdominal pain and reduced oral intake
symptoms_not_in_common: Diffuse miliary pulmonary micronodules are more suggestive of disseminated infection than lymphoma
Fine bibasal rales are not a typical primary lymphoma finding
White tongue exudate is more consistent with oral candidiasis
Long-standing hyperpigmented lesions are not typical of lymphoma
Fever with diffuse lung findings may be better explained by opportunistic infection

data.description: 65-year-old Haitian man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, hypertension, bicuspid aortic valve with ascending/aortic-root aneurysm, prior treated secondary syphilis, prior positive tuberculin skin test, and recent HTLV-1 positivity. He presented with a leg injury and diffuse pruritic rash, with 12 kg unintentional weight loss over 2 years. Exam showed bilateral wrinkling axillary plaques, multiple thin brown macules and patches with collarette scale on the palms and some soles, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.

data.diagnosis: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) with cutaneous involvement
data.description: An aggressive mature CD4-positive T-cell neoplasm caused by HTLV-1 infection. It commonly affects people from HTLV-1-endemic regions, including the Caribbean, and may produce pruritic papules, patches, plaques, tumors, lymphadenopathy, and systemic symptoms. The biopsy appearance of epidermotropic atypical lymphocytes is compatible with cutaneous involvement by a T-cell lymphoma.
symptoms_in_common: Thin brown macules and patches with scale
Skin biopsy with atypical epidermotropic lymphoid infiltrates
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported hypercalcemia
No reported leukemic lymphocytosis or circulating 'flower cells'
No reported lytic bone lesions
End-stage renal disease is not a typical direct manifestation of ATLL

data.description: Mycosis fungoides is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. It typically presents with slowly progressive pruritic patches and plaques and shows epidermotropism of atypical T lymphocytes, sometimes with Pautrier microabscesses, on skin biopsy.
symptoms_in_common: Brown patches and thin plaques with fine scale
Skin lesions involving multiple body sites
Weight loss can occur in more advanced disease
Lymphadenopathy can occur with advanced-stage disease
symptoms_not_in_common: HTLV-1 positivity strongly favors ATLL over classic mycosis fungoides
Caribbean HTLV-1 epidemiologic background is more characteristic of ATLL
Palmar and sole involvement is less typical than trunk, buttock, and proximal-extremity involvement
Prominent inguinal lymphadenopathy at presentation is less typical of early mycosis fungoides

data.description: Secondary syphilis is a systemic manifestation of Treponema pallidum infection that may cause a diffuse papulosquamous eruption, often including the palms and soles, generalized lymphadenopathy, and constitutional symptoms. It is an important clinical mimic of cutaneous lymphoma.
symptoms_in_common: Brown macules and patches with scale
symptoms_not_in_common: The eruption is described as pruritic, whereas secondary syphilis is often nonpruritic
Wrinkled axillary plaques are not a classic secondary syphilis morphology
The biopsy shows epidermotropic atypical lymphocytes rather than the typical plasmacyte-rich infiltrate of syphilis
Prior treated syphilis makes recurrent active disease less likely without supporting serologic evidence
HTLV-1 positivity and the lymphoma-like histology favor ATLL

data.description: 52-year-old man with a 2-week history of exertional central chest fullness without radiation and dyspnea, absent at rest; no light-headedness or syncope. Past history: type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP, and family history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Prior screening echocardiogram 3 years earlier showed mild left ventricular hypertrophy with otherwise normal structure and function. On exam: afebrile, BP 146/70 mmHg, HR 70/min, RR 14/min, BMI 36.2; normal JVP, regular rhythm without murmurs/rubs/gallops, normal lung and abdominal exams, and no leg edema. Labs showed creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), potassium 5.4 mmol/L, WBC 10,900/mm³, and normal INR, BUN, sodium, thyrotropin, and troponin I.

A rare, rapidly progressive autoimmune inflammatory myocarditis characterized histologically by myocardial necrosis, lymphocytic inflammation, and multinucleated giant cells. It can cause ventricular arrhythmias, atrioventricular block, heart failure, and sudden cardiac death. The biopsy image is most consistent with giant cell myocarditis.
symptoms_in_common: New ventricular tachycardia on ECG image
Prior mild left ventricular hypertrophy that may represent early inflammatory remodeling
Normal troponin can occur despite active myocarditis
symptoms_not_in_common: No resting dyspnea
No clinical signs of heart failure such as edema, elevated JVP, or pulmonary crackles
No syncope or presyncope
No reported viral prodrome, fever, or systemic inflammatory symptoms

data.description: Granulomatous inflammation involving the myocardium that may produce ventricular arrhythmias, conduction disease, myocardial thickening or scar, and heart failure. Histology can show giant cells, although well-formed noncaseating granulomas would be more typical than the diffuse necrotizing giant-cell inflammation shown.
symptoms_in_common: Possible myocardial inflammatory infiltrates with giant cells on biopsy
Possible left ventricular hypertrophy or structural myocardial abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: No known pulmonary sarcoidosis, hilar adenopathy, skin lesions, or eye disease
No documented high-grade atrioventricular block
No fever, weight loss, or other systemic sarcoidosis symptoms
Histology appears more compatible with giant cell myocarditis than with discrete noncaseating granulomas

data.description: An inherited disorder characterized by otherwise unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, often involving the interventricular septum, which can cause exertional chest pain, dyspnea, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death.
symptoms_in_common: Prior echocardiogram showing mild left ventricular hypertrophy
Ventricular tachycardia can occur in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: No murmur suggesting dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
No syncope or presyncope
No documented asymmetric septal hypertrophy, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, or outflow obstruction
Myocardial biopsy with giant cells and inflammation is not typical of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

data.diagnosis: Chronic coronary syndrome due to obstructive coronary artery disease
data.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary arteries causing exertional myocardial ischemia, typically producing exertional chest pressure and dyspnea. Diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity substantially increase risk.
symptoms_in_common: Exertional central chest fullness relieved by rest
symptoms_not_in_common: No radiation of chest discomfort
Normal troponin I
Sustained ventricular tachycardia without evidence of acute myocardial infarction is less typical as the initial manifestation
Myocardial biopsy showing giant-cell inflammatory myocarditis is not explained by coronary artery disease
No reported ischemic ST-segment changes specifically diagnostic of acute coronary occlusion

data.description: 32-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, with a history of CIN II treated by loop excision 2 years earlier, bilateral breast reduction 13 years earlier, and chronic hypertension diagnosed at 18 weeks’ gestation. At 31 weeks and 4 days of pregnancy, she presented with 2 weeks of flu-like symptoms followed by lower abdominal pain and fever. Exam showed temperature 38.3°C, uterine contractions, fundal height measuring 29 weeks, cervix 1 cm dilated and fully effaced with intact membranes. Ultrasound revealed fetal growth at the 5th percentile and oligohydramnios; fetal monitoring showed baseline heart rate 160 bpm with late decelerations. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia and elevated C-reactive protein. After cesarean section for suspected fetal distress, she developed persistent fever, increasing inflammatory markers, and a non-healing surgical wound despite standard wound care and antibiotics.

A rare neutrophilic inflammatory dermatosis causing rapidly progressive, painful sterile ulceration, often triggered by surgical trauma (pathergy). Cesarean-section wounds may enlarge and fail to heal despite antibiotics or debridement; lesions often have violaceous undermined borders and purulent-appearing bases.
symptoms_in_common: Non-healing cesarean surgical wound despite antibiotics and standard wound care
Large ulcerative wound with purulent-appearing granulating base
Violaceous/purple wound borders visible in the image
Persistent fever and increasing inflammatory markers
Worsening after surgical trauma, consistent with pathergy
symptoms_not_in_common: Lower abdominal pain and uterine contractions before cesarean delivery
Fetal growth restriction
Oligohydramnios
Late fetal heart-rate decelerations
Chronic hypertension

data.diagnosis: Post-cesarean surgical-site infection with wound dehiscence
data.description: A bacterial infection involving a cesarean incision can cause fever, neutrophilic leukocytosis, wound separation, drainage, tissue breakdown, and delayed healing. Common organisms include polymicrobial genital-tract flora, Staphylococcus species, and streptococci.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent systemic inflammation after cesarean section
Purulent-appearing wound exudate and tissue slough
symptoms_not_in_common: Failure to improve despite appropriate antibiotics
Violaceous undermined-appearing wound margins, which are more suggestive of pyoderma gangrenosum
Flu-like illness beginning before the obstetric presentation
Fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios

data.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissue that may occur after surgery or childbirth. It produces severe systemic illness, fever, rising inflammatory markers, tissue necrosis, and wound breakdown.
symptoms_in_common: Postoperative wound breakdown with necrotic/sloughing tissue
Persistent illness despite routine antibiotic treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: No described rapidly escalating severe pain out of proportion to examination
No reported crepitus, skin anesthesia, bullae, or gas in soft tissues
No reported shock or multiorgan failure
Violaceous undermined ulcer margins are more characteristic of pyoderma gangrenosum
Fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios are not typical manifestations

data.description: Infection of the amniotic fluid, placenta, membranes, or uterine lining can cause maternal fever, uterine tenderness or pain, leukocytosis, fetal tachycardia, preterm labor, and postpartum fever. It may coexist with a postoperative wound complication.
symptoms_in_common: Uterine contractions and cervical dilation at 31 weeks
Fetal tachycardia with baseline heart rate of 160 bpm
symptoms_not_in_common: Large non-healing ulcerative cesarean wound
Violaceous wound margins
Persistent wound deterioration despite antibiotics and wound care
Fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios are not classic primary features

data.description: An 87-year-old man presented with a one-year history of difficulty swallowing, with episodes of choking and aspiration that progressively increased in frequency. Laryngeal examination revealed extraluminal obstruction from behind. The patient had multiple comorbidities as mentioned in the case.

data.diagnosis: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) causing anterior cervical osteophyte compression
data.description: A noninflammatory disorder characterized by extensive flowing calcification and ossification along the anterior spine. Large anterior cervical osteophytes can mechanically compress the pharynx or esophagus, producing progressive dysphagia and aspiration. The image is suggestive of prominent anterior cervical bony overgrowth.
symptoms_in_common: Extraluminal posterior compression seen on laryngeal examination
Imaging appearance of bulky anterior cervical osteophyte formation

data.diagnosis: Cervical spondylosis with large anterior cervical osteophytes
data.description: Degenerative cervical spine disease can produce osteophytes. When unusually large, anterior osteophytes may indent the hypopharynx or cervical esophagus and cause swallowing difficulty, choking, and aspiration.
symptoms_in_common: Posterior extraluminal obstruction of the laryngopharynx
Cervical bony degenerative changes/osteophytes visible on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No neck pain, radicular arm pain, or myelopathic symptoms were reported

data.diagnosis: Ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament
data.description: Ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament, frequently occurring as part of DISH, may form a rigid bony prominence along the anterior cervical vertebrae. This can compress adjacent swallowing structures and lead to dysphagia and aspiration.
symptoms_in_common: Mechanical extrinsic compression from behind the larynx
Anterior cervical spinal ossification suggested by the image
symptoms_not_in_common: No neck stiffness or cervical pain was described

data.description: A 22-year-old African American/Asian college-age woman presented with a 3-month history of mild exertional dyspnea that progressively worsened despite treatment with inhalers for suspected reactive airway disease. She reported shortness of breath with mild exertion, nonproductive cough for several weeks, and a 5-lb weight loss. She denied fever, chills, headaches, syncope, dizziness, bone pain, nausea, or vomiting. Physical examination was unremarkable except for decreased breath sounds and slight dullness to percussion on the left. Routine laboratory work-up was unremarkable. Initially, chest x-ray showed mediastinal widening, which led to further imaging and biopsy. An open mediastinal biopsy was performed after CT-guided biopsy failed, revealing a poorly differentiated carcinoma initially thought to be thymic carcinoma. Flow cytometry from tissue showed T cells and polyclonal B cells with no immunophenotypic evidence of malignancy.

data.diagnosis: NUT carcinoma (NUTM1-rearranged poorly differentiated carcinoma of the mediastinum)
data.description: A rare, aggressive poorly differentiated carcinoma driven by a NUTM1 gene rearrangement, often arising in the midline thorax/mediastinum of young patients and frequently initially misclassified as thymic carcinoma.
symptoms_in_common: Large mediastinal mass with mediastinal widening on chest radiograph
Pathology showing poorly differentiated carcinoma initially interpreted as thymic carcinoma
Absence of a clonal lymphoid population on flow cytometry
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or chills
No headaches
No bone pain
Unremarkable routine laboratory studies

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from the thymus, usually located in the anterior mediastinum. It can cause respiratory symptoms from compression of the lungs, airways, vessels, or pleura.
symptoms_in_common: Decreased left-sided breath sounds and dullness to percussion suggesting mass effect or pleural fluid
Biopsy initially interpreted as poorly differentiated thymic carcinoma
symptoms_not_in_common: Very young age for typical thymic carcinoma
No chest pain
No superior vena cava syndrome symptoms such as facial swelling or venous distention
No myasthenia gravis symptoms

data.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that commonly occurs in young women and presents as a bulky anterior mediastinal mass, often producing cough, dyspnea, and constitutional symptoms. Tissue flow cytometry can be nondiagnostic when the specimen is fibrotic or limited.
symptoms_in_common: Bulky mediastinal mass with mediastinal widening
Possible pleural involvement or effusion suggested by left-sided dullness and decreased breath sounds
symptoms_not_in_common: Biopsy described as poorly differentiated carcinoma rather than lymphoma
Flow cytometry showed no immunophenotypic evidence of a clonal B-cell malignancy
No fever, chills, or other prominent B symptoms besides weight loss
Routine laboratory work-up was unremarkable

data.diagnosis: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis type
data.description: A lymphoma that frequently affects young adults and may present with a large anterior mediastinal mass. Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma is especially common in young women and may have nondiagnostic flow cytometry because malignant Reed-Sternberg cells are sparse.
symptoms_in_common: Mediastinal widening due to a mediastinal mass
Flow cytometry without a clear malignant lymphoid population can occur in Hodgkin lymphoma
symptoms_not_in_common: Pathology was interpreted as poorly differentiated carcinoma
No fever or chills
No night sweats reported
No peripheral lymphadenopathy reported
No pruritus reported

data.description: Primary mediastinal germ cell tumors arise in the anterior mediastinum and can become large enough to compress adjacent lungs and airways. Teratoma, seminoma, and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors are included in this category.
symptoms_in_common: Large mediastinal mass with mediastinal widening
Decreased breath sounds and dullness on the left from mass effect or pleural fluid
symptoms_not_in_common: Female sex is less typical for malignant primary mediastinal germ cell tumors
No elevated tumor markers reported
Biopsy described as poorly differentiated carcinoma rather than germ cell tumor
No nausea, vomiting, or abdominal symptoms

data.description: 71-year-old woman with hematuria, long-standing easy skin bruising that worsened at age 66, prior nephrolithiasis at age 41, and osteoporosis (left femoral neck T-score -2.6). Physical examination showed bruising on the lower extremities. Serial testing at a tertiary center showed elevated late-night serum cortisol and a Dex-CRH test with cortisol of 1.8 µg/dL at 0 minutes and 2 µg/dL at 15 minutes.

data.diagnosis: Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (PBMAH) causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
data.description: A disorder characterized by bilateral adrenal enlargement with nodular hyperplasia and autonomous cortisol production, often presenting as mild or subclinical Cushing syndrome in older adults. The CT images show bilateral adrenal enlargement/nodularity.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated late-night serum cortisol indicating loss of normal cortisol circadian rhythm
Abnormal Dex-CRH testing compatible with endogenous hypercortisolism
Prior nephrolithiasis, which can occur with chronic cortisol excess through hypercalciuria
symptoms_not_in_common: Hematuria is not a typical direct manifestation of PBMAH or Cushing syndrome

data.diagnosis: ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome due to bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
data.description: Endogenous cortisol excess caused by autonomous adrenal cortisol secretion rather than pituitary or ectopic ACTH stimulation. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is suggested by enlargement of both adrenal glands on the CT images.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal cortisol response on Dex-CRH testing
Easy bruising due to cortisol-related skin and connective-tissue fragility
Osteoporosis due to chronic glucocorticoid excess
History of kidney stones, potentially related to cortisol-associated calcium loss in urine
symptoms_not_in_common: Hematuria is not usually caused directly by cortisol excess
Classic overt Cushing features such as central weight gain, facial rounding, proximal muscle weakness, diabetes, and hypertension are not described

data.diagnosis: Subclinical or mild autonomous cortisol secretion from bilateral adrenal incidentalomas
data.description: Mild autonomous cortisol secretion is a low-grade form of adrenal cortisol excess that may lack obvious classic Cushingoid appearance but can cause bruising, bone loss, metabolic complications, and abnormal cortisol suppression or circadian testing. Bilateral adrenal nodular lesions/enlargement support an adrenal source.
symptoms_in_common: Evidence of autonomous cortisol secretion on specialized endocrine testing
symptoms_not_in_common: Hematuria is not typical
Nephrolithiasis is possible with cortisol excess but is not a defining feature
Marked clinical Cushingoid changes are not reported

data.description: 40-year-old woman with 10 months of progressive bilateral leg edema, starting as episodic foot and ankle swelling/pain in the evenings after prolonged standing and later extending to the lower legs and thighs. Five months before evaluation, she developed left back and flank pain, along with abdominal distention and pain. Past history includes hypothyroidism, latent tuberculosis, hysterectomy for fibroid uterus, appendectomy, two vaginal deliveries, and one ectopic pregnancy. Examination showed 2+ edema of the lower and upper legs, jugular venous pressure 8 cm H2O, and a distended, mildly tender abdomen with healed surgical scars. Laboratory studies showed marked hypoalbuminemia and hypoproteinemia, hypocalcemia, elevated TSH with low free thyroxine, and urinalysis with 3+ protein and 1+ blood.

data.diagnosis: Inferior vena cava thrombosis with bilateral iliac/renal venous thrombosis
data.description: Extensive thrombosis of the inferior vena cava and pelvic/renal venous drainage can cause severe bilateral lower-extremity edema, abdominal/flank pain, venous collateral formation, and abdominal wall/subcutaneous edema. The CT images show findings consistent with thrombosed central venous structures and extensive collateral veins.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive bilateral foot, ankle, leg, and thigh edema
CT appearance of central venous obstruction with collateral venous pathways
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked proteinuria
Severe hypoalbuminemia and hypoproteinemia
Low free thyroxine with elevated TSH

data.description: Nephrotic syndrome is heavy urinary protein loss due to glomerular disease, producing hypoalbuminemia, edema, and increased risk of venous thromboembolism, including renal-vein and inferior-vena-cava thrombosis.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive peripheral edema involving the legs and thighs
Abdominal distention, possibly from ascites or generalized fluid retention
Increased risk for the extensive venous thrombosis suggested on CT
Hypocalcemia, which may occur with low albumin and urinary loss of vitamin-D-binding protein
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent unilateral left flank pain is not a usual primary manifestation unless renal vein thrombosis is present
Hematuria is not required in uncomplicated nephrotic syndrome
Elevated TSH with low free thyroxine is not a primary feature, although urinary loss of thyroid-binding proteins can worsen hypothyroidism

data.description: Renal vein thrombosis is a thrombotic occlusion of renal venous drainage, often associated with nephrotic syndrome. It may produce flank pain, hematuria, proteinuria, impaired renal drainage, and extension into the inferior vena cava.
symptoms_in_common: CT findings compatible with central venous/renal venous thrombotic disease
Potential extension into the inferior vena cava
symptoms_not_in_common: Long-standing symmetric bilateral leg edema is more suggestive of inferior vena cava or iliac venous obstruction than isolated renal vein thrombosis
Abdominal distention is not typical of isolated renal vein thrombosis
Severe hypothyroidism is not a direct manifestation

data.description: Hypothyroidism can cause edema, weight gain, fatigue, serous-cavity effusions, and worsening of fluid retention. In this case it may contribute to edema but does not adequately explain the heavy proteinuria or CT evidence of extensive venous obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Leg swelling and generalized fluid retention
Possible abdominal distention from fluid accumulation
symptoms_not_in_common: 3+ proteinuria
Marked hypoalbuminemia and hypoproteinemia
Hematuria
Flank pain
CT findings of extensive venous thrombosis and collateral veins
Progressive edema extending from the feet to thighs in a pattern consistent with venous obstruction

diagnoses.name: Membranous nephropathy
diagnoses.title: Glomerular disease associated with thin basement membrane nephropathy

data.description: A 22 year old man presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain, jaundice, itching, and fever. His urine was dark and stools pale. Physical examination revealed temperature of 38.7°C, icterus, abdominal tenderness worst in the right upper quadrant with negative Murphy's sign, impalpable gall bladder, inflamed oropharynx with cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy.
