data.description: Male infant born at term to healthy nonconsanguineous parents, with no family history of immune deficiency, presented at 20 days of age with profound T-cell lymphopenia detected on newborn screening showing absent TRECs. Physical examination showed neonatal teeth, hypotonia, umbilical hernia, and erythematous psoriaform dermatitis. Imaging revealed wormian skull bones, mild pulmonary artery stenosis, and absence of the corpus callosum. No evidence of maternal engraftment was found.

A genetic disorder caused by pathogenic BCL11B variants, characterized by impaired thymic T-cell development, severe T-cell lymphopenia or SCID, craniofacial dysmorphism, neurodevelopmental abnormalities, skin findings, and occasionally congenital anomalies.
symptoms_in_common: Profound neonatal T-cell lymphopenia with absent TRECs
Early presentation compatible with severe combined immunodeficiency
Dysmorphic facial appearance visible in the image
Congenital dental abnormality such as neonatal teeth can occur in syndromic developmental disorders affecting BCL11B pathways
symptoms_not_in_common: Wormian skull bones are not a classic defining feature
Umbilical hernia is not a typical hallmark
Mild pulmonary artery stenosis is not a consistent feature

data.description: FOXN1 deficiency is an autosomal-recessive thymic epithelial-cell disorder causing profound T-cell immunodeficiency, absent or severely reduced TRECs, and ectodermal abnormalities involving hair, skin, and nails.
symptoms_in_common: Profound T-cell lymphopenia detected by absent TRECs
Abnormal hair or ectodermal appearance suggested by the clinical photographs
symptoms_not_in_common: Neonatal teeth are not typical
Wormian skull bones are not typical
Absence of the corpus callosum is not typical
Pulmonary artery stenosis is not typical
Umbilical hernia is not a usual feature
Hypotonia is not a defining feature

data.diagnosis: PAX1 deficiency (otofaciocervical syndrome type 2 with severe T-cell immunodeficiency)
data.description: Biallelic PAX1 deficiency can cause a syndromic form of severe T-cell immunodeficiency due to abnormal thymic development, often accompanied by craniofacial, skeletal, and other congenital developmental abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Profound T-cell lymphopenia with absent TRECs
Congenital craniofacial dysmorphism visible in the image
Skeletal abnormality such as wormian skull bones
Hypotonia and other developmental abnormalities may occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Neonatal teeth are not a classic feature
Psoriaform dermatitis is not typical
Absence of the corpus callosum is not a core feature
Umbilical hernia is not a defining finding

data.diagnosis: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome with severe thymic hypoplasia or athymia
data.description: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome can cause variable T-cell lymphopenia from thymic hypoplasia; rare patients have congenital athymia and a SCID-like phenotype. Congenital heart defects, craniofacial differences, and neurologic abnormalities may coexist.
symptoms_in_common: Marked neonatal T-cell lymphopenia with absent TRECs
Congenital heart defect, including pulmonary artery abnormalities
Facial dysmorphism visible in the image
Central nervous system abnormality, including possible corpus callosum defects
Umbilical hernia can occur among congenital anomalies
symptoms_not_in_common: Neonatal teeth are unusual
Wormian skull bones are not typical
Psoriaform dermatitis is not a classic presentation
Profound SCID-range T-cell lymphopenia is uncommon except in complete athymia

data.diagnosis: Omenn syndrome due to hypomorphic RAG1/RAG2 or related SCID genes
data.description: Omenn syndrome is a form of leaky severe combined immunodeficiency in which impaired lymphocyte development is accompanied by inflammatory erythroderma, activated oligoclonal T cells, lymphadenopathy, and susceptibility to severe infection.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal newborn screening with absent TRECs
symptoms_not_in_common: Neonatal teeth are not typical
Wormian skull bones are not typical
Pulmonary artery stenosis is not typical
Absence of the corpus callosum is not typical
Umbilical hernia is not typical

data.description: 47-year-old male with tenesmus and mucoid stool. Past history notable for pulmonary tuberculosis 20 years ago treated for 9 months; 20-pack-year smoking history, no alcohol use. On admission he had no weight loss, fever, or night sweats and appeared well. Exam was largely unremarkable except for a depressed anterior chest wall; no lymphadenopathy, lungs clear, heart normal. Vital signs were stable. Labs were largely within normal limits. Chest radiograph showed a right upper lung scar consistent with prior tuberculosis. Upper endoscopy revealed a healed duodenal bulb ulcer with negative H. pylori test. Abdominal CT, β2-microglobulin, serum protein electrophoresis, and bone marrow studies showed no remarkable abnormalities.

A rare localized plasma-cell neoplasm arising outside the bone marrow, which can involve the rectum or colon. The endoscopic lesions and biopsy appearance of dense plasma-cell infiltration support this diagnosis; normal serum protein studies and bone marrow findings support a primary extramedullary lesion rather than multiple myeloma.
symptoms_in_common: No evidence of bone marrow involvement
Normal serum protein electrophoresis and beta-2-microglobulin
symptoms_not_in_common: No weight loss
No fever
No night sweats
No lymphadenopathy
Remote history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis

data.description: A benign or reactive disorder characterized by prominent plasma-cell infiltration of colonic or rectal mucosa, potentially causing erythema, nodularity, mucus production, and defecatory urgency. Demonstration of polyclonal plasma cells would favor this over plasmacytoma.
symptoms_in_common: Marked plasma-cell infiltration in the biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Remote pulmonary tuberculosis history
Healed duodenal ulcer
Depressed anterior chest wall

data.diagnosis: Colorectal mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation
data.description: An indolent extranodal B-cell lymphoma that may involve the colon or rectum and can show extensive plasmacytic differentiation. It may produce mucosal nodules or masses and can mimic a plasma-cell neoplasm on limited biopsy.
symptoms_in_common: Normal bone marrow studies can occur in localized disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No lymphadenopathy
No weight loss
No fever
No night sweats
Remote history of pulmonary tuberculosis is not a typical feature

data.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease causing continuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum. Plasma cells may be prominent in the lamina propria, particularly in chronic disease, and rectal involvement can cause tenesmus and mucus.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic inflammatory infiltrate with plasma cells in mucosal biopsies
symptoms_not_in_common: No bloody diarrhea reported
No abdominal pain reported
No fever
No weight loss
Histology appears dominated by a dense plasma-cell population rather than typical diffuse chronic active colitis

data.diagnosis: Intestinal tuberculosis involving the colon or rectum
data.description: Gastrointestinal infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can cause ulceration, strictures, nodules, and inflammatory bowel symptoms. Prior pulmonary tuberculosis increases clinical consideration, although the pathology shown would more typically demonstrate granulomatous inflammation rather than a predominantly plasma-cell infiltrate.
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No night sweats
No weight loss

No reported granulomas or acid-fast bacilli on biopsy
Normal abdominal CT without typical bowel-wall thickening or lymphadenopathy

data.description: 24-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with 2 days of left leg crampy pain radiating to the left lower abdomen and buttock, associated with generalized leg swelling and exertional dyspnea. She denied fever, chest pain, dyspnea at rest, or trauma. Vital signs showed mild tachycardia (102 bpm). Exam revealed pitting edema, erythema, and increased warmth of the left leg from thigh to calf. History included long-term oral contraceptive use, prior light smoking, and family history of DVT in her father after surgery. Labs showed mild leukocytosis; hemoglobin, platelets, coagulation studies, troponin T, and NT-proBNP were normal.

Obstruction of pulmonary arterial branches by thrombus, usually embolized from a deep venous thrombosis. The chest CT image shows intraluminal filling defects in bilateral pulmonary arterial branches consistent with pulmonary emboli.
symptoms_in_common: Risk factors for venous thromboembolism including long-term oral contraceptive use and prior smoking
Clinical evidence of left-leg deep venous thrombosis as a likely embolic source
symptoms_not_in_common: No chest pain
No dyspnea at rest
Prominent unilateral leg erythema, warmth, swelling, and pain are due to the associated DVT rather than pulmonary embolism itself

data.diagnosis: Acute extensive left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis
data.description: Acute thrombosis involving the deep veins of the left lower extremity and pelvic/iliac venous system. The pelvic CT image is consistent with thrombosis of the left iliac venous region, and the clinical presentation strongly supports extensive proximal DVT.
symptoms_in_common: Pain radiating to the left lower abdomen and buttock
Increased warmth from thigh to calf
symptoms_not_in_common: Exertional dyspnea is not caused by DVT alone and is better explained by associated pulmonary embolism
No trauma or recent surgery, which are common provoking factors but are not required

data.diagnosis: May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein compression syndrome) with acute thrombosis
data.description: An anatomic venous outflow disorder in which the left common iliac vein is compressed by the overlying right common iliac artery and adjacent spine, predisposing young women to left-sided iliofemoral DVT. The pelvic imaging and extensive left-sided proximal thrombosis are compatible with this condition.
symptoms_in_common: Young woman with acute left-sided proximal leg swelling
Pulmonary embolism as a complication of DVT
Additional thrombotic risk from estrogen-containing oral contraceptive use
symptoms_not_in_common: Exertional dyspnea is not a direct manifestation of iliac vein compression and reflects pulmonary embolism
Leg erythema and warmth can occur with severe DVT but are not specific for May-Thurner syndrome
Mild leukocytosis is nonspecific

data.diagnosis: Phlegmasia alba dolens due to extensive proximal DVT
data.description: A severe form of extensive iliofemoral deep venous thrombosis causing marked limb edema and pain from major venous outflow obstruction. It may progress to phlegmasia cerulea dolens if cyanosis and threatened limb perfusion develop.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse swelling involving much of the left leg
Warmth and erythema of the affected limb
symptoms_not_in_common: No pallor of the limb described
No cyanosis, skin blistering, arterial compromise, or threatened limb viability described
Exertional dyspnea is due to associated pulmonary embolism rather than phlegmasia itself

data.description: 3-year-old boy, born at 41 weeks gestation without perinatal problems, birth weight 3.4kg. Parents were not consanguineous and had no medical history. History of 3 prior hospitalizations for viral pneumonia at 12, 18, and 27 months. Presented with recurrent and persistent pneumonia. Current symptoms included cough, sputum and fever. Physical exam showed: temperature 39.5°C, pulse 129/min, respiration 28/min, BP 95/55 mmHg. Weight 15.3kg (50-75th percentile), height 96.5cm (50-75th percentile). Two 3mm ulcers in uvula, fine crackles in both lung fields, palpable liver 1 finger-breadth below right costal margin, palpable spleen tip.

A primary immunodeficiency caused by defective NADPH oxidase in phagocytes, resulting in impaired oxidative burst and susceptibility to recurrent severe bacterial and fungal infections. The absent/markedly reduced rhodamine oxidation response on flow cytometry and sequencing image are highly supportive.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent and persistent pneumonia beginning in early childhood
Multiple prior hospitalizations for respiratory infections
High fever, cough, sputum production, and bilateral crackles consistent with severe lower respiratory infection
Chest radiograph and CT showing bilateral pulmonary infiltrates/consolidation
Mild hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, which may occur with recurrent infection or granulomatous inflammation
Male child, consistent with possible X-linked inheritance
Markedly impaired oxidative burst pattern on rhodamine-based flow cytometry
symptoms_not_in_common: Reported prior infections were described as viral pneumonia, whereas CGD classically predisposes to catalase-positive bacterial and fungal pathogens
No documented abscesses, lymphadenitis, osteomyelitis, or invasive fungal infection
Normal growth percentiles despite recurrent severe infections

data.description: CGD can also result from autosomal recessive defects in NADPH oxidase components such as NCF1, NCF2, NCF4, or CYBA. It produces defective neutrophil oxidative burst and recurrent serious pulmonary and systemic infections.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent pulmonary infection with fever, cough, and sputum
Abnormal rhodamine oxidative-burst flow-cytometry result compatible with NADPH oxidase dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: The sequencing image may suggest a specific X-linked mutation rather than an autosomal recessive defect
No known family history or consanguinity, although autosomal recessive disease can still occur without either
No reported deep-seated abscesses, fungal disease, or granulomatous gastrointestinal/urinary manifestations

data.description: A neutrophil enzyme deficiency that can cause abnormal oxidation-dependent fluorescence testing and, rarely, increased susceptibility to Candida infection. Most affected individuals are asymptomatic or have mild infections.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent respiratory infections can occur occasionally
An abnormal flow-cytometric oxidation assay may raise this differential
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe recurrent pneumonia requiring repeated hospitalizations is much more typical of CGD than myeloperoxidase deficiency
No mucocutaneous or invasive Candida infection is described
Hepatosplenomegaly is not a typical feature
The markedly absent oxidative-burst pattern is more consistent with CGD

data.description: A primary immunodeficiency, often due to STAT3-pathway abnormalities, characterized by recurrent bacterial pneumonias, skin infections, markedly elevated IgE, eczema, and characteristic skeletal or dental findings.
symptoms_in_common: Cough, fever, sputum, and pulmonary consolidation
Possible recurrent severe bacterial respiratory infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No eczema, recurrent skin abscesses, or chronic candidiasis is reported
No retained primary teeth, fractures, scoliosis, or characteristic facial features are reported
The abnormal oxidative-burst flow-cytometry pattern is not typical of hyper-IgE syndrome
Mild hepatosplenomegaly is not a classic presenting finding

data.description: A 34-year-old woman presented with acute abdominal and back pain 3 years before evaluation at the oncology clinic. She had been well until this onset. Her medical history was notable for migraines. She did not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. She worked full time as a social worker and lived in New Jersey with her husband and child. Family history included breast cancer in maternal grandmother (70s), uterine cancer in paternal aunt (40s), and colon cancer in two paternal cousins (30s and 50s). On physical examination: temperature 36.5°C, blood pressure 108/78 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats per minute, body-mass index 27.7. The abdomen had well-healed surgical scars; remainder of physical examination was normal. Laboratory results showed elevated tumor marker CA 19-9 at 110 IU per milliliter (reference <35), while alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen levels were normal.

A primary adenocarcinoma arising from the intrahepatic bile ducts. It commonly produces a desmoplastic gland-forming tumor on pathology and can present as multifocal liver masses with elevated CA 19-9.
symptoms_in_common: Restricted diffusion and enhancing liver lesions suspicious for malignancy
Gland-forming adenocarcinoma with prominent fibrous/desmoplastic stroma on histology
Normal alpha-fetoprotein, which is less supportive of hepatocellular carcinoma
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age of 34 years, since intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is more common in older adults
No reported jaundice, pruritus, fever, or weight loss

data.diagnosis: Metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to the liver
data.description: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is an aggressive gland-forming malignancy that frequently elevates CA 19-9 and metastasizes to the liver. It may cause epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple liver lesions compatible with metastatic disease
Adenocarcinoma with desmoplastic stromal reaction on pathology
symptoms_not_in_common: No definite pancreatic primary mass is demonstrated in the provided images
No reported jaundice, new diabetes, weight loss, anorexia, or steatorrhea
Young age of 34 years is unusual for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma

data.diagnosis: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma involving the liver
data.description: Colorectal adenocarcinoma commonly spreads hematogenously to the liver and can show gland-forming malignant cells on histology. A family history of early colon cancer raises concern for a hereditary colorectal cancer predisposition.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple liver lesions that could represent metastases
Family history of colon cancer in paternal cousins
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal carcinoembryonic antigen level
Elevated CA 19-9 is less typical than elevated carcinoembryonic antigen
No reported change in bowel habits, rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, or known colorectal primary tumor
Imaging and tumor-marker pattern more strongly support a pancreaticobiliary primary

data.description: A 37-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of right facial pain and a 3-month history of progressive painful swelling beneath the right ear lobe. Physical examination revealed a soft swelling in the anteroinferior auricular area that was smooth, elastic, mobile and painful on pressure, but not fluctuant. The facial nerve function was normal and the cervical lymph node was not palpable. There were no systemic symptoms. The patient was screened for metastases, and no lung or abdomen lesions were detected.

A rare benign smooth-muscle tumor arising in or adjacent to the parotid gland, often from vascular smooth muscle. Histology typically shows bland spindle cells arranged in interlacing fascicles or whorls, with smooth-muscle-marker positivity and no malignant cytologic features.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly progressive, mobile soft-tissue swelling beneath the ear
No systemic symptoms or distant lesions
Imaging appearance of a localized parotid/periparotid mass
Histology showing bland spindle cells in intersecting fascicular/whorled patterns

data.diagnosis: Schwannoma of the intraparotid facial nerve or adjacent peripheral nerve
data.description: A benign nerve-sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells. It may present as a slow-growing parotid-region mass, usually with preserved facial nerve function, and histology can show spindle cells in fascicular arrangements.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive mobile mass in the parotid/infra-auricular region
Normal facial nerve function can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked tenderness is less typical for a schwannoma than for an angioleiomyoma
The reported smooth-muscle-type immunohistochemical pattern would not be typical if S-100 staining is negative

data.diagnosis: Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland
data.description: The most common benign salivary-gland tumor, generally presenting as a slow-growing, well-circumscribed and mobile parotid mass. It contains epithelial and myoepithelial elements in a variable stromal background.
symptoms_in_common: Adult patient with a gradually enlarging parotid-region mass
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain and pressure tenderness are less typical, as pleomorphic adenomas are usually painless
Spindle-cell fascicles without characteristic epithelial or chondromyxoid components are not typical
Immunohistochemical findings favoring smooth-muscle differentiation would not be typical

data.description: A benign salivary-gland neoplasm composed predominantly of myoepithelial cells, which can have spindle-cell morphology and may resemble mesenchymal tumors on routine microscopy.
symptoms_in_common: Absence of cervical lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: Painful and pressure-tender presentation is less typical
Pure smooth-muscle fascicular morphology is less characteristic than myoepithelial cellular patterns
Lack of epithelial/myoepithelial marker expression would argue against this diagnosis

data.diagnosis: Low-grade fibromatosis or other benign fibroblastic spindle-cell tumor
data.description: Benign fibroblastic/myofibroblastic tumors may form infiltrative or circumscribed spindle-cell masses in the head and neck. They can show fascicular spindle-cell proliferation but usually lack the vascular smooth-muscle differentiation of angioleiomyoma.
symptoms_not_in_common: A mobile and well-localized painful infra-auricular mass is less typical for infiltrative fibromatosis
Pain on palpation is less characteristic
The imaging and histologic suggestion of a circumscribed smooth-muscle tumor would not be typical

data.description: At the age of 30 months, the patient began presenting an evolving framework of severe cognitive and neurological impairment, with tetraparesis and mixed spastic-dystonic features, language delay and deafness. Moreover, she has coarse facial features, presenting a high forehead and hypertelorism; her tongue is protruding due to macroglossia.

A lysosomal storage disorder causing progressive accumulation of heparan sulfate, with early developmental delay followed by severe neurodegeneration; somatic features may be milder than in other mucopolysaccharidoses. Brain MRI can show delayed or abnormal white-matter maturation, cerebral atrophy, and ventricular enlargement.
symptoms_in_common: Onset of progressive neurodevelopmental impairment in early childhood
MRI appearance compatible with diffuse white-matter abnormality and cerebral volume loss/ventricular prominence
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent macroglossia is more characteristic of some other mucopolysaccharidoses than of Sanfilippo syndrome
Severe early tetraparesis may occur later in the disease course rather than being an initial dominant manifestation

data.description: An X-linked lysosomal disorder caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, producing dermatan- and heparan-sulfate accumulation. It causes coarse facies, macroglossia, hearing loss, developmental delay, and progressive neurologic decline; neuroimaging may demonstrate white-matter lesions and ventriculomegaly.
symptoms_in_common: MRI white-matter abnormalities and ventricular prominence
symptoms_not_in_common: The patient is described as female, whereas classic Hunter syndrome primarily affects males because it is X-linked
No skeletal deformity, hepatosplenomegaly, joint stiffness, or respiratory disease is reported

data.diagnosis: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syndrome / severe MPS I)
data.description: A lysosomal storage disorder due to alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency. The severe form causes progressive developmental delay, coarse facies, macroglossia, hearing loss, skeletal disease, and progressive neurologic involvement. MRI can show white-matter signal abnormalities, enlarged perivascular spaces, atrophy, and hydrocephalus or ventriculomegaly.
symptoms_in_common: MRI findings suggesting diffuse white-matter involvement and ventricular enlargement
symptoms_not_in_common: No corneal clouding is reported
No hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis multiplex, joint contractures, or cardiac disease is reported
Dystonia is less classically emphasized than skeletal and systemic manifestations

data.diagnosis: GM1 gangliosidosis type II (late-infantile GM1 gangliosidosis)
data.description: A neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disease caused by beta-galactosidase deficiency. The late-infantile form often begins between 1 and 3 years with developmental regression, progressive cognitive decline, dystonia, spasticity, hearing impairment, and coarse facial features. MRI may show delayed myelination, diffuse white-matter signal change, and cerebral atrophy.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive severe cognitive and neurologic deterioration
MRI findings compatible with white-matter disease and cerebral atrophy
symptoms_not_in_common: No developmental regression, seizures, skeletal abnormalities, or hepatosplenomegaly are specifically reported
A cherry-red macular spot, which may occur in GM1 gangliosidosis, is not reported

data.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-mannosidase deficiency. It produces intellectual disability, speech delay, hearing loss, coarse facies, skeletal abnormalities, immune dysfunction, and progressive motor impairment; MRI may show white-matter abnormalities and cerebral or cerebellar atrophy.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe spastic-dystonic tetraparesis in early childhood is less typical than ataxia, hypotonia, and milder motor impairment
No recurrent infections, immune deficiency, skeletal abnormalities, or psychiatric manifestations are reported

data.description: A male neonate, born at 36+1 weeks gestation via cesarean section due to scarred uterus and fetal heart rate deceleration, weighing 2700g with Apgar scores of 2-8-9. The infant experienced severe asphyxia at birth requiring intubation and chest compressions. After resuscitation, he presented with respiratory distress and difficulty breathing. Following extubation from mechanical ventilation on day 6, the patient developed recurrent inspiratory dyspnea and stridor. The infant had no relevant family history and no history of laryngeal or thoracic surgery.

Immobility of both vocal folds, usually in a paramedian position, causing a markedly narrowed glottic airway. In neonates it can be congenital or associated with neurologic injury, hypoxic-ischemic injury, or birth trauma. The endoscopic images are compatible with a narrow glottic opening and impaired vocal-fold abduction.
symptoms_in_common: Severe airway obstruction requiring prior intubation and mechanical ventilation
History of severe perinatal asphyxia, which may be associated with neurologic injury affecting vocal-fold motion
Endoscopic appearance of a very narrow glottic airway
symptoms_not_in_common: No relevant family history
No prior laryngeal or thoracic surgery

data.description: A neonatal form of bilateral vocal-fold immobility present from birth or becoming apparent shortly after extubation. It commonly presents with stridor, respiratory distress, and difficulty weaning from ventilatory support; some cases are idiopathic and others are neurologic.
symptoms_in_common: Narrow glottic aperture on laryngoscopic images
No history of laryngeal or thoracic surgery, supporting a non-iatrogenic congenital or neurologic cause
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe asphyxia at birth is not required for congenital idiopathic cases
Initial respiratory failure immediately after delivery may also reflect pulmonary or hypoxic-ischemic complications rather than isolated congenital vocal-cord paralysis

data.diagnosis: Posterior glottic stenosis or cricoarytenoid fixation after intubation
data.description: Scarring, inflammation, or fixation involving the posterior glottis and cricoarytenoid joints can prevent vocal-fold abduction and mimic bilateral vocal-fold paralysis. It may occur after traumatic or prolonged endotracheal intubation.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent respiratory distress after mechanical ventilation
Narrow glottic airway on endoscopic examination
History of endotracheal intubation for several days
symptoms_not_in_common: Only approximately 6 days of intubation, which is relatively short for severe mature posterior glottic scar formation
Airway difficulty was associated with severe birth asphyxia, suggesting a possible neurologic cause rather than purely acquired intubation injury
No history of prior laryngeal surgery

data.description: A common congenital dynamic supraglottic airway disorder caused by collapse of immature supraglottic structures during inspiration. It usually causes inspiratory stridor that is worse with feeding, crying, or supine positioning.
symptoms_not_in_common: Endoscopic images suggest a restricted glottic opening rather than supraglottic collapse
Severe airway obstruction requiring intubation is less typical in uncomplicated laryngomalacia
The presentation after extubation with apparent glottic-level obstruction is less typical
No reported worsening with feeding, crying, or supine positioning

diagnoses.name: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis
diagnoses.title: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx[Bilateral]

data.description: 24-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of swelling on the left side of neck and fever. Past medical history included two similar neck abscesses 2 years and 6 years ago, which were treated with antibiotics and drainage. Physical examination showed a 2 cm diameter swelling at the level of thyroid cartilage.

data.diagnosis: Left piriform sinus fistula (third or fourth branchial pouch anomaly) with recurrent cervical abscess
data.description: A congenital epithelial tract arising from the piriform sinus, most often on the left, can permit pharyngeal bacteria to enter the neck or thyroid region and cause recurrent deep neck infections/abscesses. The CT appearance of a tract or air-containing inflammatory focus near the left hypopharynx supports this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Location near the thyroid cartilage/lower anterior neck
Prior episodes requiring antibiotics and drainage
CT finding suggestive of a left-sided fistulous tract near the piriform sinus

data.description: A branchial cleft cyst is a congenital lateral neck cyst that may become infected, producing a tender neck mass, fever, and abscess formation. Second branchial cleft anomalies are the most common type and usually occur in the upper lateral neck.
symptoms_in_common: Previous need for drainage and antibiotics
symptoms_not_in_common: Mass is at the level of the thyroid cartilage/lower neck rather than the typical upper anterior sternocleidomastoid region
Repeated left-sided deep neck infections favor a piriform sinus fistula more strongly
CT suggestion of a tract near the hypopharynx/piriform sinus is not typical of a second branchial cleft cyst

data.diagnosis: Acute suppurative thyroiditis with thyroid abscess
data.description: Acute bacterial infection of the thyroid gland is uncommon but can cause fever, painful anterior neck swelling, and abscess formation. In young patients with recurrent left-sided disease, it may be secondary to an underlying piriform sinus fistula.
symptoms_in_common: Anterior/lower lateral neck swelling near the thyroid cartilage
Prior response requiring antibiotic therapy and drainage
Possible inflammatory process adjacent to the thyroid region on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported thyroid tenderness, dysphagia, odynophagia, hoarseness, or thyroid-function symptoms
Recurrent episodes over many years are unusual without an underlying congenital fistula
A visible fistulous tract toward the piriform sinus would indicate an underlying branchial pouch anomaly rather than isolated thyroiditis

data.description: 35-year-old female with a history of intermittent rhinitis presented with 5 days of urticaria, fever, headache, myalgia, and arthralgia. She developed pruritic, painful wheals and erythematous macules >1 cm on the limbs with burning sensation; lesions lasted >24 hours and left skin pigmentation changes. She also had nonpitting angioedema of the hands, fingers, ankles, and feet. Symptoms included severe headache and myalgia affecting daily activities, with fever up to 39.5°C. She had taken over-the-counter diet pills starting 18 days before symptom onset and had been evaluated 6 days earlier for dehydration and violaceous hives on the palms, after which she stopped the pills. Examination showed large confluent wheals and macules on the limbs with marked pruritus and muscle pain. Labs showed lymphopenia and elevated C-reactive protein; other routine tests, complement, thyroid studies, and antinuclear antibodies were normal or negative. Skin biopsy showed papillary dermal edema with superficial and perivascular lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrate, focal fibrin deposits in vessel walls, and erythrocyte extravasation.

A small-vessel immune-mediated skin vasculitis presenting with urticarial-appearing lesions that are painful or burning, persist for at least 24 hours, and may leave bruising or hyperpigmentation. It may be triggered by medications or supplements and can cause systemic symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Recent exposure to over-the-counter diet pills before onset
Angioedema of hands, feet, ankles, and fingers
Biopsy with perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, focal fibrin in vessel walls, and erythrocyte extravasation
Normal complement levels, compatible with normocomplementemic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: None of the major reported findings are atypical, although severe myalgia and headache are less common than skin and joint manifestations

data.description: A medication-associated hypersensitivity reaction characterized by fever, urticarial or morbilliform rash, joint pain, muscle aches, and sometimes angioedema. Unlike true serum sickness, complement levels are often normal and major organ involvement is uncommon.
symptoms_in_common: Symptoms began after a new medication or supplement exposure
symptoms_not_in_common: Painful burning lesions that persist for 24 hours and leave pigmentation are more characteristic of urticarial vasculitis
Biopsy showing fibrin deposits in vessel walls and erythrocyte extravasation suggests vasculitis rather than a typical serum sickness-like reaction
Lymphopenia is not a classic defining feature

data.description: An acute mast-cell-mediated eruption of transient itchy wheals, often caused by drugs, foods, infections, or supplements, with possible swelling of deeper tissues such as the hands, feet, lips, or eyelids.
symptoms_in_common: Erythematous macules and large confluent urticarial plaques
Angioedema involving hands, fingers, ankles, and feet
Temporal association with over-the-counter diet pills
Dermal edema and eosinophilic infiltrate on biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: High fever
Severe headache and myalgia affecting daily activity
Arthralgia
Lesions lasting about 24 hours rather than resolving within hours
Postinflammatory pigmentation changes
Fibrin deposits in vessel walls and erythrocyte extravasation on biopsy
Elevated C-reactive protein and lymphopenia

data.description: A systemic form of urticarial vasculitis associated with low complement levels and potentially with joint, eye, lung, kidney, or gastrointestinal involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Inflammatory biopsy findings involving small vessels
symptoms_not_in_common: Complement levels were normal rather than low
No reported kidney, pulmonary, ocular, or gastrointestinal involvement
No reported anti-C1q antibody positivity
Clear temporal association with diet-pill exposure favors drug-induced normocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis

data.description: A systemic inflammatory disorder characterized by high spiking fever, arthritis or arthralgia, myalgia, elevated inflammatory markers, and a transient salmon-colored rash.
symptoms_not_in_common: Rash is pruritic, painful, burning, and urticarial rather than a typical nonpruritic salmon-colored eruption
Angioedema is not typical
Lesions persist for approximately 24 hours and leave pigmentation
Biopsy shows eosinophilic perivascular inflammation with fibrin deposits, favoring urticarial vasculitis
No persistent inflammatory arthritis, leukocytosis, or reported marked ferritin elevation
Recent diet-pill exposure provides a more plausible trigger

data.description: 16-year-old girl with 4 weeks of intermittent abdominal pain that became more frequent over 2 weeks, progressing to twice daily episodes lasting 2 to 15 minutes. Pain was sharp, severe, worst in the epigastrium and upper quadrants, and later associated with nausea and repeated vomiting; it was not related to menstruation, position, time of day, or eating. She developed decreased appetite, fatigue, dizziness, generalized weakness, worsening constipation, and missed school. Exam showed dry mucous membranes and diffuse abdominal tenderness with guarding in the epigastrium and upper quadrants. Initial labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, mild anemia, thrombocytosis, and elevated ESR; urinalysis was normal and abdominal/pelvic ultrasonography was unrevealing. Past history included iron-deficiency anemia and anxiety disorder; medications included iron supplementation, oral contraception, and famotidine.

data.diagnosis: Rapunzel syndrome (gastric trichobezoar with intestinal extension)
data.description: A large mass of swallowed hair (trichobezoar) fills the stomach and extends beyond the pylorus into the small intestine. The endoscopic and CT images show a large hair-containing gastric mass with a long tail, characteristic of Rapunzel syndrome.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent severe epigastric and upper-quadrant abdominal pain
Early functional gastric outlet obstruction symptoms
Diffuse abdominal tenderness with upper-abdominal guarding
Leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, and elevated ESR consistent with inflammation or obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain not related to eating
No reported history of hair pulling or hair ingestion
No palpable upper-abdominal mass reported

data.description: A trichobezoar is a compact intragastric accumulation of swallowed hair. It can cause gastric irritation, partial outlet obstruction, malnutrition, anemia, and vomiting; in this case the images indicate an exceptionally large trichobezoar.
symptoms_in_common: Weight or nutritional compromise suggested by poor intake
symptoms_not_in_common: Very brief episodic pain lasting only 2 to 15 minutes is less typical than persistent postprandial discomfort
No reported early satiety
No reported halitosis
No reported alopecia or other physical evidence of trichotillomania

data.diagnosis: Small-bowel obstruction due to bezoar extension
data.description: The intestinal tail of a gastric trichobezoar can mechanically obstruct the duodenum or small bowel, producing intermittent crampy pain, vomiting, constipation, dehydration, and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Progressively more frequent abdominal pain episodes
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is mainly epigastric and upper-quadrant rather than predominantly central or lower abdominal
No reported abdominal distension
No reported inability to pass flatus
No reported bilious or feculent vomiting

data.diagnosis: Gastric outlet obstruction secondary to a large gastric bezoar
data.description: A large intragastric bezoar can obstruct gastric emptying at the pylorus, causing upper abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, poor oral intake, dehydration, and nutritional deficiencies.
symptoms_not_in_common: Vomiting was not specifically described as occurring after meals
Pain was not related to eating
No reported early satiety or postprandial fullness
Constipation is less specific for isolated gastric outlet obstruction

data.description: A 45-year-old white man was found dead at home and underwent autopsy as the cause of death was not apparent. He had recently been under review by the respiratory team for poor respiratory function and patchy fibronodular lung changes. His medical history included osteomyelitis of the elbow, congenital kyphoscoliosis, and testicular seminoma, which had been treated with orchidectomy and chemotherapy. At postmortem examination, the abdominal cavity contained copious pus covering the serosal aspect of the small bowel. There was an obvious perforation at the level of the mid-ileum, as well as three ulcers on the mucosal aspect of the ileum, one of which had perforated. Widespread pale nodules measuring up to 5 mm each were noted throughout the parenchyma of both lungs and a small pale lesion was present in the left kidney. No abnormalities were seen in the cardiovascular, endocrine, or central nervous systems.

data.diagnosis: Disseminated tuberculosis with intestinal ileal tuberculosis and perforation
data.description: Systemic infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis causing granulomatous disease in multiple organs. Ileal tuberculosis can produce ulceration, transmural inflammation, perforation, and fatal peritonitis; pulmonary and renal nodules may represent disseminated involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Patchy fibronodular lung changes and poor respiratory function
Ileal mucosal ulcers with one ulcer perforating through the bowel wall
Copious purulent peritonitis due to ileal perforation
Small pale renal lesion compatible with extrapulmonary mycobacterial involvement
Histology showing granulomatous inflammation with necrotic areas
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented fever, night sweats, weight loss, or chronic cough
No reported lymph-node enlargement
Sudden unexpected death without a known diagnosis of tuberculosis

data.diagnosis: Disseminated nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, especially Mycobacterium avium complex
data.description: A systemic infection caused by environmental mycobacteria, often occurring in immunocompromised individuals. It may involve lungs, gastrointestinal tract, bone, kidney, and other organs, with abundant acid-fast bacilli in tissue.
symptoms_in_common: Poor respiratory function with fibronodular pulmonary abnormalities
Numerous small pale nodules throughout both lungs
History of osteomyelitis, which can occur with disseminated mycobacterial infection
Ileal ulceration and perforation with peritonitis
Prior chemotherapy for seminoma, which may have contributed to impaired host defenses
symptoms_not_in_common: No stated severe immunodeficiency, HIV infection, transplant history, or long-term immunosuppressive treatment
No documented chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, or weight loss
Well-formed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation is often more characteristic of tuberculosis than disseminated MAC

data.description: Localized or disseminated tuberculosis involving the ileum, where it causes ulcerative granulomatous inflammation. Deep ulceration can penetrate the bowel wall and result in perforation, diffuse peritonitis, and sepsis.
symptoms_in_common: Acid-fast organisms in the inflammatory tissue
Concurrent pulmonary fibronodular disease supporting a pulmonary source for intestinal tuberculosis
symptoms_not_in_common: No recorded preceding abdominal pain, bowel obstruction, diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, fever, or weight loss
No described mesenteric lymphadenopathy, ascites, or peritoneal tubercles
Extensive pulmonary and renal lesions suggest disease broader than isolated intestinal tuberculosis

data.diagnosis: Crohn disease with ileal ulceration and perforation
data.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that commonly affects the terminal ileum and may cause transmural inflammation, deep ulcers, strictures, fistulas, and rarely free bowel perforation. Granulomas can be present but are noncaseating and acid-fast organisms are not expected.
symptoms_in_common: Transmural inflammatory process in the bowel wall
symptoms_not_in_common: Acid-fast bacilli in tissue
Widespread pulmonary pale nodules and fibronodular lung disease
Renal lesion compatible with disseminated infection
No reported chronic diarrhea, recurrent abdominal pain, weight loss, fistulas, strictures, or perianal disease
Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation is not typical of Crohn disease

data.description: 33-year-old man admitted with chest pain that began 2 hours earlier as epigastric pain and progressed to central chest pain, associated with one episode of vomiting, dizziness, dyspnea, diaphoresis, and distal paresthesias; pain had resolved on admission. Later he developed nausea, diaphoresis, pallor, blurred vision, muffled hearing, and tingling in both hands, with systolic blood pressure falling to 89 mm Hg and cardiac monitoring showing a 3–4 second pause without P waves. History included syncope with phlebotomy and recent flu-like symptoms; his daughter had gastroenteritis. Physical examinations were normal.

data.diagnosis: Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope (reflex syncope with sinus pause)
data.description: A neurally mediated reflex causing increased vagal tone, producing hypotension, bradycardia or transient sinus arrest, and presyncopal symptoms. It is often triggered by pain, nausea, vomiting, emotional stress, dehydration, or medical procedures.
symptoms_in_common: Hypotension with systolic blood pressure of 89 mm Hg
Transient 3-4 second pause without P waves, consistent with sinus arrest
Normal physical examination after symptom resolution
symptoms_not_in_common: Initial central chest pain
Dyspnea during the first episode

data.description: Myocardial ischemia caused by reduced coronary blood flow, ranging from unstable angina to myocardial infarction. It commonly causes central chest discomfort with autonomic symptoms.

data.description: A 21-year-old man presented to his general practitioner with intermittent left-sided pain in the anterior chest wall associated with neck discomfort. The pain was described as 'stabbing' in nature and had arisen suddenly while watching television, with no history of trauma before onset. The pain was not exacerbated by inspiration or effort. His medical history and physical examination were initially unremarkable. Several days later, he attended the emergency department with worsening chest pain and dyspnea. On examination, chest expansion was equal and breath sounds were normal, although there was crepitus on auscultation of the precordium. Palpation of the neck and supraclavicular fossae detected subcutaneous emphysema. His respiratory rate was 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturations were 100%. His full blood count and inflammatory markers were within normal limits.

Free air in the mediastinum occurring without trauma or an invasive procedure, often from alveolar rupture with air tracking along bronchovascular sheaths (the Macklin effect). The CT image shows mediastinal air adjacent to the trachea, and the clinical precordial crepitus with cervical subcutaneous emphysema is highly characteristic.
symptoms_in_common: Subcutaneous emphysema in the neck and supraclavicular fossae
Normal inflammatory markers and full blood count

data.diagnosis: Esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome or other esophageal rupture)
data.description: A full-thickness tear of the esophagus causing leakage of air and/or gastrointestinal contents into the mediastinum. It can produce pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema but usually follows forceful vomiting, instrumentation, or severe retching and may rapidly cause mediastinitis.
symptoms_not_in_common: No vomiting, retching, or dysphagia reported
No history of esophageal instrumentation or trauma
Normal inflammatory markers and full blood count
No fever or systemic toxicity
Pain developed while resting and was initially intermittent

data.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse, often presenting in young adults with sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. symptoms_not_in_common: Pain was not worsened by inspiration
Breath sounds were normal and chest expansion was equal

Chest radiograph does not demonstrate a visible pneumothorax or lung collapse
CT demonstrates mediastinal rather than pleural air

data.description: 34-year-old man in Scotland presented with an expanding itchy rash on the right flank that persisted for three months. He did not recall any insect bite or foreign travel history, but regularly visits the Scottish highlands. Initial Borrelia serology performed at 4 weeks after rash onset was negative.

The characteristic expanding annular skin lesion of Lyme borreliosis, caused by Borrelia infection transmitted by Ixodes ticks. Serology can be negative early in infection and erythema migrans is primarily a clinical diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Expanding red annular rash with central clearing
Regular exposure to Scottish Highlands, where tick exposure and Lyme disease occur
No recalled tick or insect bite, which is common in Lyme disease
Negative Borrelia serology early after rash onset can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent itch is less typical than minimal or absent symptoms
Persistence for three months is longer than the usual duration of untreated erythema migrans

data.description: A superficial dermatophyte fungal infection that commonly causes an itchy, enlarging ring-shaped rash with a more active red edge and central clearing.
symptoms_not_in_common: The border appears relatively smooth rather than distinctly scaly or raised
No reported exposure to infected people, pets, or contaminated surfaces
Very large expanding plaque without obvious scale is less typical

data.description: A reactive inflammatory skin eruption producing slowly enlarging annular red plaques, often on the trunk or proximal limbs; lesions may be mildly itchy and can persist for weeks to months.

Flank location is less typical than distal extremity involvement

data.description: A 39-year-old man with a history of current smoking and no other medical history presented with left-sided squeezing chest pain that was worse in the early morning after drinking alcohol and lasted 30 minutes. Initial vital signs showed blood pressure of 132/89 mmHg and pulse rate of 98 beats/minute. Initial laboratory findings revealed creatine kinase 118 U/L (normal 58-348), CK-MB 1.7 ug/L (normal 0-5.0), elevated highly sensitive troponin-T 0.027 ng/mL (normal 0-0.014), and microcytic hypochromic anemia with hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL. Echocardiography showed normal-sized cardiac chambers with good left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction of 61%) and no regional wall motion abnormality.

data.diagnosis: Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) with transient coronary artery spasm
data.description: Episodic myocardial ischemia caused by transient vasoconstriction of an epicardial coronary artery, often occurring at rest in the early morning. Smoking and alcohol can precipitate coronary spasm. Angiographic narrowing that resolves and intravascular imaging without major fixed plaque support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Squeezing left-sided chest pain occurring at rest
Mildly elevated high-sensitivity troponin-T indicating transient myocardial injury
Preserved left-ventricular function and no regional wall-motion abnormality
Coronary angiographic appearance compatible with dynamic narrowing rather than severe fixed obstructive disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Microcytic hypochromic anemia is not a typical direct manifestation of coronary vasospasm
No documented transient ST-segment elevation during the pain episode

data.diagnosis: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction due to coronary vasospasm (vasospasm-related MINOCA)
data.description: A myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) can result from prolonged coronary vasospasm, causing transient ischemia and troponin release without a persistent occlusive atherosclerotic lesion.
symptoms_in_common: Acute squeezing chest pain suggestive of myocardial ischemia
Possible ischemic ST-T abnormalities on the ECG
No regional wall-motion abnormality despite biochemical myocardial injury
Coronary imaging without clear severe fixed obstructive coronary disease
Smoking, which is a major risk factor for coronary vasospasm
symptoms_not_in_common: Initial CK and CK-MB levels are normal
The troponin elevation is relatively small
No persistent ST-segment elevation is described
Microcytic hypochromic anemia is not itself a typical infarction symptom

data.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome from atherosclerotic coronary artery disease
data.description: Acute coronary syndrome occurs when coronary atherosclerotic plaque rupture, erosion, or thrombosis causes reduced coronary blood flow and myocardial ischemia or infarction.
symptoms_in_common: Current smoking as a coronary risk factor
ECG changes that may represent myocardial ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age with few conventional atherosclerotic risk factors other than smoking
Pain occurred at rest in the early morning after alcohol use, a pattern more suggestive of vasospasm
Normal left-ventricular systolic function and no regional wall-motion abnormality
Coronary angiography and intravascular imaging appear not to show a major fixed obstructive plaque lesion
Microcytic hypochromic anemia is not typical of plaque-mediated acute coronary syndrome

data.diagnosis: Type 2 myocardial infarction or demand-related myocardial injury associated with anemia
data.description: Reduced oxygen delivery from significant anemia can contribute to myocardial oxygen supply-demand mismatch, producing ischemic chest discomfort and mild troponin elevation, particularly when another trigger such as tachycardia or coronary spasm is present.
symptoms_in_common: Hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic anemia
Pulse rate of 98 beats per minute
Chest pain potentially consistent with myocardial oxygen supply-demand imbalance
No regional wall-motion abnormality on echocardiography
symptoms_not_in_common: The chest pain was episodic, early morning, and alcohol-associated, which is more characteristic of coronary vasospasm
No severe tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxemia, sepsis, or other strong systemic demand trigger is reported
Dynamic coronary narrowing on angiography would not be explained by anemia alone
Smoking is more specifically associated with vasospastic angina than isolated anemia-related myocardial injury

data.description: 12-year-old Saudi boy presented with severe spontaneous dental pain for 3 days. He was the fourth of five siblings. Parents were not related. His mother had 5 previous spontaneous abortions in first trimester. Mother took acetazolamide 1000mg/day for idiopathic intracranial hypertension before and throughout pregnancy. Patient was born at full term via spontaneous vaginal delivery, weighing 2,270g (below 5th percentile). He presented without major dysmorphic features, was intelligent with good behavior, and had normal skin, hair and nails. Intraoral exam showed mixed dentition with retained primary lower central incisors, hypocalcified permanent upper incisors, and multiple carious teeth. Tongue, floor of mouth, upper lip, hard and soft palate were normal.

A congenital limb malformation characterized by absence or underdevelopment of central fingers and toes, producing a split-hand/split-foot appearance; it can occur with congenital absence of multiple teeth (oligodontia).
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral malformed hands with absent or hypoplastic digits consistent with ectrodactyly
Bilateral malformed feet with absent or hypoplastic toes
Panoramic radiograph showing multiple missing permanent tooth germs consistent with oligodontia
Retained primary lower central incisors, compatible with absent or delayed permanent successors
Multiple carious teeth, which may occur because of abnormal enamel and missing/abnormal dentition
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe spontaneous dental pain for 3 days
Maternal acetazolamide exposure throughout pregnancy
History of five maternal first-trimester spontaneous abortions

data.diagnosis: Ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefting syndrome (EEC syndrome, TP63-related disorder)
data.description: A TP63-related developmental disorder commonly causing split-hand/split-foot malformation, abnormalities of teeth and enamel, and variable ectodermal or cleft lip/palate findings. Expression is highly variable.
symptoms_in_common: Dental caries associated with enamel defects
symptoms_not_in_common: No cleft lip or cleft palate
Normal upper lip, hard palate and soft palate
Normal skin, hair and nails without obvious ectodermal dysplasia
No major dysmorphic facial features reported
Maternal acetazolamide exposure is not a typical feature of an inherited TP63 disorder

data.diagnosis: Acetazolamide embryopathy (teratogenic fetal exposure to acetazolamide)
data.description: A pattern of congenital abnormalities potentially associated with prenatal acetazolamide exposure. Reported concerns include fetal growth restriction and limb or craniofacial developmental abnormalities, although causality in individual cases can be difficult to establish.
symptoms_in_common: Documented maternal acetazolamide use before and throughout pregnancy
Low birth weight below the 5th percentile
Congenital bilateral hand and foot malformations
Dental developmental abnormalities including multiple missing teeth and enamel hypocalcification
symptoms_not_in_common: A classic, well-defined acetazolamide-specific syndrome is not established
Normal intelligence and behavior
No major craniofacial dysmorphism
No cleft lip or palate
Normal skin, hair and nails

data.description: A TP63-related ectodermal dysplasia syndrome that may include ectrodactyly or syndactyly, hypodontia/oligodontia, enamel defects, nail abnormalities, skin findings and lacrimal-duct abnormalities; clefting is usually absent.
symptoms_in_common: Retained primary incisors due to missing permanent teeth
Extensive dental caries associated with abnormal dental development
Absence of cleft lip and palate is compatible with ADULT syndrome
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal nails
Normal skin and hair
No reported lacrimal-duct obstruction or excessive tearing
No reported freckling or pigmentary skin changes
Maternal acetazolamide exposure is not a typical feature of this genetic syndrome

data.description: 62-year-old man with hypertension on amlodipine presented with one week of recurrent palpitations occurring four times, associated with rapid heartbeat and shortness of breath; two episodes followed alcohol intake. He denied chest pain and syncope. Physical examination showed blood pressure 160/90 mm Hg, regular pulse 82 bpm, and normal heart and respiratory examinations. Holter monitoring recorded frequent supraventricular ectopy and two episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.

An intermittent cardiac arrhythmia characterized by chaotic atrial electrical activity and irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm that spontaneously terminates within 7 days, often causing episodic palpitations and breathlessness.
symptoms_in_common: Shortness of breath associated with episodes
Holter documentation of two episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Frequent supraventricular ectopic beats, couplets, and runs
Alcohol intake preceding two episodes, a recognized trigger
Hypertension, an important risk factor for atrial fibrillation
symptoms_not_in_common: No chest pain
No syncope
Normal regular pulse between episodes

data.description: A form of atrial arrhythmia, commonly atrial fibrillation, precipitated by recent alcohol consumption, sometimes occurring even without chronic heavy alcohol use or structural heart disease.
symptoms_in_common: Documented paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on Holter monitoring
Episodes that are intermittent rather than continuously present
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypertension, which is an additional non-alcohol-related risk factor
No reported binge drinking quantity or chronic heavy alcohol use
Some episodes were not clearly linked to alcohol intake

data.diagnosis: Frequent premature atrial contractions with atrial tachyarrhythmia
data.description: Premature atrial contractions are early beats originating in the atria. A high burden of atrial ectopy, including couplets and short runs, can cause palpitations and may trigger atrial fibrillation or other supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.
symptoms_in_common: Holter showing very frequent supraventricular ectopic beats
Holter showing supraventricular couplets and runs
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, which can be triggered by frequent atrial ectopy
symptoms_not_in_common: No persistent irregular pulse on examination
No chest pain
No syncope

data.description: A 58-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. He also experienced urinary symptoms including frequency, urgency, and dysuria. Initial colonoscopy revealed prominent congestion and edema, loss of vascular pattern, and multiple moth-eaten ulcers with purulent exudates involving the entire colon. A repeat colonoscopy showed scattered irregular ulcers with with granular background mucosa and 'fuzzy' vasculature. The ileum appeared normal.

data.diagnosis: Primary colorectal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
data.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that can infiltrate the colon diffusely and cause ulceration, inflammatory-appearing mucosa, abdominal symptoms, and weight loss. The dense atypical lymphoid infiltrate and immunohistochemical staining in the images support a lymphoproliferative process.

Urinary urgency
Dysuria

Urinary urgency

No reported perianal disease, fistula, stricture, or granulomas
Urinary frequency
Urinary urgency

Biopsy appearance suggesting a lymphoproliferative lesion rather than classic Crohn inflammation

data.description: An opportunistic viral colitis that can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and large irregular colonic ulcers, especially in immunocompromised patients or those receiving immunosuppressive therapy. data.description: A previously healthy 9-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of left chest pain and increasing respiratory distress. His vital signs showed a respiratory rate of 40/min and heart rate of 105/min. Physical examination revealed unremarkable cardiac auscultation, while auscultation of lung fields showed diminished breath sounds over the left side.

Presence of both air and fluid in the left pleural space, causing partial collapse of the left lung. The radiographs show a large left-sided horizontal air-fluid level and a visible pleural line with compressed lung.

Partial collapse/compression of the left lung on imaging

data.description: 63-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension and diabetes was referred from primary clinic due to hepatic mass found on ultrasonography. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory findings showed normal hematological indexes, liver function tests, and renal functions. Patient was negative for viral markers with normal α-fetoprotein levels. Bone marrow biopsy showed 30% marrow cellularity but was otherwise normal. Serum calcium, β-2 microglobulin, and serum/urine protein immunoelectrophoresis were normal. Skeletal radiography revealed no abnormalities.

data.diagnosis: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
data.description: A localized monoclonal plasma-cell tumor occurring outside the bone marrow. Primary hepatic involvement is very rare. The liver lesion and plasma-cell-rich histology with plasma-cell immunophenotype support this diagnosis, while normal marrow, serum/urine immunoelectrophoresis, calcium, and skeletal survey support a solitary extramedullary process rather than systemic myeloma.
symptoms_in_common: Normal liver function tests despite a liver mass
Normal bone marrow examination without clonal marrow involvement
Normal serum and urine protein immunoelectrophoresis
Histology showing sheets of plasma-cell-like cells
Immunohistochemical staining consistent with plasma-cell differentiation

data.description: A systemic malignant plasma-cell disorder that may rarely involve the liver as a focal plasmacytoma or diffuse infiltration. It usually has bone marrow involvement, monoclonal protein production, lytic bone lesions, anemia, renal impairment, or hypercalcemia.

data.description: Young female European traveler presented to a medical clinic in central Australia with vaginal discharge after having sex with a new European traveler partner 1 week earlier in Sydney.

data.description: A 44-year-old man with a 17-year history of tobacco and cannabis use presented with acute dyspnoea and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. He had no other medical conditions and took no regular medications. On examination, he was thin and hypoxic, with a silent, hyper-resonant left hemithorax. Laboratory results showed normal α-1 antitrypsin concentration (1.4 g/L), normal immunoglobulins, and specific IgE for Aspergillus. Spirometry revealed severe obstruction with FVC of 2.95 L (57% predicted), FEV1 of 1.37 L (34% predicted), and FEV1/FVC ratio of 59% predicted.

A severe form of bullous emphysema in which giant air-filled bullae, usually upper-lobe predominant, occupy a large portion of a hemithorax and compress residual functioning lung. It is strongly associated with cigarette smoking and cannabis use.
symptoms_in_common: Long history of tobacco and cannabis smoking
Severe obstructive spirometry with markedly reduced FEV1 and reduced FEV1/FVC ratio
Chest radiograph and CT showing a very large left-sided air-filled bulla with compression of adjacent lung

data.diagnosis: Smoking-related chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with bullous emphysema
data.description: COPD/emphysema is chronic irreversible airflow obstruction caused most commonly by smoking. Destruction of alveolar walls may form bullae, including very large bullae in advanced disease.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging evidence of emphysematous bullous destruction

data.diagnosis: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due to rupture of an emphysematous bulla
data.description: A spontaneous pneumothorax can occur when a subpleural bleb or emphysematous bulla ruptures, allowing air into the pleural space. It commonly presents with sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness and is more likely in smokers with emphysema.

Severe chronic airflow obstruction indicates substantial underlying emphysema rather than an isolated primary pneumothorax
No described mediastinal shift or haemodynamic instability suggesting tension pneumothorax

Acute dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain, which can result from bullous disease or pneumothorax

data.description: 62-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes presented with 3 months of progressive fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, and vague upper abdominal pain. History includes a 40-pack-year smoking history (quit 2 years earlier), moderate alcohol use, and family history of smoking-related lung cancer. On presentation he had renal insufficiency (creatinine 3.2 mg/dL), severe anemia (hemoglobin 7 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (77,000/µL), hypercalcemia (12.7 mg/dL), elevated total protein (>10 g/dL), biochemical evidence of tumor lysis syndrome (LDH 1,157 U/L, uric acid 20.8 mg/dL), and coagulopathy consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation (prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer and fibrin split products).

An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with an extremely high proliferation rate. It commonly produces bulky abdominal/retroperitoneal disease, marrow involvement, spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome, and a 'starry-sky' histologic pattern; the image findings are consistent with a high-grade CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma.
symptoms_in_common: Marked hyperuricemia and spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome
Histology showing a high-grade lymphoid infiltrate with starry-sky appearance
B-cell immunophenotype compatible with CD20 positivity
symptoms_not_in_common: Older age is less typical than in endemic or pediatric Burkitt lymphoma, although sporadic adult cases occur
Smoking history is not a typical Burkitt lymphoma feature
Family history of smoking-related lung cancer is not specifically associated with Burkitt lymphoma

data.description: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults and may present with constitutional symptoms, abdominal masses, marrow involvement, elevated LDH, and tumor lysis syndrome. It is generally composed of larger atypical B cells rather than the classic uniform medium-sized cells of Burkitt lymphoma.
symptoms_in_common: Possible DIC in advanced aggressive disease

Very high uric acid and rapid-turnover clinical pattern are less typical for conventional diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

data.description: A clonal plasma-cell malignancy that commonly causes anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, and elevated serum protein due to monoclonal immunoglobulin production. It can cause bone lesions and marrow failure but does not usually produce a high-grade abdominal lymphoma mass or profound spontaneous tumor lysis.

Severe hyperuricemia and very high LDH are less typical

Histology of high-grade lymphoid cells with starry-sky pattern is not typical
CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma morphology is not typical of plasma-cell myeloma

data.description: A rapidly proliferative precursor lymphoid neoplasm that can cause cytopenias, high LDH, tumor lysis syndrome, organ infiltration, and occasionally bulky nodal or abdominal disease. It is distinguished from Burkitt lymphoma by precursor-cell morphology and immunophenotypic markers such as TdT.
symptoms_in_common: Possible abdominal mass or marrow involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation at age 62 is less typical, particularly for B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma
Hypercalcemia is not a common presenting feature
The described starry-sky high-grade mature B-cell morphology favors Burkitt lymphoma
CD20-positive mature B-cell staining pattern is less consistent with lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma
DIC is less characteristic than in some other acute leukemias

data.description: A 26-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of rash on her lower legs, abdomen, and arms, accompanied by a six-month history of paraesthesia in her right hand and left foot. She had no history of fatigue, weight loss, fever, or arthralgia. Neurological examination showed reduced sensation to light touch in the right ring and little fingers, the lateral palmar and dorsal hand, the left lateral calf, and the dorsum of the left foot. She experienced clumsiness in her right hand causing difficulty with writing, but no weakness was noted. Blood tests, including a full autoimmune screen, were normal. Electromyography demonstrated sensory damage in the right ulnar nerve and asymmetrical superficial sensory damage in the peroneal nerve, with greater involvement on the left side.

data.diagnosis: Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneous PAN) with mononeuritis multiplex
data.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of small- to medium-sized arteries confined predominantly to the skin, sometimes with peripheral nerve involvement. The image shows livedoid/purpuric lesions, and the biopsy is compatible with necrotizing vasculitis of a muscular vessel.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic purpuric or livedoid rash on the legs, abdomen, and arms
Skin lesions with a violaceous, reticular appearance
Paresthesia in multiple noncontiguous peripheral nerve distributions
Hand clumsiness related to sensory dysfunction
Absence of constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and fatigue
symptoms_not_in_common: No significant limb pain, nodules, ulcers, or livedo-related painful skin lesions were reported
No motor weakness was noted

data.description: A necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that can cause skin purpura or livedo reticularis and mononeuritis multiplex, often with renal, gastrointestinal, muscular, or constitutional involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Mononeuritis multiplex pattern involving the ulnar and peroneal nerves
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No fatigue
No weight loss
No arthralgia
No reported hypertension or renal involvement
No abdominal pain or gastrointestinal ischemic symptoms
No myalgia or muscle weakness
No other systemic organ involvement reported

data.diagnosis: ANCA-associated vasculitic neuropathy (for example microscopic polyangiitis)
data.description: Small-vessel systemic vasculitis may produce palpable purpura and painful asymmetric peripheral neuropathy or mononeuritis multiplex; it commonly affects the kidneys and/or lungs.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal autoimmune screen, with no reported ANCA positivity
No renal symptoms or reported urinary abnormalities
No respiratory symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, or hemoptysis
No constitutional symptoms
Biopsy appearance of muscular-vessel necrotizing arteritis is more characteristic of polyarteritis nodosa than microscopic polyangiitis

data.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis that can cause lower-extremity purpura, peripheral neuropathy, arthralgia, renal disease, and systemic symptoms, often associated with hepatitis C or autoimmune disease.
symptoms_in_common: Asymmetric nerve involvement can occur in vasculitic neuropathy
symptoms_not_in_common: No arthralgia
No fatigue, fever, or weight loss
No renal manifestations reported
Normal autoimmune testing
Rash also involves the abdomen and arms rather than being predominantly dependent lower-extremity palpable purpura
Biopsy of a medium-sized muscular artery is less typical than the small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis expected in cryoglobulinemia

data.description: 17-year-old male with high myopia and craniofacial-skeletal abnormalities. Full-term vaginal birth; birth weight 4.3 kg. Height tracked around the 80th percentile until age 15, then plateaued around the 55th percentile. History includes pectus excavatum present since birth, dental crowding and class III dentofacial growth pattern at age 12, retroclined lower teeth on exam, and a grade 3/6 systolic heart murmur noted at age 13. Current findings include scoliosis with loss of normal upper thoracic curvature. Measurements: weight 66.3 kg, height 177.5 cm, head circumference 58.5 cm. Laboratory testing showed markedly elevated homocysteine (237.0) with normal methionine, methylmalonic acid, vitamin B12, folate, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and MCV.

data.diagnosis: Classical homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) deficiency
data.description: An autosomal-recessive disorder of sulfur amino-acid metabolism causing markedly elevated homocysteine. It commonly produces a marfanoid skeletal phenotype, ectopia lentis/high myopia, osteoporosis, scoliosis, chest-wall deformity, and thromboembolic risk.
symptoms_in_common: Ocular findings on the images consistent with lens subluxation/ectopia lentis
Scoliosis and loss of normal thoracic spinal curvature
Low bone mineral density and vertebral deformity/compression changes on spinal imaging
Dental crowding and class III dentofacial growth pattern
Relatively tall stature earlier in adolescence
Heart murmur, which may occur with associated cardiovascular involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal methionine, since untreated CBS deficiency often causes elevated methionine
No reported thromboembolic event
No reported developmental delay or intellectual disability

data.diagnosis: Homocystinuria due to a remethylation defect (for example, MTHFR deficiency or cobalamin-processing disorder)
data.description: A group of inherited disorders that impair conversion of homocysteine to methionine, producing severe hyperhomocysteinemia with normal or low methionine. Neurologic, psychiatric, hematologic, and vascular manifestations are common, although presentations vary.
symptoms_in_common: Normal methylmalonic acid, which can be compatible with isolated remethylation disorders such as MTHFR deficiency
Normal vitamin B12 and folate levels despite hyperhomocysteinemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Pectus excavatum
Scoliosis and thoracic skeletal deformity
Dental crowding and class III dentofacial pattern
Lens subluxation/ectopia lentis and high myopia
Low bone mineral density with vertebral changes
No reported neurologic deterioration, seizures, cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms, or megaloblastic anemia

data.description: An autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder, usually caused by FBN1 variants, characterized by skeletal overgrowth, pectus deformity, scoliosis, ectopia lentis, myopia, and aortic-root disease.
symptoms_in_common: Ocular findings compatible with ectopia lentis
Dental crowding and craniofacial skeletal abnormalities
Heart murmur that could suggest structural cardiovascular involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated homocysteine
Normal methionine with severe hyperhomocysteinemia
Low bone mineral density and vertebral compression-type deformity are not defining Marfan features
Height plateauing during adolescence is less characteristic than progressive long-bone overgrowth

data.description: A heritable connective-tissue disorder involving TGF-beta signaling, characterized by arterial aneurysm/tortuosity risk, pectus deformity, scoliosis, craniofacial abnormalities, and sometimes myopia.
symptoms_in_common: Heart murmur, potentially reflecting cardiovascular involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated homocysteine
Normal methionine with severe hyperhomocysteinemia
Lens subluxation is less typical than in homocystinuria or Marfan syndrome
No reported arterial aneurysm, arterial tortuosity, hypertelorism, bifid uvula, or cleft palate

data.description: 29-year-old right-hand dominant male with hypothyroidism on thyroxine, presented with 4 days of progressive dull left-sided neck pain radiating to the head, diplopia, right-sided numbness, dropping objects, and unsteady gait. He denied alcohol or illicit drug use, seizure activity, head injury, or loss of consciousness. On examination, he was alert and oriented with mild hypertension, right-sided weakness mainly in the upper limb with pronator drift, reduced pinprick/light touch/proprioception on the right, resting and intention tremor with dysdiadochokinesia worse on the right, broad-based cerebellar ataxic gait, and an upgoing right plantar response. Pupils were equal and reactive; diplopia was present on extreme gaze without ocular palsy or papilloedema.

data.diagnosis: Pontine hemorrhage due to a brainstem cavernous malformation (cavernoma)
data.description: A cavernous malformation is a cluster of fragile, low-flow blood vessels that can bleed repeatedly. In the pons, even a small hemorrhage can cause prominent long-tract, cerebellar, sensory, and ocular symptoms. The CT images show a focal hyperdense pontine lesion consistent with acute hemorrhage, with associated ventricular enlargement; MRI supports a focal brainstem hemorrhagic lesion.
symptoms_in_common: Acute progressive headache and left-sided neck pain
Right-sided loss of pinprick, light touch, and proprioception
Right-sided upper motor neuron sign with upgoing plantar response
Dropping objects due to weakness and incoordination
Relatively preserved consciousness despite focal brainstem deficits
symptoms_not_in_common: No prior history of recurrent neurologic episodes or known familial cavernous malformations
Mild hypertension is not a defining feature of cavernoma-related hemorrhage

data.description: A pontine hemorrhage is bleeding within the pons, commonly related to chronic hypertension and rupture of small penetrating arteries.
