symptoms_not_in_common: No palpable abdominal mass or lymphadenopathy
No weight loss or constitutional cancer symptoms described
Elevated serum IgG4 favors IgG4-related fibroinflammatory disease over malignancy
No discrete primary tumor is described on the provided imaging

data.description: A 19-year-old man with no previous medical problems presented with a six-day history of breathlessness and left-sided chest pain that had started acutely. On examination, his respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute with oxygen saturations of 95% on room air. The patient had no significant past medical history and no other baseline characteristics were reported.

Air in the pleural space causing partial or near-complete collapse of a lung, occurring without trauma or known underlying lung disease; it is most common in young men. The radiograph shows a large left pneumothorax with absent peripheral lung markings and a collapsed left lung medially.
symptoms_in_common: Tachypnea with respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute
Young male with no known medical history
Chest radiograph showing marked left-sided hyperlucency with absent peripheral vascular markings

data.description: A pneumothorax in which intrapleural pressure rises sufficiently to compress the affected lung and potentially shift mediastinal structures, impairing venous return and causing hemodynamic compromise. A very large left pneumothorax is visible on the radiograph.
symptoms_in_common: Large left pneumothorax on chest radiograph
symptoms_not_in_common: Oxygen saturation of 95% on room air is relatively preserved for clinically significant tension physiology
No reported hypotension, tachycardia, severe hypoxemia, altered consciousness, or cardiovascular instability

data.description: A large air-filled space within the lung caused by destruction of alveolar tissue, which can mimic a pneumothorax on chest radiography. In this case, the visible collapsed lung edge and lack of peripheral markings favor pneumothorax rather than a bulla.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral hyperlucency of the left hemithorax on chest radiograph
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute onset of symptoms is more typical of pneumothorax than a stable giant bulla
No reported history of smoking, chronic lung disease, or prior bullous disease
Radiographic appearance of a pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings is more typical of pneumothorax

data.description: 28-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with fatigue, intermittent low-grade fevers, and migratory joint pain/swelling: initial right foot/ankle pain and swelling limiting walking for several days, followed by knee and hip pain and right elbow pain/swelling. Exam showed fever (38.3°C), diffuse joint tenderness without erythema or swelling, normal range of motion, and tachycardia; chest radiograph was clear. Five days later she returned with progressive orthopnea and dyspnea, with decreased joint pain except persistent right knee pain and stiffness. Repeat exam showed mild fever, tachycardia, elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral crackles, holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla, and a warm left knee with limited range of motion and severe pain on flexion. She was born in Brazil, moved to the northeastern United States 10 years earlier, and recalled childhood exertional shortness of breath.

data.diagnosis: Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic carditis causing severe mitral regurgitation
data.description: An immune-mediated complication of prior group A streptococcal streptococcal infection. It commonly causes migratory polyarthritis and carditis, with mitral-valve inflammation leading to mitral regurgitation and acute heart failure. The echocardiographic images are consistent with significant mitral regurgitation.
symptoms_in_common: Migratory joint pain and swelling involving ankle, knee, hip, and elbow
Large-joint arthritis with severe knee pain and stiffness
New holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla, consistent with mitral regurgitation
Orthopnea and progressive dyspnea from heart failure
Elevated jugular venous pressure and bilateral crackles
Echocardiographic appearance of important mitral-valve regurgitation
Childhood exertional shortness of breath, which may suggest previous rheumatic valvular disease
Birth and childhood in Brazil, where rheumatic fever remains more prevalent
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported preceding sore throat or documented recent streptococcal pharyngitis
No erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules, or chorea reported

data.diagnosis: Infective endocarditis with mitral-valve regurgitation and heart failure
data.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, that can produce fever, a new regurgitant murmur, embolic or immune-mediated joint manifestations, and heart failure when valve destruction is severe.
symptoms_in_common: New holosystolic murmur compatible with mitral regurgitation
Elevated jugular venous pressure and pulmonary crackles indicating heart failure
Arthralgias or arthritis can occur as an immune-mediated manifestation
symptoms_not_in_common: Migratory large-joint arthritis is more characteristic of acute rheumatic fever
No reported persistent high fever, chills, weight loss, or night sweats
No reported intravenous drug use, prosthetic valve, recent procedure, or known bacteremia risk factor
No reported peripheral endocarditis findings such as petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, or embolic events
No valvular vegetation is described on the provided echocardiographic images

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with Libman-Sacks endocarditis or lupus-associated valvular disease
data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause constitutional symptoms, inflammatory polyarthralgia or arthritis, and nonbacterial valvular lesions. Valvular involvement may cause regurgitation, although severe acute mitral regurgitation is less typical than in rheumatic carditis or infective endocarditis.
symptoms_in_common: Mitral-valve regurgitation with a holosystolic apical murmur
Dyspnea and orthopnea due to cardiac dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: No malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, alopecia, Raynaud phenomenon, or serositis reported
No renal, hematologic, or neurologic manifestations reported
The abrupt migratory large-joint pattern is more typical of acute rheumatic fever
The degree of acute heart failure from mitral regurgitation is less typical for lupus valvular disease

data.diagnosis: Disseminated gonococcal infection with migratory polyarthritis
data.description: Hematogenous spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae that may cause fever, migratory arthralgias, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and occasionally septic arthritis of a single joint. It does not usually cause valvular disease or heart failure.
symptoms_in_common: Migratory joint pains involving several joints
Progression to a prominently painful warm knee with limited motion
Minimal visible swelling early in the course can occur with migratory arthralgias
symptoms_not_in_common: New severe mitral regurgitation is not typical
Orthopnea, elevated jugular venous pressure, and pulmonary crackles indicating heart failure are not typical
No rash or tenosynovitis reported
No genitourinary symptoms or sexual exposure history reported
The echocardiographic valvular abnormality strongly suggests a cardiac process beyond uncomplicated disseminated gonococcal infection

data.description: A 56-year-old female patient presented with low-back and hip pain radiating down to her left leg for 12 months. She did not respond to initial management with conservative therapy of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications.

data.diagnosis: Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst (juxtafacet cyst), likely at L3-L4
data.description: A fluid-filled degenerative cyst arising from a lumbar facet joint that can protrude into the spinal canal or lateral recess and compress a nerve root. The MRI appearance of a well-circumscribed posterior-lateral cystic lesion adjacent to the facet joint is most consistent with this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral left leg-radiating pain consistent with lumbar radiculopathy
Persistent symptoms despite conservative NSAID treatment
Age in the typical degenerative-risk range

data.diagnosis: Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerative facet arthropathy with lateral recess compression
data.description: Degenerative enlargement of facet joints, ligamentous tissues, and disc-related changes can narrow the spinal canal or lateral recess, causing compression of lumbar nerve roots. The facet-associated cyst seen on MRI may be a focal contributor to stenosis.
symptoms_in_common: Pain radiating from the back/hip into one leg
Older age with likely degenerative spinal changes
symptoms_not_in_common: No neurogenic claudication or walking-induced bilateral leg symptoms were reported

data.description: Protrusion or extrusion of intervertebral disc material can compress a lumbar nerve root and produce sciatica. Disc degeneration is present on the images, although the focal cystic facet-adjacent lesion is more suggestive of a synovial cyst than a primary disc extrusion.
symptoms_in_common: Left-sided pain radiating down the leg
Failure of initial conservative anti-inflammatory treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: The 12-month persistent course is less typical of an acute disc herniation
MRI appearance favors a posterior facet-associated cystic lesion rather than a typical ventral disc extrusion

data.description: A 57-year-old male patient presented with a three-month history of fatigue, recurrent sore throats, and a persistent 'cold sore.' The patient had no relevant medical history, drank little alcohol, and was a non-smoker.

data.diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with possible cervical lymph-node metastasis
data.description: A malignant tumor of squamous cells, commonly presenting as a persistent nonhealing, crusted or ulcerated lesion on the lip. Regional lymph-node enlargement can indicate spread.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent ulcerated and crusted lesion at the lip corner described as a 'cold sore'
Nonhealing lesion present for approximately three months
Visible enlarged submandibular/upper cervical neck swelling
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent sore throats are not a classic presenting symptom of an isolated lip squamous cell carcinoma
Absence of smoking and substantial alcohol use lowers, but does not exclude, risk

data.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus infection (persistent herpes labialis)
data.description: HSV-1 commonly causes recurrent painful grouped blisters and crusted erosions on or around the lips, often called cold sores. Persistent or unusually severe disease may occur with immune dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Lesion described as a persistent 'cold sore'
Crusted ulcerative lesion at the lip margin
Recurrent sore throats may occur during viral illnesses
symptoms_not_in_common: A lesion persisting for three months without healing is atypical for uncomplicated herpes labialis
A prominent unilateral cervical/submandibular neck mass is not typical of routine recurrent cold sores
The lesion appears solitary and indurated/ulcerated rather than typical clusters of transient vesicles

data.diagnosis: Basal cell carcinoma of the perioral skin
data.description: Basal cell carcinoma is a slow-growing skin cancer that can present as a persistent ulcerated, crusted, or bleeding lesion on sun-exposed facial skin, including the area around the lips.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent nonhealing crusted ulcer near the lip
symptoms_not_in_common: Cervical lymph-node enlargement is unusual because basal cell carcinoma rarely metastasizes
Recurrent sore throats are not typical
Fatigue is not usually caused by localized basal cell carcinoma

diagnoses.name: Perioral lesion with plasma cell rich infiltrate
diagnoses.title: Plasma cell neoplasms

data.description: 28-year-old male patient admitted on November 27, 2013, complaining of diarrhea (loose stool, three to five times per day) for over 10 years and hematochezia for about 1 month. Had been diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia 5 months after birth, with hemoglobin level remaining 70-80 g/L (normal range 110-150 g/L) for most of the time. On admission, albumin level was 26 g/L (normal range 35-52 g/L). Liver and renal function were otherwise normal. Patient reported recurrent arthralgia in the knee and ankle joints.

An inherited hamartomatous polyposis syndrome characterized by multiple gastrointestinal polyps, especially in the small bowel, which can cause bleeding, anemia, intussusception, obstruction, diarrhea, and protein loss.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging suggestive of small-bowel intussusception related to polypoid lesions
Multiple polypoid gastrointestinal lesions on endoscopy
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent knee and ankle arthralgia
No reported mucocutaneous melanin pigmentation

data.description: A hamartomatous polyposis disorder with multiple juvenile polyps, usually involving the colon and stomach, causing rectal bleeding, chronic anemia, diarrhea, and protein-losing enteropathy.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic iron deficiency anemia beginning early in life
Low albumin suggesting intestinal protein loss
Multiple gastrointestinal polypoid lesions on endoscopy
Possible bowel intussusception due to polyps
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent knee and ankle arthralgia
Prominent small-bowel involvement is less typical than colonic involvement

data.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and may cause diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, bowel narrowing, and inflammatory arthritis.
symptoms_in_common: Possible bowel wall thickening or narrowing on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Anemia diagnosed at 5 months of age
Multiple polyp-like lesions and apparent intussusception are less characteristic than inflammatory strictures or ulcers

data.description: A disorder of dilated intestinal lymphatic vessels causing protein-losing enteropathy, chronic diarrhea, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and occasionally gastrointestinal bleeding or polypoid intestinal lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Polypoid or nodular intestinal lesions may occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Hematochezia is not a dominant typical feature
Severe iron deficiency anemia is less typical
Recurrent knee and ankle arthralgia is not typical
Intussusception from multiple polyps is uncommon

data.diagnosis: Common variable immunodeficiency with nodular lymphoid hyperplasia
data.description: An immune-deficiency disorder that can produce chronic infectious or inflammatory diarrhea, malabsorption, nodular lymphoid hyperplasia of the intestine, anemia, and low serum protein levels.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple small nodular or polypoid intestinal lesions can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Hematochezia is less typical
No history of recurrent respiratory or other infections is reported
Recurrent arthralgia is not a typical primary manifestation
Intussusception related to hamartomatous-appearing polyps is less typical

data.description: A 65-year-old male retired farmer presented with an inability to fully straighten the ring finger and little finger of his right hand, which had progressed over the past two years. He had recently noticed a 'rope like' swelling in his palm with no history of trauma. His medical history was unremarkable except for smoking cessation 10 years earlier with a 90 pack-year history. His father had a similar deformity. On examination, he had palpable cords to his middle, ring, and little fingers with palpable nodules on the volar aspect of all proximal phalanges, causing flexion contractures of the proximal interphalangeal joints. The cord and nodules in the ring finger were adherent to the overlying skin.

A benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia causing nodules and cord formation, progressively pulling the fingers into flexion. It commonly affects the ring and little fingers in older men and may be familial.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive inability to fully straighten the ring and little fingers over two years
Palpable rope-like swelling/cord in the palm
Palmar nodules and cords extending toward the middle, ring, and little fingers
Flexion contractures of the proximal interphalangeal joints
Adherence of the ring-finger cord and nodules to the overlying skin
Positive family history in his father
History of heavy smoking, a recognized association
symptoms_not_in_common: No major atypical symptoms are described

data.description: Inflammation and thickening around the flexor tendon pulley, usually at the metacarpophalangeal joint, causing painful clicking, catching, or locking during finger movement.
symptoms_in_common: Palpable palmar thickening near the finger flexor tendons
Involvement of the ring finger can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: No pain, clicking, catching, or intermittent locking is reported
Palpable cords extending into multiple fingers are not typical
Skin adherence over a cord is not typical
Fixed progressive proximal interphalangeal flexion contractures are less typical

Simultaneous involvement of middle, ring, and little fingers with palmar fascial nodules is not typical

data.description: A congenital or developmental condition characterized by a flexion contracture of the proximal interphalangeal joint, most often affecting the little finger.
symptoms_in_common: Flexion contractures of the proximal interphalangeal joints
symptoms_not_in_common: Late onset at age 63 with progression over two years is not typical
Palmar rope-like cords and nodules are not typical
Ring and middle finger involvement with palpable fascial cords is not typical
Adherence of nodules and cords to the skin is not typical
The condition is usually present in childhood or adolescence rather than newly developing in an older adult

data.diagnosis: Flexor tendon contracture or adhesions after hand trauma
data.description: Scarring or shortening of flexor tendons and surrounding tissues can limit finger extension after laceration, fracture, surgery, or prolonged immobilization.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to fully extend the affected fingers
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of trauma, hand surgery, fracture, or immobilization
Palpable rope-like palmar cords are not typical of tendon adhesions
Multiple palmar nodules and skin adherence are not typical
Family history of the same deformity is not typical
Typical tendon adhesions do not preferentially involve the ring and little fingers with characteristic palmar fascial cords

data.description: 57-year-old man with 8-year HIV infection and a 10-year history of bilateral inguinal hernias, left larger than right, previously reducible. Over 3 months he developed increasing pain with the bulge, and in the 3 weeks before presentation worsening left inguinal pain, enlarging hernia, intermittent subjective fevers, night sweats, and hard, tender lumps adjacent to the hernia; oral temperature reached 38.1°C the night before presentation. Past history includes Kaposi sarcoma, molluscum contagiosum, anal dysplasia, pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection, pneumocystis pneumonia, thrush, preseptal cellulitis, and cryptosporidium-related diarrhea. HIV was well controlled on antiretroviral therapy (CD4 250/mm³, undetectable viral load). Exam showed bilateral easily reducible inguinal hernias with bulky, slightly tender left inguinal lymphadenopathy, including three nodes up to 3 cm.

data.diagnosis: Syphilitic lymphadenitis (secondary syphilis with inguinal lymph-node involvement)
data.description: Lymph-node inflammation caused by Treponema pallidum, often occurring in secondary syphilis. It can produce prominent regional or generalized lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, follicular hyperplasia, plasmacytosis, and detectable spirochetes on immunostaining.
symptoms_in_common: Bulky tender left inguinal lymphadenopathy with nodes up to 3 cm
HIV infection, which is associated with increased risk of syphilis and sometimes atypical presentations
CT evidence of enlarged left inguinal lymph nodes
Lymph-node histology with reactive changes and immunostaining showing spirochete-like organisms
symptoms_not_in_common: Long-standing bilateral reducible inguinal hernias
Progressive hernia enlargement over several months
No reported genital ulcer, rash, mucous patches, or palmoplantar eruption

data.description: An invasive sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3. It may cause painful inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy, systemic symptoms, and inflammatory lymph-node disease, especially in men with HIV.
symptoms_in_common: Tender enlarged lymph nodes adjacent to the groin
Subacute progression over weeks to months
symptoms_not_in_common: Spirochete-like organisms demonstrated in the lymph node favor syphilis rather than Chlamydia infection
No reported transient genital papule or ulcer
No reported proctitis, rectal pain, discharge, or tenesmus
Bilateral chronic inguinal hernias are not caused by LGV

data.diagnosis: HIV-associated lymphoma (such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)
data.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurs at increased frequency in people with HIV and may present with enlarging lymph nodes, fever, night sweats, and extranodal disease. Inguinal nodes can be involved, although isolated regional painful adenopathy is less specific.
symptoms_in_common: HIV infection with prior opportunistic illnesses
CT evidence of enlarged inguinal lymph nodes
symptoms_not_in_common: Nodes are described as slightly tender, whereas lymphoma nodes are often painless
Spirochete-positive lymph-node staining supports an infectious cause rather than lymphoma
Histology appears reactive/inflammatory rather than a monomorphic malignant lymphoid proliferation
Hernia-associated pain and long-standing reducible hernias are not typical lymphoma manifestations

data.diagnosis: Mycobacterial lymphadenitis, including recurrent Mycobacterium avium complex infection
data.description: Mycobacterial infection can cause lymph-node enlargement, fever, night sweats, and constitutional symptoms in immunocompromised patients. Disseminated MAC is most common with advanced HIV immunosuppression, while localized mycobacterial lymphadenitis may occur at higher CD4 counts.
symptoms_in_common: Prior pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection
symptoms_not_in_common: CD4 count of 250 cells/mm3 and undetectable viral load make disseminated MAC less typical
No reported weight loss, persistent diarrhea, hepatosplenomegaly, or diffuse lymphadenopathy
Spirochetes identified in lymph-node tissue favor syphilitic lymphadenitis
No described granulomas or acid-fast organisms on histology

diagnoses.name: Necrotizing lymphadenitis
diagnoses.title: Histiocytic necrotising lymphadenitis of Kikuchi and Fujimoto

data.description: A 16-year-old girl presented with acute left shoulder pain, left-sided chest pain, and shortness of breath. She had a 4-month history of intermittent left shoulder and left-sided chest pain following a dance recital, which had been treated with analgesia and physiotherapy. She denied fever, cough, orthopnea, weight loss, and appetite change. Physical examination revealed tenderness at the location of the left fifth rib and reduced left chest expansion.

data.diagnosis: Solitary eosinophilic granuloma of the rib (osseous Langerhans cell histiocytosis)
data.description: A localized form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis causing a destructive lytic bone lesion, commonly involving flat bones such as ribs. It can produce adjacent soft-tissue inflammation, pleural reaction, and chest pain. The imaging appearance of a focal rib lesion with adjacent pleural abnormality and the histology showing inflammatory/Langerhans-type cells support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Localized tenderness over the left fifth rib
Left shoulder pain referred from the chest wall/pleura
Acute shortness of breath in the setting of pleural involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt worsening after a dance recital may suggest trauma but is not a typical cause of eosinophilic granuloma
Acute onset of severe shortness of breath is less typical unless there is associated pleural effusion or pneumothorax

data.diagnosis: Ewing sarcoma of the rib / Askin tumor
data.description: Ewing sarcoma is a malignant small round cell tumor that can arise from a rib and extend into adjacent soft tissue or pleura. It may cause a chest-wall mass, pleural effusion, chest pain, and respiratory symptoms in adolescents.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent focal rib and chest-wall pain
Imaging evidence of a chest-wall/rib-associated process with pleural involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No weight loss
No appetite change
No reported palpable chest-wall mass

data.diagnosis: Rib osteomyelitis with pleuritis or empyema
data.description: Infection of a rib can cause focal bony destruction, chest-wall pain, adjacent pleural inflammation, pleural effusion, and reduced expansion of the affected hemithorax. Infection can occasionally be indolent and present without marked systemic symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Possible adjacent pleural fluid/inflammatory change on imaging
Several months of intermittent pain before acute worsening
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No cough
No reported systemic illness
No appetite change
No reported preceding skin, respiratory, or bloodstream infection

data.diagnosis: Tuberculous osteomyelitis of the rib with a chest-wall cold abscess
data.description: Tuberculosis can rarely involve a rib, producing chronic localized pain, lytic rib destruction, chest-wall soft-tissue inflammation or abscess, and pleural disease. Constitutional symptoms may be absent, particularly in localized disease.
symptoms_in_common: Focal tenderness over the fifth rib
Possible lytic rib lesion with adjacent soft-tissue/pleural abnormality
Shortness of breath related to pleural involvement
Lack of high fever can occur in indolent tuberculosis
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No cough
No weight loss
No appetite change
Relatively acute respiratory deterioration is less characteristic of slowly progressive rib tuberculosis

data.diagnosis: Pathologic rib fracture or stress injury with reactive pleural effusion
data.description: A rib stress injury or pathologic fracture can cause focal chest-wall pain after strenuous physical activity and may be associated with pleural irritation, small effusion, or reduced expansion. A destructive-appearing rib lesion, however, would raise concern for an underlying bone disorder rather than an uncomplicated athletic injury.
symptoms_in_common: Pain beginning after strenuous dance activity
Localized pain and tenderness at the left fifth rib
Pain persisting despite analgesia and physiotherapy
Chest pain worsened enough to limit chest expansion
Shoulder pain can be referred from chest-wall or pleural irritation
Shortness of breath can occur with painful splinting or pleural irritation
symptoms_not_in_common: Four months of persistent symptoms is longer than expected for many uncomplicated rib strains
Pleural/chest-wall mass-like imaging findings are not typical of a simple stress injury
Acute shortness of breath is not typical without pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pleural effusion

diagnoses.name: Rib osteosarcoma
diagnoses.title: Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage of ribs, sternum or clavicle

data.description: A 66-year-old man presented with a 4 to 5-month history of fever, chills, drenching night sweats, and unintentional 35-kg weight loss. He had previously undergone work-up for fever of unknown origin including evaluation for infectious causes such as tuberculosis, typhoid, and brucellosis, but these were not revealing. On physical examination, his spleen was palpable but no adenopathy was detected. Blood tests revealed anemia with hemoglobin of 9.0 g/dL (normal 13.0-18.0 g/dL), microcytosis with mean corpuscular volume of 75 fl (normal 80.0-94.0 fl), normal platelet count of 354,000/μL, and elevated international normalized ratio of 1.30 (normal 0.85-1.20). His serum ferritin level was significantly elevated at 1,796.0 ng/mL (normal 25-310 ng/mL).

data.diagnosis: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
data.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma arising predominantly in the spleen. It can present as a solitary splenic mass with constitutional B symptoms and may occur without peripheral lymphadenopathy.
symptoms_in_common: No detectable peripheral adenopathy, which can occur in primary splenic lymphoma
Cytology showing atypical large cells and immunostaining compatible with a hematolymphoid malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Microcytic anemia is not a classic specific feature and may reflect chronic inflammation or iron deficiency
Elevated INR is not a typical presenting feature
Very high ferritin is nonspecific and may reflect inflammation or associated hemophagocytic activation

data.description: A rare, highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor of the spleen that may form a splenic mass and cause systemic symptoms, anemia, coagulopathy, and splenomegaly.
symptoms_in_common: Mildly elevated INR, which can occur with tumor-related coagulopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Drenching night sweats are more characteristic of lymphoma than angiosarcoma
Normal platelet count is less typical because splenic angiosarcoma often causes thrombocytopenia or consumptive coagulopathy
Marked ferritin elevation is not a characteristic specific finding

data.description: A rare lymphoma confined mainly to the spleen at presentation. It may cause B symptoms, splenomegaly, anemia, and a focal splenic lesion, sometimes without palpable lymph nodes.
symptoms_in_common: No peripheral adenopathy can occur in rare primary splenic presentations
symptoms_not_in_common: Microcytosis is not a typical defining feature
Elevated INR is not typical
Marked hyperferritinemia is nonspecific rather than characteristic
Primary splenic Hodgkin lymphoma is much rarer than nodal Hodgkin lymphoma

data.description: A systemic parasitic infection caused by Leishmania species, classically producing prolonged fever, weight loss, splenomegaly, anemia, hyperferritinemia, and macrophages containing intracellular organisms in tissue aspirates.
symptoms_in_common: Possible macrophage-rich cytology with intracellular structures that can resemble amastigotes
symptoms_not_in_common: A discrete dominant splenic mass is less typical than diffuse splenic enlargement
Normal platelet count is less typical because pancytopenia or thrombocytopenia is common
The reported negative infectious work-up does not exclude leishmaniasis but makes common infectious explanations less likely
No exposure, travel, or endemic-area history is provided

diagnoses.name: Splenic involvement
diagnoses.title: Fibrosis of spleen[Schistosomiasis involving the skin]

data.description: 52-year-old man with history of hypertension, BPH with obstructive nephropathy, chronic renal insufficiency requiring dialysis until a living-related renal transplant 1 year earlier, and hyperparathyroidism with bilateral cataract surgery, presented with acute palpitations and chest pressure. Two days earlier he developed epigastric burning, fatigue, weakness, and vomiting, partially relieved by antacids. He denied fever, chills, or other localizing symptoms. On arrival, heart rate was 200 bpm with atrial fibrillation and rapid ventricular response; after cardioversion, pulse was 53 bpm and blood pressure 128/90 mmHg. Exam showed a diffuse, laterally displaced apical impulse, loud second heart sound, and fourth heart sound, without murmurs or jugular venous distention. Labs showed creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, troponin T 1.04 ng/mL, normal electrolytes and liver tests, WBC 6100/mm³, hematocrit 37.9%, platelets 148,000/mm³, normal TSH, tacrolimus 8.2 ng/mL, and urinalysis with 2+ proteinuria. Serum protein electrophoresis and free light-chain ratio were unremarkable, and leukocyte α-galactosidase activity was markedly reduced.

data.diagnosis: Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease) with cardiac involvement
data.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, resulting in globotriaosylceramide accumulation in the kidneys, heart, nervous system, skin, and eyes. Cardiac involvement commonly produces concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, and myocardial fibrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic renal insufficiency progressing to dialysis and renal transplantation
Left-ventricular hypertrophy suggested by laterally displaced apical impulse and ECG voltage
Echocardiographic appearance consistent with marked concentric ventricular hypertrophy
Fourth heart sound, consistent with impaired ventricular relaxation/diastolic dysfunction
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Elevated troponin without an alternative systemic inflammatory explanation
History of bilateral cataract surgery, which may reflect ocular involvement
Gastrointestinal symptoms including epigastric burning, vomiting, fatigue, and weakness
symptoms_not_in_common: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with obstructive nephropathy
Hypertension, which may be comorbid and can independently contribute to left-ventricular hypertrophy
No reported angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, hypohidrosis, or heat intolerance

data.diagnosis: Hypertensive heart disease with concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy
data.description: Long-standing systemic hypertension can cause concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, reduced ventricular compliance, diastolic dysfunction, left-atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation, and myocardial oxygen-demand ischemia with mild troponin elevation.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse and laterally displaced apical impulse
ECG findings compatible with left-ventricular hypertrophy and repolarization abnormality
Elevated troponin, potentially from demand ischemia during tachyarrhythmia
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly reduced leukocyte alpha-galactosidase activity
Renal failure and proteinuria at a relatively young age that may reflect a systemic storage disorder
Cataract history and gastrointestinal symptoms are not characteristic manifestations of hypertensive heart disease
The degree and systemic pattern of disease are not fully explained by uncomplicated hypertension

data.description: An infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular amyloid protein deposition. It can produce increased ventricular wall thickness, restrictive physiology, atrial arrhythmias, conduction disease, proteinuria, renal dysfunction, and elevated cardiac biomarkers.
symptoms_in_common: Fourth heart sound and probable diastolic dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light-chain ratio are unremarkable, arguing against AL amyloidosis
Markedly reduced leukocyte alpha-galactosidase activity strongly favors Fabry disease instead
No described low-voltage ECG; the ECG instead suggests hypertrophy
No reported heart failure symptoms, edema, orthostatic hypotension, neuropathy, macroglossia, or purpura

data.description: A genetic myocardial disease characterized by otherwise unexplained left-ventricular hypertrophy, often asymmetric but sometimes concentric, with diastolic dysfunction, myocardial ischemia, atrial enlargement, and atrial or ventricular arrhythmias.
symptoms_in_common: Marked left-ventricular hypertrophy on ECG and echocardiography
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe renal disease with proteinuria and renal transplantation is not typical of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Marked alpha-galactosidase deficiency is not a feature of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
No reported family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden cardiac death
No described systolic murmur or dynamic left-ventricular outflow tract obstruction

data.description: Male infant, 22 hours old, admitted for repeated right-sided limb clonic seizures for 16 hours. Born at 40+6 weeks by cesarean section after frequent variable fetal heart decelerations; amniotic fluid was reduced and grade I turbid, with no premature rupture of membranes. Apgar scores were 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes; birth weight 3380 g. Seizures began 6 hours after birth, involved the right limbs, were not accompanied by altered consciousness or cyanosis, resolved spontaneously, and occurred 4 times. On admission, vital signs were stable; the infant was alert with good responsiveness, normal skin color, flat anterior fontanelle, normal pupils and light reflexes, coarse breath sounds without rales, normal cardiac exam, soft abdomen without masses, and normal limb activity, muscle tone, and primitive reflexes.

data.diagnosis: Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left middle cerebral artery territory infarction)
data.description: An acute interruption of arterial cerebral blood flow causing focal brain infarction. The diffusion-weighted MRI shows a focal area of restricted diffusion in the left cerebral hemisphere, consistent with an acute ischemic infarct, likely in a left middle cerebral artery cortical territory.
symptoms_in_common: Focal clonic seizures involving the right-sided limbs
Seizure onset within the first day of life
Normal general neurologic examination can occur early in neonatal stroke
MRI evidence of unilateral focal diffusion restriction in the left cerebral hemisphere
Contralateral relationship between left cerebral lesion and right-sided seizures
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear persistent focal weakness or asymmetric tone was documented
No documented laterality-specific reduction in spontaneous limb movement

data.diagnosis: Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke due to left middle cerebral artery branch occlusion
data.description: A subtype of neonatal stroke caused by thrombotic or embolic occlusion of a cerebral artery around the time of birth. Vascular imaging may show reduced visualization or narrowing of a left middle cerebral artery branch, while MRI demonstrates acute infarction.
symptoms_in_common: Early neonatal presentation at 6 hours after birth
Diffusion-restricted lesion in the left cerebral hemisphere
Imaging pattern compatible with an arterial vascular territory lesion
Fetal heart-rate decelerations, which may reflect perinatal stress and are a possible associated risk factor
symptoms_not_in_common: Apgar scores were normal at 1, 5, and 10 minutes
No documented congenital heart disease, placental thrombus, or known coagulation disorder
No persistent neurologic deficit was identified at admission

data.description: Brain injury from impaired oxygen delivery and/or blood flow around birth. It commonly causes neonatal seizures, but classic HIE usually produces diffuse or bilateral brain injury rather than a sharply focal unilateral arterial-territory lesion.
symptoms_in_common: Seizures beginning during the first day of life
History of frequent variable fetal heart decelerations before delivery
Reduced and turbid amniotic fluid, which may accompany intrapartum stress
symptoms_not_in_common: Seizures were consistently focal and limited to the right limbs rather than generalized or multifocal
Infant was alert and responsive with normal tone and primitive reflexes
No low Apgar scores or need for resuscitation
No cyanosis or depressed consciousness during seizures
MRI lesion appears focal and unilateral, favoring arterial infarction rather than typical diffuse HIE

data.description: Bleeding into the brain parenchyma, ventricles, or subarachnoid space can provoke seizures in newborns. However, the described MRI diffusion abnormality and apparent vascular-territory distribution are more suggestive of ischemic infarction than hemorrhage.
symptoms_in_common: Focal clonic seizure activity can occur with a focal cerebral hemorrhage
Potential perinatal stress before cesarean delivery
symptoms_not_in_common: No bulging fontanelle
No lethargy, coma, pallor, apnea, or hemodynamic instability
No anemia or bleeding manifestations were reported
MRI appearance is described as focal diffusion restriction rather than a hemorrhagic signal pattern
No intraventricular or extra-axial blood collection is evident from the provided images

data.description: 19-year-old woman with 3 weeks of right shoulder and right flank pain, followed 2 weeks later by progressive exertional dyspnea and nonproductive cough that worsened over an 8-day cruise to severe dyspnea with walking, requiring a wheelchair. On presentation she was ill-appearing with increased work of breathing, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and a murmur. She also had intermittent back pain for 6 months, visible chest pulsations and labored breathing during sleep for 2 weeks, and two episodes of diarrhea during the cruise. History included asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection 2 months earlier, dental cleaning 5 weeks earlier, anxiety, and anemia. Initial labs showed microcytic anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, elevated ESR and CRP, and low albumin.

data.diagnosis: Takayasu arteritis with severe aortic regurgitation and heart failure
data.description: A chronic large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, typically in young women. Imaging is consistent with diffuse aortic wall disease and branch-vessel stenoses; aortic-root involvement can cause severe aortic regurgitation and acute decompensated heart failure.
symptoms_in_common: Visible chest pulsations and labored breathing during sleep
Imaging evidence of aortitis and stenotic disease involving the aorta and branch vessels
Echocardiographic evidence compatible with severe aortic regurgitation
symptoms_not_in_common: Two isolated episodes of diarrhea during the cruise
Recent dental cleaning
Remote asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection

data.diagnosis: Severe chronic aortic regurgitation causing acute decompensated heart failure
data.description: Aortic valve incompetence causes diastolic blood flow from the aorta back into the left ventricle. Severe regurgitation produces a murmur, wide pulsatile circulation, pulmonary congestion, dyspnea, and eventual heart failure. In this case, the likely cause is inflammatory aortic-root disease from Takayasu arteritis.
symptoms_in_common: Echocardiographic color Doppler evidence of marked aortic regurgitation
Diastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta on Doppler imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Six months of intermittent back pain
Right flank pain
Elevated ESR and CRP as a primary finding
Leukocytosis and thrombocytosis
Two episodes of diarrhea

data.diagnosis: Infective endocarditis involving the aortic valve
data.description: Infective endocarditis is microbial infection of the endocardial surface, often involving a cardiac valve. Aortic-valve infection can cause new severe aortic regurgitation, heart failure, systemic inflammation, and embolic or musculoskeletal pain. It is an important alternative because of the murmur, inflammatory markers, and recent dental procedure.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive dyspnea from possible severe aortic regurgitation
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported fever or chills
No reported positive blood cultures
No reported peripheral stigmata of endocarditis
Diffuse aortic and branch-vessel stenoses on CT are not typical of isolated infective endocarditis
Young woman demographic is more characteristic of Takayasu arteritis than endocarditis-related diffuse aortitis

data.diagnosis: Aortitis due to another inflammatory vasculitis, such as Behcet disease or isolated idiopathic aortitis
data.description: Inflammatory aortitis can thicken the aortic wall, cause aneurysmal or stenotic changes, involve major branches, and produce aortic-valve regurgitation. Behcet disease and isolated idiopathic aortitis can occasionally mimic Takayasu arteritis, although the demographic and vascular pattern favor Takayasu disease.
symptoms_in_common: Aortic wall and major branch-vessel abnormalities on CT
Back, shoulder, and flank pain that may reflect vascular inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: No recurrent oral ulcers
No genital ulcers
No uveitis or other inflammatory eye disease
No characteristic skin lesions
No reported recurrent thrombosis
No reported inflammatory bowel disease symptoms beyond two brief diarrhea episodes

data.description: Giant cell arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that can involve the thoracic aorta and cause aortic regurgitation or aortic aneurysmal disease. It can produce elevated inflammatory markers and constitutional illness, but it overwhelmingly affects adults older than 50 years.
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 19 years is profoundly atypical
No headache
No scalp tenderness
No jaw claudication
No visual symptoms
Extensive branch-vessel stenoses in a young woman are more typical of Takayasu arteritis

data.description: 56-year-old man with a 7-day history of worsening epigastric pain with nausea and belching. Past history includes traumatic splenectomy, hyperlipidaemia, obesity, and Bell’s palsy; prior CT showed multiple abdominal nodules consistent with splenunculi. He had started orlistat about 10 days before symptom onset. On exam he was haemodynamically stable, mildly febrile (37.5°C), with epigastric and left iliac fossa tenderness; rectal exam was negative for blood, masses, or melaena. Labs showed mild neutrophilia and elevated CRP with normal liver, renal, amylase, and lipase results. Pain persisted despite analgesia and high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy, and inflammatory markers worsened while awaiting endoscopy.

data.diagnosis: Torsion and infarction of an accessory spleen (torsed splenunculus)
data.description: An accessory spleen can remain after traumatic splenectomy and may rarely twist on its vascular pedicle, causing venous congestion, infarction, local inflammation, and acute abdominal pain. The CT appearances of an inflamed mesenteric mass with a twisted vascular pedicle are highly suggestive.
symptoms_in_common: Known multiple splenunculi after prior traumatic splenectomy
Normal amylase and lipase despite persistent pain
symptoms_not_in_common: Belching
Recent initiation of orlistat

data.diagnosis: Infarction of accessory splenic tissue without torsion
data.description: Accessory splenic tissue may become infarcted because of compromised arterial or venous supply. It produces localized abdominal pain and inflammatory-marker elevation, with CT potentially showing poorly enhancing or inflamed ectopic splenic tissue.
symptoms_in_common: Epigastric and left iliac fossa tenderness
History of splenectomy with documented abdominal splenunculi
No biochemical evidence of pancreatitis or hepatobiliary disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Belching
Temporal association with orlistat use

data.description: Mesenteric panniculitis is inflammatory change within mesenteric fat that can cause abdominal pain, nausea, low-grade fever, and raised inflammatory markers. CT typically demonstrates mesenteric fat stranding, soft-tissue nodules, and inflammatory change around mesenteric vessels.
symptoms_in_common: CT evidence of mesenteric inflammatory change
symptoms_not_in_common: Known splenunculi, which more strongly support an accessory-spleen complication
Acute severe progression over only 7 days
Focal left iliac fossa tenderness

data.description: Acute inflammation of the pancreas commonly causes severe epigastric pain with nausea and elevated pancreatic enzymes; CT may show peripancreatic inflammatory change in established disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal amylase
Normal lipase
No described pancreatic enlargement or peripancreatic inflammatory changes on CT
Left iliac fossa tenderness
Known accessory spleens with imaging suggesting a focal mesenteric lesion

data.description: A 12-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 48-hour history of abdominal pain localised in the hypogastrium, which had progressively worsened in the last few hours. The patient mentioned previous episodes of less intense abdominal pain. Considering the clinical suspicion of acute appendicitis, an abdominal ultrasound was requested.

Obstruction of menstrual outflow by an imperforate hymen causes accumulation of blood in the vagina and often uterus (hematocolpos/hematometra). Ultrasound may show a large midline pelvic cystic structure containing homogeneous low-level internal echoes consistent with retained blood.
symptoms_in_common: Previous recurrent episodes of less intense abdominal pain

data.diagnosis: Obstructed hemivagina with hematometrocolpos (OHVIRA syndrome or other Müllerian outflow obstruction)
data.description: A congenital Müllerian anomaly, such as an obstructed hemivagina, can lead to retained menstrual blood in one side of the vagina and uterus. It may present after menarche with cyclic or recurrent pelvic pain and a complex fluid-filled pelvic mass on ultrasound.
symptoms_in_common: Prior recurrent episodes of abdominal pain
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain described as a continuous 48-hour episode rather than clearly cyclic

data.description: An endometrioma is an ovarian cyst containing old blood from endometriosis. On ultrasound it commonly has homogeneous low-level 'ground-glass' internal echoes, although it is uncommon at 12 years of age.
symptoms_in_common: Previous episodes of less intense abdominal pain
Cystic pelvic lesion with internal low-level echoes on ultrasound
symptoms_not_in_common: Very young age for typical endometrioma presentation
Rapid progression to severe pain over 48 hours is less typical without cyst rupture or torsion

data.diagnosis: Ovarian torsion associated with an ovarian cyst
data.description: Ovarian torsion is twisting of the ovary and its vascular pedicle, often around a cyst or enlarged ovary. It causes acute pelvic pain and requires urgent evaluation; ultrasound may show an enlarged cystic ovarian mass, though Doppler findings are needed for assessment.
symptoms_in_common: Possible pelvic cystic mass on ultrasound
symptoms_not_in_common: History of previous recurrent milder abdominal pain is less characteristic of a single acute torsion episode
Pain is described as hypogastric rather than clearly unilateral

data.description: Acute appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix and is a common cause of acute abdominal pain in children. Pain often begins centrally and localizes to the right lower quadrant, although pelvic appendicitis can produce hypogastric pain.
symptoms_in_common: Progressively worsening pain over approximately 48 hours
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain localized to the hypogastrium rather than the typical right lower quadrant
Previous recurrent episodes of milder abdominal pain
Large midline complex fluid-filled pelvic structure on ultrasound is not typical of uncomplicated appendicitis

data.description: 8-year-old Korean boy with severe global developmental delay and multiple exostoses. Developmental delay was first noted at 3 months of age with poor eye contact and head control. He was born at 40 weeks to healthy non-consanguineous parents, with no perinatal problems. Examination showed hypotonia, ptosis, nystagmus, microcephaly, severe growth retardation, and characteristic facial features including sparse eyebrows, prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic nare, down-turned mouth, and high-arched palate. He could not sit or walk independently. At 5 years, testing showed severe intellectual disability. Multiple exostoses were first observed at 6 years as protrusions of the right wrist and knee.

A contiguous gene-deletion syndrome caused by deletion of 11p11.2, commonly involving EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A. It is characterized by multiple osteochondromas/exostoses, parietal foramina or other skull ossification defects, developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, growth retardation, and distinctive craniofacial features.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple exostoses of the wrist, knee, and other long-bone metaphyses on radiographs
Severe global developmental delay and severe intellectual disability
Early hypotonia and inability to sit or walk independently
Microcephaly and severe postnatal growth retardation
Characteristic facial appearance including sparse eyebrows, prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic nares, down-turned mouth, and high-arched palate
Skull imaging showing bilateral parietal ossification defects/parietal foramina
Chromosomal microarray showing an 11p deletion involving EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A
symptoms_not_in_common: No major symptoms are clearly atypical; the presentation is highly characteristic of Potocki-Shaffer syndrome

data.description: An autosomal dominant skeletal disorder, usually caused by pathogenic variants in EXT1 or EXT2, producing multiple cartilage-capped bony outgrowths near the metaphyses of long bones during childhood.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple bony protrusions/exostoses emerging in childhood
Radiographic osteochondromas involving the wrist/forearm and knees
Growth impairment can occur in more severe cases
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe global developmental delay
Severe intellectual disability
Marked hypotonia from infancy
Microcephaly
Distinctive dysmorphic facial features
Ptosis and nystagmus
Parietal foramina/skull ossification defects
Deletion involving multiple 11p11.2 genes rather than an isolated EXT1 or EXT2 disorder

data.description: A contiguous gene-deletion disorder involving 8q23-q24, typically including EXT1 and TRPS1. It causes multiple exostoses, short stature, characteristic facial features, sparse hair, and variable developmental delay.
symptoms_in_common: Short stature or severe growth retardation
Prominent nasal bridge and nasal abnormalities can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe neonatal-onset hypotonia and profound motor impairment are less typical
Microcephaly is not a defining feature
Parietal foramina or large parietal skull ossification defects are not typical
Ptosis and nystagmus are not classic findings
The detected deletion is on chromosome 11p and includes EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A rather than chromosome 8q involving EXT1 and TRPS1

data.description: 15-year-old boy with congenital neutropenia due to an ELA2 mutation and refractory anemia with excess blasts 2, referred for bone marrow transplantation. Since infancy, he had chronic severe neutropenia (ANC 200–1,000/µL) requiring granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and antibiotics for recurrent bacterial skin and lung infections. For several weeks, he had multiple nonpruritic skin ulcerations on the right abdomen, scalp, and left ankle. Exam showed these ulcerations. Labs while on G-CSF showed normal ANC, normal lymphocyte and eosinophil counts, markedly elevated IgG, and normal IgE.
A contagious infestation by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite. The biopsy image directly shows a mite within the stratum corneum, supporting this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple skin lesions involving the scalp, abdomen, and ankle
Histologic identification of a mite in the stratum corneum
Dermal inflammatory infiltrate beneath involved epidermis
Immunocompromised state, which can produce atypical scabies presentations
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of pruritus; classic scabies is usually intensely itchy
Prominent ulceration is not typical of uncomplicated scabies
Scalp involvement is uncommon in immunocompetent adolescents and adults
Chronic severe congenital neutropenia is not caused by scabies
Recurrent bacterial lung infections are not typical manifestations of scabies

data.description: A severe, highly contagious form of scabies occurring most often in patients with impaired immune function or reduced ability to scratch. It may cause extensive crusted, hyperkeratotic, erosive, or ulcerated lesions and can be minimally pruritic.
symptoms_in_common: Immunocompromised host with congenital neutropenia and marrow disease
Widespread lesions at multiple body sites
Crusted and ulcerated scalp and truncal lesions
Mite demonstrated histologically in the stratum corneum
symptoms_not_in_common: The images do not show the classic diffuse thick hyperkeratotic scale expected in many cases of crusted scabies
Only a limited number of mites are apparent in the provided histology; crusted scabies often has a very high mite burden
Normal lymphocyte count is less typical than the profound cellular immune dysfunction often associated with severe crusted scabies
Recurrent bacterial pulmonary infections are not a direct feature of crusted scabies

data.diagnosis: Secondary bacterial infection of scabetic lesions (impetiginized scabies/ecthyma)
data.description: Scabies lesions can become secondarily infected with bacteria, particularly Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. In a patient with severe neutropenia, superficial lesions may progress to erosions, ulcers, and crusting.
symptoms_in_common: History of recurrent bacterial skin infections
Severe congenital neutropenia predisposing to bacterial skin infection
Underlying scabies infestation that can disrupt the skin barrier
symptoms_not_in_common: A visible mite in the stratum corneum indicates scabies as the primary process rather than isolated bacterial ecthyma
No reported fever, purulent drainage, cellulitis, or systemic illness
Normal ANC while receiving G-CSF makes severe invasive bacterial infection less directly supported at the time of evaluation
Nonpruritic lesions are not specifically characteristic of bacterial impetigo or ecthyma

data.description: 16-year-old male with 4 weeks of weakness, malaise, anorexia, nausea, fever, and vomiting. No rash, joint pain, oral ulcers, or herbal medicine use. Exam showed pallor, bilateral pitting pedal edema, and hypertension (160/90 mmHg); systemic exam otherwise unremarkable. Labs: hemoglobin 90 g/L, leukocyte count 6600/mm³, platelets 2×10⁹/mm³, 3+ proteinuria with 24-hour urine protein 2.4 g, hematuria with RBC casts, blood urea 46.4 mmol/L (130 mg/dL), and creatinine 265.2 μmol/L (3 mg/dL) rising to 884 μmol/L (10 mg/dL) over 7 days. ANA and ANCA were negative; HBsAg, anti-HCV, and HIV were negative; complement levels were normal. Ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys, CT chest/abdomen was normal, and fundus examination was unremarkable.

data.diagnosis: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy)
data.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by platelet-rich microthrombi in renal vessels and glomeruli, causing thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, severe acute kidney injury, hypertension, and active urinary sediment. The biopsy image is compatible with glomerular thrombotic microangiopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Malaise, weakness, fever, nausea, and vomiting
Renal biopsy appearance consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy
No reported diarrheal prodrome, which supports atypical rather than Shiga-toxin-associated HUS
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal complement levels do not exclude atypical HUS but are less supportive of some complement-mediated forms
No documented evidence of microangiopathic hemolysis such as schistocytes, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, or indirect hyperbilirubinemia

data.description: A severe ADAMTS13-deficiency-associated thrombotic microangiopathy causing marked thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, fever, and variable renal and neurologic involvement. Renal biopsy may show thrombotic microangiopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Histologic appearance compatible with thrombotic microangiopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe renal-predominant failure is more typical of hemolytic uremic syndrome than classic TTP
No neurologic manifestations such as confusion, headache, seizures, or focal deficits
No documented microangiopathic hemolysis findings such as schistocytes or elevated LDH
Proteinuria, hematuria, and red-cell casts are prominent and suggest substantial glomerular injury

data.description: Severe hypertension can injure renal arterioles and glomerular capillaries, producing endothelial damage, thrombotic microangiopathy, hematuria, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.
symptoms_in_common: Renal biopsy appearance potentially consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg is elevated but not clearly in the usual malignant-hypertension range
Fundus examination was unremarkable, without hypertensive retinopathy
No reported hypertensive encephalopathy, severe headache, visual symptoms, or cardiac failure
The degree of thrombocytopenia is unusually profound for hypertension alone

data.description: A 44-year-old man was hospitalized because of jaundice. Physical examination revealed normal findings except jaundice, and his past medical history was unremarkable. Complete blood count showed hemoglobin of 15 g/dL, white blood cell count of 8,200/μL with differential of 79% segmented neutrophils, 15% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, and 1% eosinophils, and platelet count of 248,000/μL. Liver function test showed elevation of total bilirubin (15.3 mg/dL), direct bilirubin (9.4 mg/dL), and alkaline phosphatase (298 IU/L). Immunohistochemical stains showed tumor cells positive for leukocyte common antigen (CD 45) and negative for CD 3,4,5,8,10,21,23,56 and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showed neither significant abnormalities nor evidence of myelodysplasia or leukemic infiltration.

data.diagnosis: Primary myeloid sarcoma of the extrahepatic bile duct (isolated granulocytic sarcoma)
data.description: A localized extramedullary tumor composed of immature myeloid cells. It can occur without detectable bone marrow leukemia and may infiltrate the bile duct, producing obstructive jaundice. The histology and leukocyte-marker positivity with absence of T-cell, B-cell, NK-cell, and precursor lymphoid markers support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Marked elevation of total and direct bilirubin
Elevated alkaline phosphatase consistent with biliary obstruction
Imaging evidence of biliary obstruction at the hepatic hilum/extrahepatic bile duct
Dense infiltration of atypical hematolymphoid tumor cells around bile ducts
Tumor-cell positivity for leukocyte common antigen (CD45)
Normal bone marrow without leukemic infiltration can occur in isolated myeloid sarcoma
symptoms_not_in_common: No peripheral blood cytopenias
No circulating blasts reported
No bone marrow evidence of acute myeloid leukemia
No fever, weight loss, night sweats, or other systemic symptoms reported

data.diagnosis: Primary extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the bile duct
data.description: An uncommon lymphoma arising in or infiltrating the biliary tract that can mimic cholangiocarcinoma and cause obstructive jaundice. Lymphomas are generally CD45-positive, but the reported negative lymphoid immunophenotype makes a conventional B-cell or T-cell lymphoma less likely.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated direct bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase
Histologic infiltrate of atypical hematolymphoid cells
symptoms_not_in_common: Tumor cells are negative for CD3, CD4, CD5, CD8, CD10, CD21, and CD23, which is not typical for most defined T-cell or B-cell lymphomas
No lymphadenopathy described
No splenomegaly described
No B symptoms reported
Normal bone marrow

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the bile ducts that commonly presents with painless obstructive jaundice and intrahepatic biliary dilatation. However, the pathology in this case favors a hematologic tumor rather than an epithelial carcinoma.
symptoms_in_common: Obstructing hilar/extrahepatic biliary lesion on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Tumor cells are CD45-positive, whereas cholangiocarcinoma is typically negative for leukocyte markers
Histology shows diffuse atypical hematolymphoid-cell infiltration rather than malignant gland-forming epithelial cells
No reported epithelial-marker positivity
Relatively young age for typical cholangiocarcinoma presentation
